en: [Page 197] But is it not the case that as much as is said by "one should sacrifice" (yajeta), so much is also said by "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*"?
Therefore, since it serves no purpose, the sense is that it cannot be a name. He refutes this: This would indeed be so if the means of knowledge were to follow the purpose.
The purpose, however, follows from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, even if a lack of purpose were to follow from the *pramāṇa*, it would not be a defect. This [assertion] is merely a concession; for a purpose does indeed exist. As it has been said: "And the utility of names for the sake of other sentences is observed.

Or rather, their function as being connected to qualities and fruits is seen even in other sentences. Thus, even a lack of purpose is not at all established. Therefore, the independence of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is proven.

Regarding the statement that "in which there is an instruction on qualities," and the claim that "the name also will become meaningful by being connected with qualities and results"— considering that to be improper, the propriety of this [name] in a specific context is now established. By this, the fault of lack of connection to the chapter is addressed.
[The author] refutes [the objection]: how it is unreasonable is stated as follows. First, for the purpose of connecting a quality (*guṇopabandha*), [it is said]: "There are fifteen *ājya* [stotras].

By means of the word *ājya*, having designated a specific *stotra* by its name, the quality of the number fifteen is enjoined therein. Thus, the name is meaningful through that connection with a quality. For the purpose of connecting a result (*phalopabandha*), [it is said]: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrā*."

"Curd, honey, ghee, water, parched grain, and rice—this mixture constitutes the *prājāpatya* sacrifice"; thus, in the context of the established sacrifice, the connection with the fruit is made by means of the word *citrā*.

Herein lies the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*): it is indeed appropriate that [the word] "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" and so forth [should be names].

The status of being a name [is established] because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Likewise, for *ājya* and the others as well, their status as names of praise is established because of their coreferentiality with the meaning of praise in such expressions as "they praise with the *ājyas*" and "they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*. However, where coreferentiality with the meaning of an action (*bhāvārtha*) is not perceived—as in the case of "the *ājyas* are fifteen"—there is no comprehension that it is a name.
He asks "Why? and says:
199] Even though the meaning is inclusive, it is called a name because of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).

Even in the case of words such as *udbhid* and others, which possess a consistent etymological meaning, their status as names has been stated on account of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, such coreferentiality does not exist here; for this very reason...

Regarding the statement "there are fifteen *ājya* [hymns]," the word *ājya* does not function as a name for a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). Therefore, it cannot be asserted that the name possesses meaningfulness through its connection with a quality (*guṇopabandha*). To this, an objection is raised: "It may well be appropriate in the case of a connection with a quality..."
It is not that the name lacks meaningfulness; rather, since grammatical coreferentiality is possible when there is a connection with a result,
why would it lack meaningfulness upon the utterance of the word "sacrificer"?
It can be said [that this applies] to the passage, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā.
He refutes this: It is said—in reply—that there is no purposefulness [in that case].

It can be said that by the very word *yajeta* (one should sacrifice), which denotes the subject matter at hand, the connection of the specific sacrifice with the fruit is established; for why? He says: because in that case, the specific sacrifice is obtained simply through proximity (*sannidhāna*).
Not by name. Here he raises an objection: "Let it not be that there is an understanding of a specific sacrifice by way of its name; for as for being a name—"

It cannot be set aside because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He refutes this: "Who has said that its status as a name (*nāmatva*) is being rejected? The objection is based merely on the fact that there is no purpose [for it being a name]. But how, then, can it be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*), as in "one should sacrifice with the *citrayā*"?
"Desiring cattle"? This is the intended meaning: even if there is no [other] purpose, why should it not be a name?
How then is it an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)? The answer is: it is an injunction of a quality in this way; for here, [the substance] is already known.
A specific sacrifice is enjoined for the sake of a result.

Let it be so; nevertheless, what follows? He says: For when a specific [sacrifice] is already known, the comprehension of another word is neither applicable to the absence of specificity nor to [another] specificity.
Why? The answer is: precisely because it has already been ascertained.

From the sentence "curd, honey, and ghee," the sacrifice in its specific form is ascertained; by the very root *yaj* (to sacrifice), which denotes the subject matter at hand in the injunction "one desiring cattle should sacrifice," that specific [sacrifice] is ascertained.

For where the meaning of an injunction is understood solely from the words connected within its own sentence— that is, from the understanding of the word-meanings connected within its own injunctive sentence— it is precisely from that [sentence] itself that the specific qualification is understood.

As in the case of "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," a term whose meaning is already determined by another sentence does not require a syntactic connection (*padānvaya*) within its own sentence for the sake of self-understanding. And for that which is independent [of such a requirement], there can be no verbal grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) are the causes of a relationship. Furthermore, in the sentence "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*), the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) does not require a name for the sake of knowing its specific nature, because that specific nature is already known from another sentence. Therefore, due to the absence of such a syntactic connection, it is not a name.

Therefore, in the case of the word "citrayā," variegatedness (citratva) is to be understood as that which is being enjoined. To this, an objection is raised: "In cases where the specific detail is understood from the accompanying word (upapada) itself—since that which is enjoined is not the subject under discussion—let there be a purpose for the name, because the specific detail is understood by its power alone. [The author] replies: "In this instance, it has merely been illustrated that such a thing does not exist at all; moreover, even when the subject is not under discussion, the status of being a name (nāmadheyatā) does not provide any assistance."

Even in a case where a sentence containing a name not previously mentioned enjoins a sacrifice for the sake of a result, there too the name does not function as a name [of that sacrifice]. Why? He says: because in the case of what is not previously mentioned, it is indeed a different ritual action (karmāntara), since the result [is connected to it].

Because the action is subject to injunction, and because the action is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛtatvāt*), it constitutes a distinct action (*karmāntaratva*). In that case, there is the injunction of the meanings of two words.

Even by means of the name (*nāman*), a similarity to the primary action based on its utility (*upakāra*) is enjoined. By the word expressing the "meaning of being" (*bhāvārtha-śabda*), the injunction of the meaning of being is also [enjoined]; thus, the "meaning of being" (*bhāvārtha*) has been demonstrated.
It has been shown that in the case of the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*, the injunction "he offers the *agnihotra*" refers to the well-known *agnihotra*.

Therefore, a name is not purposeful either by being attached as a fruit to a primary rite already established, or by being attached as a fruit to a distinct rite currently arising. Consequently, the term "citrayā" is applicable only where it is appropriate.

This is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the animal sacrifice; in this case, the following injunction of a quality must be formulated: because clarified butter, vegetable offerings, milk-offerings (*sānnāyya*), and so forth lack the quality of being "variegated" (*citra*), and because the statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" does not require such a qualification, it is impossible for [the word *citrayā*] to form a single syntactical unit with that [injunction]. Therefore, having split the sentence, the word *citrayā* alone serves to enjoin a quality, while "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" enjoins the fruit for the sacrifice under discussion. Furthermore, the word *citrayā* is displaced from its original context in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice.

It is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, in the case of the statement "the Ājya-stotras are fifteen," it is an injunction of fifteen Ājyas for the stotra. Therefore, the claim that [the sentence] is purposeful by being connected to a quality and a result is incorrect.
To this, the following reply is given:

This is not incorrect, for it is purposeful by way of being connected with the fruit of a subordinate quality (guṇaphala). Why? He says: "Where another subordinate quality is enjoined," as for example:

In the case of diversity, there is femininity [in the word *striyaḥ*], and likewise the number fifteen in the *ājya* verses; in that context, it is only the application of the previously established name of the ritual action (*karman*) that becomes meaningful. For a quality (*guṇa*) cannot be enjoined in relation to something that is not a ritual action, according to the stated principle that "the performance [of a ritual] is dependent [on its name]. Indeed, the injunction of a quality occurs through the injunction of a ritual action colored by that quality; therefore, there is no injunction of a quality in relation to what is not a ritual action.
And because the establishment of an action occurs through a name— since a name possesses meaning by being connected with a quality—

and because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in other sentences such as "they praise with the *ājya*s," once its status as a name is established, the phrase "the *ājya*s are fifteen" can indeed function as a name.

It is not possible to establish [the meaning] by means of a name. Therefore, it is logical that a name possesses purpose through its connection with a quality (*guṇa*). This is appropriate in the case of *ājya* and similar terms, because two things cannot both be enjoined due to the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Since one must function as the subject of reference (*uddeśaka*), and because the word *ājya* itself functions as the subject of reference by virtue of denoting the substance (*karma-vacanatā*), the name possesses purpose. However, as for the term *citrayā*, [it is different].
How can there be meaningfulness? For in that case, because the specific [meaning] is understood precisely from the fact that it is the subject under discussion,
its meaningfulness cannot be asserted.

The answer: Certainly. Even in that case, it is possible [to maintain this], provided that there were no injunction regarding the fruit of what has already arisen, for that would contradict the scriptural mention of the accessory (*guṇa*).
This very point is shown by the statement: "This is for the sake of the fruit."

It is not for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), because no distinction is perceived. This hearing of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is solely for the purpose of connecting it with a result, and no distinction—that it is not for the purpose of connecting it with a subordinate quality—is perceived. And when no such distinction is perceived, there is indecision (*anadhyavasāya*).

It might be argued that there is invalidity due to a lack of definitive determination; this is refuted by [the fact that] it is a name, because a name is subject to injunction and because there is certainty regarding the connection with the result—as in the case of "citrayā" (with the variegated offering)—this is logical. Here, the *pūrvapakṣa* (*Bhāṣya*) states: "And these are not etymological."
Thus [the opponent] objects: "Of what use is the refutation of its being etymological (*yaugikatva*)? He replies:
"The intention is this: for if it were etymological, the denotation of the sacrifice under discussion would be established, just as..."

In the expression "Give wages to the cook," even though there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a specific person, the successful denotation of the cook under discussion is established.

Likewise here as well, if the etymological view (*yaugika-pakṣa*) were accepted, there would be a reference to the sacrifice under discussion; consequently, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) would not be established. Therefore, it was stated that these [words] are not etymological.
Now, one might ask: even if they denote a genus (*jāti*), why should they not be names?

To this, he says: "It is not so. For when the genus (*jāti*) is denoted, it is logically proper that the genus itself be the thing enjoined (*vidheya*). Denotation of the individual (*vyakti*), however, requires a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*). Moreover, [the word *citrayā*] cannot denote the individual through its etymological meaning (*ayaugika*). Thus, because *citrayā* denotes only a quality (*guṇa*), it is equivalent to those words that denote a genus. Therefore, this [word] also does not denote the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*). [The word is] *citrayā*.

What is demonstrated by this commentary passage, "And 'one should sacrifice' is a restatement (anuvāda) of the sacrifice because it is already known, not an injunction (vidhi) of the sacrifice"? (Page 198)

The answer: [it is] the state of not being expected (anākāṅkṣitatva). Because the name—that is, the word *citrā*—is not expected, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since its specific quality is already known.
A name does not require a specific cognition; and for that which is not required, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Due to the absence of that, it is not a name. Therefore, in the injunction of a result, its utility is not understood by way of being a name. Consequently, when assuming a quality and a result, the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is not intended [as a mere name].
What is it that this proponent (pūrvapakṣin), by speaking thus, intends to refute?

Surely it is the very connection between the quality (guṇa) and the fruit (phala) that is being stated; that [connection] is not to be suspected, for the proponent [accepts] the connection between the quality and the fruit.

It must be established that the name has no meaningful referent; for it is precisely on account of that [referent] which would give the name its meaning that such a doubt might arise. Furthermore, even when there is a connection between a quality and a fruit, the name still lacks a meaningful referent. Thus he says: "Because even in the case of a connection between a quality and a fruit, by virtue of that very connection, the name [remains without a referent]."
On the contrary, this must be refuted by the proponent who asserts that the name possesses meaning;
therefore, this fragment of the Bhāṣya turns out to be entirely irrelevant as it revolves in the mind.
The respondent said: To this it is replied—regarding the conceptualization of qualities and results [p. 205].
Indeed, it cannot be set aside; therefore, the proponent refutes the connection between the quality and the fruit.

Why can it not be set aside? He says: "It can [be set aside]. The answer is: because there is no intention to express the sacrifice (*yajati*). And when there is no intention to express it, [the sacrifice] remains unattached.

The meaning is that a quality (*guṇa*) cannot be enjoined for the sake of a result unless it is dependent upon a verbal root meaning (*bhāvārtha*). Why, then, is the sacrifice (*yajati*) not intended to be expressed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the engagement [in action] from another source is the cause for the connection between the ritual act and the result of the quality."

Since the action proceeds from something other than the injunction, the understanding arises that the fruit results from a subordinate element when [the sacrifice] is not being enjoined. And there is no other motivator for the sacrifice (*yajya*) apart from the injunction for one who desires cattle; for nothing else can be a motivator for the purpose of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not intended to be significant [as a primary factor]. However, the word *citrā* is connected with the desire for cattle.
Therefore, since the connection with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*) is not abandoned, the word *citrayā* remains nothing more than a name (*nāmadheya*). Thus,
the proponent [of the prima facie view] concludes.

Even by resorting to a connection between the quality (*guṇa*) and the fruit (*phala*) for the word *citrā*, he absolutely rejects its connection with one who desires cattle (*paśukāma*). For he thinks: "If I were to admit a connection with one who desires cattle even through a connection between the quality and the fruit for the word *citrā*, then [that would be untenable] because of the impossibility of a connection between the quality and the fruit."

When that [objection] is refuted, there is syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) because of the non-abandonment of the sense of "you" (tvam). Otherwise, syntactic unity would be impossible between the words *citrā* and *paśukāma*.

Otherwise, the word *citrayā* would result in being a mere name (*nāmadheya*). Therefore, by that very effort, I utterly reject the possibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) even through the connection of a quality with a fruit.
Consequently, because there is no mutual expectancy (*anākāṅkṣitatva*) between the two—the term "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*)—[they cannot form a single sentence].
In some cases, the word *citrā* should be understood as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) corresponding to a quality;
[in such cases] there is no connection between the meaning of the verbal root and the person entitled to perform the rite (*adhikārin*).

The word *citrā* (variegated), which signifies a non-existence [of a specific quality], is not required by the word *paśukāma* (desirous of cattle) for the sake of establishing a connection. Furthermore, the sacrifice, whose specific nature is already known, does not require a name to provide knowledge of its own particulars. Therefore, this injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not to be understood as applying where this quality called "variegated" is incapable of being enjoined. He explains another portion of the Bhāṣya that supports the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Even in the assumption of an injunction of a quality, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For it has been stated that the defect of relying on figurative indication is that the matter would then become cognizable through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs everywhere only after one has cognized an object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and determined the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) therein; moreover, this would be a great defect in the case of the Veda. This is because it would entail the undesirable consequence that mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśa*) would depend upon other means of valid cognition. Furthermore, it has been stated that such [intention] is not present here either, due to the absence of a connection between words in grammatical apposition.

For in this case, regarding the term *udabhid*, if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by resorting to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice (*yāga*), such that the quality would be the thing enjoined, then the fault of "implication of possessive meaning" (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) has been stated.

In this case, by resorting to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is no injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); rather, it is through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) alone that [the meaning is]: "That which one should sacrifice with an animal, that [sacrifice] should be variegated. Therefore, since there is no fault of metaphorical indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the injunction of a quality is established.

Therefore, it is established that [the name] is not purposeful through its connection with a quality or a result. It is replied: An injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible here. For, when there is an injunction of the meaning of a name, since an already established thing cannot be enjoined by itself, it must be enjoined as entering into an action, and not as something to be accomplished in its own right.

The meaning is that the quality itself is not enjoined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). What follows from this? This results in the following: where this injunction of a quality is already established, it attains its utility for the ritual action; in that case, the quality is to be enjoined, and its injunction pertains to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).

Because it is possible for the animal to possess variegated color. Even if this were so, what follows? To this he says: "In that case, while variegated color is being enjoined, another quality of this animal, namely 'femaleness' (strītva), would have to be enjoined as well."

Furthermore, even in the case of an injunction for excellence (*utkarṣa*), there would be another syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Moreover, if there were an injunction regarding the *sārasvatī* [offering], then— even if the feminine gender were not enjoined there—
the connection with the term "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma-pada*) which is understood [from the context] would have to be abandoned, whether that [gender] is enjoined or not.
[The injunction] occurs. Furthermore, the attainment of the specific qualities of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] must be set aside in the case of the Sārasvatī [offering].

For in the Agniṣomīya, a specific color is fixed; that which is obtained through extended application (atideśa) must be set aside. Therefore, since a split of the sentence (vākyabheda) is inevitable, this [injunction] is prescribed for the Agniṣomīya—which serves as the archetype (prakṛti) for all sacrifices performed with living beings as the material—because it has been excluded from connection with its own [original] sentence.
In that case, both the quality of being variegated (*citratva*) and the quality of being female (*strītva*) would have to be enjoined anew;

consequently, there would again be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, it is not possible for this to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, it is logical to assume that its status as a cause (*nimittatā*) is based on the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) that is perceived and the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) that is likewise perceived. And that [unity] here resides in the name (*nāman*).

And it has been stated that this [designation] is not possible without a name; therefore, its status as a name is established. By this, it is also demonstrated that it possesses purposefulness through its connection with a fruit.

For if it were a quality (guṇa), there would be uncertainty as to whether this sentence is intended for the sake of connecting a quality or for the sake of connecting a fruit; such uncertainty is resolved by its being a name.

That this is refuted has already been demonstrated. Likewise, under the view that "the fifteen *ājya* [verses] are [to be used]" is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), there would be the injunction of two qualities, because both the number and the *ājyas* would be enjoined; and that is not possible, because of the requirement of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore, one word within the mantra must be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the indicator [of the ritual action]. And that [word] refers to the ritual...

...is connected. Therefore, it is appropriate that the word *ājya* itself—which denotes a ritual action already known from another sentence—serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*). Thus, the mutual—

The comprehension of the relationship is not abandoned here, as in the case of the statement: "In this [context], there are fifteen *ājya* offerings. Furthermore, what was said—that even in the view that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is also incorrect. Why? Because wherever the *ājyas* are enjoined by the words "the *ājyas* are," that [sentence] must be expressed by the verb "are" (*bhavanti*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the hymns (stotras) are "possessing ghee" (ājyavanti). For this reason also, they are "possessing ghee" here; that is precisely the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). As for what was stated—that the status of being a name for the ritual action is not well-established—that is established because it serves as a definition of the action.

Since the ritual action is indicated by the word "ājya," its status as a name for the action is established, and since the ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta) exists everywhere—as in the passage "they went toward the race" (yadājimīyuḥ), and so forth.
On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya has raised an objection: "Now, why are the *ājya* verses, qualified by the number fifteen, not enjoined for the stotras? (B.
adds *ājyāni*).
Thus, he raises an objection to that: "What has been set forth here that was not already refuted? The answer is:
"This has been set forth; for the meaning of two words [found] elsewhere is also present here."
"It is enjoined. What will happen in this way?
The answer is: the intention is that there will be no repetition of the sentence.
Since the two word-meanings stand in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified, they are both enjoined by this single injunction; thus, there is no [need for] further activity.
Thus there is no recurrence. This is the commentary on the refutation of this objection: "Because of the absence of a word that denotes [the qualified].
He explains that: "In this way, it is indeed established."
If the meaning of both words were to be enjoined by a single injunction, then their relationship would have to be established prior to that injunction—just as in the case of "Agni Pāvaka.
For instance, the quality of being "pāvaka" (purifying) is already established for Agni prior to its formal injunction. And this is not the case here.

[210] Likewise, here too, it is established that there are exactly fifteen *ājya* [stotras], as stated by B. "Fifteen indeed. Thus he says: "But this [number] does not exist [as a separate entity]. Therefore, these two are caused respectively by the injunction (*vidhi*) and the statement of the subject matter (*uddeśa*).
Thus, this is the relationship between these two; therefore, it is not possible for the meaning of both words to be the object of an injunction.
Now, why is it that an injunction is not possible even for two things that are unrelated to each other, such as Agni and Prajāpati, as is the case in the Agnihotra?

The meaning is: why does this not occur here as well—namely, that Agni and Prajāpati, who are otherwise unrelated, are enjoined by a single injunction through the phrase "to Agni and to Prajāpati"? B. The answer:

[The author] does not reject it; rather, such an injunction of two unrelated things is not possible because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it. Therefore, it must be accepted as being caused solely by the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*).
Therefore, it is established that this is also a name.
211] And there is another scriptural passage that makes that known. But by what distinction is there here a suspicion that this might be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)?

This section is commenced in order to refute [the opponent's view]. The reply is as follows: since there is no need for a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established even by treating it as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

This term *agnihotram* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; thus, grammatical coreferentiality is achieved even without a possessive indication. It is on this specific ground that the suspicion arises here that it is an injunction of a quality. And so it has been shown: "that in which the offering (*hotra*) is made to Agni is the *agnihotra*."

B. & C. This very compound is a statement regarding the oblation (*homa*), because the oblation itself constitutes the meaning of the other member of the compound. Even by enjoining the meaning of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), it certainly becomes an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), just as in the case of "the priests wearing golden garlands."
[They] come into being. Therefore, in this case, Agni, having become a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), is prescribed as the deity.

It is indeed appropriate that *agnihotraṃ juhoti* ("he offers the agnihotra") be an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhāna*). But as for *āghāram āghārayati* ("he pours the libation"), [page 212]...
How so?

The answer is: there is no purpose here for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); since the status of being a word denoting an action (*karmavacanatā*) is not perceived here, it is simply an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

The word *āghāra* does not denote an action, but rather refers to the substance to be poured; this pouring (*āghāraṇa*) is prescribed as a purificatory refinement (*saṃskāra*) or an accessory (*guṇa*) for that substance. This very point is stated: this pouring is to be performed only where the substance to be poured exists, namely in the *upāṃśuyāja*.

"It is enjoined. Now, an objection is raised: since the sacrifice whose substance is the *āghāra* is to be accomplished in the *āhavanīya* fire, it already possesses the *āghāra* by virtue of being a sacrifice;

for all sacrifices are performed while standing, are accomplished in the *āhavanīya*, and the *homa* is offered in the *āhavanīya*. Thus, the act of pouring a long stream of liquid as the substance of the sacrifice is already established. What, then, is the purpose of enjoining the *āghāra*? [The answer is: Because an injunction serves to bring about what has not yet been established. To this, the reply is:
—The intention is that this [act] is a different *āghāra* from the *homa-āghāra*, and it is for the purpose of purifying the substance (*dravya-saṃskāra*).

Since an injunction (*vidhi*) brings about what has not been previously established, it serves as the means for the ritual action (*karma-sādhana*). This is stated by one who considers the word *āghāra* to be formed with the suffix *-ghañ* according to the rule "in the sense of a non-agentive *kāraka* when it is a name" (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*). From this...

Thus, this is a consecratory refinement (*saṃskāra*); for this very reason, it has been demonstrated that [the term] is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Therefore, in this example, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based solely on the fact that [the word] does not denote an action. However, in the case of the *agnihotra*, even though it denotes an action, [it is still a name].
It has been stated that because there is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not contradictory.
To this, it is replied: an injunction of a quality is not possible here.
Because the qualities have already been obtained. He explains this very point:
those qualities which are presented here as being enjoined are already obtained from elsewhere. First, as for Agni, [they are obtained] from the [text]: "And to Agni and to Prajāpati..."

Since this is already established from this very sentence, it is not something to be enjoined; therefore, it is not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), but the word *agnihotra* is merely a name (*nāmadheya*).
The same applies to the pouring of the libation (*āghāraṇa*), as in "he pours the libation continuously," "he pours the libation straight," and so forth.

But surely, since these sentences—such as "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*)—are intended to enjoin qualities like continuity (*sāntatya*) by way of restating the act of pouring (*āghāraṇa*), how can the pouring itself be established from them?

If it is argued that the sentences concerning continuity and so forth actually enjoin the pouring as qualified by continuity, that is not correct; for, as in the case of "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), those [sentences] are understood to be concerned with subordinate qualities (*guṇa*) because they are recited in proximity to the injunction of the pouring. To this it is replied: first of all, the lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) for the injunction of the pouring is unavoidable. For instance, let that [injunction] not exist; in its absence, the sentences concerning continuity and so forth would themselves be the enjoiners of the qualified pouring.

[The sentence] "Let [them] be" is not an injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*). Nor should it be argued that if sentences such as "He pours the *santata* [libation]" were intended to enjoin a common substrate (*āghāra*), a distinction [between them] would result;

for in the case of subordinate actions (*guṇa-karman*), no distinction is perceived when there is no difference in their purpose, as is the case with the purchase of Soma (*somakraya*). The statement "He offers the *agnihotra*" serves this purpose [of establishing the rite], whereas if statements such as "He offers with curd" were injunctions of distinct rites, it would entail a distinction [between them]. Furthermore, when meaningfulness is possible, it is not proper to assume meaninglessness. And meaningfulness is indeed possible for the sentence "He pours the *āghāra*," by way of its enjoining a sacrifice. For if it were not...

In that case, the sentences concerning "continuity" (*santata*) and so forth would be intended solely as injunctions for the *upāṃśuyāja* itself. But since it is established that they are injunctions for a sacrifice,
in that case—

In that very context which prescribes the sacrifice, the pouring (*āghāraṇa*)—which is established as having clarified butter (*ājya*) as its substance—is taken for granted; these sentences are intended to enjoin properties such as continuity (*sāntatya*), etc. However, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has here raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by relying on an injunction regarding the substance, namely the phrase "fourfold-drawn" (*caturgṛhīta*).

And because the substance has already been obtained, this is the established conclusion (*rāddhāntita*). In that regard, first of all, how can there be an injunction for clarified butter (*ājya*) by the statement "this [is] indeed the fourfold-drawn [portion]" (*caturgṛhītaṃ vā etad*) in the context of the *upāṃśuyāja*? For the *upāṃśuyāja* cannot be denoted by the word "āghāra" (libation). If it were said that it is called "āghāra" because it consists of a substance to be poured (*āghārya*), then a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*) would result. It is replied: by the statement "this [is] indeed the fourfold-drawn," this is taught [to be performed] with clarified butter.

"One should perform the ritual action with what has been taken four times. Since that [action] lacks a material substance, it remains as the *upāṃśuyāja* (whispered sacrifice) alone. And since its material is clarified butter (*ājya*), the term "āghāra" (libation) is merely a restatement of what is already established by the sense; thus, there is no fault. And this has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya as follows:

"Whether the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is supported by an injunction regarding the material or by an injunction regarding the preparation of the material for the pouring, even so, because of the injunction [established] by another scripture..."

"Because the statement of the opponent is possible, the injunction is untenable; therefore, it is a name. He raises an objection against this very conclusion: "What is this that is being said so incoherently? The proponent asks: "What here is incoherent? The objector says: "This is what is incoherent here:"

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asserts that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) regarding the ladle-oblation (darvihoma). Furthermore, there is no such injunction as "to Agni and to Prajāpati" in the case of the ladle-oblation, nor is there such an offering (āghāraṇa) in the case of the silent sacrifice (upāṃśuyāja).
The proponent has stated: "Nor are *santata* and the others injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*.
He concludes: "This appears like the word *viyat* [in the phrase *ākāśe śyenaḥ*]. He provides the resolution: "To this we reply:"

Under the view that these are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), this injunction—"he offers the *agnihotra*"—pertains specifically to the *darvihoma*; likewise, "he pours the *āghāra* libation" pertains to the *upāṃśuyāja*. Consequently, finding no proximate substratum, the injunction regarding the deity—"that which [is offered] to Agni"—and the injunction regarding continuity—"he pours the *āghāra* continuously"—both apply to the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. And since they are already enjoined by those two [injunctions], the *agnihotra*...

The intention is that it has been correctly stated that the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not tenable in the case of [the word] "āghāra. Failing to understand this very point, the opponent objects: "In that case, the principle of 'being known from elsewhere' (*tatprakhyatā*) is not the reason for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), because qualities are enjoined in the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. Here...

And [the phrase] "and that which for Agni" is not present [in those cases], because of the absence of proximity. If the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) were suspected to occur only in its own original location, then, due to the proximity there of the words "and that which for Agni" and so forth, the principle of "being designated by that" (tatprakhyatā) would serve as the reason in the final conclusion (rāddhānta). However, regarding the Darvihoma and the Upāṃśuyāja, since there is no suspicion of an injunction of a quality, and because the words "and that which for Agni" and so forth are not present there, it is impossible to demonstrate that "there is another scriptural statement designating it. The respondent says: "Certainly, it is the reason in the final conclusion. How so? The answer is: "The principle of being designated by that (tatprakhyatā) also [applies]."
For it is indeed a *darvihoma* sacrifice.
In that view, even the injunction "to Agni" is a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*), because it depends upon the context.
In that very case, it occurs just as in the statement "he performs the *agnihotra*.

Just as, under the view that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), the sentence "he performs the *agnihotra*" extends to the *darvihoma* because it requires a similar [context], so too does the phrase "that which is for Agni" [apply]. Likewise, the statement "he pours the libation continuously" (*santatam āghārayati*) refers to the *upāṃśuyāja* itself, because it requires a purposeful substance.

It is like the injunctions for ritual preparations [where one says], "he offers the Āghāra libations. He objects: "If, then, because of the existence of another scriptural passage that describes it as such, there is no injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) in the case of the Darvihoma or the Upāṃśuyāja, then is it not also a name?"

In that case, it would follow that [the rule] applies only to those *darvihomas* and to the *upāṃśuyāja*. He refutes this: "The 'Beloved of the Gods' (devānāṃ priyaḥ) does not understand what has not been established."

The meaning is that he is ignorant of logic (*nyāya*). Since the prescription of the qualities is established from another source, and because once [the action] is established, the name cannot be prescribed— given that the name itself is not something to be enjoined—
what else could be understood from this sentence other than the prescription of the meaning of the verb, namely, "one performs the *agnihotra* oblation"?

When the status of [the sentence] as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) has been refuted, then it must be an injunction of an action (*karmavidhi*). And once the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) has been enjoined, the phrases "to Agni" and "to Prajāpati" remain applicable only to that specific context due to the force of the ritual section (*prakaraṇa*).

Consequently, by virtue of that very connection with the qualities, this name also belongs to that very other action which is enjoined by this injunction. Thus he says: "Therefore, it is established that this is the name of this very [action]. Likewise, when the injunction of a quality in the case of "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*) has been refuted, what else could the injunction enjoin apart from the meaning of the verbal suffix?
He alone is capable; he alone is the object to be enjoined as the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*),
because, like the root *harati*, the root *yajati* [denotes an action] through the connection between the substance and the deity.

Just as in the case of the *prastarapraharaṇa* (the throwing of the grass-bundle), there is the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) because of the connection between the substance and the deity, so too *āghāraṇa* (the pouring of the libation) is indeed *yaji*. Therefore, qualities such as *santata* (continuous) and so forth also belong to that very [act]. Consequently, this word *āghāra* is also [a name for] that [sacrifice].
It is established that this refers to the name of that very [Agni].

This being the case, what is the meaning of the expression "he pours the āghāra continuously"? The meaning is that he brings about the āghāra offering continuously. Now, if the injunction regarding the deity is "to Agni," then how is it that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here?
Because, insofar as [the text says] "to Agni and to Prajāpati," there is the injunction of multiple qualities in the form of Agni and Prajāpati.
It must indeed be understood that there is a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
He refutes this: "There is no syntactical split known as the injunction of multiple attributes when there is the injunction of qualifiers for a single kāraka.
This is the meaning:

For here, because Agni and Prajāpati are construed as qualifiers of a single factor called the deity, there is no injunction of multiple qualities regarding Prajāpati; how, then, could there be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)? Indeed, it is the injunction of another related entity that is termed "multiple qualities," not the injunction of another substance.

For where there is an injunction of multiple related factors for an action that is not [otherwise] connected to an action, there is an injunction of multiple qualities (*anekaguṇavidhāna*); whereas where only a single factor related to the action is enjoined— provided, at most, that it is based on a single substance.

That very object, which is composed of multiple substances, is the locus for the injunction of multiple qualities; it is not [the case] that this occurs when [the object] is non-existent. And here, Agni and Prajāpati are taken as the substratum of the deity-status (*devatātva*), but not as the deity-status itself. Furthermore, it is the deity as related to the ritual action (*karma*) that is enjoined as being related to the ritual action, and not [anything else].

Because the deities are presiding [simultaneously], there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, since the connection of the deity with the ritual action is established through each individual presiding presence, the repetition of the ritual action is also justified; thus, this constitutes a single instruction (*ekaśāstra*). And because of the word "and" (*ca*), this is faultless.
There is also the designation of that [single instruction].

Here, the author of the Bhāṣya first establishes that only the words *śyena*, *iṣu*, and *saṃdaṃśa* are names of rites (*nāmadheya*). Fearing that someone might take the examples to be restricted solely to *ājya* and so forth, he says: "In this context, the conventional (*rūḍhi*) words such as *śyena*, *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and others are the examples. But what is the distinction between this section and the section on *udbhid*, by which this new section is commenced? For just as there, the status of being a name of a rite was asserted out of fear of the implication of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), so too here it can be established in the same way.

Thus it can be said that the name belongs to the side of [the former]. The reply is: there is this distinction—that etymological derivation (*yoga*) conforms to the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the case of an action, whereas conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), on the other hand, does not follow etymological derivation.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding these words such as *ājyapṛṣṭha* and so forth, if they are considered names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), their etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) must be asserted; whereas if they are considered injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), they possess conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Conventional meaning is stronger than the etymological, because the etymological depends upon the application of its constituent parts and is thus dependent, while the conventional is independent. Therefore, rather than resorting to conventional meaning, it is better to accept the indication of a possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); thus, the status of being an injunction of an accessory is again suspected here. Consequently, this [discussion] is connected with the section concerning the *udbhid* (the *udbhidadhikaraṇa*).

This is the distinction: since words such as *udbhid* are etymological (*yaugika*) in both positions, how then is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) reached? It is said: because the sentence is intent upon enjoining an action, it is improper to enjoin the meaning of the qualifying word (*upapada*). As for the fact that in some cases an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) is resorted to, that is because the connection with another word has no other possible recourse. However, where there is an available, though delayed, etymological derivation, there is no justification for enjoining an action qualified by a quality by resorting to the indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Regarding this specific example, he raises an objection: "But surely..."

Even on the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), one need not assume that the term *śyena* follows its etymological derivation. Rather, even under the view that it is the name of the ritual action, one must accept a figurative designation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*) in the sense of "the Śyena-like [sacrifice] is called Śyena. Furthermore, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not preclude figurative usage, because figurative expression is rooted in conventional usage. Therefore, since the elision of the possessive suffix (*matub-lopa*) lacks any basis of proof, there is no possibility of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) being maintained there; rather, it is better to simply resort to figurative usage. He [the author of the commentary] refutes this: this very [objection] was cited by the venerable Commentator (Śabara) in order to dispel such ignorance.

Precisely because a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is difficult to maintain in this example, the Commentator has cited, among all the conventional (*rūḍhi*) words serving as examples, only those cases where even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is no loss of their conventional status. One might think that this is not a valid example due to the absence of a prima facie argument; however, he demonstrates how such an absence exists here: it is appropriate to say that in the case of *udbhid* and similar terms, they are names (*nāmadheya*) by resorting to etymological derivation (*yoga*) out of fear of dropping the possessive suffix *-matup*. But this does not imply a loss of their conventional status.
Resorting to another elision out of fear of an elision—

such as resorting to the elision of the suffix *vati* in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice out of fear of the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*— is not appropriate under the view that the term is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇapakṣa*).

For the application of figurative (gauṇa) words occurs through the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*). Therefore, it is better to rely on the elision of the *matup* itself, because [the word] is understood as being connected with its literal meaning.

In the view that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the literal meaning of the word *śyena* is what becomes connected with the ritual action; however, [in the other view], it is not [that literal meaning].

Therefore, even when there is the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*), the connection of the literal meaning still occurs; thus, that [literal sense] alone is logical. However, it was further argued as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that in the case of a figurative interpretation (*gauṇapakṣa*), the literal meaning does not connect with the ritual action, and therefore it is weak.
He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), which is common to all examples: "It is said: [The response: It is said, ...
It was stated that [the former] follows [the latter].
The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) says: "Just as conventional usage does not follow etymological derivation, so too etymological derivation does not follow conventional usage."
It does not follow conventional usage at all.
Therefore, what is the distinction of conventional usage if there is no mutual following? He reveals the intention of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):
"But here..."
An established usage (*rūḍhi*) that has operated previously prevails over etymological derivation (*yoga*) due to its independence [from analysis].
The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) states his own position:
"It is true that established usage would prevail over etymological derivation, provided that the meaning of the sentence were preceded by the comprehension of the etymological cause."

If it were to be understood [in that way], then, because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger in the state of the primary signifier (*nimitta*), there would be a subversion of the etymological connection (*yoga*);
that is, the etymological connection would be abandoned. But if, on the other hand, the status of being a signifier is preceded by the comprehension of the function (*kārya*), then— [p.

Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not override [the etymological sense]. When, having understood the purpose of the sentence, the comprehension of that purpose occurs within the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) itself, and when one ceases [from further analysis] and follows the cause [of the action], then—because the sentence has a single meaning—the object of injunction (*vidheya*) is the verbal root-meaning alone; for if one were to resort to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*). In that case...

Therefore, when considering how a single meaning can be established, one must resort to *yoga* (etymological derivation) itself; thus, *rūḍhi* (conventional usage) does not override *yoga*. Now, even if the sentence is intent upon enjoining a single action, why should it be intent solely on enjoining a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)? He says "no": [it is] "pertaining to the verbal root-meaning" (*bhāvārthagatā*) and "dependent on the verbal root-meaning" (*bhāvārthāśritā*).

Since the comprehension of the task (kārya) is the object of an injunction only when there is an action-meaning (bhāvārtha), an injunction is not possible regarding a mere quality (guṇa) in its isolated state;

therefore, because it conforms to the comprehension of the task residing in an action-meaning, the etymological derivation (yoga) is perceived first, and thus the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) is not accepted.

For even in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) of words such as *ājya* has been demonstrated—for instance, in the passage beginning, "Because they went toward the race (*ājim īyuḥ*), that is the reason for the *ājya*-ness of the *ājyas*. Otherwise, the statement regarding their etymological nature in the supplementary passage would be groundless. In this regard:
The opponent objects: "It is reasonable that *ājya* and the like are names; but how can *śyena* be a name? The questioner’s underlying intention is this:

a word is a name by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And the word *śyena*, which denotes the genus of the hawk, cannot have coreferentiality with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) even in a figurative sense. However, for *ājya* and the others, which are derived etymologically (*yaugika*), it is indeed possible for them to be names through coreferentiality. The reply:

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the name-status applies even to the *śyena* sacrifice. Now, one might object that there is no such coreferentiality at all; to this he replies: "For coreferentiality remains uncontradicted even in cases of figurative denotation (*gauṇābhidhāna*), because the sense of the suffix *-vat* is what is being prescribed."

For if the meaning of the suffix -vat were not something to be enjoined, then, because it would be subordinate to that [suffix], there would be no subordination to the verb; consequently, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would not occur. However, when the meaning of the suffix -vat is not non-enjoined, but rather serves merely as the occasion for the application of the action toward the object, then, because it is subordinate to the object, coreferentiality is established, and thus [the word] functions as a name (nāmadheya).

[It] occurs. Furthermore, if there were an elision of the *matup* suffix (*matub-lope*), a difference of substratum (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*) would be unavoidable, because the possessive meaning (*matvartha*) would be that which is enjoined, whereas the ritual action (*karman*) would be that which is enjoined.

Therefore, since enjoining multiple meanings contradicts the comprehension of a single meaning, it is better to assume the elision of the *vat* suffix rather than the elision of the *matup* suffix; thus, its status as a name (*nāmadheyatva*) is established.
The same applies to the word *śyena*.
[This is so] because of the mention of a quality within a name. For what purpose is this section?
It is so that it might be considered whether [the term] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

In that case, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) would be intended for the purpose of refuting that [position]; however, such a refutation is not possible. For it has been established that names consist of both etymological meanings and conventional meanings. Furthermore, it is possible to assert the status of "being named after something else" (*tatprakhyatā*) in the case of the *vājapeya*, because the drinking of *surā* is enjoined therein.
That *surā* would be of the nature of a drink, since its consumption is prescribed.

Because the word-form (*peyarūpa*) has been established as *vāja*, he states the rebuttal: "This section, during the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), implies all [the other] pronouns.
He asks "Why? and says: because of the presentation of the simultaneous designation (*tantrābhidhāna*).
Through simultaneous designation, the sacrifice offers its own meaning with respect to both the result and the quality.

Now, one might object that even the simultaneous designation must be abandoned due to the consequence of mutual dependence; to this he replies: and in the case of simultaneous designation, there is indeed no dependence of the word even when a quality is being enjoined.

Since both the status of being the object of an injunction (*vidheya*) and the status of being the subject (*uddeśyatva*) are understood from a single utterance, and since it is impossible for that which is being enjoined to simultaneously possess the status of the subject, there is no requirement for another substratum in the case of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); thus, the designation [of the name] as a "tantra" (simultaneous application) cannot be maintained. Therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute the theory of *tantrābhidhāna*. If that is so, then terms such as *udbhid* and others would also be examples here; consequently, the point is that the introduction of other examples would be redundant. He refutes this: "Certainly... (*bāḍham*).
The *udbhid* and other [names] are also examples here. The objector asks:

"Why, then, was only 'one desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*' cited as an example? He replies: "This is like questioning a *śiṃśapā* tree; for even when the *udbhid* and others have been cited as examples, one could just as well ask why the *udbhid* specifically was chosen."
Therefore, this objection which we raise is indeed not to be challenged. And he states another solution: "A certain distinction can also be stated here—that it is because the two actions are equal."
By this sūtra, the mention of the *dīkṣā*, *upasad*, and so forth refers specifically to what pertains to the Vājapeya;
therefore, the Vājapeya is cited there in order to demonstrate the reason for its superiority.

Now, one might object: "If this is so, does it not follow that, according to the evidence of the scriptural text (*darśana*), the Vājapeya alone was intended by the author of the sūtra as the illustrative example? To this, he says:
Furthermore, that perception is indeed universal;

since perception preceded by reasoning is universal, and reasoning is the same everywhere, perception as well is again universal. For this very reason, this section is meaningful because it refutes the designation of a specific system (tantra). Therefore, this is stated:
In this case, the position that [terms like *udbhid*] enjoin a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is indeed superior.

Why is it superior? To this he says: for in this way, the word-meaning such as *udbhid* becomes something connected to the action (*kāryānvayin*). On the other hand, under the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), the word-meaning would be merely the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Why? The answer [p.
because of that which has been enjoined.
In the view that [the word] is the name of the ritual action (*karman*), being "udbhid" means being denotable by the word *udbhid*;
it does not mean the enunciation (*abhidhāna*) or the injunction (*vidhāna*) of the *udbhid*. Therefore, it is not the cause for the commencement [of the action].

Therefore, if the name were the cause, it would serve the purpose of non-activity, whereas the sentence serves the purpose of activity; thus, there would be an inconsistency between the effect and its cause.

There would be a contradiction in that the action (kārya) consists of activity (pravṛtti), while the cause (nimitta) consists of a name (nāman); however, this contradiction does not exist under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi). Therefore, the injunction of a quality is superior. But [one might object]:
in the case of an injunction of a quality, there is the figurative indication of possessive meaning (matvarthalakṣaṇā).
It has been stated in the *Udbhid-ādhikaraṇa* that [the name] must be accepted as having no literal meaning; he refutes this by saying: "That very thing does not exist.
How does it not exist?
The reply is as follows: For the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha) is understood to be of a single form even in the relationship between cause and effect.
Whether it is understood as an effect or as a cause, the meaning of the verbal suffix is apprehended by a single form; it is precisely that which is being brought into existence (sādhyamāna).

For the meaning of the verbal root does not constitute the means (*sādhana*). When both [the instrument and the action] are understood, why would there be a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)? Because the relationship is understood through a non-co-referential connection: "The sacrifice is to be performed by means of the *udbhid*, and by that sacrifice, cattle [are obtained]. Therefore, this meaning is established: "By means of the *vājapeya* [there is] a sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice, self-sovereignty."

There is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). But if this were so, there would be a clear syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); to this he replies: "The expression is otherwise because of what is observed."

In ultimate reality, however, that which possesses the nature of both the probandum and the probans is expressed all at once by the verb. Thus it is said: "In the comprehension of the meaning of a word, there is no perception of distinction. But surely this is a property of the thing itself?

The meaning is that since it is only while being accomplished (*sādhyamāna*) that something becomes a means (*sādhana*), the word [itself] does not possess the property [of denoting both]; for instance, in the case of "sovereignty through sacrifice," the word is not able to denote the state of having both forms simultaneously. Otherwise, the word would cause one to understand [the object] as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), whereas otherwise it causes one to understand it as something to be referred to (*uddeśya*).
He refutes this: It is true that, because it possesses both forms, it is denotable in that way;
yet even when both are denoted, the word "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) is capable of conveying the two related entities because it possesses both forms.
Because the sacrifice possesses the nature of both the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it is denoted by the word exactly as it is;
for although it is expressed as having both forms, it is nonetheless [expressed] as being related to both the result and the quality which are its correlates.

But the word "he should sacrifice" (yajeta) is capable of expressing the dedication of the two related parties; if it is so capable, then the injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) is established.
And validity is established. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "It is not so; for those two related entities—the fruit and the quality—are incapable of being connected with the sacrifice.

Indeed, the fruit is not capable of being connected with that which consists of both the goal and the means. Nor is the quality [capable], because the fruit is connected only with the means, and the quality is connected only with the goal. If they were capable of being connected..."
There being nothing,
what capacity for denotation will it exercise?
Therefore, because each is capable of being related [to the result] individually, they are denoted here as distinct entities.
Consequently, since two objects are enjoined, this sentence results in a dual function: "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice."

The injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya" would be mutually disconnected. If this were so, what would happen? The answer is: the understanding of mutual connection would be abandoned, and a meaning that is not actually perceived would have to be imagined. Thus, this very state of mutual dependence arises; for otherwise, the imagination of a meaning not perceived from the words themselves would be untenable. Now, regarding the claim that syntactic unity is achieved by resorting to the indication of possessive significance (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), he says: "And the indication of possessive significance is contradictory. Therefore, by the arguments stated in the *Udbhid* section and the *Tatprakhya* section...

Furthermore, the arguments were stated in the section concerning designation by that [name]; by those arguments, the position that it is a name alone is logical. As for the inconsistency regarding the cause and the effect mentioned in the sentence, that does not exist, because there is no contradiction.

There is no inconsistency because the sign (nimitta) does not obstruct the effect. Now, one might object that there is indeed an inconsistency even if [the name] is not conducive to the purpose; to this he says: "Inconsistency exists in the case of obstruction, not in the case of being non-conducive.
Although the name lacks conduciveness to activity, nevertheless there is no inconsistency; such is the meaning.
Therefore, there is no fault;
there is no fault characterized by a contradiction between the effect and its cause.
As for its qualities: for what purpose is this section (adhikaraṇa) commenced?
A partisan (ekadeśin) offers the answer: "What is this question?
Is it not already known that the Āgneya and other offerings are injunctions of qualities (guṇavidhi) and not names?"

The objector refutes this: It is correct that names possess the status of being designations based on etymological derivation (*yaugika*), conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), or established meaning (*prāpta*); however, the status of being a name is not possible in the case of "the *āgneya* [cake] on eight potsherds.
Why? He says: For the status of being a name is asserted on the basis of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the verb.

In a sentence whose primary purport is the injunction of the meaning of a verb, since it is impossible for another thing to be the object of that injunction, even the other words must have the meaning of the verb as their primary purport; for this reason, they are called "nouns" (nāman). One might ask: "Let it be so; nevertheless, what follows? To this he says: "And here, even the verb 'bhavati' (it exists) does not have the sense of an action (bhāvārtha), because its meaning is not something to be enjoined. This verb 'bhavati' is not of the nature of an action. Why is it not of the nature of an action? To this it is replied: "Because its meaning is not something to be enjoined."

If the meaning of the word *bhavati* is also of the nature of an existent (*bhāva-rūpa*), why does it not take the form of something to be enjoined (*vidheya*)? And since it is not something to be enjoined, we understand from that non-enjoinability that it does not have the nature of an existent. (B) Because, if it were not of the nature of an existent, the sentence would lack the purpose of enjoining that [existent]; therefore, since the sentence has the purpose of enjoining when there is the nature of an existent, the status of *Āgneya* as a name is established through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [enjoined existent]. Furthermore, there is no other reason for its being a name than the aforementioned reason, which consists in its coreferentiality with the meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyāta-artha*) being enjoined.

With this intention, our question is: "For what purpose is this section (*adhikaraṇa*) commenced? The meaning is that because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is weak, this section should not have been commenced. The respondent says:
To this it is replied: here again, the very same dependence is being questioned.

Having raised the objection regarding the dependence of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced in order to state its independence in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). The meaning is that it ought to be commenced.

This is the meaning. How is dependence suspected? The answer is: just as the status of being a name is not possible because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a verbal action, so too is the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) impossible because no verbal action is heard.
For an injunction of a quality is dependent upon a verbal action; and here, no verbal action is heard.

If this were an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*), and if neither the status of an injunction regarding a quality nor the status of a name (*nāmatva*) were possible, then, due to the absence of any other alternative, non-authoritativeness would necessarily follow. And that [non-authoritativeness] does not belong to the word by its very nature, but rather is produced by its being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*). By virtue of being of human origin—

And therefore, because it would follow that [the Veda] is of human origin, the entire collection of the Vedas would necessarily depend upon other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Now, since the expression "āgneya" is heard as a conjunction of substance and deity,
and since that [conjunction] is untenable without the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) must be the act of sacrificing.

And therefore, in that case, either a name or an injunction of qualities is indeed possible. How [then] can there be a lack of authority? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "True, if a connection between a substance and a deity were heard. The objector says: "But surely 'Āgneya' is what is heard."
The proponent says: "True, provided that it were not concerned with the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake baked on eight potsherds).

For the *aṣṭākapāla* is heard [in scripture] as belonging to Agni (*āgneya*). Since that [connection] is not possible here, the relationship between the substance and the deity is effectively unheard. The objector asks: "If it were indeed concerned with the *aṣṭākapāla*..."

There would be a connection between the substance and the deity; what follows from that? The implication is that the eight-potherd cake (aṣṭākapāla) would indeed possess the character of being dedicated to Agni (āgneyatva). The proponent states the reply: "From that, this follows: the state of being an eight-potherd cake must be understood as not being enjoined [by the primary injunction], because it is merely the object of reference (uddeśya)."

And there is no such thing as an "eight-potherd" (aṣṭākapāla) that has not been prescribed. But surely, that which is cooked on eight potsherds will be the referent— whether it be worldly or based on the scriptural injunction— "he cooks [the oblation] on potsherds."

The meaning of this is as follows: Alternatively, let it not be that the worldly [fire] is the intended referent, because of the statement, "he cooks in the potsherds. Rather, let it be based solely on the scriptural injunction. In any case, by this very statement, the status of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) can be enjoined even for that which has not been previously prescribed.
The proponent refutes this: "First of all, it cannot be based on direct scriptural statement (*vācanika*), because the number eight is heard [in the text].

For the state of being prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapālatā*) is not obtained unless there is an injunction for the number eight in the scriptural statement. If it is argued that that number itself is what is enjoined, he refutes this:"
—No, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). [The argument would be: "In the *āgneya* there is the number; in the number, the *āgneya*.

By way of restating the *āgneya*, the number eight would have to be enjoined: "That which is the *āgneya* should be made eight-potherded"; and likewise, "that which is eight-potherded is the *āgneya*."
B. Regarding the "connection with a deity" (*devatāsamyoga*):

since the quality of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) is stated by way of reference to the eight-potsherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*), an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is therefore not possible; nor indeed can it be otherwise.
It has been stated that [the cognition] arises;

therefore, it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*). If the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was intended to show a lack of authority, why then did the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) say "nāma" (by name)? The respondent says: Where was it said?

The objector says: It was stated in the introduction whether this is a name or an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). This was introduced at the time of the doubt. In that regard, "it is a name" is the formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while "it is an injunction of a quality" is the formulation of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thus, at the time of adopting the prima facie view, there is a negation of the injunction of a quality.
And by performing [this], it is stated that, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is a name (*nāmadheya*).
He provides the resolution: "It is true that it has been stated to be a name; however, it is not [a name]."

The meaning is that it has not been stated that "this is the name of the verbal root-meaning which is to be enjoined. What, then, has been stated? He says: "By the mention of the name, its status as a well-known referent is demonstrated."

The term *āgneya* does not function as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), but rather as a well-known meaning (*prasiddhārtha*), as it has been stated that even a name possesses a well-known meaning. Even if this be so, how is its dependence (*sāpekṣatā*) explained? To this he says:
"And since well-knownness is not possible without another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), the dependence of the application [of the word] is demonstrated."

He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): This would indeed be so if there were a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*) regarding the connection with number and the connection with the deity. But that is not the case. [Objection:
But surely this is the case.
[Question: How is it not the case? [Answer: The reply is: for the injunction of the deity applies to the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake baked on eight potsherds).

He recalls the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "But was it not said that this [Brahman] is not well-known? The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) replies: "Is it not well-known even as something denotable?"

The meaning is that it is well-known as something denotable. And it is by relying on its renown as a denotation that its injunction is possible. The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says: it is not well-known as something denotable, but rather as something to be accomplished (kārya).

Since it is established that "an offering on eight potsherds must be made," its lack of prior establishment is stated. The final conclusion (rāddhānta) says: this very lack of prior establishment by way of being something to be accomplished is indeed desired; for it is precisely because it is not previously established as something to be accomplished that [the injunction is necessary].

It is thus established. He concludes: Therefore, the non-establishment of the designation (of the term) subverts its injunction; however, it is not the non-establishment [of the object] by way of being something to be produced (*kāryatayā*). Consequently, just as in the case of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is an injunction for the meaning of "eight-potsherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) as well. Furthermore, the fact that [the meaning] is understood through a well-known designation has been demonstrated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) when he says, "one does not take what has been cooked by another.

For if the meaning were not well-established, the taking of what was cooked by another would not even be a possibility that required refutation, such that it would be appropriate to state [the prohibition]. [This applies] to the potsherds (*kapāleṣu*).

Because of the statement "he cooks," one does not take what has been cooked by another; therefore, this meaning of the *taddhita* suffix is as well-established as the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Just as the meaning of the root *yaj* is established through its direct hearing in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), so too is the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix established. Consequently, there is no risk of [the word] being dependent on something else.
Because independence is established through the injunction of an action qualified by specific qualities;
nor, in this case, is there the possibility of the meaning being already established, as is the case with the eight-pot-sherd [offering] in relation to the *agnihotra*.

Thus, it is also prescribed that just as in the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra," the fire is not prescribed as the deity because the deity Fire is already established, so too it is not possible here [to prescribe the deity]. Furthermore,
this [text] expresses a well-known meaning.
[Page 234] Regarding the *barhis* and the clarified butter (*ājya*):
what, then, is the intermediate connection? To this he says: "This section is incidental."

What, then, is the logical consequence here? The answer is: even with a meaning that is to be enjoined, the connection of a noun's meaning is observed, as in the case of "the eight-pot-sherd offering" (*aṣṭākapāla*).
Furthermore, this word *ājya* is also seen in common usage to be based solely on the action [of preparation].
In common usage, this word *ājya* is based on the act of refinement (*saṃskāra*).
It is observed that the word *ājya* is employed only in its processed state. Therefore, this [word] also is connected with the action (*kāryānvayī*).

The connection of the word *ājya* with the purpose of the action means it is connected as something to be produced (*kāryatayānvayī*). This very point is demonstrated by the statement: "One should make *ājya* by means of processing. The meaning is:
