"One should process the *ājya* by means of melting."

But surely, the word *ājya* is observed in certain regions even without reference to a ritual action, as in the expressions "ghee is for sale" and "having taken the sacrificial grass, the cows have gone.
Therefore, how can it be said with certainty that the word is based solely on a ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*)?

It can be determined. He refutes [the objection]: indeed, the usage that is heard in the Veda ought to be universal (*sārvabhauma*). Usage that originates from only one region and is based on refinement (*saṃskāra*) cannot be universal.
First, for those who employ words in the refined form (*saṃskṛta*), their usage is indeed based on refinement;
however, as for those who do not employ words when refinement is absent, [their usage is not so].
For them, it is clear that [the word] has the conditioned (*saṃskāra*) as its cause. Even those who employ [the word] in the sense of mere genus (*jāti*) employ it in reference to the conditioned;
thus, its scope being the conditioned is universal. And that alone is the Vedic sense. As for its denoting the genus in a particular instance, that is figurative (*gauṇa*).
Why is this so? The answer is: because of what is well-known (*prasiddha*).
For a word can possess a figurative sense only when its primary meaning is well-established, not when it is unknown;
for just as the word "fire," which is well-known to denote burning, becomes used figuratively when applied to a young boy due to his similarity to fire, so it is for all [words].

The status of being a cause for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is well-established; thus, when applied to mere birth (*jāti*), it is a secondary usage occurring in only one part [of its meaning]. However, for those who maintain that the term is used only in reference to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) itself, the usage is primary because there is no other usage. Furthermore, this term is not universally established as denoting clarified butter (*ghṛta*);
and for that which is not so established, a secondary application to clarified butter elsewhere would not be logical.

Those who consider sound to have its cause in *saṃskāra* (mental impressions) do not employ sound even in another birth; in that case, it is not logical for it to be secondary (*gauṇa*), because primary usage is not observed elsewhere. On the other hand, if its cause were action (*karman*), then when it is employed in one part [of a word], such as *ghṛta*, [it would follow accordingly].

Even in the case of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), since there is usage there based on the cause of ritual action (*karmanimittaka*), the secondary sense is established; for elsewhere, the primary usage is established, as the secondary sense is established in the case of *ghṛta* (clarified butter). Therefore, because words such as *ājya* have ritual action as their cause, it is logical that they refer solely to the purpose of the ritual act (*kāryārthatā*). To this, it is replied: the syntactical connection as referring to the purpose of the ritual act is not tenable, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). [This applies] to the *barhis*...
"The sprinkling of what already exists, and the sacrificial grass by means of sprinkling.

Indeed, that which is consecrated by sprinkling and other such rites is called "barhis" (sacrificial grass). Since sprinkling and other rites are prescribed with reference to the *barhis*, it is not understood [from the statement alone] of what they are the rites.

[The opponent says: "Sprinkling and so forth are enjoined. [The author asks: "If that is so, there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*); how then is there no mutual dependence in the case of the 'eight-potherd' (*aṣṭākapāla*) offering?

The answer is: "There is no mutual dependence because the designation is established through common usage (*prasiddhi*)," as it has been stated. But here, the designation occurs precisely through the function (*kārya*).
Thus, there is a discrepancy regarding the charge of mutual dependence.
However, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asks: "How is it with respect to the sacrificial post (yūpa)?
For it is heard in scripture: 'He fashions the sacrificial post.'"

Furthermore, the word *yūpa* denotes a ritual action (*kārya*) and a consecration (*saṃskāra*); in that case, a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident. Since there is no means of establishing it through anything else, this is a recourse of last resort (*agatikā gatiḥ*).
Just as in the case of *barhis* and so forth, there is establishment through something else because its usage is observed in reference to the genus alone, so it is here.

Since it does not exist in the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and since there is no other possible course, this resort is taken: that which is fit for carving and which is the object of the act of carving, one makes into a sacrificial post by means of carving. What kind of desperate resort is this?
He says in a single sentence: "Is it not understood from the scripture itself?"

The intention is this: if it were understood from scripture, then the same would apply to *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and other such items as well. The answer is: when there is common worldly usage (*prasiddhi*), one does not understand it from scripture; where something is already established by another means, it is not proper to employ a general term, because only the specific meaning is understood. In that case, this understanding derived from scripture is not obtained: that which is fit for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and serves as the object of the action of sprinkling—that is *barhis*.

That [substance] is consecrated by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). However, when the meaning of a word is not already established, because the purpose of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) remains unobstructed, it is postulated; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the injunction's purpose being frustrated. As for what was stated—that the universal application (*sārvabhauma-prayoga*) cannot be secondary (*gauṇa*)—that is not possible.

Regarding the argument that [the secondary sense] is not established because the Vedic meaning is unknown, it is replied: people in the world do not necessarily employ a secondary sense only when the Vedic primary meaning is well-known, as is the case with the word "king" (*rājan*). For instance, even non-Aryans use the word "king" despite its Vedic primary meaning being unknown to them.
Likewise, they employ figurative expressions such as the word *barhis* (sacrificial grass). He raises an objection: "In that case, the same fault applies even to the word *rājan* (king).

He states this in a single passage: "For they employ a figurative expression for the purpose of conveying a similarity to the primary object; yet it is figurative even when there is no cognition of that [primary object]."
This is called "forceful application" (haṭha);

for a word is used figuratively (gauṇa) precisely to convey a resemblance to its primary meaning. Since that resemblance cannot be known if the primary meaning is not understood, the figurative application would be without cause if the cognition of resemblance were absent.

It is without cause. To this it is replied: the relationship between a word and its meaning does not depend upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). For intention depends upon a [pre-existing] relationship.

The meaning of this is as follows: although the speaker employs [the word] with a figurative understanding and the person being addressed likewise understands it, nevertheless, an observer standing by...

A child, not having observed the usage [of a word] in its primary sense, understands only that primary sense. Having understood it thus, he would also engage in linguistic practice accordingly. Therefore, for a bystander, the relationship between a word and its meaning does not depend upon the speaker's intention; rather, whatever primary relationship between word and meaning the bystander perceives, that very same one he intends when engaging in linguistic practice at a later time. This very point is illustrated by means of an example:

He demonstrates this: for it is stated in the *Gopotalikā* and other texts that, due to the lack of knowledge regarding the non-origination from incapacity, people employ words as if they were beginningless, just like those who possess beginningless vision (*anādṛk*). Thus.

Furthermore, because a speaker does not fully understand the intention of another speaker, one might employ a word devoid of that intention toward a different object. For instance, someone who knows the primary meaning of a word to refer to a universal (*jāti*) may, due to the presence of a single shared characteristic, apply it figuratively (*gauṇa*) even to something belonging to a different class that possesses a connection with the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) associated with that figurative usage.

The word *barhis* and others have been employed here; for one who does not know another primary meaning, there is an intention to convey a secondary meaning. Thus, for one who does not know this, the cognition of the primary meaning proceeds. Just as, in the case of [the words] *gopotalikā* and so forth, those who do not know [their etymology] have a cognition of beginninglessness and a lack of origin from incapacity, and the linguistic usage of word and meaning is based upon that. But how is this understood?

[Objection: This primary linguistic usage regarding the term *saṃskṛta* (consecrated) is based on error. [Response: No, because such usage is observed both in common worldly practice and in the Veda. In the Veda, for instance, having prescribed *ājya* (clarified butter), it sometimes praises it using the word *ghṛta* (butter).

In that case, if the word *ājya* were expressive of the consecration (*saṃskāra*), then the word *ghṛta* in that praise would have to be used merely as a figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). However, if it denotes the genus (*jāti*), then it retains its own primary meaning. Therefore, by examining the Veda, it is determined that the word indeed denotes the genus.

In common worldly usage as well, one observes the employment of the word "to be purchased" (*krayyam*) twice—as in "ghee is to be purchased"—independently of any specific action that would require it.

That is, even in the world, usage is seen that is independent of that for which the action is the means; namely, that whose means is the action itself in the form of a consecration (*saṃskāra*). Now, one might object: "But even in those cases, there is an unstated intention (*avivakṣā*)."
It can be said:

A. Even though the word "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) has its primary meaning [in relation to the person], it is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) in reference to the caste because of its connection with that [refinement]; or, even if it denotes refinement alone, the word is used figuratively for the caste by virtue of the caste's mere fitness for such refinement.

In that case, since B. was engaged [in the debate] without fully understanding the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), it can also be said that because of this lack of understanding of the intention, the notion of a primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) indeed arose for someone; therefore, [p.

How is the certainty [established]? He provides the answer: "The resolution regarding the reed-grass (*vetasa*) and so forth has already been stated. Furthermore, when there is a conflict regarding the refinement of the genus (*jāti-saṃskāra*) or a conflict regarding worldly usage concerning an object of common experience, the determination is made through the general analogy with Vedic usage.

Therefore, here too, because of the similarity to Vedic usage, the primary sense (*mukhyatā*) applies to the genus (*jāti*). However, regarding the word *saṃskṛta*, its secondary usage (*gauṇaḥ prayogaḥ*) arises from its connection with the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belonging to that [genus]. If this is so, then the matter is already settled by that very same section (*adhikaraṇa*). It is replied: this section is commenced to dispel the doubt that a secondary usage occurs only for one who already knows the primary usage. The examples, however, are both *barhis* and *vetasa*, which apply in both cases. But what is the relevance of this incidental discussion?
What is the purpose of defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The answer is: it is precisely to avoid non-determination; that is, to avoid the non-determination of the meaning of words.

In the linguistic usage of words, there would otherwise be a lack of determination as to which [meaning] is primary and which is secondary. Consequently, even in the case of the Veda, there would be invalidity due to such non-determination. Therefore, non-determination is indeed the motivating factor for this section (*adhikaraṇa*). But surely, by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)...

The distinction has been shown only with respect to the object (*karman*), not with respect to the cognition (*avagati*). He refutes this: precisely because there is a distinction regarding the object, for that very reason non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) is the purpose;
non-determination is the motivator for the formal inquiry (*adhikaraṇa*) in order to eliminate it. If there were no distinction regarding the object...

In that case, there would be no distinction in practice; and due to the absence of a distinction in practice, there would be a lack of determination (*anadhyavasāya*) which cannot be removed. This is not a fault, and it is for the sake of its removal that this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been commenced. However, once certainty is reached through determination, the purpose is already established.

[Page 240] Regarding the *prokṣaṇī* waters: for what purpose is this a separate section? The answer is: an exception (*apavāda*) is stated based on traditional law (*smṛti*) concerning two types of ritual performance—that which pertains to the entire earth and that which pertains to only a portion of it.

The application [of words] based on *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement) is universal, whereas that based on *jāti* (genus) originates only in a specific region. Having considered the traditional memory (*smṛti*) regarding these two, an exception is stated: that the word *prokṣaṇī* is etymological (*yaugika*). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) asks:
"But how can an exception to usage be stated on the basis of traditional memory, since the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is rooted in actual usage? How [can it override it]?"

The sense is that he is refuting the application [of the rule]. He states the final conclusion: for the application is indeed consistent with the traditional teaching (smṛti). For the application certainly conforms to the traditional teaching. Why? He says: because the connection of both parts is possible.
Even he who...

The application [of a word] is based on a refinement (*saṃskāra*), and in that case too, a connection (*yoga*) is possible; and it is also the case where the application is based on a genus (*jāti*). Consequently, since the application is not incompatible with the connection, it does not sublate the connection. In this regard, the application "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters" is based on a refinement.
"We are distressed by the sprinkling waters"— this is based on the [caste] species. Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the determination is made according to the Smṛti.
The rest has been stated.
Likewise regarding the *nirmanthya* fire. What is added here?

The answer: this is excessive here. The traditional rule (*smṛti*) is also over-extensive, because we observe its application even to that which has not been churned for long, and likewise we observe its application even to that which is unrefined.
"We shall cook [the food] by means of that which is being churned.

Thus, it does not have the production of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) as its cause. Likewise, etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) is also impossible, because usage is observed even when the fire has been churned not long ago; if it were etymologically derived, usage would occur only when it has been churned for a long time.

It might be so; however, it cannot be based on the genus (*jāti*), because the term is used for fire in general. Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that even from traditional usage (*smṛti*), no definitive conclusion can be reached.
He states the established conclusion: because the Smṛti text expresses the term without distinction, it is not capable of obstructing the specific application [of the word].

For if, in the Smṛti, the word *nirmanthya* were considered correct whether applied to wood that has been rubbed for a long time or to wood that has been rubbed recently; [then the specific usage would be invalidated].
If it were remembered [at that time], then the specific application would obstruct the memory; but this is not the case.

If it is argued that "it obstructs non-specific knowledge," meaning that the application obstructs the non-specific knowledge derived from memory, [the author] refutes this: it does not obstruct [memory], because non-specificity is subsumed within the specific.

If that which is non-distinctive in the *smṛti* were to be restricted as distinctive by the force of its application (*prayoga*), then there would be no fault whatsoever. Therefore, this case is also like the previous one; thus it was said, "it is so.
Regarding the *vaiśvadeva*: how, then, does a doubt arise here concerning whether it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*)?

To the extent that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), it is more appropriate here for [the word] to be a name (*nāmadheya*). The reply: In this case, grammatical coreferentiality is more appropriately established under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Since the meaning of the verbal root is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is not appropriate for it to be a name; rather, the view that it is an injunction of a quality is indeed correct. Even in the case of an injunction of a quality, because there is no implication of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—since in the expression "of this sacrifice, the Viśvedevas are the deities" (*viśvedevā devatā asya yāgasya*), the sacrifice itself is the meaning of the suffix—the grammatical coreferentiality is established through its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*). He objects again: If the injunction of a quality is indeed more appropriate, why...

The presentation as a name provides the resolution: because there is no subject matter for the injunction of a quality, an injunction of a quality is also not tenable, since there is no subject matter for the quality to be enjoined. Why is there no subject matter? The answer is: by means of Agni and so forth.

Because the deities of the rites under discussion are already established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), those very rites that are under discussion are occupied by Agni and others who are enjoined by their original injunctions (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*); therefore, it is not possible to enjoin another deity therein. If it is impossible to enjoin another deity in the context of the established rites...

In that case, why does this not become a separate ritual qualified by a deity? That too is not determined, because the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Viśvedevas is the subject under discussion. For in the injunction of a separate ritual, there would be an injunction of a qualification—that is, an injunction of a qualified entity—and that occurs only when no other alternative is possible.

[This would be] logical if it existed; yet here there is another alternative, because—due to its association with the *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā* sacrifice—it is possible for it to be construed as a name (*nāmadheya*) for the sacrifices under discussion, according to the maxim of the "man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Therefore, even the status of being a name is not possible here, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) can be established even by way of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*). Nor is it an injunction of a quality, because the sacrifices under discussion are already occupied by qualities prescribed at their origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*). Thus he says: "Therefore, it is not a name..."
Nor can independence be understood on the basis of the qualities;
such is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position. A proponent of the final view (rāddhāntaikadeśin) says:
"If you think that it is impossible to determine independence, then let the determination be made through the injunction of qualities."

For the relationship between the meanings of nouns and verbs is understood in that manner. [Objection: But was it not stated that there is no object [for such a relationship]? [Reply: He refutes this: "That was poorly stated. [Objection: How is it poorly stated?
The answer: For the postulation of an effect arises from scripture (śruti), not scripture from the effect.

What is this that is being said? The answer: This is this; for the obstruction by a quality taught in the originative injunction (utpatti-śiṣṭa) is indeed the cause of non-comprehension, but not the sublation of what has already been comprehended.

The contradiction lies solely in the apprehension of a connection with another quality due to the obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origin; it does not, however, effect the sublation of that which has already been apprehended. One might grant this, but even so, what follows? He says: this word *vaiśvadeva* applies only to the meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyātārtha*) as it occurs in the context, and not to Agni and the others. [This is] in order to prevent the related meaning of the verbal root from being excluded from being denoted by the word *vaiśvadeva*.
[They are] capable.
He says in a single passage: B. another related factor.

They exclude the status of being the object of another related entity, but they do not exclude the status of being denotable. What follows from this? The answer is: for the sake of establishing the status of being denotable, the fire and other deities who are connected by way of origin do not obstruct the attainment of another deity as a further related entity; just as [they do not obstruct] when [a thing] is to be consecrated.

Since the consumption [of the *phalacamasa*] is connected as a consecration (or remnant) of the sacrificial residue (*yāgaśeṣa*), its status as a means of accomplishing the sacrifice—which could not otherwise be established—is implied; thus, the Soma does not obstruct it. Therefore, for the sake of making possible the designation by the term "Vaiśvadeva" as heard in the text, one must postulate a function for the Viśvedevas.

It is logical. The meaning is that it is logical for [the Vaiśvadeva] to enter as a deity into the sacrifices under discussion; however, the completion of the sacrifice is not their function. Considering that this [completion] is accomplished by Agni and the others alone, it is not logical to assume an incorrect status for what is directly stated—that is, to assume an incorrect referent for the denotation of the term "Vaiśvadeva. Since the connection as a deity is for the sake of making the designation possible, therefore, when the performance is carried out together with Agni and the others...
Because it is independent of conceptual construction, determination is appropriate.
He states the ultimate conclusion: "If this is so..."

The assumption of a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is merely for the sake of establishing the application of the word; if that is so, let it rather be a name (*nāmadheya*). For it is for the purpose of making the designation intelligible that there is a connection with another quality.
It is postulated through logical necessity (*anupapatti*). However, for those things enjoined by unequal means of knowledge, there is no such conceptualization.

For fire and the others are enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), whereas the Viśvedevas are enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*). In that case, the injunction is logically consistent as being a name (*nāmadheya*). But [it may be objected]: "Is it not so..."

If [the word] were a mere name, the meaning derived from its constituent parts would not be connected to the ritual action (*kārya*). For if, by following the meaning of the parts, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) belonging to the Viśvedevas were perceived, it would be unconnected with the ritual action; this is the sense. He refutes this: "It is not logical for that which is already connected to be further connected; and this meaning is already connected to the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture). Therefore, the lack of connection with the ritual action is not capable of precluding the denotation [of the deity]."

Since that which is already connected [to the action] in one instance may be understood as a name (*nāmadheya*)—on the analogy of the "man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*)—even when it is not connected elsewhere, its status as a cause (*nimittatva*) is not contradicted, just like the staff itself.
Therefore, it is impossible to assume an option (*vikalpa*), nor is there a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the ritual act. Consequently, it is logical to determine that it is a name.
[247] But how, again, is there the designation "vaiśvadeva" for the sacrifice to Agni and the other deities within the *vaiśvadeva* [parvan]?

[The objection is: "It is established [that the term 'āmikṣā'] lacks a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) because it is prescribed again in the injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), since a basis for application is possible there. He refutes this: "True, this would be so if it were established solely through the act of prescription; however, in the case of *āmikṣā*, it would follow that it is not denoted [by the word]."

For since the Viśvedevas are already established in connection with the *āmikṣā*, they cannot be the object of an injunction; thus, the application of the designation [of the sacrifice] as something to be enjoined does not succeed in an absolute sense. Now, one might argue that by abandoning the *āmikṣā* [as the primary referent], the designation as something to be enjoined will succeed; to this he says: "And the state of being the subject matter is equal [for both];
therefore, the sacrifice of the *āmikṣā* is not [the intended meaning]."

It cannot be avoided. Here, an objection is raised: "Which of these two is stronger?"—namely, between this naming of what is not a Vaiśvadeva as 'Vaiśvadeva' and the naming of that which is enjoined by means of that which is not enjoined, which of these two is stronger? The author replies: "The naming of that which is enjoined by means of that which is not enjoined [is not stronger]."

It is possible. For that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is made known when it is unknown, whereas that which is the denotable object (*abhidheya*) is already known. And it is not possible for a single entity to be both known and unknown at the same time. Furthermore, the denotation by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is possible for things that share a common connection, as in the case of the expression "the staff-bearers are going. This would be the case under the view that [the word] is a name (*nāmadheya*).

Just as the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) applies by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) even to those who do not possess a staff due to association, so too here the word "vaiśvadeva" will apply both to that which is not a vaiśvadeva and to that which is a vaiśvadeva. Therefore, this position—that the term "vaiśvadeva" denotes what is not a vaiśvadeva—is superior; this position is better.
[Page 248] Furthermore, this must be addressed here: why is the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" not applied specifically to the Āmikṣā sacrifice alone?

For in that case, no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) would have to be resorted to regarding the word *vaiśvadeva*. And even if the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) were to apply to that [Āmikṣā sacrifice] as well, nevertheless...

There is no inconsistency in this. To this it is replied: by the rule that the word *vaiśvadeva* applies to a hymn (*sūkta*) or an oblation (*havis*), it functions primarily in reference to either a hymn or an oblation. Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *yajati*, which itself functions in the sense of a sacrifice, this word *vaiśvadeva* cannot restrict the application of the term *yajati*. Nor can there be a connection between the word *vaiśvadeva* and the verb *yajati* through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Because, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *āmikṣā*, it would follow that it must be feminine; and because when coreferential connection is possible, a non-coreferential connection is untenable. "Those [words] preceded by [other means of knowledge] are not for the purpose of injunction. It has been stated that the authority [of the Veda] is established through injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, names, and injunctions of qualities.
In this case, however, in the offerings on eight potsherds or twelve potsherds, there is no status as a mantra and no status as a reminder; therefore, it functions as an injunction (codaka).

Since it does not serve as a reminder of what has already been enjoined, it cannot even be a name (*nāmadheya*). Furthermore, because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the "eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth—

there being no coreferentiality with the meaning of the action being enjoined in the phrase "when it becomes eight-potsherded"— the possibility of it being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) such as the number eight found in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) remains indeed doubtful.
In that regard, first of all, there is no doubt concerning the prescription of qualities; it is possible.
Because of the absence of an object;
because it is absolutely impossible to enjoin a quality [where none exists]. How is there an absence of an object?
The answer is: because of the cessation of one set of qualities and the arising of another set of qualities.

Regarding the injunction "one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," the sacrifice to Vaiśvānara is already restricted by the number twelve prescribed in its originative injunction. As for the potsherds upon which the sacrificial cake is placed, since they are not yet established [by that originative injunction] and because the act of placing is not the primary purpose [of the injunction], they do not constitute the subject matter [of the restrictive rule]. Likewise, there is no doubt regarding the explanatory passage (arthavāda) either.

The connection [is as follows]. Why? He says: because by means of the number twelve, other numbers such as eight and so forth are excluded. It is not a praise by virtue of being connected to that [number], as in the case of "Water is indeed peaceful.

If it is argued that just as the praise of water as "water is peaceful" is appropriate because it refers to water connected with the reed-grass (vetasa) which is the thing to be enjoined, so too is it appropriate here; [we reply: praise by way of a connection is indeed appropriate.
However, there is no praise of another number, because the number twelve has no such connection. Therefore, [the objection] is merely a misconception.
Furthermore, there is an objection regarding independence.
This being the case, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) remains as follows:
A certain proponent of a partial conclusion considers its validity to arise through the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*). What is his intention?
Thinking thus, does he not perceive the obstruction of the [original] production by another quality?
Because he thinks thus: [the answer is] "No, it is not that he does not see;
rather, he certainly sees. This is because one who considers this to be a single sentence falls into the error of taking it as a single syntactical unit.
Due to the confusion of the sentence, one considers the act of offering to be joined with all the numbers,
because of its syntactic unity: [namely] the eight-potsherd, the nine-potsherd, the ten-potsherd, and the eleven-potsherd.

"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds"— thinking that this prescribes an offering endowed with the total number [of potsherds], and considering this to be a single sentence because it constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the intention is that there is either a repetition of the ritual action or an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the subordinate elements (*guṇa*). [Regarding] Vaiśvānara...
The phrase "on twelve potsherds" is considered to be an introductory statement for the sake of the deity.

Therefore, by that single sentence, there is an injunction for the Vaiśvānara sacrifice endowed with the total number [of potsherds]. Because of this injunction, there is an origination [of the rite];
consequently, there is no obstruction by a quality already enjoined at the time of origination (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa*).

[Page 251] But this is for the purpose of enjoining a subordinate element (*guṇa*). To this it is replied: validity cannot be asserted on the basis of enjoining a subordinate element, because there is no subject matter (*viṣaya*). Now, it was argued that the ritual action having Vaiśvānara as its deity is the subject matter.

The rebuttal is as follows: that is not the subject [of the injunction], because it contradicts the twelve-fold division. By such statements as "that which is on eight potsherds" (yad-aṣṭākapāla), there is a plurality [of offerings].
B. nānā.

The injunction regarding the number of potsherds as "eighteen" is contained in a single sentence; therefore, the statement that there is no obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origination is ill-stated.
How so?

The answer is: because the word *vaiśvānara* expresses a case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting a meaning distinct [from the nominal stem], the term *vaiśvānaram* ends in the accusative case and expresses a meaning distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *dvādaśakapāla* is based on direct Vedic statement (*śrauta*).

Therefore, it is first understood that "one should offer the *vaiśvānara* [cake] on twelve potsherds. As for the [clause] "when [it is] on eight potsherds" (*yadaṣṭākapāla*), [it is a subordinate clause].
Because terms such as these are connected with the words *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster) and *punāti* (purifies), they are not understood to have the word *vaiśvānara* as their substratum.

However, a connection must be postulated on the grounds that the praise expressed by the word *punāti* would otherwise be inexplicable. And it has already been stated that such a postulation is not tenable when a [direct] connection already exists.
The meaning of this is as follows: here, the status of being a single unified sentence (sahavākyārthatva) is not possible, because words such as "a cake on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*),
which end in the nominative case, are connected with the word *vaiśvānara*, which ends in the accusative case.

Because there is no connection with the word [dvādaśakapāla]. However, while it might be intended to postulate a connection with Vaiśvānara on the grounds that praise would otherwise be inexplicable, such a postulation cannot even gain a foothold because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dvādaśakapāla* itself, which ends in the accusative case. Therefore, it remains established that [the sacrifice] is already occupied by a quality prescribed at its origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇa*). If, by the word *vaiśvānara*...
There is no connection between the eight-potherd [offering] and the others; if that is so, then it is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*). He refutes this:

"It is not intuition, because it is logically established as being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). But how is its purpose of praise established, given that the previous number has already been set aside by another number? As it was said: [it is established] by another number.
The answer: For the exclusion is by way of designation (abhidhāna), not by way of existence (sadbhāva) nor by way of non-existence (asadbhāva);
[for example], the number eight and so forth [is excluded] by the word "twelve."

It is not denoted. However, while the numbers eight and so forth can exist within the number twelve, their relation is based on their actual presence and not on the cause of verbal denotation. Since they do exist, their separate denotation is justified;
it is logical to denote the substances by isolating the numbers eight and so forth.
[Objection: But surely, if [the word] is separated [from its context], the understanding of the relationship [between the parts] would not occur;
and consequently, the praise would be untenable. [The author] replies:
Separation is possible for the sake of denotation, but the state of being related cannot itself be separated.
The meaning of this is as follows:
it is possible to apply the word "eight" to designate those eight potsherds which constitute a single portion of the twelve potsherds.

It is possible to perform [the ritual], but one cannot, however, logically establish that they actually possess the status of being included within the number twelve. Therefore, since their actual connection [to that number] is not established, the praise of the number twelve is indeed valid as a figurative praise of them. Now, one might ask: how can there be a lack of logical connection for the sake of denotation, yet not in reality? To this he says: "For denotation follows the speaker's intention (vivakṣā), not the objective reality.
Therefore, even though their actual number is twelve, when there is an intention to refer to only a portion of them, it is entirely appropriate to denote them by the word 'eight' and so forth."

Therefore, because the relationship [between the parts] is not being established, the praise is appropriate, just as in the case of "the waters are peaceful. And so it has been shown: "The felly and hub of this wheel are beautiful."
The praise of the whole occurs through the praise of its parts;

therefore, by praising the number eight which constitutes the parts, there is praise of the number twelve. [Objection: But let it be that the number twelve, being enjoined as part of the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), exists for the sake of the fruit, because there is no connection with the ninefold arrangement.

[Page 255] To the objection that the injunction of [subsidiary acts] such as the eightfold oblation (*aṣṭatva*) might apply to that very same ritual action, he replies: "Even the injunction of a connection between a quality and a fruit is not possible on this basis alone. Why not? The answer is: "Because it is understood to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) for the purpose of praise (*stuti*)."

Furthermore, because a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result if there were a connection between the quality and the fruit, and because the unity of the sentence has been demonstrated through the opening and the conclusion, it is established that [the Veda] is independent, as this is justified by its being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). That is established. It has been stated that praise is possible through a connection even when [the quality] is mentioned separately.

Even though there is thus a separate mention [of the quality], nevertheless, because the state of being related has not been separately joined, it is said that by the praise of that [quality], the praise of the related entity also occurs. However, where the state of being related is not understood in any way whatsoever due to a mutual lack of syntactic connection,
and where the enjoining of a quality is not possible—

Because of impossibility, as in the cases of "the sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd" (ekakapāla) or "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (prastara), and so forth— how can there be authority in such instances?
The meaning is that there is indeed no authority.
B. Nor are qualities enjoined.
But is it not established in the section concerning the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya-adhikaraṇa*) that there is a secondary relationship even for words denoting different meanings?
"It exists.
Because of this, since mutual connection is possible, the praise of both the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is justified. He refutes this:
"That very point is not accepted."

Only a figurative application (gauṇīvṛtti) is implied. Why is it not accepted? The answer is: figurative application is simply not possible because [the word] is connected with a different meaning. How is it not possible?
The answer is: for in a figurative expression...
It is logical that qualities alone possess denotability.

Regarding this so-called figurative designation (*gauṇābhidhāna*), if it is the case that qualities themselves are what is denoted, then the comprehension of specific qualities is established; otherwise, it is not. Thus he says: "For otherwise..."

In the expression "Devadatta is a lion," the word "lion" conveys only the quality of bravery in Devadatta. Likewise, in the expression "the boy is fire," the word "fire" does not establish the presence of actual flames in the boy, but rather his ruddy complexion; thus [the literal sense] is not tenable.
To the question "Why?", he says here: "The activity of the lion species" (siṃhajāti-pravṛtti).

The word "lion" (*siṃha*), when expressing qualities through its primary meaning, would express all those qualities whatsoever that are connected with the genus [of lions], because there is no distinction in the means of expression. Now, if you think that it expresses only as many as one intends to speak of...

If it is argued that "only that quality which is intended to be expressed is perceived, and no other," [the author] refutes this: "In that case, the word follows the intention [of the speaker], not the denotable object."
In that case, the word follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) and not the actual object.

Even though the object does not exist, the word nevertheless functions by the power of the speaker's intention. What follows from this? The answer is: that which has a superimposed nature is figurative (*gauṇa*).

[It would follow that one] attains [the fire-nature]. Since the state of being fire, which does not exist in the boy, is superimposed and intended to be expressed, it results that the word is used figuratively (*gauṇa*). Even so, why is this? He says: "And in the case of superimposition, there is no connection with another object;
that is, the word 'fire' has no connection with the boy. Why is this? The answer is: for superimposition has as its object only an already apprehended thing.
It grasps only an object that has already been apprehended, even if it is currently non-existent, and does not touch an object not yet apprehended;
just as in the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is grasped as "that very thing" and not as "something similar to it. This is the cognition: "This is indeed silver."

It is not, however, "similar to silver. Therefore, it perceives only non-existent silver, and not something like mother-of-pearl that is similar to silver. Furthermore, whatever is perceived as the object of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is precisely the object of figurative (*gauṇa*) language as well; therefore, in the praise of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), [the word "fire" refers to them].
The word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is not capable [of being the subject]. Well then, let it be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
The answer is: that too is not possible because of impossibility;
for a quality being enjoined is not seen to have a purpose in terms of the ritual action (kārya).
In this context, it is prescribed for the sake of the ritual purpose; however, that [purpose] is not tenable in either case.

It has been demonstrated that the injunction of the *prastara* and the single potsherd (*ekapāla*) is not for the sake of the sacrificer’s purpose, nor is the sacrificer’s purpose for the sake of those two.
The author of the Commentary has stated that this is an injunction regarding the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Therefore, this very same suspicion regarding a figurative interpretation (*pratibhā-śaṅkā*) arises; to this, it is replied: It is true that an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, but an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) cannot be ruled out. [Objection: But surely, because of the connection with another meaning... [A. ...it is not so.
And because there is no connection with the actual meaning, it was stated that this is not an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). He refutes this: "What has been said is incorrect. How is it incorrect?
The answer is: for figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) is indeed possible precisely through a connection with its own primary meaning.

The meaning is that a word becomes secondary (gauṇa) when, having denoted its own primary meaning, it relies upon an intention directed toward something similar to that meaning which has been presented by it. But was it not stated that this is not the case because there is no cognition of any quality merely related to the primary meaning?

He refutes [the objection]: "The distinction arises from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); this too has already been stated. He raises an objection: "It is true that you have said this; however, it has also been stated that in the case of the speaker's intention, there is no connection with the denotable object (*abhidheya*).
[Regarding] the speaker's intention...

In the case of a restrictive [injunction], that which is the expressed primary meaning (*svārtha*) of the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) does not become a related entity [to the act]. For in that case, there would be a superimposition (*adhyāropa*); the word expresses a meaning that is non-existent and constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpanā*), rather than a real, ultimate meaning. Consequently, praise (*stuti*) would be untenable.

Likewise, the occurrence of [words like] "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*) is explained: since a word has as its object mere conceptualization independent of an external referent, the employment of the term "sky-flower" is logically consistent.
But if the word were connected to the denoted object, it would be logically untenable; for with what would it be connected?

By which meaning is the word "what" (kiṃ) here connected? To this it is replied: you are indeed ignorant of the unrestricted nature of words; for when there is no intention to denote a specific referent, [the word functions]. You are truly ignorant of the scope [of linguistic usage].
The utterance of a specific word would be without basis.

For it is the object (*artha*) that, for the sake of its own cognition, necessitates the word; thus, the utterance of a specific word is logical. In the absence of that [object], however, the utterance of a specific word would be baseless. Furthermore, the designation through superimposition (*adhyāropa*) by means of another word is likewise not at all tenable.
To this, he objects: "Foolish man, do not speak thus! For it is by way of having a superimposed object that the referent of the word 'lion' is intended;
indeed, words have superimposed objects, and thus the meaning of a superimposed lion is what is intended."
Nor, however, does it [the word "lion"] apply to the boy by way of a connection with those qualities. Furthermore, this referent "lion" cannot occur as something superimposed without the word "lion.
Therefore, the utterance of the word "lion" is not without a basis.
"Since the very object that is superimposed is the one whose word is uttered, the utterance of a specific term is not without cause. The proponent replies: "But indeed, this has been stated by us;
the specific cause has been explained."
B. The prohibition of binding is not [due] to the absence of the boy, but rather because of his connection with the dawn;
C. the utterance of the word "liṅga."

[Page 261] Why is it that the meaning of "lion" alone is superimposed upon Devadatta? If you say, "Because of perceiving his qualities"—that is, because one perceives the qualities of a lion in Devadatta—the author refutes this: "In that case, it follows that the representation must be based on a connection with the primary referent."

The word "lion" denotes Devadatta by virtue of his connection with—that is, his similarity to—the primary referent of the word "lion. In this case, since the essential nature of the substance (Devadatta) is already apprehended through the word "Devadatta," the purpose [of the word "lion"] is solely to convey similarity. Furthermore, since the lion's similarity is based on the possession of common qualities, the purpose is to convey those qualities of the lion. If it is asked, "How is the specific quality understood? the answer is: through the observation of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because figurative usage (*gauṇa*) is preceded by such [direct] perception.

It is understood through the force of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) that this usage is secondary (*gauṇa*). For, having learned through another means of valid cognition that this word for one thing is being applied to another, the determination of its secondary nature occurs. And in that case, it is understood that the word is applied to that [other object] by virtue of its connection with a certain quality (*guṇa*) which is perceived through another means of valid cognition; thus, the establishment of the comprehension of that specific quality is achieved. He states this in a single passage: "Even in the case of words such as 'cook' (*pācaka*), the primary meaning is restricted to a particular [individual] by the force of another means of valid cognition."
It is established [as secondary].
What is the reasoning for saying it is not secondary?
If every word functions solely through a connection with an object, then how is it that the term "sky-flower" [functions]?
The use of the word [“existent”] refers to existence. The reply is: “just as ‘a sky-flower’.
The word “iti” here is intended to indicate that cognition; by this, the following is stated:

Just as there is the cognition "it is like a sky-flower," so too is the verbal usage "it is like a sky-flower. For instance, one cognition has the mere sky as its object, while another has the mere flower as its object. In that case, even though there is no mutual connection between the two, one who does not perceive their non-connection nevertheless engages in the linguistic practice of perceiving a connection. This should be described according to the principles established in the *Nyāyavīthī* as being based on the perception of a commonality between the two related entities through their proximity and simultaneous utterance. Therefore, the status of the explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is established. What happens?
The purpose [of this discussion] and how it is so are explained in the Bhāṣya: "The genus (jāti). The same application of validity should be made for the genus and so forth as well;

there too, validity is established by resorting to the status of being an explanatory passage (arthavāda). If this is so, why then are there separate topical sections (adhikaraṇas)? To this he says: "But the separate topical sections are due to the difference in the refutations; the application is also [different]."
These are for the purpose of illustration.
In that regard, the response is that the statement "the Brāhmaṇa is of Agni" is a figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) based on similarity due to their originating from the same source.
The statement "the sacrificial post is the sun" is based on similarity to the sacrificial post; the statement "others than cows and horses are indeed non-animals;

cows and horses are animals" uses the word "animal" figuratively for cows and horses by way of praise. Likewise, in the cases "he places the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks" and "he places the *prāṇabhṛt*-bricks," [the usage is figurative] by virtue of abundance.

The separate treatment of these topics as distinct *adhikaraṇas* is intended to show the resolution that "definition (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs through the inherence of the indicative mark (*liṅga-samavāya*). Therefore, it is established that even words with secondary meanings (*gauṇārtha*) possess authority by way of being explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), as do those with metaphorical meanings (*lākṣaṇikārtha*). But how can even those things that serve as the indicators (*lakṣaṇa*) in passages such as the *sṛṣṭi* (creation) hymns be themselves the objects of indication (*lakṣya*)? For in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the Gaṅgā, which serves as the indicator, is not itself the object of indication. The answer is: because of their connection to the same action as the objects of indication. That is, the indicator has a connection to the same action as those things which are the actual objects of indication; and since that action is itself the object of indication, [the indicator is also included].

For being a cause (*nimitta*) is indeed the reason for being characterized by a secondary application (*upadhāna*); and this state of being characterized by a secondary application exists even for the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras and others that function as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in [the mantras] being both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). As for how the word "animal" (*paśu*) can apply to horses and the like through secondary application (*lakṣaṇā*) in cases such as the *apaśu* [rite]: [it is because they are excluded from the class of animals].
How is the word "animal" (*paśu*) applied by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to horses and other such creatures?

In the case of horses and so forth, [the word] is applied primarily (*mukhya*) alone. And here, the non-acceptance of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not the deciding factor, because in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the figurative (*gauṇa*) sense is intended. The meaning is that in every respect there is only primary application here, neither figurative nor indicative. Regarding the subsequent point, because the usage is preceded by a prohibition—the generic term (*jātiśabda*) being prohibited in other members of that class—when it is employed for other members of that same class, it obtains its usage only through figurative application. For in this case, among the other animals, they are not [truly] "animals" (*paśavaḥ*).

Having established the prohibition [of the term "animal"] specifically with respect to cattle and horses among the species of animals, the application of the word "animal" (*paśu*) to them is merely figurative (*gauṇa*).

Why? Because when a generic term (*jātiśabda*) is prohibited from its own specific class, it becomes the object of the prohibition precisely as a quality inherent in that class which is itself being prohibited.
Because the genus (jāti) does not depart [from the object], the genus cannot be denied; nevertheless, he asks "why? and says:
"Furthermore, because of the denial of the quality (guṇa), when [the word] is applied to another member of that same genus, it is understood as having only a figurative meaning (gauṇārtha)."

The meaning is that, since the qualities have been negated in the preceding statements, a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding those very qualities is appropriate. Therefore, even the word denoting the genus (*jātiśabda*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), because it functions through its connection with the qualities of the denoted object; thus, there is no contradiction. Consequently, the independence [of the Veda] is established.

"Regarding doubtful cases. [Objection: But surely, in the case of *yava*, *varāha*, *vetasa*, and so forth, the removal of doubt has already been accomplished through the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*); therefore, this [present discussion] is redundant. [The author] replies: True; however, that [removal of doubt] concerned the meaning of the word itself. Here, the word-meaning—which is being doubted as to whether it is innate (*autpattika*) or not—is determined in each respective instance by the remainder of the passage.
Here he raises an objection: "Does the word have an object [meaning] such that the doubt concerning it may be removed? The sense is that it does not exist at all. He replies:
—Certainly it exists;

for through the distinction between insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*), one perceives the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word-meanings. If it is certain that a word denotes only its own meaning and that there is no sentence distinct from words, then how can the innate (*autpattika*) relationship between sentence and sentence-meaning be established through the linguistic usage of elders?

Objection: It is true that there is an innate relationship between a sentence and its meaning; however, it has been stated in the section on *tadbhūtānām* that the meaning of a sentence is communicated by the sentence through its constituent parts.

"Because it is connected with the purpose of action," as we have stated in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*. Therefore, in that case, there is doubt regarding what has become that [action]; but here, the sentence-meaning itself has the purpose of action.

This, then, is the distinction between sentence and sentence-meaning from word and word-meaning; and this has been demonstrated in detail. Therefore, even due to doubt regarding the purpose of action, there is a lack of authoritative validity.
Due to the contradiction between the opening and the conclusion, there is doubt regarding the very meaning of the passage.

This being the case regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), some who hold a portion of the final conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*) consider it appropriate to determine the meaning of the concluding passage on the basis of the opening statement (*upakrama*).
Because there is no contradiction.
To the question "How is there no contradiction?", he says: For a universal resides both in itself and in its particulars. If by that...

It has been said by someone that [the term] "anointed" (akta) can apply even when it is not actually anointed; likewise, although [the substance] is anointed with clarified butter (ghṛta), the word "clarified butter" must be explained in the concluding passage by virtue of the opening statement, just as in the case of the phrase "he lays down the sṛṣṭis," which applies to both those bricks that are sṛṣṭis and those that are not.
Just as in the expression "he lays down the sṛṣṭis," [the term refers to all bricks] whether they are actual sṛṣṭis or not.

Furthermore, the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) [should be explained] in that manner, and the word "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) should be explained as applying both to what is clarified butter and what is not clarified butter. To this it is said: this might indeed be so, if by that [reasoning]...

In other cases, the general sense [of a word] would be established by another sentence; however, here, because it constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the comprehension of the connection extends only as far as the specific detail.

In a single sentence, the meaning of the sentence is understood after considering the mutual relationship of the words. In that context, because the word *akta* (anointed) is connected with the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter), it is understood that its object is specifically clarified butter. Otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *ghṛta*, but not for the word *akta*.

There is a certain contradiction between the word and its meaning. Therefore, it is established that the status of being for the sake of action depends upon the supplementary portion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*);
thus it is settled in the *vākyaśeṣa*.
It is established that the sentence’s capacity to convey the meaning of the sentence depends upon that [word] which contains the term *ghṛta*.
Or rather, it follows from the sense (*arthāt*). Even where there is doubt regarding the performance [of an action], the scripture itself is considered to be doubtful;
therefore, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
[Page 270] But is this not improper? For, due to doubt regarding the performance [of the ritual], the scripture itself would be doubtful.
Since performance is preceded by the scripture, it is established that [the scripture] conveys the meaning of the sentence. Even if the performance is doubtful, nevertheless—
The meaning is that the treatise (śāstra) is doubtful. He refutes this: "True, as you have said;

however, even when there is doubt regarding the performance [of an act], the instruction concerning what is already established (siddhānuśāsana) is not itself doubtful. But in the case of an instruction concerning what is to be accomplished (kāryānuśāsana), doubt regarding the performance indeed arises."
The scripture. The objector says: Is there any practice that is not preceded by scripture, such that the scripture would be subject to doubt when that practice is doubted?

For if that [the injunction] were antecedent, even the performance would be subject to doubt, whereas the scripture is not doubted. It is true that when there is a connection [to a result], it is preceded by scripture;

the meaning is that at the stage of its origination, it is preceded by scripture. The performance exists because of the reality of the object of the injunction; the injunction does not establish the performance as its own proof.

Therefore, when even that [the injunction] is doubtful, the scripture itself is doubtful, because the scripture culminates in that [injunction]. Consequently, doubt regarding the meaning of the injunction is justified;
for doubt regarding its performance is also justified, since the injunction culminates in that [performance]. He states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "But that..."
That which is the intended meaning must be determined through implication, and it has been so determined by the author of the Commentary. He concludes the subject matter of the chapter:
"Because it is a synonym for that."

Therefore, having established the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) by demonstrating its independence through the performance of injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, traditional law (*smṛti*), and names;
It has been stated that "validity" is the subject, and it was promised that there shall be an investigation into the cause of that which possesses validity.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first book in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, composed by the Great Teacher Śālikanātha.
In the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*,
the commentary on the second chapter.
The first quarter:
[the section on] those whose meaning consists in being. In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been completed.
It has been stated that "the conduct" (vṛtta) refers to this commentary.
For the first chapter indeed ought to be cited as the reason; yet, not by the entire chapter is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) [established].
The definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.

What then? It was stated by way of a portion of it, namely through the definitions of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. Anticipating the objection that this does not serve as the reason for the division of the treatise (*śāstra*), he says:
"In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition has occurred," which means that it has been explained how verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition.

The meaning of this is as follows: the meaning of the commentary on the phrase "in the first chapter" is this—the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that independence (*anapekṣatva*), by which mode of being independent verbal testimony (*śabda*) is characterized as a means of valid cognition; that independence is the definition.

"Released" (*muktam*). By this, the entire subject matter of the chapter is proclaimed. Furthermore, we shall explain that independence (*anapekṣatva*) serves as the reason for the distinction between scriptures (*śāstra-bheda*). Now, one might object: "The investigation of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth was performed in the first chapter; however, the manner in which the word possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) has not been stated.
Thinking thus, he asks: "From where? (*kutaḥ*)?

Thus [he says]. He introduces the commentary as a response: "Since injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and traditional texts (*smṛti*) have been determined according to their true nature, and both subordinate injunctions (*guṇavidhi*) and names (*nāmadheya*) have been examined; and the determination of doubtful matters through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and through the sense (*artha*) has been stated."

Therefore, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated. But how, when only this much has been said, is the meaning of "the definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated" expressed? To that he says:
"And these..."

Explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, when understood otherwise than they truly are, do not invalidate validity; however, when correctly comprehended, they do not obstruct it. Therefore, because they have been determined according to their true nature, it is said that "the definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated."

The determination of the true nature of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, was stated solely for the purpose of establishing validity; thus, in the first chapter, only the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was set forth. Therefore, it was rightly said that "the definition of the means of valid cognition was stated in the first chapter. By the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating, "That must not be forgotten," [the author] indicates—by saying that this independence (*anapekṣatva*) must not be forgotten—that the discussion of difference and non-difference is dependent upon that independence, since he demonstrates that the remembrance of that [independence] alone is what is useful. Why [is this so]?...

Is the statement regarding difference and non-difference dependent upon dependence on something else? The answer is: for it is the difference and non-difference of the effect that is being stated, and that is based on independence [from other factors].
Why? He says: for when a word is dependent upon something else, it is not possible to state the distinction of the effect from the word alone.
He summarizes: "Therefore, that must not be forgotten" by means of this [phrase] "because of independence. In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows:

The distinction between treatises (*śāstra*), the subject matter of the chapters (*adhyāya-artha*), the distinction between the goals to be accomplished (*sādhya-bheda*), and the distinction between the auxiliary factors (*anubandha-bheda*) are stated here as the causes for that [distinction]. That goal to be accomplished is accessible through verbal testimony (*śabda*) alone; therefore, the independence of verbal testimony is required. Furthermore, that distinction of auxiliary factors which is the cause for the distinction between treatises is also dependent upon the distinction between effects (*kārya-bheda*). For if the *apūrva* were to differ by virtue of its connection with sacrifices (*yāga*) and so forth, then the status of the auxiliary factors of those sacrifices and so forth would likewise differ.

The scripture (*śāstra*) would also be divided by virtue of its presenting distinct subordinate elements (*anubandha*). However, if the unseen potency (*apūrva*) is not divided by the subordinate element of the sacrifice, then, due to the absence of a division in the subordinate elements, the scripture is not divided. Therefore, even for the sake of establishing a division of subordinate elements, a division of the *kārya* (the "thing to be done") must indeed be asserted. And since that [division] cannot be stated without dependence (*apekṣā*) and independence (*anapekṣatva*), it stands in dependence upon that independence. Subsequently, the primary and secondary elements are examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct.
Thus [ends] the commentary. Immediately after the classification of the treatises (*śāstrabheda*), G. states that the classification of the treatises must be explained next.
He asks for the reason therein: "Why immediately after?"

By the mention of "single" (ekagrahaṇena), he says: for even other definitions, such as that based on remainder (śeṣa) and so forth, depend precisely upon the absence of dependence on anything else; it is only by means of this [absence of dependence] that the nature [of the object] can be determined from the word.

Therefore, by what distinction is the definition of the differentiation of the scriptures (*śāstrabheda*) commenced immediately after the definition of independence (*anapekṣatva*)? The answer is: it is true that even the "subsidiary nature" (*śeṣatva*) and so forth can be determined from verbal testimony (*śabda*) only in dependence upon independence, but not immediately thereafter.

G. Furthermore, with the intention that "this alone [follows] immediately after," the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Immediately after [the mention of the primary], the primary and non-primary [factors]."
Thus [it is asked]: why is this very [topic] presented immediately after [the definition of the means of valid cognition], rather than the definition of the remainder (śeṣalakṣaṇa) and so forth?
The answer is: because everything that follows is preceded by a distinction of function (kāryabheda).

The fact that it is preceded by a difference in function, however, is because it is preceded by a difference in scripture, and because a difference in function serves as the reason for a difference in scripture. And how it is preceded by a difference in scripture [p.

The definition of the remainder has been shown in the same way in the first [chapter] of the third [book]. The commentary, which states that "the primary and secondary [factors], whether distinct or non-distinct, will be examined," is challenged by the question: "What are these 'primary and secondary' factors?"
He says in a single passage: "If it is connected [to the previous context] as 'first,
the primary and secondary [elements] will be examined,' then one thing would be proposed and another would be examined."

Consequently, there is a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the examination (*parīkṣā*). He explains this very point: for immediately following [the section on] difference and non-difference, the examination of the primary (*pradhāna*) and the non-primary (*apradhāna*) is not seen.
[Objection: But surely the rest is for the sake of that, according to the principle: "But those by which a substance is intended to be produced, in that case [it is] a quality (*guṇa*)."
And the examination of the primary and the secondary is indeed seen immediately following [the statement] "it is understood.
He refutes [this objection]: for that which is established by the third...
That [distinction] has been brought forward here for the sake of conventional usage, in order to establish the distinction between ritual actions—
which serves as the cause for the distinction between the Śāstras.
And so it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:

In the third chapter, it was stated by [the author] himself: "Now, in that case, regarding those things for which a substance is intended to be prepared, there the quality should be understood"—thereby, the status of being for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) was excluded for verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) that have a visible purpose. But here, the definition of all subsidiaries (*śeṣa*) is being stated. [The opponent says: "They are primary (*pradhāna*). [The author replies: That is incorrect.
Therefore, to say "they are both primary and non-primary" is incoherent.
It is said: by the terms "principal" (*pradhāna*) and "non-principal" (*apradhāna*), the objectives (*sādhya*) and the adjuncts (*anubandha*) are denoted.

By the word "objective," the fourfold group beginning with origination (*utpatti*), the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*), the intermediate operation of the instrument (*karaṇāvāntaravyāpāra*), and the entitlement characterized by sovereignty (*aiśvaryalakṣaṇādhikāra*) are expressed. These objectives are designated by the term "principal," while the adjuncts of the injunction (*niyoga*) are designated by the term "non-principal."
They have become the objects [of inquiry]. Therefore, those primary and secondary [actions] will be examined as to whether they are different or non-different;
the meaning is that the difference and non-difference of both the goals (*sādhya*) and the auxiliary factors (*anubandha*) will be investigated.
First, the difference among the auxiliary factors is as follows: "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations."

The distinction between the scriptures arises from the distinction between those [actions]. There is also non-distinction in the ancillary factors (*anubandha*), as in: "One who, knowing thus, performs the Full Moon sacrifice.
And because of that non-distinction, there is non-distinction of the scripture. Likewise...

There is also a difference in the effects [of actions], which constitutes the distinction between these two scriptural injunctions: "One threshes the rice" and "One sprinkles the rice. The effect of threshing is the removal of the husks and chaff, permeated by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*). The effect of sprinkling, however, is an unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, [the texts state]: "One threshes the rice," "One [sprinkles] the rice."

There is a distinction between these two scriptural injunctions, such as "he sprinkles" (*prokṣati*). Although these two scriptures are mutually distinct, they do not differ from the injunction of a mere *bhāvārtha* (action-oriented meaning), because there is no difference in their *anubandhas* (subsidiary elements). For the *anubandha* is the object of the *niyoga* (the mandate), and we shall explain later that threshing (*avaghāta*) and the like are not objects of the *niyoga*. Furthermore, a difference in the *sādhya* (the end to be accomplished) that is independent of one another is a cause for the distinction between scriptures. Now, the task of threshing and so forth does not have as its *sādhya* an *apūrva* (unseen potency) that is independent of the *Āgneya* sacrifice and others. However, in the case of subordinate acts (*guṇakarman*), a distinction between scriptures is indeed appropriate due to the difference in their mutually independent *sādhyas*.

This has been stated in the *Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*: "But [it may be argued] that even in the case of an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the cup (*camasa*), this would indeed be a separate scripture (*śāstrāntara*). [The reply is: No; this is merely another sentence (*vākyāntara*), not a separate scripture. A separate scripture occurs only with reference to the injunction of another subordinate quality that serves an equal purpose, but not with reference to the injunction of a subordinate quality consisting of mere existence. (Bṛhatī 2.3.24)

And here, the equality intended is that of effects which are mutually independent. By this, it should be understood that there is a distinction between scriptures based on the difference in the goals to be accomplished—such as the invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from restrictive rules—in cases such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). Likewise, in the *Paurṇamāsī* section, the relationship between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is set forth.

Even regarding the two sets of procedures (*itikartavyatā*), a distinction will be stated based on the difference between the scriptures and the difference between the goals to be accomplished (*sādhya*). For, in the case of the procedure, the goal to be accomplished is the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇa*);
however, for the instruments, there is another intermediate operation (*vyāpārāntara*).

Actions (*kāryāṇi*) are of the nature of activity (*vyāpāra*). Likewise, regarding the statement "practice for as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīviko ’bhyāsaḥ*), it will be explained that there is a distinction between scriptures (*śāstra*) due to the difference in the goals to be accomplished (*sādhyabheda*)—namely, the qualification based on living (*jīvanādhikāra*) and the qualification based on desire (*kāmādhikāra*). Furthermore, there is non-difference (*abheda*) of the goal to be accomplished.

In the cases of "He offers the *samidh*s" and "He offers to *Tanūnapāt*," because they share a single goal through what is called "contextual connection" (*adhikāra*), such as "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni," although the scriptural injunctions regarding the *samidh*s, Agni, and so forth are distinct due to the difference in their subordinate elements (*anubandha*), they are nonetheless non-distinct because the goal (*sādhya*) is the same. Therefore, it is well said that the primary and secondary rites will be examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct.

This alone is the meaning to be described and no other; this is the explanation of the word "immediately following" (*ānantarya*). And since this is the connection between the chapters, it is the statement of the reason for that immediate succession.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because"—that is, because this connection between chapters exists, therefore the definition of the differentiation of the scriptures (*śāstrabheda*) must be presented immediately after. We have already demonstrated how this serves as a logical reason (*hetu*).

Thus, sixfold differentiation of ritual action (*karmabheda*) will be explained here: difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*).
The restatement of the commentary. He objects: "How is it that 'difference' (*bheda*) is a difference in words (*śabdāntara*)?

This objection is raised by taking the word *bheda* as denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*). He replies: "It is differentiated (*bhidyate*) by this," thus *bheda* is a term denoting the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*).
