The word "distinction" (bheda) [refers to this]: that which is distinguished from another word and so forth, and that which is [the object of] the verbal root—that is the meaning of "action" (karma-bhāvārtha). By the six means of distinction, such as "another word" (śabdāntara) and the rest, there is only a distinction between actions (bhāvārtha); there is no distinction of subsidiaries (anubandha), nor a distinction of injunctions (śāstra), nor a distinction of apūrva-niyoga. This is by way of number.

In the case of the statement "seventeen [animals] for Prajāpati," there is no difference in the status of the adjuncts (*anubandha*), because the injunction (*niyoga*) is established by their proximity to the substances and deities conveyed by the nominal stem *prājāpatya*. This is because they constitute a single object of the injunction; and in the case of a simultaneous connection (*tantrasambandha*), the status as an object of the injunction does not differ, just as in the expression "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Furthermore, the author of the *Nibandhana*, who maintains that the power of the word is paramount, considers the connection between substance and deity to be the object of the injunction. On this point, there are these verses: [The verses follow here.]
In the second chapter, the teacher described the differentiation of the treatise within his commentary and exposition by means of the goal to be accomplished and the various types of connections.
However, when that which is to be proven is independent of one another, it constitutes a division of the treatises;
due to the specific differences among the means of proof, those divisions are declared in many ways.

The distinctions of connection (anubandha), however, are differentiated by means of different designations, repetition, mention of qualities, and different procedures; these are the causes for the division of the scriptures.
Even though there is identity with the self as a continuous sequence, it differentiates the mere entities;
because it is their differentiation and because there is no distinction in its being the differentiator, number is also formulated in this very context.

Since the word *bheda* (difference) has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), it is therefore stated as "the difference of actions" (*karma-bheda*). The out-of-order presentation of "different words" (*śabdāntara*) and the other criteria, without regard for the order to be explained later, is for the purpose of demonstrating that order is not a useful factor [in establishing difference].

The meaning is that when "different words" and the others function as differentiators of the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), there is no mutual dependence on their sequence. Here, an objection is raised: "That which is to be explained later is mentioned here in the form of a proposition (*pratijñā*"; i.e., it is stated with the intention of being a formal proposition).

For what purpose? The Naiyāyikas maintain that it is logical to state the proposition (*pratijñā*) at the very time of stating the reason (*hetu*); those who practice logic (*nyāyavyavahārin*) hold this view. It is for the sake of introducing the reason—that is, for the sake of stating the reason.
For the proposition (*pratijñā*) is indeed stated, yet it is properly [stated] at the very time of the statement of the reason (*hetu*). He replies: "True;

where an object is stated as something to be proven (*sādhya*), there it is so. However, for the sake of grasping the subject (*dharmin*), this demonstration of the distinction between the experienced and the subsequent connection will be made as a reason. He will do so.
When this has been said, the intellect of the listener— whose mind is drawn by the desire to know that [subject]— being composed,

proceeds with ease toward the classification of the treatise as it is being explained. By stating, "This is called the chapter characterized by various ritual acts (*karma*)," he demonstrates the established terminology of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*) in order to declare the beginninglessness of the system (*nyāya*).
This principle is beginningless;

it is merely being recorded in its own treatise by Jaimini and others through some specific occasion. This is done for the purpose of avoiding the fault of investigating matters not promised, namely that which is other than the introduction (*upoddhāta*), as well as what follows from what is relevant (*prasaktānuprasakta*).

Furthermore, even that which is considered other than the primary subject of the treatise as it was initially proposed is treated as an introductory digression (*upoddhāta*), just as this very first section is. And there are further incidental discussions (*prasaktānuprasakta*)—such as the definition of *mantras* and their various types. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. First, then, this is considered: in the first chapter it was stated that "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). An injunction is a sentence that expresses an action, and the meaning of a sentence resides in its constituent words.
In that regard, is Dharma expressed by each individual word, or is it expressed by all the words together as one?
The restatement of the commentary. He raises an objection:

"It is indeed appropriate that this should first be considered—whether dharma is expressed by each individual word or by all of them together as a single syntactical connection. The particle *iti* should be understood here [at the end of the sentence]. What is the meaning of the statement, "This was said in the first chapter"? [End of fragment]
With what context is this treatise connected? Therefore, we do not know how it is to be explained.
To this, it is replied: Is the property [dharma] [to be understood] word by word?

It is said: when only this much has been stated, someone might think there is a contradiction with the method of our own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta-prakriyā*), because of the assertion that the relationship between a sentence and its meaning is innate (*autpattika*).
For when [the meaning] is [conveyed] by the sentence itself—

When the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is being stated, the word-meaning (*padārtha*) has no separate meaning of its own at that time. Therefore, how can it be suspected that the meaning denoted by each individual word is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*)? For one who considers such a view to contradict the established method (*prakriyā*), the following is the response given in the first chapter of the *Bhāṣya*: "In the first chapter, it was stated that Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). He explains the meaning of this: "It is true that in the first chapter it was said that Dharma is a matter characterized by injunction; and an injunction is a sentence."

Therefore, it was stated in the *Codanā-lakṣaṇa* sūtra that the meaning of a sentence consists precisely in the definition of the sentence itself. Nevertheless, it was also stated that the meaning of the words exists within the sentence as well. [The author] maintains that the words themselves—which are denoted by the term "sentence"—express the meanings of the words as already connected, and thus denote the meaning of the sentence; for it is said: "Those [words] which have [already] come into being are recited together with a word denoting action. This is the view of the author of the *Granthakalpaka*.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the established procedure. Consequently, this is logical: is the property (dharma) expressed by each word individually, or is it expressed by all of them together as one?

Now, this might be considered improper. For it is not the case that every single word denotes dharma; rather, one might object that it is the word itself, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which expresses dharma in its nature as the unseen potency (*apūrva*). Anticipating this, he explains: "This is what is meant. Does the connection with the task (*kārya*) belong to the meaning expressed by each individual word, or to that [meaning] which depends upon mutual relationship?

When the meaning expressed by a word is connected with the task—that is, when it is the object of the mandate (*niyoga*)—then the mandate is said to be expressed by that word, because the knowledge of the mandate does not arise from the word "mandate" alone. But how can it be suspected that an object, which is understood as being mutually related [with other objects], has a connection with the task only while unrelated to the meanings of the other words? [The answer is: Because of the mutual relationship being understood, the connection of all [objects] with the mandate is not understood [as a whole].

He refutes [this objection]: For it is observed that in the case of the *aruṇa* (red) and other such instances, there is an understanding of the connection with the action (*kārya*), even though the substance and the quality are mutually related to one another.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in understanding a mutual relationship when there is a connection with a purposeful action (*kārya*). But was it not said that in that case there is no understanding of a mutual relationship between the substance and the quality, because the connection with the purchase (*kraya*) is understood through the force of the instrumental case-ending? He replies: "True; indeed, by virtue of being for the sake of this [action] (*aidamarthyena*), there is none."

It has been stated that there is a mutual relationship; however, this does not mean that there is no relationship even by way of the quality (guṇa) and the possessor of the quality (guṇin); rather, the meaning is that such a relationship certainly exists. For otherwise...
If a mutual relationship were not perceived, then there would be no restriction at all;
for the purchase could be made with a one-year-old cow that is not red, or even with a multi-colored cow that is red. Yet, such a restriction does exist;
therefore, there is indeed the perception of a mutual relationship. This is likewise the case here between the noun and the verb.

Is the connection with the *niyoga* independent of the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*), or is it established precisely without abandoning that relationship between the action and its factors? Thus, the doubt is justified.

That which does not abandon the relationship between action and its factors is "not abandoning the relationship between action and its factors"; for that indeed is the connection with the injunction (*niyoga*). What, then, is the prima facie position? This means: in this doubt, what is logical? The word *prāpta* here functions in the sense of the word *yukta* (logical). The answer is: it is logical that there is a connection with the religious duty (*dharma*) for each individual word. Why?
The answer is: because the utterance of all words has the injunction (*niyoga*) as its purpose.

All words indeed have as their primary aim the communication of word-meanings that have been brought under the purview of the injunction. This is because the utterance of all words is for the sake of an action (*kārya*). [Objection: But surely, the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*) is also understood here;
therefore—

Since it is understood that the action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*) share the same purpose (*aidamarthya*), it is logical that all of them directly possess the status of being for the sake of the *niyoga* (the mandate), without abandoning that [shared] purpose. He replies: "True, a relationship characterized by action and its factors is indeed understood; however, there is no proof for the factors having the action as their sole purpose. This is because the object of the *niyoga*, being independent, is understood as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*)."

If there is no mutual *raidadarthya* (purposefulness) between the action and the factor of action (*kāraka*), then one of dull intellect, considering that the relationship between the action and the factor of action would likewise not exist, raises this objection: "But how can a factor of action, being entirely devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*), bring about the fulfillment of the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*)?"

For that which has become a *kāraka* (a factor of action) brings about the fulfillment of the meaning of the *niyoga* by virtue of being subordinated to it through the *niyoga*'s own purpose. [Objection: How can there be the status of a *kāraka* without a relationship between an action and its factors? Or how can an object (*karman*) that is not being acted upon, and which has not itself acquired existence, bring about the fulfillment of the *niyoga*? [The author] answers: Let this relationship between action and its factors exist as a matter of fact.

The relationship between the quality and the possessor of the quality is like that between substance and quality; however, "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya) exists solely for the purpose of the injunction,
for "being for the sake of that" is indeed something distinct.
G. Karma.
G. The meaning is precisely that of an injunction.

And the intention is that there would be another relationship between the action and its factors (kriyākāraka). Therefore, there would be a distinct dharma for each word. To this, it is said: this is not tenable. Why? He says: for if the status of being the object of the injunction (niyogārthatā) did not belong to those words which do not abandon their perceived meaning, then there would be a distinct dharma for each word. This is the meaning.

Because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is everywhere more powerful, even a perceived mutual relationship is appropriate only if, by accepting it, the intended meaning regarding the injunction (*niyoga*) is not lost. However, where the comprehension of a relationship is indeed required for consistency, the abandonment of that [relationship] would result in the very abandonment of what is heard in the text (*śrutahāna*). And this is not the case here.

G. adds: Nor is it logical that this cognition [of the relationship] should result from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). For if there were a connection with the *dharma* at every word, the understanding of a mutual relationship would have to be abandoned, precisely because of the absence of a cause. Indeed, the entry of substance and quality into a single action called "purchase" is the cause for the understanding of their mutual relationship. In this case, however, because there is a difference in the injunctions (*niyoga*) due to the difference in the subordinate elements (*anubandha*) at every word, [the two] enter into different injunctions.

Even though it is understood that the mutual relationship between the noun (*nāman*) and the verb (*ākhyāta*) is seedless (i.e., lacks an inherent basis), it must nevertheless be abandoned [as a mere appearance]. Moreover, that [relationship] is required by the injunction (*vidhi*). For without an action (*kriyā*), the status of being a factor (*kāraka*) is impossible; and without a factor, the accomplishment of an action is not possible. Therefore, it is logical that one [of the two] is supported by the other for the sake of the injunction. And since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is fulfilled even through an indirect succession, there is no fault.
In this way, the postulation of an inference of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) will be minimized.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Here, in this very *Bhāṣya*, it is understood as follows: if merit (*dharma*) were [inherent] in each individual word, then a new transcendental potency (*apūrva*) would have to be postulated for every single word. And these [potencies] are to be known through the inference of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). For what logicians call "inference of the unperceived" is designated by the term *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. Thus it has been said: "And touch is not among those things perceived [by the senses]; therefore, air has an unperceived mark (*liṅga*)."

Thus, this is the connection between the sections of the treatise: in this way, from an inference based on what is not perceived (*adṛṣṭānumāna*) concerning an unprecedented object (*apūrva-viṣaya*), there arises a conceptual extension (*prasaṅga-kalpanā*) based on an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭānumāna*). Here, an objection is raised: "What, then, is this conceptual extension based on an inference of the unperceived? For even from verbal testimony (*śabda*), that which is perceived is indeed perceived."

For if there were the postulation of an unobserved entity (*adṛṣṭa*), then it would be appropriate to say, "In this way, there will be a postulation involving the consequence of inferring an unobserved entity," and "In this way, it will be a very slight [postulation]. But here, there is no postulation of an unobserved entity.

[The opponent argues: "Because the *apūrva* (unseen force) is denotable by words. [The author] refutes this: "True, as you have said, there is no postulation of an unseen entity based on a name alone.

When one postulates a *dharma* for every single word, the resulting contingency of a relationship between substratum and superstratum would require an inference of a restrictive rule; such an unseen entity would be without authority (*apramāṇaka*). An unseen entity is only established when it is supported by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."

The meaning is that [the agent] attains [the action]. Since it is impossible for that which is devoid of action to function as a *kāraka*, action must be understood as being supported by the *kāraka* through its status as a *kāraka*. Furthermore, by means of action, [the *kāraka*] itself...

The agent (*kāraka*), being the substratum, is to be apprehended as already established in itself; and therein lies the understanding of the restriction: "Depending upon this very action, this agent accomplishes this specific injunction," and "Depending upon this very agent, this action [occurs]. Such a conceptualization of an unseen relationship between substrate and superstrate would be without any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*), because it differs from the logic of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow). And in that case, how could there not be the contingency of postulating many unseen factors? The answer is: first of all, in this way, the status of being a substrate belongs to the agents, and the status of being a superstrate [belongs to the action].

Furthermore, regarding actions, there is their relationship as the means and the end for the sake of that [result], as well as the specific restriction [of cause and effect]. On the other hand, in the position supported by either [of the two alternatives], there will be the assumption of an inference of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) with fewer complications. What is this "assumption of an inference of the unseen"?
The answer is: the unseen is that which lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

That which is indeed unobserved (*adṛṣṭa*) lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). Inference (*anumāna*) is the inference of a necessary connection (*niyamānumāna*). For that undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding the relationship between locus and located (*āśrayāśrayitva*), this is the "consequence of the inference of the unobserved" (*adṛṣṭānumānaprasaṅga*); it is both an inference of the unobserved and a consequence. Thus, the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of that is very slight (*alpīyasī*).
But surely, no such conceptualization occurs; why do you say it is "very slight"?

He refutes [this objection]: even in the case where one side is favored, there exists the conceptual construction that the object to be enjoined is indeed the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), and the favoring belongs to that alone. Furthermore, as for this "favoring" (*anugraha*)...

That which is being performed is not to be accepted as consisting of its own form alone, because that would contradict the meaning of the *niyoga* (the injunction). Now, one might object: "Is this not already expressed by the words? Why is it being postulated here? He replies: "We shall explain in the ninth [book] that its comprehension arises from the effect (*kārya*)."

By accepting that [the injunction] is prompted by something unprecedented (*apūrva*), the employment of the expression "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) becomes consistent. Anticipating the objection that if the understanding [of the injunction] arises from its effect (*kārya*), it would then not be verbal (*śābda*), he says: "But it is verbal because it is rooted in a purpose understood through words. Therefore, it has been rightly stated: "In this way, there will be a conceptual construction involving the inference of a very small amount of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)."
Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya concludes that there is "one apūrva," which [the opponent] challenges: "What is this 'one apūrva'? He replies: "Is it not this very thing?
This meaning is indeed quite clear. Again he challenges: "It is not so; it is not so."
"From one [action], the apūrva [arises]"—this is the context.
Therefore, it must be concluded that "from one [action] comes the apūrva," and not that "the apūrva is one. To this, it is replied: when...
If the ritual duty pertains to each individual word in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then there must be a distinction of injunctions for each word.
Why?
The answer is: because there is a distinction of the subordinate elements (*anubandha*) for each word.

Furthermore, when there is an application according to the rule (*vidhi*) of those [factors] which are mutually connected—that is, a prescribed injunction (*vidhi-niyoga*)—then there is only a single subordinate element (*anubandha*). And for this reason, it is concluded that there is a single *apūrva*. Now, even so, does the *apūrva* arise from a single [factor]?

"Why was it not withdrawn? By what means of result is it withdrawn? To this he says: and in order to demonstrate this very difference in the effect within the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) on page 286...

The Blessed Commentator has concluded with the result that "therefore, there is a single apūrva," and the observation of a difference in the effects was presented as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) because of their mutual lack of connection.

In order to establish the reasoning of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it must be shown that the comprehension of mutual relationship [between words] would otherwise result in being baseless. Here, since the utterance of words has the *niyoga* (the mandate) as its purpose, every word is directly connected to the *niyoga*. Since a direct connection is possible, it is illogical to resort to an indirect one; therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that all words have the *niyoga* as their object. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: if all words had the *niyoga* as their object, there would be a contradiction with the comprehension of their mutual relationship. Consequently, there is a distinct *niyoga* for each individual word. For those words that enter into these distinct *niyogas*, [there is no such contradiction].

Because a connection [between them] is untenable, it is logical that there be a distinction of objects according to their respective applications (*viniyoga*). Thus, one of the two is the object of the other as it is supported by the latter. And when recourse is taken to a mutual relationship, the understanding of the application (*viniyoga*) is itself understood through the application (*niyoga*).
Thus is the authoritative means [of knowledge].

When [an action] is something new from a single [word], then there is doubt: does it arise from words denoting an action (*bhāva-śabda*) or from words denoting substance and quality (*dravya-guṇa-śabda*)?
Regarding this, he asks: by the mention of "words denoting an action," what is being included?
The proponent of a partial view (ekadeśin) offers an answer: "Of verbal roots alone.
He then raises an objection: "If that is so, then by pointing out the doubt, [the question remains] whether it is from nominal words or from verbal roots?"
It must be stated: what is this being said—is it from words denoting states (bhāva-śabda) or from words denoting substances and qualities (dravya-guṇa-śabda)? [To the objector, p.

He asks: G. What is there [in this], or what is superior here [to that], such that even in the author of the Bhāṣya’s presentation of the doubt, there is nothing additional by which [this would differ]?
It is raised as a question whether it is more appropriate to derive [the meaning] from nouns or from verbs. The objector says: "The noun is repeated unnecessarily;
if the inclusion of substance-words and quality-words were made, there would be no need for verb-words."

The inclusion of both types of words [nouns and verbs] by means of two terms [“name” and “verbal root”]: when the term *bhāvaśabda* (word denoting a state/being) is employed—that is, when recourse is taken to the term *bhāvaśabda*—the terms *dravya* (substance) and *guṇa* (quality) must be included as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).

For in that case, the word is indicated by way of its denotation (*vācya-avacchedena*); thus, the distinct terms *dravya* and *guṇa* must be uttered as the objects to be presented by the word. However, in the case of employing the term *ākhyāta* (verb), since the word is indicated by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), the term *nāma* (name) indicates the word’s own form.

Thus it must be employed. And consequently, the non-utterance of two words is for the sake of brevity. The supreme resolver says: "For you are ignorant of the intended meaning; if it were stated whether [the suffix] comes from verbal roots or from nominal stems, then it would be determined."
If it were held that the *apūrva* arises only from verbs (*ākhyāta*), then the statement "the cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo’ṣṭākapālaḥ*) would lack a ritual action as its purpose.

The connection between the substance and the deity would not be the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), because the word *āgneya* is a noun (*nāman*). Furthermore, the meaning of "it comes into being" (*bhavati*)—which refers to the act of becoming—would be the object of the injunction as a ritual action, because it is a verb (*ākhyāta*).
Regarding the word *bhavati*: both of these [interpretations] are undesirable. This is because the meaning of "becoming" (*bhavati*) cannot be that which is enjoined;

for an already existing thing cannot be enjoined to "become," and that which has not yet come into being cannot be enjoined because it does not exist of its own accord. Therefore, the meaning of "becoming" is not something to be enjoined. Furthermore, it is the relationship between the substance and the deity that must be enjoined.
Therefore,
so that an undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti) does not arise, the mention of nouns and verbs was not made.

Not by the Blessed One, the author of the commentary; rather, [it is] by whichever nature the verbal root can possess the sense of an injunction, and by whichever nature the noun can possess the sense of an injunction.

Therefore, it is not possible for the Bhagavat, as the author of the commentary, to have made his presentation by means of that very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva). It is possible [only] to ask: by which intrinsic nature does the meaning of the verb possess the sense of an injunction, and by which [nature] is the function of the noun not excluded?
Thus it is possible.
To the two questions, there are two answers respectively:
because the meaning of the verb consists in the sense of "being," it has injunctive force; whereas because a noun denotes a substance or a quality, it does not have injunctive force.
We shall explain how this is so further below.
Here, the commentary asks: "What, then, is 'being' (bhāva), or what are the words for 'being'?
It explains this as follows: "What indeed is this thing called 'being' that is distinct from the meaning of a verb? And what is this word for 'being' that is distinct from a verbal word?"

He explains the *Uttarabhāṣya*: "The reply, however—the answer—is that the meaning of these [terms] 'one should sacrifice,' 'one should give,' and 'one should offer' is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*); and these are words denoting action (*bhāvaśabda*). Now, one might object: are these not simply the words 'sacrifice,' 'give,' and 'offer'?

This is the *parihāra-bhāṣya* (the explanatory passage providing the rebuttal). He explains it as follows: "But is this not that very same meaning of the verb, and are these not those very same verbal words?"—this is the objection (*ākṣepa*). "It is not so; and these are words such as 'sacrifice' (*yāga*) and the like"—he explains this rebuttal passage (*parihāra-bhāṣya*) as follows:
"The resolution, however, is that the meaning of the verb alone [is not intended] in cases such as 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*), 'one gives' (*dadāti*), and 'one offers oblations' (*juhoti*)."
What, then, is understood? It is also the production of another object;

that is, it is understood as the producer of an object other than the agent. Not only is the temporal sequence [of the action] understood—as in "it happens"—but the mere temporal sequence is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). The meaning of the verbal suffix is merely the temporal sequence.

"One should not meditate in that way"—here, in the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is the production of another [entity]. That quality of being the meaning of the verbal root does not exist in the case of "it exists" (*bhavati*), because there it is understood as the arising of the agent itself. What we have stated here has also been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "And from this, the meaning of sacrifice and so forth is understood, as well as 'one should bring about' (*bhāvayet*)."
By this commentary [the author says]. Now, thinking that the meaning of this commentary is something entirely different, he asks: "What has been stated by this commentary? The answer is:
—From this, both the relation of priority and posteriority and the state of being a producer of another are understood;
in that case, where the effect and the meaning of the sacrifice and so forth are understood from it, G. [states].

By this, the understanding of sacrifice and the like as consisting of prior and subsequent stages has been stated. "One should bring about" (bhāvayet) conveys the understanding of the production of something else. Furthermore, this meaning has been made explicit by the author of the Bhāṣya: "One should strive in such a way that something comes into being."
The meaning is that human effort conducive to the production of something else is understood. Therefore, even these verbal forms (*ākhyāta-śabda*) are called "action-words" (*bhāva-śabda*).

For that object whose nature is to bring about a sequence of prior and posterior stages is the "meaning of action" (*bhāvārtha*), and words whose referent is that [action] are "action-words. Consequently, the mention of "substance-words" (*dravya-śabda*) and "quality-words" (*guṇa-śabda*) is also included.
Indeed, if the term "noun" (*nāman*) were used, the counter-correlative would not be specified; for among nouns as well, some...

Because it has consciousness as its essential nature. Now, if someone should think: "Even so, that intrinsic nature by which there is the state of having action as its purpose, yet the state of not having action as its purpose is not specified, would remain unindicated.
He replies to that: "Because they produce cognition of substances and qualities, they do not have action as their purpose, simply because they are names.

This is because names such as "Āgneya" (dedicated to Agni) are seen to have action as their purpose. What, then, is the prima facie position? That they are so without distinction. What is the intention [of this objection]?
This is said by the author of the Bhāṣya.

The reply is: whether it be the substance that exists for the sake of the action, or the action that exists for the sake of the substance, in any case, the connection with the effect is precisely one that does not abandon the relationship between the action and its factors (kāraka). If the injunction (niyoga) has the action as its object, then everything else is for the sake of that [action].

According to logic, a substance exists for the sake of action; however, when the substance is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), then the action exists for the sake of the substance. In both of these positions—this being the position that action exists for the sake of the substance—the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*) is not contradicted. Therefore, since no specific distinction is perceived, either one may be the object of the injunction. Nor does this lead to a lack of authority due to indecision, because the performance of the rite is indeed determined. It is of a single form.

For in both these positions, there would be performance [of the rite], and because of the lack of determination regarding that performance, there would be a lack of authority [for the Veda]. To this it is replied: in this way, the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka) is not established. For when the action has the substance as its purpose, then the injunction (niyoga) has the substance as its object; in that case, the relationship between action and its factors is simply abandoned. Why?

The answer is as follows: At that time, the substance (*dravya*) is the object (*karman*), being the primary element in the action because it is what is intended to be reached by the action. And that which is intended to be reached becomes the object. Furthermore, the object is not the agent (*kāraka*);
for we shall explain that "the arising [of an action] resides in the agent" and thus constitutes the object.
The *kāraka* [is defined as follows]: that state which arises from the locus of the *kāraka* is the *karman* (object), not merely the state of being a *kāraka*.

If the *karman* does not itself constitute a *kāraka*, how then is the traditional rule (*āgama*) "the second case ending is used for the *kāraka* that is the object" to be understood? Likewise, [the rule] "that which is desired by the agent... [is explained].
And in the section on grammatical factors (*kāraka*), it is stated that "darkness is the object" (*tamaḥ karma*).
By reflecting upon this traditional authority (*āgama*) as well, it is understood that the status of being a factor (*kārakatva*) belongs to the object (*karman*). Regarding the object...

This is because of the indication of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the rule "the second case [is used] for the *kāraka*," and likewise because of the statement that "that *kāraka* which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) is the object (*karman*). He provides the resolution: the meaning of the sūtra is that the *kāraka* in which the fruit of the action is produced is the object.

The status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to a factor of action (*kāraka*) by virtue of its participation in the fruit of the action; it does not, however, consist in the mere production of the action. Nor is the status of being a factor of action anything other than the production of the action. Why is the meaning of the Sūtra to be understood in this way? To this he says: otherwise, the mention of the term "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) would be purposeless.

For that which brings about an action is not the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) by means of that action; rather, the state of being the recipient of the fruit produced by the action is what constitutes the most desired object. Therefore, it is also established that the accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs when there is an objective factor (*karma-kāraka*).
Because it is connected with two states; therefore,
when a verb (ākhyāta) serves the purpose of action, the purpose of injunction, or provides the object of the injunction—

Only then would there be the establishment of substance and quality as factors of action (*kāraka*), and their mention [in scripture] would be by way of being such factors; it is not for the sake of favoring this that the meaning of the verbal suffix alone is determined to be the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*).

Therefore, he says: "From those words which denote an action (*bhāvārtha*) and are terms for ritual acts (*karmaśabda*), such as 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) and so forth, the action (*kriyā*) is to be understood."

In this context, the author of the Sūtras, by stating that "action should be understood from those [words] whose meaning is being," has stated that the very fact of having an ontological meaning (*bhāvārthatva*) is the reason, since no other reason is provided.
With this in mind, he asks: "Why? He explains that: "The question 'Why? means: what is it here?"
How else could the status of being a "bhāvārtha" (an action signifying an activity) be lost?

For even that status of being a bhāvārtha would itself be lost if it were not the object of an injunction (niyoga). In that case, this would indeed be a valid reason; however, the point is that this is not the case.

The answer: Certainly, [the action] is lost, for the status of being a verbal meaning (bhāvārthatva) belongs to a word denoting an action (bhāva-śabda) precisely because it denotes a sequence of prior and posterior stages (pūrvāparībhāva). Even so, he asks: "And what of it? He replies: And that sequence of prior and posterior stages occurs here when the substance and the quality are for the sake of that [action].
Otherwise, as in the case of "one desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a milking vessel," there would be only the comprehension of a substratum (āśraya). It is not [so here].
And it is understood that the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) is to be accomplished by means of the milking of the cows.

The meaning of this is as follows: for when something is a "goal to be accomplished" (*sādhya*), it possesses the nature of being a verbal action (*bhāvārthatva*). And when a verbal action is the object of an injunction (*niyoga*), substances and qualities serve its purpose; thus, the verbal action attains the status of being the goal to be accomplished. But as for substances and qualities...

If [the suffix] has the sense of *niyoga* (an injunction), then the meaning of the verbal roots would be understood merely as the substratum (*āśrayamātra*), and not as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*), as is the case in the expression "one desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel. But is it not the case that even in the sentence "one desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel," the fetching (*praṇayana*) is indeed characterized by a sequence of prior and posterior stages?

It is so understood; and the *godohana* is indeed an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*). He refutes this: True, it is so understood, but not as the meaning of the sentence being "one should lead [the water] by means of the *godohana*."

In this sentence, because the *godohana* (the milking vessel) constitutes the meaning of the sentence and because the *praṇayana* (the act of carrying) is subservient to it, a reversed relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is understood. However, this worldly relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is what is actually conveyed by the word. Therefore, even under the view of non-restriction (*aniyamapakṣa*), the fact that the sentence has the nature of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*) is not perceived as being abandoned by the relationship of action and factor, since that relationship persists through restriction.

When, first of all, the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) is action (*kriyā*), then there is no abandonment of the perceived relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*). However, in the case of substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*), since they are stated to exist for the sake of action, by the aforementioned reasoning, there is indeed an abandonment of the relationship between action and its factors; thus, there is no lack of restriction. Rather, it is only that which has "being" as its meaning (*bhāvārtha*) that constitutes the meaning of the injunction. Therefore, this was said: "precisely because it has being as its meaning. [p. 293]
This is what is meant: "precisely because the relationship is understood in this very way.

That is to say, since the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) constitutes the object of the injunction (niyoga), it possesses the status of being that which is to be accomplished (sādhya), whereas substance (dravya) and quality (guṇa) possess only the status of being means of accomplishment (sādhana). Thus it is.
The meaning is that the relationship is understood, and not otherwise. Now,
he elaborates upon that object denoted by the word *bhāva* (action), which is distinct from a sequence of prior and posterior states—

elaborating on that object consisting of the production of something else, for the sake of explaining which the term "verbal suffix" (*ākhyāta*) was not employed, but rather the phrase "that whose meaning is action" (*bhāvārtha*) was used.

As for those who say that one should bring something into being (*bhāvayet*), they would say that one should bring heaven into being (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*) because of its connection with the word "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). Herein this is intended: having perceived the activity occurring immediately after hearing a sentence containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, it is determined that the optative suffixes and the like denote an object that impels to action. And since it is understood that the "task to be accomplished" (*kārya*) is what impels to action, it is concluded that the optative suffixes and the like also signify that very task. Furthermore, the task to be accomplished is said to be that which is achievable through human effort (*kṛti*) and is primary (*pradhāna*) with respect to that effort. As it has been said: "That which is achievable through effort is the primary [object]."

As for that which is called the "effect" (*kārya*), its designation is not possible without designating an effort (*kṛti*); therefore, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others also designate effort. And since effort itself is the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) of that which is to come into being, it is termed "productive operation" (*bhāvanā*). Consequently, from expressions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the production of something else is understood. And that production of something else, through its connection with the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), is the "production of heaven" (*svargabhāvanā*).

It is understood thus. Here, an objection is raised: "Why is it said that 'one should bring about heaven' (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*) because of its connection with the word *svargakāma*? It would be more appropriate to say 'one should bring about the one who desires heaven' (*svargakāmaṃ bhāvayet*). For the relation of one word-meaning with another word-meaning is what is logical; and here, the word-meaning is the one who desires heaven, not heaven itself. Therefore, this [interpretation] appears to be incorrect. To this, it is replied: True, [the primary meaning is] the one who desires heaven.

The meaning of the word is the person (*puruṣa*), because this word has the person as its primary referent; and that very person [is connected] with another word-meaning expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.
It is connected to the effect by way of being that which is enjoined. However, this connection, which culminates in the realization of heaven, has heaven as its ultimate goal.
Thus,
the Bhāṣyakāra has demonstrated here that the "ultimate purpose" (aidaṃparya) consists in reaching as far as the connection with heaven; this is what is meant by "finality" (paratva).

Now, one might ask: for what purpose has the production of another [result] been elaborated by resorting to heaven (*svarga*), when it could instead have been elaborated by directly resorting to the *apūrva* itself? To this he says: "For the purpose of demonstrating that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The intention is as follows: if the word "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*) culminates in the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) directed toward heaven, then only at that point, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the section on the *apūrva*, would the *apūrva* be a causal effect distinct from the action.

[The instrumental nature] is established. Otherwise, the action itself would be the result (*kārya*). Consequently, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) would possess only the status of an object (*karman*), not that of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

It is only when there is a result distinct from the action that the instrumental status of the meaning of the verbal root with respect to that [result] is established. Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of demonstrating this instrumental status? To this he says: "For he will state later that once this section is settled, there will be an inquiry as to whether [the word in question] is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*). This is what is meant: the mention of "the meaning of the verbal root" (*bhāvārtha*) is made here for the purpose of refuting the view that it is a name.

The establishment of the names of the *śyena* and other such words occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And the establishment of this coreferentiality occurs when the sacrifice functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the words *śyena* and so forth are joined with the instrumental case-ending. Therefore, without the establishment of the instrument, it is impossible to explain the very apprehension of the verbal root's meaning (*bhāvārtha*); thus, in order to demonstrate its status as an instrument, its productivity with respect to heaven (*svarga*) is shown. But how can there be such a focus [on the result] as "one should bring about heaven"?

Regarding the sentence, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and so forth—the answer is that we shall explain how it has such a purport in the section on qualification (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*) and in the sūtra, *vṛttyarthaṃ cābhi-saṃyogāt*. Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya concluded: "From them, the action (*kriyā*) is to be understood. But what, then, is this action here?
The answer: "The meaning of the injunction" refers to that meaning which has the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, it has been stated that the performance of the fruit is action (*kriyā*).

And the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the fruit, not the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*); for if it were the meaning of the injunction, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would not be the meaning of the sentence (*avākyārthatva*). It is said in reply: just as the meaning of the injunction [is established].
We shall explain the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the section defining qualification (*adhikāra*); nor is it the meaning of the sentence or the meaning of the commentary,
because it is based on instrumentality solely for the sake of the self (*ātman*).
As it has been said:
"In order to establish an agent who is conducive to the realization of the self,
even that which produces heaven and so forth must be, for us, primarily the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished) itself."

And here too, the Commentator, by stating that "those [words] connected with sacrifice, gift, and oblation declare the production of heaven," has declared that the meaning of the injunction itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

This is the meaning of this commentary: those words denoting action (*bhāva-śabda*), being connected as designators with the things to be designated—namely, sacrifice, gift, and oblation—declare the meaning of the injunction, which consists in making those [actions] its object.

They express a new meaning (apūrvārtha) by means of denoting that object. And in that context, by employing the word "origination" (*utpatti*) for the sense of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), it is stated that the sense of the injunction functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the production of heaven.

The word "origination" (*utpatti*) is derived in the sense of an instrument, according to the rule: "That by which something is produced is 'origination'. [Objection: But since sacrifice and the like are accepted as the instruments, how can the sense of the injunction be the instrument?
To the objection that this is not tenable, he replies: "Because of its connection with that [apūrva], the sacrifice and so forth possess the status of an instrument;

for the verbal root-meaning possesses the status of an instrument precisely by way of producing the apūrva which has become the instrument, and not otherwise. Thus there is no fault. To the question "Why is this so?", [the reply is: "How, moreover, can the niyoga (obligatory injunction) have the status of an instrument?"
The intention is that its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is understood.

The meaning is: how can the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists of the effect (*kārya*), serve as an instrument for the accomplishment of the result? But the respondent [says] on page 296:

For this is what is enjoined: it shows the meaning established by the definition of the *adhikāra* (qualification for ritual performance), namely, "one who desires heaven should achieve heaven by means of sacrifice and so forth.

Indeed, in the first section of the sixth book (*Ṣaṣṭhādya*), regarding the sacrifice as the instrument for the fulfillment of the desire of the desirer who is being enjoined to the ritual act—of whom [is this the instrument]?
Having raised the objection that this is merely the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the word, this point was stated with effort: "By what [means] would one accomplish heaven? By sacrifice and so forth.
What is demonstrated by this passage? The answer is: it is precisely that same reasoning pertaining to qualification (*adhikārika-yukti*).

The very same reasoning that was stated in the section on the definition of qualification (*adhikāra*) regarding the fact that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), has been expressed by this passage. Why? He says: "For it will be established that qualification belongs to one who seeks to accomplish heaven."
He will state that the qualification of one who desires [a result] extends up to the attainment of that desired object. Therefore, this is the meaning of the Bhāṣya:

"One who desires heaven indeed wishes to accomplish heaven. When there arises the expectancy, "By what means shall he accomplish heaven?", the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is prescribed. And since the fruit is accomplished by the meaning of that word through the mediation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), and not otherwise, the *apūrva* is thereby understood.

Therefore, since the word that denotes it [the sacrifice] conveys the *apūrva*, the *apūrva* is understood from that [word]. As for how this resolves the contradiction between what precedes and what follows, he asks:

"From where is the contradiction between the preceding and the following suspected? To this he replies: "For previously it was stated that 'the fruit arises from the *niyoga*,' whereas now you say 'the fruit arises from the sacrifice'—this is the contradiction. He resolves it: "By the phrase 'having produced the *apūrva* by means of that [sacrifice],' there is no contradiction."

Since the instrumentality of the sacrifice also exists by way of the accomplishment of the apūrva which has become the instrument, there is no contradiction due to this correspondence; therefore, the apūrva is understood.

He explains the commentary with its supplementary gloss (*sopaskāram*): "From that, it is understood that the *apūrva* alone is the means to the fruit; 'the means to the fruit' is the supplementary gloss.

Since the status of sacrifice and the like as instruments is established through the mediation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), therefore the *apūrva* alone is the ultimate cause. Consequently, that which denotes it makes the *apūrva* understood; thus, we maintain that verbal roots (*bhāva-śabda*) are denoters of the *apūrva*.
Having thus restated the Bhāṣya by its opening phrase (*pratīkena*), [the author proceeds].

He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*): "Therefore, that which is its denoter"—this is the conclusion (*nigamana*). The meaning is that this is the summary. He explains the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*): "Since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), while bringing about the unprecedented (*apūrva*), produces the fruit and not otherwise due to its momentariness; therefore, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) regarding that [unprecedented] is conveyed by the optative suffixes (*liṅgādi*) and so forth, and of that..."

Since that which is being conveyed depends upon its object for comprehension, and since verbal roots (bhāva-arthas) convey their objects, it is said that the *apūrva* is understood from them; however, these words denoting action (*bhāva-śabda*) are not the direct designators (*vācaka*) of the *apūrva*.

Demonstrating this, the author of the Bhāṣya explains the sūtra, *tebhyaḥ kriyā pratīyeta*, as follows: "When it is said that action (*kriyā*) is understood from those [words] whose meaning is 'being' (*bhāvārtha*), that is not intended to mean that they are direct denoters (*sākṣād-vācaka*); rather, it is by way of expressing their object (*viṣaya-abhidhāna*).
To the question, "Why is the sūtra explained in this manner? the author of the Bhāṣya replies: "For there is no word whatsoever that is a direct denoter of the *apūrva*."

Thus [ends the passage]. Some consider this commentary to be incorrect. For by this very commentary, it is stated that there is no word whatsoever that denotes the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) in any way; and that is incorrect, because words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) do denote it. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But there is no word that directly denotes the *apūrva"—this statement has the sense of the *bhāvārtha* (the meaning consisting of the action) in mind. (R. *bhāvārtha*)
In paragraph [p.

298], the denial of denotative power is intended with reference to words whose meaning consists in a [transitive] action (*bhāvārtha*), not with reference to words in general. Thus he says: "Furthermore, even words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) do not fail to express an injunction (*niyoga*)."

Now, one might object: "Even if it is understood from the Sūtra that action (*kriyā*) is cognized from those [verbal roots], and thus it is determined that only those words whose meaning is 'being' (*bhāvārtha*) denote the mandate (*niyoga*), nevertheless, this doubt is not appropriate because there is no evidence for it; therefore, this [Sūtra] is stated not to refute such a doubt, but rather to show that no word whatsoever directly denotes the *apūrva*. To this he says: "But how can there even be a suspicion that [the verbal root] denotes [the mandate] through its meaning as 'being'?"

The answer is: because the word for injunction (*niyoga*), such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, is never used in isolation. If the meaning of an injunction were determined—or indeed enjoined—by the optative suffix and the like when used alone, apart from the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

In that case, there would be no suspicion that it expresses the meaning of a verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). Nor is there ever the usage of a word in isolation, because its application is invariably restricted to being followed by a verbal base (*prakṛti*), since only that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is employed.

Even when the meaning of the abstract state (*bhāvārtha*) is expressed, it is used only in its verbal form (*tiṅanta*), not in its pure form. Therefore, for those who are mistaken, the denotative capacity (*vācakatā*) follows only as far as the actual usage;
that is, as long as a word consisting of both stem and suffix is employed, the denotative capacity conforms precisely to that. It is exactly so.

For those who are deluded into thinking that it is the word itself which possesses denotative power, the limited scope of usage cannot be established through any other means than by the comprehension of meaning.

If even a single [phoneme] were expressive, why then is it not used alone? For there is no means for determining the extent of usage other than the mutual comprehension of meaning; indeed, only as much as is required to convey the meaning is employed. It was stated that [the phoneme] is "not expressive" in order to refute this view.
Now, if expressiveness is suspected on the grounds that its usage would otherwise be inexplicable, then that is not correct.
He states [the following] in a single passage to refute [this]: "Or rather, how else could the number of formal arguments (*prayoga*) be established,
by which or for which [reason] that argument..."

To the extent that the capacity to denote [meaning] is being refuted as following from mere usage, he offers this rebuttal: "Is even the comprehension of meaning to be denied? Or, since the comprehension of meaning is understood through differentiation, how can it be set aside?"
It is possible;
[it occurs] by means of the very first [word], even without the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*).

In such cases as "he offers" (*juhoti*) and "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), meanings consisting of the process of becoming (*bhāvārtha*) are understood; yet, when verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) are employed with a different root, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is comprehended. Thus, by the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the optative suffix and others alone denote the *apūrva*.

However, the fact that the verbal root expresses the meaning of the process of becoming, which is thus understood, cannot be denied. Therefore, meanings consisting of the process of becoming do not possess the capacity to denote the *apūrva*.
If expressiveness belongs to [the suffixes] individually, what then is the cause for the restriction on usage?
Why is the word *liṅ* and so forth not used alone? The answer is: it is simply usage.

The reason for the restriction to usage [is as follows]. Now, one might object: "If it is asked what the cause of usage itself is, it is not a proper answer to say that usage itself is the cause. To this he says: "Just as with denotative capacity (*vācakatva*), the beginninglessness of usage has also been stated, as follows:"

The denotative capacity of words is due to their beginninglessness, and their usage is likewise established through a succession of the linguistic practice of elders, since beginninglessness has been demonstrated in the *Vimalāñjana*. Therefore, for subsequent persons, the very usage of preceding individuals is the cause of the restriction. For a word that is observed to be denotative when used in a certain manner is used in that very same manner; thus, the restriction is established. Consequently:

It is well said that the meaning of *niyoga* is not denoted by the word *bhāva*. By such expressions as "something must be brought about (*bhāvayitavya*) through those things whose meaning is *bhāva*," [the author] demonstrates the non-distinctive relationship between the fruit, the *niyoga*, and the *bhāvārtha*. Since this relationship is non-distinctive, it is established that it is not merely *niyogic*. For otherwise, if it were thus...
In that case, it is not demonstrated because there is no application; someone, following the rule of separate injunctions, considers it to be unrelated, like Bādari.

One might indeed think: "Even so, what harm is there in this? To this he replies: "And therefore, while this subject matter remains unsettled, it cannot be said that an investigation will take place as to whether [terms like *udbhid*] are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names (*nāmadheya*).
For without [the status of] being an instrument (*karaṇatā*), [terms such as] *udbhid* and the like—"

This has already been stated previously: "It is not by name. What, then, is the reason? That is to say, for what reason does this relationship not possess the characteristic of being established by application (*viniyoga*)? The answer is: because of the absence of the means of application, such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest. How is there an absence?

This is the intention of the questioner: why is the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and the like not itself considered "Śruti"? The answer is: because the relationship [between them] is not apprehended, if...

If a relationship characterized by *aidamarthya* (subservience to a specific purpose) were understood immediately following the hearing of the injunction (*yajyādiśruti*), then there would be the occurrence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). However, such [a relationship] is not understood. Thinking that it has been stated that there is no understanding of a relationship other than through a general one, [the opponent] objects: "But surely this relationship exists: 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice' (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*. [The author] replies: "Certainly it exists, but it is not characterized by *aidamarthya*; rather, it is characterized by *adhikāra* (qualification)."

Now, one might object: "If direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means of proof do not exist, how then can even the relationship characterized by qualification (*adhikāra*) be understood? To this, he says: "And it has been stated in the sūtra *śeṣaḥ parārthatvāt* that the application (*viniyoga*) is understood through the fact of being for the sake of this [purpose]."

And in that regard, since the means of application (*viniyoga*) are based on direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*)— defined as being for the sake of another— is established; and within that subsidiarity, which is defined as being for the purpose of that [principal], by stating that "direct statement and the rest are the causes for application by way of subsidiarity," [the author] asserts that being for the purpose of that [principal] (*aidamarthya*)...
Now begins the fourth quarter.
It has been stated that the Vedic corpus has this purpose. But is this not rather a definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?

In this chapter, because of the formal propositions "words are stated according to their means of valid cognition" and "an investigation of its causes," he will state in the second [chapter] and thereafter: "the definition of the means of valid cognition has been declared."
Therefore, [the opponent asks]: "What is this that has been proposed?

What is this that is being said? Are words such as *udbhid* injunctions regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? The respondent asks: "Or rather, why is this proposal not applicable in the section on the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*)?"
The objector replies:
"Quite so;
it is simply not possible. For [this would be so] only if validity were already established."
The deliberation for the ascertainment of a specific object is established.

That deliberation which is for the sake of the ascertainment of a specific object—that deliberation is "the deliberation for the ascertainment of a specific object. However, in the case of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), such deliberation does not arise because there is no object [to be ascertained].
[Page 181] What is this consideration regarding the specific meaning?

He states another objection: "And it has been said that the Vedic corpus has a purpose [beyond mere injunction]. That which was explained as being possible through the prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is also not tenable; for the impossibility of [the passage] being a mantra or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not constitute a reason for its being a prescription of a quality.
[Objection: What then is the reason? [Response: The very fact that [the word] cannot be attained through [mere] action is the reason for its being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Thus, the Sūtra has been explained as meaning that because it is impossible for the word *udbhidā* to be a reminder (*smāraka*) and because it is impossible for it to be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it must have the purpose of enjoining a quality. That is untenable;

for it is not the case that something which cannot function as a reminder or as a matter of praise is necessarily an injunction of a quality. What then? [It is an injunction of a quality] when [it pertains to] an action...

When [the action] has already been established, the hearing of its qualities is the reason for it being an injunction of qualities; as the Commentator himself stated: "The injunction of qualities regarding an action that is not [already] enjoined would be purposeless."

Thus, by saying this, it is stated that the prescription of a subsidiary (guṇavidhāna) is possible only when an action has already been enjoined. Therefore, the very attainment of the action is the reason for [the injunction] being a prescription of a subsidiary. And if the impossibility of being either a mantra or an explanatory passage (arthavāda) were the reason for being a prescription of a subsidiary, then even the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) would become a prescription of a subsidiary.

[Page 182] Even for one desiring heaven, it is impossible for there to be a mantra or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). He states another objection: as for what was said—that in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the Jyotiṣṭoma, the injunction of an accessory (*guṇa*) will be purposeful—that too is incorrect, for even there an accessory word is heard.

[The opponent argues: "In the case of [the injunction] *jyotiṣṭomena*, that too is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), because even there an injunction of an action (*karmavidhāna*) is impossible. Therefore, how can there be an injunction of qualities such as *udbhid* based on that [action] here? Now, in that case...

The intention is that in the Jyotiṣṭoma there will be a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna); since the action itself is enjoined therein, the injunction of the accessory (guṇavidhi) will be dependent upon it.
He refutes this: "Why then does a qualified injunction not also occur here in the case of 'udbhidā'?"
He introduces another objection:
"Now, when it is established that [the sacrifice] is one in the case of 'by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma,' then the other..."
"In 'udbhidā' there is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhāna) in that very same [context].

He refutes this: "In this case, since the ritual action is already established by means of a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna) in the phrase 'udbhidā', the injunction of a quality in the subsequent phrase 'jyotiṣṭomena' [is what must be explained]."

Why is it not possible? We see no reason for such a restriction. He states another objection: "And there is the prescription of a qualified [action] regarding the arising of a qualified property. (B. reads *viśiṣṭadharmotpattau*).
It is understood in the arising of the ritual action,
both in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and in that which is qualified by the attributes of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

When a ritual action has already been established, even the phrase "udbhidā" is understood as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) itself, not as an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*). Why? He says: "And it is not proper to enjoin another quality when the ritual action has already been produced as qualified [by other qualities]; because of the obstruction by the quality enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇāvarodha*). [As stated in the *Tantravārttika*: "And a quality [is enjoined] when there is a connection with something new (*apūrva*), [provided there is no conflict] between two sentences."
Because of the statement of the principle that "it is due to equality," he concludes:
therefore, there is neither inclusion within the definition nor the statement of a formal argument (nyāya).
"Since the prescription of qualities is possible," [says] B. "We do not know how this came about here, nor do we know how this commentary arrived at such a point. The respondent says:

To this it is replied: This is indeed the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, it was argued that in the definition of a means of valid cognition, a consideration regarding the determination of a specific object is not appropriate.
He refutes this: It is not at all this determination of a specific object that has been set forth here. What then?
The question posed? The answer is: does an injunction of an action (*karmavidhāna*) occur here, or is there merely an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*)?
In the case of it being a name (*nāmadheya*), there is an injunction of an action.

In the view that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it has been set forth that there is only an injunction of a quality and not an injunction of an action (*karmavidhāna*). Regarding this, he adopts the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "And when an injunction of a quality is possible, an injunction of an action is not logical, because the sentence is intent upon the quality, like the case of 'the red cloth' (*raktapaṭavat*).
The meaning of this is: the application (*niyoga*) is understood to be dependent upon the object (*viṣaya*), according to its specific assignment (*viniyoga*).
Because the understanding of that [meaning] is dependent upon the application (viniyoga), and because by virtue of the application in cases such as "udbhid" and so forth,
only the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) is perceived; therefore, just as in the sentence "the cloth becomes red," it is for the purpose of connecting it with the quality of redness alone.

Similarly here as well, in the statement "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," because it is intent upon enjoining the *udbhid* and so forth, it does not culminate in an injunction for a ritual action (*karman*).
Therefore, since an injunction for a ritual action is impossible, [the Veda] lacks authority. How is it so in the case of the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)?
The answer is: because it relies upon a worldly action (*laukikakarman*). For when a sentence is intent on enjoining a quality (*guṇavidhi*), a worldly action must necessarily be relied upon.
Here, an objection is raised: what fault is there in relying upon a Vedic action?

Therefore, something worldly must be resorted to; indeed, there is no fault in this. However, Vedic ritual action is impossible. Why is it impossible? Because in every case, due to the hearing of a subordinate term (*upapada*), a single word is not employed independently. Since the sentence, because of the hearing of a subordinate term in every instance, is intent upon enjoining the meaning of that subordinate term, it is impossible for it to enjoin a ritual action; thus, Vedic ritual action is impossible. Here, an objection is raised: even so, why is there a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*)?
The answer is: regarding the meaning of the verbal root, activity must be sought from another source, namely another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is from another [source]...

"In that case, the activity [of the injunction] must be sought elsewhere, which entails the consequence of its being dependent [on something else]. Since the activity regarding the meaning of the verbal root depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because it is dependent, its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) follows as a matter of course.

The opponent says: "But if, on the contrary, there were independence due to the prescription of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*), as in the cases of eating, sexual intercourse with a wife, and so forth, then how could there be a lack of authority?"
Just as when eating has already commenced from another source, one says, "One should eat the foods facing eastward"; or as it is said, "One should approach [one's wife] during her season."

Regarding the approach to a woman: the meaning is that since there is independence in both cases, it will be the same here as well, and thus there will be no lack of authority. He refutes this: this would be so if all injunctions everywhere were solely for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*). However, some injunctions are perceived as being for the sake of ritual action (*karmārtha*) as well; in those cases, such a restriction is not possible.

The meaning of this is as follows: if, first of all, everything were for the sake of human purpose (puruṣārtha)—as in the case of "one should eat food facing the east"—then there would be independence [from other factors]. However, some injunctions are perceived as being for the sake of ritual action (karma).

Since the nature of the action is established by that [text] and because it is observed through other qualities as well, no restriction is possible. Consequently, there is a dependence on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of that restriction. He objects: "Furthermore, in the injunction 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' what is being restricted? Is it not the agent?"

It is restricted. [The opponent] objects: "Just as this [restriction] does not apply as a qualification of the agent, so it has been demonstrated in the eleventh [book]. However, because the fruit is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), a restriction is impossible;

and because it is the primary element (*pradhānabhūta*) and thus not something to be undertaken (*anupādeya*), the fruit is not enjoined. Therefore, a restriction upon it is not possible. Regarding the fruit:

If it is argued that "action is what is being enjoined," he refutes this: it has already been stated that actions are not objects of injunction, because sentences have as their primary purport other categories of meaning (padārtha). Therefore, it must be understood that one must seek another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or else this is merely the intuition of the blind. Since no other means of knowledge is possible, it should be considered that this is the intuition of the blind due to a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). Here, an objection is raised: why is there not an injunction of action possessing qualities?

Why is it that the action itself, as qualified by a quality, is not enjoined? Just as in the case of the command "bring the man with the staff," there is a cognition of a person qualified by a staff, so too here, because of the cognition of an action qualified by a quality, that very [action] should be the object of the injunction. The answer is: because such an action qualified by a quality is not understood. Why? He says: for in this case, the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is not expressed by means of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth.

It is established as follows: for that meaning, namely "possessing that" (tadvattā), belongs only to words ending in the suffix *mat*, not to words ending in case-suffixes (*sub*). Now, [regarding the word] *udbhid*...

If it is argued that [the word] "gives" is understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), he refutes this: in that case, dependence [on something else] follows as a consequence. Why? He says: for a secondary indication cannot be asserted on the basis of the direct Vedic text (śruti).
It is not known from the direct application of the Vedic word that the term "udbhid" and so forth functions in its meaning through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā);
rather, this is understood through another means of knowledge, because its usage is perceived as referring to that which possesses the quality [denoted by the primary sense].
Therefore, there is the status of being an object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As it was stated [in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "Since the purposefulness of the Veda has been declared, therefore everything [in it] must be for that purpose. This applies when there is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), not when there is no injunction of a subordinate quality.
Regarding the term "cause" (*hetu*):

it is said in response to this—that this is indeed a cause by way of refuting the [notion of] name (*nāman*). But how, then, is the name refuted by this? Because the intended purpose (*edamarthya*) is impossible.

Because the purpose of an injunction (niyoga) is impossible [in this context]. How is it that its subservience to that purpose is not possible? The answer is: for it has been stated that the meaningfulness of the words in the injunctive statement, the mantras, and the explanatory passages (arthavādas) is established by virtue of their being for the sake of an injunction.

The meaningfulness that was stated on the basis of the purpose of *niyoga* (the injunction) applies to the words of the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and the mantras; however, this status of having *niyoga* as its meaning is not possible for a noun (*nāman*), because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*).

Now, one might object: "Granted that [the Veda] may not have its purpose realized through an injunction because it is not something to be enjoined; however, it will nonetheless have its purpose realized through direct revelation (śruti) or traditional law (smṛti). To this he replies: "Indeed, it has been stated that even those things which are not themselves to be enjoined possess purpose through śruti or smṛti. And both of these..."
Since it is not possible for it to be a name,
therefore, regarding the position that it is a name—

Since the meaning of [the word] *gaudi* is impossible [to be enjoined], the meaning of *udbhid* and so forth must be the object of injunction; and if it is the object of injunction, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Regarding this, the Commentator has stated:
"A certain portion of this [sentence] is an injunction, which enjoins a matter not previously known."
It makes known [the meaning], as in: "One should sacrifice with Soma.
He objects to that: But how can the injunctive statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" be cited as an example?

The respondent said: "Or how is it that [the injunction] is not possible? The objector said: "Because even here, there is no injunction of a sacrifice, since a subordinate term (*upapada*) is heard. The respondent said: "Let there be no injunction of a sacrifice; at least a quality (*guṇa*) is being enjoined."
With that intention, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated the words of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśapada*):
