"Some part of this is an injunction. [Objection: But even an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, because words such as *udbhid* and others are well-known as names of sacrifices (*yāganāmadheya*).
It is said: for it is in the linguistic usage of the elders that "established convention" (prasiddhi) is so called;
and yet, the word *soma* does not [arise] in the linguistic usage of the elders [in the sense of the plant].

The word *udbhid* denotes a sacrifice. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely the practice of ritualists (*yājñika*) is also nothing other than the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), for the ritualists [employ] words such as *udbhid*."

They have stated that these are "words denoting the ritual action" (*karmavacana*). Therefore, their well-known usage is indeed a valid established usage (*prasiddhi*). [Objection: If their status as words denoting the ritual action is already established, why is there a need for knowledge of their secondary qualities (*guṇajñāna*)? [The author] answers: That [well-known usage] is not a [valid] established usage, because the usage of ritualists is preceded by worldly usage; for in the world...

The words *udbhid* and so forth are well known as names of rituals; on the contrary, they are established as denoting other things, being commonly known as terms for a spade. Therefore, [the passage] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
"This [statement], 'The injunction of a quality in the Jyotiṣṭoma, which is the archetype (prakṛti), will be purposeful,' appears to be an incorrect commentary."

Why is this incorrect? The answer is: even in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the word "Jyotiṣṭoma" itself is indeed injunctive; for there too, the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) must be sought from elsewhere.

Who has stated that a text ending with an address (*ābhāṣānta*) is such that the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) need not be sought there either? If this were so, then an injunction (*vidhāna*) would not be possible in that case.
The respondent says: "In that case, the status of being the archetype for the prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhiprakṛtitā*) is observed.
He explains this very point: "What is meant is this: by [the injunction] 'one should sacrifice with soma' (*somena yajeta*), which prescribes a quality..."
If one were to proceed from another source for the accomplishment of the sacrifice, then this [argument] would also be applicable there.
The meaning is this:

in the injunction of the accessory named *soma*—namely, "one should sacrifice with *soma*"—if that which is intended as the substratum (*āśraya*) of the injunction of the accessory is either the *Jyotiṣṭoma* or something worldly...

Or rather, let even *udbhid* and the like be injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) in that very context. And the word "root" (*prakṛti*) [is used] in an injunction of quality because of the presence of the root in the injunction of quality.
[Page 189]
This is for the purpose of definition. Therefore, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is accepted as having the purpose of indicating the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Wherever there is acceptance of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there too [the principle applies]; thus, even *udbhid* and the others are injunctions of qualities—the meaning is that all injunctions of qualities should enjoin a quality.
Now, why is it not an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*)? To this he says: "The impossibility of an injunction of a qualified entity has already been stated."

To the objection that "in that case, let it be a name," he replies: furthermore, in the case of it being a name, its status as the object of an injunction (*niyoga*) is not possible, because the sacrifice (*yajña*), which is the thing to be enjoined, has already been grasped by the verbal root *yaji*.
What is the use of another name? He says: "It does not assist the injunction, since it merely presents the word for that which has already been enjoined. Now, [one might object]: "Let it be..."
Even so, he asks "what [is gained]? and replies: "The authority of the *codanā* has been stated by virtue of its being conducive to the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, even in your own position, authority must still be sought from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."

It is understood through another means of valid cognition and is not easily obtained; moreover, in our own position, even the referent of a word is well-established through the linguistic usage of elders. And in your view, validity is at least equal [in both cases].
In your view as well, the lack of authority is equal;
at best, you must resort to a non-worldly power of words,
or else [accept] that it is a mere name.

To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that this sentence refers to a quality—that is true; however, that [quality] is understood as such through the consideration of its application (*viniyoga*), and no further expectation of an application need be made.
What then?

It depends upon an existent entity (bhāva), because its object is an existent entity. And this existent entity is that which is expressed as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta). Therefore, this [injunction] has that as its object.

[The opponent argues: "It is an injunction (*niyoga*). And there is no such injunction regarding a specific object that has already been established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by virtue of which one could set that aside and enjoin merely a quality (*guṇa*). On this point, the *Bhāṣya* states: "It is a different ritual act from the Jyotiṣṭoma. That is incorrect; for [the act] designated as 'Jyotiṣṭoma'...

Anticipating the objection that there exists a ritual action by which it might be said that this is a different ritual action from the Jyotiṣṭoma, he says: "It is a different ritual action from the Jyotiṣṭoma. What is meant is this: it is established that a Vedic ritual action is distinct from a worldly one. The word "Jyotiṣṭoma" is used here as a designation for the locus of the injunction regarding the subordinate elements (guṇa). And the author of the Sūtras will demonstrate this in the aphorism: "From them, the action is understood."

Therefore, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) alone is the object of the injunction (*vidhi*). How then can there be a repetition of the word for the sake of a subordinate element (*guṇa*), if the mandate (*niyoga*) has only the meaning of the verbal root as its object? The answer is: it is intended to convey the attainment of what is to be done (*kartavyatā-prāpti*), not the application (*viniyoga*).

As for the statement that the subsequent scriptural mention (*punaḥśruti*) has the purpose of [specifying] a quality (*guṇa*), the meaning is as follows: the necessity of performing the action as delimited by the *homa* (oblation) has already been established; however, its delimitation by a specific quality has not yet been established.

Therefore, with the intention that the quality itself is not being enjoined [anew], the subsequent scriptural mention is intended solely to connect the action with the quality, through a distinction between what is already established and what is not. Regarding this, he asks: "Or rather, is the injunction not according to the application (*viniyoga*)?"

Regarding the claim that the injunction (*niyoga*) is described with disregard for the application (*viniyoga*), the reply is as follows: This is indeed the method of the author of the Sūtras, who recites: "Words denoting action have the meaning of being (*bhāva*);
from them, the action (*kriyā*) is to be understood. Is this Sūtra, which stands in opposition to the application, intended to be applied according to the specific application?

The answer is: Certainly; for otherwise, according to the principle of application (*viniyoga*), the injunctions for the *śyena* sacrifice and others would result in the status of mere ritual acts (*bhāvārtha*), following the analogy of the red-clad ascetics (*raktapaṭa*). And this has already been refuted in the section on "the meaning of being an act" (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*) by virtue of their not having the nature of an act (*abhāvārthatā*). What, then, is the root of this methodological approach?
The answer: We maintain that comprehension alone is the root;
it pertains exclusively to the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha).

Since an injunction (*niyoga*) is understood [from it], and surely there is likewise an understanding even in the case of an application (*viniyoga*); therefore, its abandonment too is not proper. He replies:

— Who has said that there is no comprehension whatsoever regarding application (* viniyoga*)? Rather, we have stated that the "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) is understood as having the entity (*bhāva*) as its object,
because the entity has the nature of an action (*kārya*).

It has been stated in the *Viṣayakaraṇīya* that an injunction (*niyoga*) has the task (*kārya*) as its object. Now, for what purpose is the understanding of the application (*viniyoga*)? The answer is: we say it is for the sake of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

That entity which has become the object of the injunction (*niyoga*) is the meaning of that [injunction]. If the application (*viniyoga*) is the meaning of the verbal root, then how is it said to be subordinate to a quality (*guṇa*)?
In this case as well, there would first of all be subordination to the action (*bhāva*). The answer is: because the action is already established.

The sentence has as its primary purport a subordinate element (*guṇa*). Now, one might object: when an accompanying word (*upapada*) is heard, the mere action (*bhāva*) is not understood as the object of the injunction at all, because it is understood as an object only when conjoined with a subordinate element, just as in the case of "the cloth becomes red. It was stated in the second chapter that it is not merely the becoming of the cloth that is perceived. To this, he replies: Who said that a word expressing a mere action attains the status of being the object [of an injunction] on its own?

But it has been stated that this [the action] is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), not its qualifier (*guṇa*). Nor does the fact that this injunction has an action as its object preclude its connection with another word;
rather, it is understood as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), like the case of "one who wears red garments" (*raktapaṭa*). But how then—
Qualities such as *rudbhida* (wood-cutter) and others, being existent, function as qualifiers of an entity (*bhāva*),
by means of which the entity qualified by them is enjoined.

Thus it is said. He refutes this: Is the relationship between qualifier and qualified established solely by way of being a quality (*guṇatā*), such that [the relationship] of the object which is a non-existence [would follow] by virtue of its being a quality?

He states that the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is the qualifier: "Insofar as even a name is seen to function as both qualifier and qualified, as in 'This Brāhmaṇa is named Ḍittha' or 'This Kṣatriya is named Ḍabittha.'"
Thus [it is asked]. But how, again, is it understood that these are names? The answer is: because of the apprehension of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Since the coreferentiality of words such as *udbhid* with the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is apprehended, there is the understanding that they are names. But how, then, is the apprehension of coreferentiality established?
The meaning is that [the word *somena*] is understood to have the same referent as the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

He states the reply according to the view of the "partialist" (*ekadeśin*): "[Because of the mention of the instrumental case, it belongs to the root *yaj*]. For indeed, the sense of the instrumental case exists there; that [instrumentality] is established for it by this [word].

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, the instrumental case-ending is heard in the case of words such as *udbhid*; therefore, it is understood that "one should bring about the *apūrva* by means of the sacrifice called *udbhid*. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) refutes this: "This is incorrect. For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not based on the use of the same case-ending; rather, coreferentiality is based on the comprehension of a single referent. Indeed, in coreferentiality, it is the state of having a single referent that is expressed, and that is not based on the same case-ending, but rather on the state of having a single referent. For if it were based on the same case-ending..."

In that case, there would be no connection of the substance and the quality with the action in the expression "aruṇayā ekahāyanyā" (with a one-year-old reddish-brown cow); rather, there would be only a mutual connection between them, as in the case of a "blue lotus."

Just as there is a mutual relationship between [the words] "blue" and "lotus" in the expression *nīlotpalam*, so too would it exist between "red" (*aruṇā*) and "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*); yet this is not accepted. Precisely because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not based on the use of a single case-ending, for that very reason coreferentiality is not perceived in expressions such as "cow, horse, man, elephant," even though they share a single case-ending.

To the question, "How then is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) understood in the case of 'This is Devadatta'? he says: "And this grammatical coreferentiality in 'This is Devadatta' is understood through [the words] having a single referent (*ekārthatā*). Therefore, it is not the case that the case-endings (*vibhakti*)..."

This is the reason for their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Now, he states his own view: "To this it is replied—it has been stated that because the meaning of a verbal root is the object [of the injunction], the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) is understood as residing in the meaning of the verb, not in the meaning of the nominal stem; and yet, this relationship is indeed perceived."
Regarding the two [terms] *udbhid* and *yāga*: if it is accepted that [the name *udbhid*] is caused by a quality (*guṇanimittaka*), then,
since [the word] is derived from the root *ud-bhid*, the term *udbhid* would have to be understood as an indication [of the object] with the suffix *matup* elided.

The meaning is that the fault lies precisely in the postulation of an unstated possessive suffix (*matvartha*). However, if it is a name (*nāmadheya*), then the relationship is based on another word that has not been postulated; and this is logically consistent.
The connection [between the two] arises from their association with the same case-ending.

It is precisely for this reason that the introduction of the third-case designation (*tṛtīyānideśa*) is presented in the Bhāṣya. The meaning is that if there were a designation using different case-endings, then there would be no syntactic connection by way of being a name (*nāmadheya*); however, such [a lack of connection] does not occur because they are designated with a single case-ending.

As for what was shown in the case of "aruṇayā," there the connection with the action (bhāva) belongs to both [the quality and the substance]; but here, since no other meaning is heard, whose connection does the instrumental case-ending express,
given that the other word denotes the action?

Just as in the case of the *aruṇa* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), a separate act (*kraya*) is heard [in the text], so here an unprecedented *bhāvanā* (*apūrvabhāvanā*) that is not subsumed under the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not perceived;
nor is a separate meaning heard. Rather, an unprecedented *bhāvanā* is perceived as being subsumed under the meaning of the root *yaj*; thus, there is a connection with the meaning of the root *yaj*.

This is the case with words such as *udbhid*. Therefore, this instrumental case ending has as its sole purpose mere designation (*nirdeśamātra*), because the meaning [of the word] is already established by its being a synonym for sacrifice (*yāga*). Now, one might object: "In the case of mere designation, the nominative case alone ought to occur. The reply is: that grammatical rule teaches non-deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not non-deviation from the meaning of the word (*pada*).
And when there is non-deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem, the nominative case occurs.

It is not non-distinct from the meaning of the word (*padārtha*). And this non-distinction from the meaning of the word is not a non-distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). This has been demonstrated by the example: "The Brahmin Ḍittha ate. But one might object: since there is no comprehension of a single unified meaning, what will the case-ending (*vibhakti*) accomplish?

The word *udbhid* cannot denote the sacrifice itself; therefore, it is better to assume here the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*). Alternatively, both [the name and the material] serve the purpose of an injunction for the sake of application (*viniyoga*).
It is like the case of the *aruṇa* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow). He refutes this: first of all, there is no status as the object of an injunction (*niyoga*) for these two;
it has already been stated that an injunction has as its object that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*). Furthermore, a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not denote an action to be accomplished.

Therefore, it is untenable for the name to be the direct object of the injunction. To this, an objection is raised: "Let it be that the name denotes an action (*kārya*) because of its connection with parts; thus, its status as the object [of the injunction] is established. He replies: "True, let it be..."

Through the well-known meaning of its constituent parts, names denote an action (*kārya*) when they do not have a distinct referent; however, when there is a distinction [of referent], because of their connection [with another word], who would deny that they possess an established referent (*siddhārthatā*)? And if they possess an established referent, it has already been stated that this is not the domain of the injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, since the application of the etymological derivation of the parts is consistent, it is established that the name does not have a distinct referent.
And because there is no distinct referent, the lack of contact with the injunction is avoided.
For in a sacrifice, the connection with the injunction is direct; likewise, for its name as well, contact with the *niyoga* (the mandate) is established through the mediation of its meaning.
197] But surely, as much as is expressed by "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), so much also is expressed by "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yajeta*).

The sense is that, because it serves no purpose, there is no name [for it]. He refutes this: this might be so if the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to follow the purpose; however, it is the purpose that follows the means of valid cognition. Therefore, even the fact that it lacks a purpose—which arises from the means of valid cognition—is not a fault. And this is merely a concession, since a purpose does indeed exist. As he says: "And the utility of names for the sake of the meaning of other sentences is observed."

The purpose of connecting qualities (*guṇa*) with results (*phala*) is observed even in other sentences; therefore, the charge of being purposeless does not hold true in this case either. Consequently, the independence of the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is established. Regarding that in which there is an instruction on a quality, it was stated that even a name will be meaningful through its connection to qualities and results; however, for one who considers that to be incorrect, the validity of [the name] is now demonstrated in a specific context.

By this, he removes the fault of the lack of connection with the chapter. How it is indeed improper is stated as follows: "First, for the purpose of connecting the qualities, it is said that there are fifteen *ājya* [verses]."

By means of the word *ājya*, a specific *stotra* is referred to by its name, and therein the quality of the number fifteen is enjoined. Thus, the name is purposeful through its connection with that quality. For the purpose of connecting it with a result, the connection with a result is made for the sacrifice under discussion by the word *citrayā* in the injunction: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*," as in: "Curd, honey, ghee, water, parched grain, and rice—this mixture belongs to Prajāpati. Thus, the connection with a result is effected for the sacrifice already established by the term *citrayā*.

In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: It is indeed appropriate that terms such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" function as names, because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Likewise, terms such as *ājya* and *pṛṣṭha* should also function as names, because of their coreferentiality with the meaning of the verb *stu* (to praise), as in "they praise with the *ājyas*" and "they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*."

[This refers to] the status of being a name based on praise (*stutināmatva*). However, where grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the verbal root is not perceived—as in the case of "the *ājya* offerings are fifteen"—there is no comprehension that it is a name.
Why is this? He says:

Even though the meaning is consistent, it is called a name because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For those [words] such as *udbhid* and others, even though their meaning is consistent, their status as names has been stated on account of coreferentiality; and that is not the case here.

There is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). Precisely because the word *ājya* lacks the status of a name for a ritual action— as seen in the expression "the fifteen *ājya* [offerings]"— it cannot be asserted that the name possesses meaningfulness through its connection with a quality (*guṇopabandha*).

Here he raises an objection: It may well be that the name has no meaningful referent when it is connected with a quality; however, in the case of its connection with a result, since grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible when the word for the sacrifice is uttered...
"Why can it not be said that there is purposefulness in the statement, 'One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā'? He replies: "It is said."

— Nor can it be said that there is a purposefulness [of the suffix] by means of the root *yaj* itself, which denotes the subject matter under discussion, as in the injunction "one desiring cattle should sacrifice."
Because the connection of a specific sacrifice with its fruit is established. Why? He says: for in that case, the specific sacrifice is obtained through mere proximity, not by name.
Here he raises an objection: mā...
From the name *bhṛt*, there is the comprehension of a specific sacrifice; indeed, its status as a name cannot be denied.

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He refutes [the objection]: "By whom was it said that its status as a name is being rejected? The objection is based merely on the fact that there is no [distinct] purpose. But how, then, can there be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) in the case of "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*"?
This is the intention: even if there is no [distinct] purpose, why should its status as a name not be accepted?

[Objection: It may be so; but how is it an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)? [Response: The answer is: thus is the injunction of a quality. For here, a specific sacrifice already known is enjoined for the sake of a result.

[Objection: Let it be so; even then, what follows? [Response: He says: for when the specific [sacrifice] is already known, the cognition from another word does not lead to a lack of specification (*aviśeṣa*).
It does not lead to a distinction;
why? The answer is: precisely because it is already known. [This refers to the phrase] "curd, honey, and ghee."

The sacrifice, which has been specifically identified through the sentence as "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*), has its specific form determined by the root *yaji* itself, which denotes the subject matter under discussion. For in a case where the meaning of an injunction is understood from words connected within its own sentence...

In a case where the meaning of a word is understood only through its own injunctive sentence, the specific qualification is understood from that very source—as in "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. However, when a term is already known from another sentence, it does not require syntactic connection (*padānvaya*) within its own sentence for the sake of its own comprehension. And for that which is not so required, there can be no verbal grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*) are the causes of syntactic connection. In the injunction "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*), the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) does not require a name for the sake of understanding the specific [nature of the rite], because that specific nature is already understood from another sentence. Therefore, since there is no such connection, it cannot be a name.

Consequently, in the word "citrayā," the quality of being variegated (*citratva*) must be understood as something to be enjoined. To this, an objection is raised: "In that case, where the specific nature is understood from the accompanying word (*upapada*) itself—since what has been enjoined is not the subject under discussion—let there be a purpose for the name."

Because a specific distinction is understood precisely through that power. He refutes [the objection]: first, it has been stated here simply that [the name] does not apply exclusively; furthermore, even when applied to what is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛta*), the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*) does not assist [the injunction].
Even if a sentence joined with a name not pertaining to the subject at hand enjoins a sacrifice for the sake of a result, [it remains so].

Even there, there is no connection of the name by way of being a designation. Why? He says: because it is indeed another action (*karmāntara*), since the action is enjoined with respect to the result. And because the action is not previously established (*aprakṛta*), it constitutes a different action. In that case, there is the injunction of the meanings of two words.

Even by means of a name, a similarity to the primary action is enjoined based on its auxiliary function; likewise, even by a word denoting a verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), there is the injunction of a verbal root-meaning. Thus, the verbal root-meaning has been demonstrated, as shown in the case of "one performs the *agnihotra*" within the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*.

Therefore, the name [citrayā] is not purposeful either by way of connecting the fruit of the primary action already arisen, or by way of connecting the fruit of another action currently arising. Consequently, wherever the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is applicable—such as in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*)—this injunction of a quality must be postulated there. This is because substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*), medicinal herbs (*oṣadha*), and the *sānnāyya* offering lack variegation (*acitratva*), and because the statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" does not require such a qualification.

Since it is impossible for it to form a single syntactical unit with that [preceding sentence], one must split the sentence; thus, the word *citrā* alone is for the purpose of enjoining a quality (*guṇavidhi*). The phrase "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*), however, is the injunction of the fruit for the sacrifice under discussion. And the word *citrā*, being transferred to the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), is the enjoiner of a quality. Likewise, in the case of the statement "the *ājya* chants are fifteen," there are fifteen *ājya* verses in the chant.
Regarding the term "injunction" (*vidhi*): therefore, the statement that [the injunction] is purposeful by way of its connection with qualities and results is incorrect. To this, the reply is given:
it is not incorrect.

"It is purposeful by way of being connected with qualities and results. Why is this so? He says: "Where another quality is enjoined"—as, for example, femininity is enjoined in relation to variegatedness, or the number fifteen in relation to the clarified butter (*ājya*); in those cases, there is simply the application of a name to an action already established.

It becomes meaningful; for a quality cannot be enjoined with respect to that which is not an action, according to the stated principle that "the performance [of an action] is dependent [on its existence]. Indeed, the injunction of a quality occurs through the injunction of an action colored by that quality; therefore, there is no injunction of a quality with respect to what is not an action. Furthermore, because the action is presented by the name, the name possesses meaning through its connection with the quality. This is also due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Since the status of [the word] as a name is established in other sentences such as "they praise with the *ājya*s," the statement "the *ājya*s are fifteen" is indeed capable of signifying the relationship between the name and the named. Therefore, it is logical that a name is purposeful through its connection with a quality; this is appropriate in the case of the *ājya*s and so forth.

Because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), both [the word *citrayā* and *ājyena*] cannot be that which is enjoined (*vidheya*). Since one must serve as the subject (*uddeśaka*), and because the word *ājya* functions as the designation of the ritual action (*karmavacana*), it alone serves as the subject;

thus, the name (*nāman*) possesses meaningfulness. But how does the word *citrayā* possess meaningfulness? For in that case, the specific [animal] is understood precisely because it is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).
[Page 203] Its meaningfulness cannot be asserted. The reply: Certainly; it can be asserted even in that case, provided that [the object] does not exist.
The prescription of a result for that which has not yet arisen is untenable, because it would contradict the scriptural mention of a quality.
He demonstrates this very point: since no distinction is perceived, one might think, "This is for the sake of the result, not for the sake of the quality."

It is not understood what the distinction is—that this mention of the sacrifice is solely for the purpose of connecting it with a result and not for the purpose of connecting it with an accessory (guṇa). And when such a distinction is not understood, there would be indecision;
and from indecision follows a lack of authoritative validity. That [objection] is refuted by [the fact that the term is] a name (nāmadheya).

Because the name is subject to being enjoined and because there is a certainty regarding its connection with the fruit, it is proper [to say] "by the *citrayā*"; in this regard, the *pūrvapakṣa* (*prima facie*) commentary states: "And these [words] are not etymological (*yaugika*). P. 198.
He objects to that: "What is the use of refuting its etymological nature?
He replies: "The intention is this: for if it were etymological, there would be the establishment of denoting the sacrifice under discussion, just as in the expression, 'Give wages to the cook.'"
Even in the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a specific person, the establishment of the expression of the "presently mentioned cook" is achieved;

likewise here too, under the view that [the term] is etymological (*yaugika*), there would be the denotation of the "presently mentioned sacrifice," and consequently, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not tenable.
It is established. Therefore, it has been stated that these [words] are not derivative (*yaugika*).
Now, one might ask: even if they denote a genus (*jāti*), why do they not function as names (*nāman*)?
To this, he says: "But when denoting a genus, there is only the state of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*)."

The [denotation of] the genus is logical; for the denotation of an individual depends upon specific qualities (*viśeṣa*). Moreover, that which is not etymologically derived (*ayaugika*) cannot denote an individual. Thus, because "with the variegated" (*citrayā*) denotes a mere quality, it is equivalent to those [words] that denote a genus.

Therefore, this too does not denote the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*). Furthermore, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the variegated" (*citrayā yajeta*), it is understood as a reference (*anuvāda*) to a sacrifice already known, and is not an injunction (*vidhi*) of a sacrifice.
What is demonstrated by this commentary? The answer is:
the state of being free from expectancy (*anākāṅkṣitatva*). [This follows] because the noun is free from expectancy.
Regarding the name *citrāpada*:

since this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), it does not require a name for the sake of knowing its specific [referent], because its particularity is already known. And for that which does not require [a name], there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

"Because that [quality] is absent, it is not a name. Therefore, in the case of an injunction of a result, it is understood that there is no utility in [the word] being a name. By this proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), who asserts that the root *yajati* ("to sacrifice") is not intended [as a primary action] when a quality and a result are postulated, what is it that must be refuted?
Is it being suspected that [the name] is to be rejected?

But surely, it is only the connection between the quality and the fruit that is being stated; this is not to be suspected. For the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) must establish that the name has no purpose by means of the connection between the quality and the fruit. Therefore, that alone is to be suspected by which the name would possess meaning. And it is not...

Even in the case of a connection between a quality and its result, the name remains meaningful. Thus he says: "Because even when there is a connection between a quality and its result, the name does not thereby become meaningless; on the contrary, this [objection] must be refuted by the proponent who asserts that the name is meaningful."
Therefore, this fragment of the Bhāṣya turns out to be entirely incoherent in the mind of the respondent (rāddhāntin).
The resolver says: "To this, it is replied."
Since it is indeed impossible to preclude the conceptualization of a relationship between qualities and results, the proponent refutes the connection between qualities and results.

Why is it impossible to turn back? He says: "It is possible. The answer is: because the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is not intended [as the primary object]. And when it is not intended, the meaning of the verbal activity (*bhāvārtha*) is not supported; nor can a quality (*guṇa*) that does not rest upon the meaning of the verbal activity be enjoined for the sake of a result.

Anticipating the question, "Why, then, is the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) not intended [as the primary injunction]? he says: "For the engagement in an action from another source is the cause for the connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a result;

because the action has been engaged in from another source, the understanding arises that 'the result comes from the quality' when it is not being enjoined [by that verb]. And there is no other motivator for the act of sacrificing than the injunction for one who desires cattle.

Since the capacity to impel another toward action belongs to that which serves the purpose of the sacrifice, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not intended [as the primary meaning here]. However, the word *citrā* is connected with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*).
Therefore, as long as the connection with the desire for cattle is not abandoned, the word *citrā* remains nothing but a name (*nāmadheya*). This is clearly understood.

Therefore, the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) absolutely rejects the connection with "one who desires cattle" even by resorting to the relationship between a quality and a result for the word *citrā*. For he thinks as follows:

If I were to absolutely exclude the connection of the word *citrā* with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*) even by means of a relationship between a quality and a fruit (*guṇaphala-sambandha*), he [the opponent] would think: "If I admit the connection of the word *citrā* with the desire for cattle even through a relationship between a quality and a fruit, then, since that [relationship] is impossible, once it is rejected, the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*) would be lost."
Because of the abandonment [of that view], otherwise, since the words *citrā* and *paśukāma* would be impossible [to connect] due to being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*),

the word *citrā* would result in being merely a name (*nāmadheya*). Therefore, by that very effort, even the connection between a quality and a fruit (*guṇaphalasaṃbandha*) is far removed from being a single sentence.
I refute this; therefore,
because the word *citrayā* has no expectancy for either the term denoting the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*) or for the sacrifice (*yāga*), [it cannot be construed with them].

In some cases, an injunction regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*) must be understood as being in accordance with those qualities. There is no connection between the efficient force (*bhāvārtha*) and the qualified agent; rather, there is a connection [between them]. Thus, the word *citrayā* (with the variegated offering), which does not itself constitute an efficient force, is not expected by the word *paśukāma* (desiring cattle). Furthermore, even by means of a sacrifice whose specific nature is already known, [the name] serves as a designation (*nāmadheya*) for the sake of knowing its own particularity.

It is not desired [that this be so]. Where this quality called *citrā* (variegated) is not fit to be enjoined, there this injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) should not be understood to apply. He explains another portion of the Bhāṣya which supports the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Even in the assumption of an injunction of a quality, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For it has been stated that the defect of relying on figurative indication consists in the fact that the meaning would then be cognizable through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
Indeed, having first cognized the object through another means of knowledge and having ascertained the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding it, [one then understands the sentence].

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs everywhere, and that is a great defect in the Veda; for it would entail the consequence that the mantras, the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), and the injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśas*) would depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Furthermore, it has been stated that this [indication] is not present here either, due to the absence of a connection between words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For in the case of "udabhidet,"...

If, by resorting to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice, it were a "guṇavidhi" (an injunction of an accessory) such that the accessory were the object to be enjoined, then the fault of "matvarthalakṣaṇā" (indirect indication of the sense of "possessing") would have been stated.
Here, however, by resorting to coreferentiality— [The sentence continues: ...by resorting to coreferentiality, [the fault of matvarthalakṣaṇā does not arise].

There is no injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); rather, it is simply that "one should sacrifice with a brindled animal" (*citrayā yajeta*) by means of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Therefore, since there is no fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of the sense of possession), the injunction of a quality is established. Thus, [the point] is established. (B. adds *na*)

"It is meaningful as a name because of its connection with a quality and a result. This is said [in response]. Here, an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible. For when there is the injunction of a name and its referent, since an already established entity cannot be enjoined in itself, it must be enjoined by way of entering into an action; however, the quality itself is not enjoined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). What follows from this? This follows: wherever this injunction of a quality occurs...

Being established, it attains the status of being instrumental to the ritual action; therefore, a quality must be enjoined therein, and its injunction applies to the animal because the variegated nature of the animal is possible. Even if this be so, he asks "what then? regarding that which is enjoined there: *tatra vidhīyamāne*.
If this animal were multicolored, another quality called "femininity" would have to be enjoined;
consequently, even in the case of displacement [to another rite], there would be a further syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, if it were enjoined in the *Sārasvatī* sacrifice, there too—
Whether the female gender is not prescribed or is indeed prescribed, the connection with the word "desiring cattle" (paśukāma), which is understood [from the context], would have to be abandoned;
furthermore, the attainment of the qualities of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] would have to be set aside in the case of the Sārasvatī [offering].

For in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, a specific color is fixed; that [color], obtained through extended application (atideśa), must be set aside. Therefore, because a syntactical split (vākyabheda) is inevitable, this [injunction] is prescribed for the Agniṣomīya—which serves as the archetype (prakṛti) for all sacrifices performed with living beings as the material—since its connection to its own sentence has been excluded.
In that context, both qualities, namely variegatedness (citratva) and femininity (strītva), which have already been obtained, must be enjoined again.

Consequently, there would again be a split in the sentence; therefore, it is not possible for this to be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Hence, since the syntactic connection is perceived and the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is perceived, it is proper to assume that this [word] serves as the cause [of that unity]. And it has been stated that this [unity] is not possible here without the name. Therefore, its status as a name (*nāmadheyatva*) is established.

By this connection with the result, it is also shown that [the sentence] possesses purposefulness. For, if [the term *ājyāni*] were a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there would be uncertainty as to whether this sentence is intended for the purpose of connecting it with a quality or for the purpose of connecting it with a result; that uncertainty is resolved by its being a name (*nāmadheya*), as has already been demonstrated. Likewise, in the case of the statement "There are fifteen *ājyāni*," if it were a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there would be the prescription of two qualities.

Because there is an injunction regarding both the number and the clarified butter (*ājya*), and that [injunction] is not possible due to the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*), therefore one word of the mantra must be understood through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the indicator (*uddeśaka*). And that [word] is connected to the ritual action. Therefore, in another sentence...

It is only for the word *ājya*, which denotes a well-known ritual action (*karman*), that the status of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) is appropriate. In this way, the understanding of their mutual relationship is not abandoned, as in the case of the statement: "In this context, there are fifteen *ājya* [stotras]."

As for what was said—that even in the view that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here—that too is incorrect. Why? Because wherever the *ājya* offerings are enjoined by the words "the *ājyas* exist" (*ājyāni bhavanti*), that must be expressed by the verb *bhavati*. Therefore, the meaning is that the stotras come to possess the *ājyas*; thus, the expression "they come to possess the *ājyas*" (*ājyavanti bhavanti*) is precisely that figurative indication. As for the claim that the status of being a name for the ritual action (*karman-nāmadheya*) is unestablished, that is established because it serves as a designation for the ritual action.

Since the word *ājya* denotes the ritual action (*karman*), its status as a name for that action is established; furthermore, the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists everywhere, as in the passage "that they went toward the race" (*yadājimīyuḥ*). On this point, the Commentator has raised an objection: "Why then are the *ājyas*, qualified by the number fifteen, not enjoined with respect to the hymns (*stotra*)?"
B. adds "ājyānī" [p.
209], and this he challenges: what has been set forth by this that was not already refuted?
The answer is: this has been proposed. [The objection is that] the meaning of two words, which is established elsewhere, is also being enjoined here. What will happen if it is so?
The answer is: the intention is that there is no repetition of the sentence.
Since the two word-meanings, standing in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified, are enjoined by a single injunction, there is no further application;
thus, there is no repetition (*anāvṛtti*). This is its meaning.
This is the commentary providing the resolution to the objection: "Because there is no word that denotes [the two] as distinct.

He explains this: "In this way, it is indeed established that the meaning of both words is enjoined by a single injunction, provided that the relationship between these two is already established prior to the injunction."

It might be argued that it is like the case of "to Agni Pāvaka. Just as the state of being *pāvaka* (purifying) is already established for Agni prior to its formal designation, and not [as something newly produced by the act of naming].

Likewise, since it is established that there are exactly fifteen *ājya* [stotras] here—as indicated by the term "fifteen" itself—it is said: "But this [number] does not exist [as a separate entity]. Therefore, the connection between these two is based solely on the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) and its cause; consequently, it is impossible for the meaning of both words to be the object of an injunction (*vidheya*).
Now, why is it that a single injunction is not possible even for two things that are unrelated, such as Agni and Prajāpati? Just as in the Agnihotra sacrifice,
by the [injunction] "to Agni and to Prajāpati," there is an injunction of Agni and Prajāpati— who are mutually unrelated— by means of a single injunction, so too here.

The meaning is: why does it not occur? B. The answer: It does not avoid [this objection]; it is not possible for there to be an injunction regarding two unrelated things, because such a thing is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it must be accepted that this is caused solely by the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*).
Consequently, it is established that this too is a name (*nāmadheya*).

[Page 211] And there is another treatise that makes this clear. But by what distinction is this section commenced here to remove the suspicion that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)? The answer is: because there is no need for a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the possessive sense (*matvartha*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible even through an injunction of a subordinate quality.

This term *agnihotra* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, even without the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established. Because of this specific feature, there arises the suspicion here that it might be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). This has been demonstrated accordingly: "In this [rite], there is an offering (*hotra*) for Agni"—thus it is *agnihotra*.
It is precisely this same [compound].

This compound expresses the act of offering (*homa*), because the offering itself constitutes the meaning of the other member of the compound. Even by enjoining the meaning of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), it remains an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), just as in the case of the statement, "The priests wear golden garlands.
Therefore, in this instance, Agni, being the subordinate member, is the deity (*devatā*).
It is enjoined. It is indeed appropriate that "He offers the Agnihotra" is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); but how is it so with "He pours the Āghāra"?

The reply is: there is no purpose here for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as the word is not perceived here as denoting an action; rather, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
The word *āghāra* does not denote an action, but rather refers to the substance to be poured; this [act] is its pouring (*āghāraṇa*).

The quality of being poured out (*āghārya*) is enjoined as a ritual action (*saṃskāra*). This is precisely what is stated: "In that very case where there is a substance to be poured out in the *upāṃśuyāja*, it is therein that this pouring out (*āghāraṇa*) is enjoined. But surely, since a sacrifice involving a substance to be poured out is accomplished in the *āhavanīya* fire, it already possesses the act of pouring out by necessity?

All sacrifices (*yajati*) consist of oblations (*homa*) performed while standing, accomplished in the *āhavanīya* fire, and the act of pouring an oblation occurs in the *āhavanīya*; thus, since the action of pouring a long stream of liquid is already established for a sacrifice where the substance to be poured is the *āghāra*, what is the purpose of the injunction for the *āghāra*? [The answer is: Because an injunction (*vidhi*) serves to bring about what has not yet been established. The reply is: This is a different *āghāra* from the *homa* and the [standard] *āghāra*.
The intention is that [the pouring] subsequent to the preparation of the substance is for the purpose of preparing the substance.

Because an injunction brings about what has not yet been attained, it serves as a means for the ritual action (*karma*). For one who considers the word *āghāra* to end in the suffix *-ghañ*—according to the rule "the suffix *-ghañ* occurs when the agent is not the primary factor and a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be expressed"—it follows that since this is a preparation (*saṃskāra*) of the thing to be poured (*āghārya*), it is therefore [performed] in the *upāṃśuyāja*.
It has been demonstrated that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Therefore, in this example, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that [the word *agnihotra*] is not a designation of an action. However, in the case of the Agnihotra, although it is a designation of an action, it has been stated that an injunction of a quality is not contradictory because there is no need for a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
To this it is replied: An injunction of qualities (guṇavidhi) is not possible here, because the qualities are already established. He explains this very point:
Those qualities which are presented here as being subject to injunction are already obtained from elsewhere; for instance, the fire [is obtained] from the passage: "To Agni and to Prajāpati...
and so forth.

Since it is obtained from two statements, it cannot be something to be enjoined; therefore, it is not an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*), but the word *agnihotra* is merely a name (*nāmadheya*).
As for the pouring (*āghāraṇa*), it is also established by such statements as "he pours continuously" (*santatam āghārayati*) and "he pours straight" (*ṛjum āghārayati*).

But [an objection may be raised]: these sentences are intended to enjoin continuity and so forth by referring back (*anuvāda*) to the act of pouring expressed in the phrase "he pours" (*āghārayati*); how then can the pouring itself be established from them?

Now, it might be argued that the sentences concerning "continuous" (*santata*) and so forth enjoin the *āghāra* (libation) as qualified by continuity. That is not so; for, like the injunction "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), these are understood to have the purpose of enjoining a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) because they are recited in proximity to the injunction for the *āghāra*. To this it is replied: First of all, the redundancy of the injunction for the *āghāra* itself is unavoidable. To explain: let that [injunction] be absent; in its absence, let the sentences concerning "continuous" and so forth themselves be the enjoiners of the qualified *āghāra*, rather than being a primary injunctive sentence. Nor should it be said that if the sentences concerning "continuous" and so forth were intended to enjoin the *āghāra*, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result.

Because there is no perception of difference when there is no difference in the effect of qualities and actions—as is the case with the purchase of *soma*—the statement "He offers the *agnihotra*" serves as its purpose; for if statements such as "He offers with curd" were injunctions of distinct actions, it would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, when meaningfulness is possible, meaninglessness is not appropriate. And the statement "He pours the *āghāra* libation" is meaningful as an injunction of a sacrifice (*yāga*), provided that it is not [an injunction of a mere quality].

In that case, the sentences concerning "continuous" (*santata*) and so forth would be merely injunctions regarding the *upāṃśuyāja* itself. However, since it is established that [the sentence] is an injunction for a sacrifice,

and since that injunction for a sacrifice [specifies] that very sacrifice as having clarified butter (*ājya*) as its substance— either by being [already] possessed of a substance or by being without a substance [previously].
These sentences are intended to enjoin continuity and other qualities by relying on the *āghāra* (libation) that has already been established.

However, the author of the Bhāṣya has here raised a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by relying on an injunction regarding the substance. Since the substance is already established by the term "fourfold-drawn" (*caturgṛhīta*), he establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). In that regard, how can there be an injunction of clarified butter (*ājya*) for the *upāṃśuyāja* by means of the phrase "this is indeed the fourfold-drawn"? For the word *āghāra* cannot denote the *upāṃśuyāja*. [Objection: But surely it [denotes it] because the *upāṃśuyāja* consists of a substance that is poured as an *āghāra*.

Thus it is said that a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) results. It is replied: by the statement "this is indeed fourfold-drawn" (*caturgṛhītam*), this is taught—that one should perform the ritual action with fourfold-drawn clarified butter (*ājya*). And because that [action] is devoid of a specific substance [otherwise], it remains restricted to the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice itself. Since its substance is clarified butter, the word *āghāra* is merely a restatement of what is already established by the sense; thus there is no fault. And this has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya as follows:

"Whether the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based on an injunction regarding the substance or on an injunction regarding the refinement of the substance used for pouring, even so, the injunction [is established] by another scriptural authority."

"Because it is possible for the opponent's statement to be [otherwise] understood, the designation [of the term] as an injunction is untenable; therefore, it must be a name. He raises an objection against this very conclusion: "Why is this being said so incoherently? The proponent asks: "What is incoherent here?
The objector replies: "This is what is incoherent here:"

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) asserts that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) regarding the *darvihoma*. Furthermore, there is no such injunction as "to Agni and to Prajāpati" in the case of the *darvihoma*, nor is there an *āghāraṇa* offering in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
The proponent has stated: "Nor are *santata* and the others injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*.
He concludes: "This appears like the word 'ether' (*viyat*). He provides the resolution: "To this we reply:"

Under the view that these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), this injunction—"he offers the *agnihotra*"—applies specifically to the *darvihoma*; likewise, "he pours the *āghāra* libation" applies to the *upāṃśuyāja*. Consequently, since the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja* do not find a proximate substratum [for their respective qualities], the injunction of the deity "to Agni" and the injunction of continuity "he pours the *āghāra* continuously" both migrate to the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. And thus, because they are already enjoined by those two [injunctions], the *agnihotra*...

The sense is that it has been correctly stated that the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not tenable in the case of the word *āghāra*. Failing to understand this very point, the opponent objects: "In that case, the principle of 'being known from another source' (*tatprakhyatā*) is not the reason for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), because [in the case of] the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*, there is an injunction of a quality. Regarding this:

And [the phrase] "and that which for Agni" is not present [in those cases]. If it were suspected that the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) occurs in its own original location, then, because of the proximity there of the phrases "and that which for Agni" and so forth, the principle of "being designated by that" (tatprakhyatā) would serve as the reason in the final conclusion (siddhānta). However, regarding the Darvihoma and the Upāṃśuyāja, since there is no suspicion of an injunction of a quality, and because the phrases "and that which for Agni" and so forth are not proximate there, it is impossible to demonstrate that "there is another scriptural text designating that. The respondent says: "Certainly, it is the reason in the final conclusion. How so? The answer is: "The principle of being designated by that (tatprakhyatā) also [applies]."
For this is indeed a *darvihoma* itself.
In that view, even the injunction "to Agni" is a prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), because it depends upon a specific subject matter.
In that very case, it occurs just as in the statement "he performs the Agnihotra.

Just as, under the view that it is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), the sentence "he performs the Agnihotra" refers to the *darvihoma* by virtue of its dependence on a specific [material], so too does the phrase "that which is for Agni" [refer to it]. Likewise, the statement "he continuously pours the libation" (*santatam āghārayati*) also applies only to the *upāṃśuyāja*, because it requires a purposeful substance.
It is like [the injunction] "he offers the Āghāra-oblation" among the rules for the ritual preparations (*saṃskāra*).

He objects: "If, then, because of the existence of another scriptural statement describing that [same thing], it is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), then [the term] would also not be a name in the case of the *darvihoma* or the *upāṃśuyāja*."

In that case, it would follow that [the rule] applies only to those very *darvihomas* and to the *upāṃśuyāja*. He refutes this: "The 'beloved of the gods' (the opponent) does not understand what is not established."

The meaning is that [the opponent] is ignorant of logic (*nyāya*). Since the prescription of the quality (*guṇa*) is established from another source, and because once the prescription is established the name (*nāman*) is also [established], and because a name is not something to be prescribed—
given that the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) in "He offers the *agnihotra*" is what is being prescribed— what else could be understood from this sentence?

When the status of [the sentence] as an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) has been refuted, then it must be an injunction of an action (*karmavidhi*). And once the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) has been enjoined, the phrase "to Agni and to Prajāpati" remains applicable only to that specific context due to the force of the section (*prakaraṇa*). Consequently, by virtue of that very connection with the accessory, this name also belongs to that very other action which is to be enjoined by this injunction. Thus he says: "Therefore, it is established that this is the name of this very [action]. In the same way, when the injunction of an accessory in the case of "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*) has been refuted, what else could the injunction enjoin apart from the meaning of the verbal suffix?

He alone is capable; that very thing to be enjoined is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*), because of the connection between the substance and the deity, just like the root *harati* (to take) [is related to its object]. Thus it is with *yajati* (to sacrifice).

Just as in the case of the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara-praharaṇa*), there is a root *yaji* (to sacrifice) due to the connection between the substance and the deity, so too the pouring of the libation (*āghāraṇa*) is indeed a *yajati*. Therefore, qualities such as "continuous" (*santata*) and so forth also belong to that very [act]. Consequently, this term *āghāra* [also] refers to that.
It is established that [the word] "of that very [sacrifice]" refers to its name.

This being the case, what is the meaning of the phrase "he pours the āghāra continuously"? The meaning is: "he brings about the āghāra continuously. Now, if the injunction regarding the deity is contained in the words "to Agni," then how is there no split of the sentence (vākyabheda) here?
Because, insofar as [the text says] "to Agni and to Prajāpati," it prescribes multiple attributes in the form of Agni and Prajāpati.
It must indeed be so through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
He refutes this: "There is no split in the sentence known as the injunction of multiple qualities when there is the injunction of qualifiers for a single factor (*kāraka*).
This is its meaning.

For here, since Agni and Prajāpati are construed as qualifiers of a single factor called the deity, there is no injunction of multiple attributes regarding Prajāpati; how, then, could there be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)? Indeed, it is the injunction of another related entity that is termed "multiple attributes," not the injunction of a different substance.

For where there is an injunction of multiple related factors for an action that is not already connected [to another injunction], there is an injunction of multiple qualities (*anekaguṇavidhāna*); whereas where only a single factor related to the action is enjoined— provided, at most, that it is a single related factor residing in a substance.

That very object, which is composed of multiple substances, is the locus for the injunction of multiple qualities; it is not [the case] when that [object] is non-existent. And here, Agni and Prajāpati are taken as the substratum of the deity, not as the deity itself. Furthermore, it is the deity as related to the ritual action that is enjoined as being related to the ritual action, not [the deity] in isolation.

Because the deities are presiding [simultaneously], there is no split in the sentence. Furthermore, since the connection of the deity with the ritual action is established through each individual presiding presence, the repetition of the ritual action is also justified; thus, this constitutes a single instruction (*eka-śāstra*). And because of the word "and" (*ca*), this is faultless.
And there is the designation of that [single instruction].

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya first establishes that the words *śyena*, *iṣu*, and *saṃdaṃśa* are indeed names [of sacrifices]. Fearing that someone, being focused solely on the examples provided here, might think that *ājya* and others are not valid examples, he says: "In this case, the examples are conventional words (*rūḍhi-śabda*), such as *śyena*, *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and so forth. Now, what is the distinction between this section and the section concerning *udbhid*, by virtue of which this new section has been commenced? For just as in that [previous] case, the status of being a name for an action was asserted out of fear of implying a possessive indication (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), so too can it be maintained here.
Thus one may speak of its being on the side of etymological derivation (*nāmadheya-pakṣatā*). The reply is:

there is this distinction—that while *yoga* (etymological derivation) conforms to the occasion for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) regarding an action, *rūḍhi* (conventional usage), however, does not follow *yoga*.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding these words such as *ājyapṛṣṭha* and so forth, if they are taken as names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), their etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) must be asserted; whereas if they are taken as injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), they possess conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Conventional meaning is stronger than the etymological, because the etymological depends upon the application of its constituent parts (*yogānuvartitva*) and is thus dependent, while the conventional is independent. Therefore, rather than relying on conventional meaning, it is better to resort to the indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); thus, the status of these as injunctions of accessory qualities is again suspected here. Consequently, this [discussion] is connected with the section concerning the *udbhid* (the *udbhid-adhikaraṇa*).
This is the distinction: since words such as *udbhid* and others are etymological (*yaugika*) in both positions, how then is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) reached? It is said:

because the sentence is intent upon enjoining an action (*karma-vidhi*), it is improper to enjoin the meaning of the subordinate term (*upapada*). As for the fact that in some cases an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*) is resorted to, that is because the connection with another word has no other possible recourse. However, where there is an available, albeit delayed, etymological derivation, there is no justification for enjoining an action qualified by a quality by resorting to the indication of possessive sense (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*). Regarding this specific example, he raises an objection: "But surely..."

Even on the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), one need not assume that the term *śyena* follows its etymological derivation. Rather, even on the view that it is the name of a ritual action, one must accept a figurative designation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*) in the sense that "it is like a hawk, therefore it is a hawk. Furthermore, conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not preclude figurative usage, because figurative designation is rooted in conventional usage. Therefore, since the elision of the possessive suffix (*matub-lopa*) lacks any basis of proof, there is no possibility of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) being applicable there; rather, it is better to resort to figurative usage itself. [The author] refutes this: the venerable Commentator cited this very point in order to dispel such ignorance.

Precisely because a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is difficult to find in this example, for that very reason the Commentator has cited, among all the conventional (*rūḍhi*) words serving as examples, only those cases where even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) the status of being a conventional term is not lost. One might think, "This is not a valid example" due to the perception that no prima facie argument exists here. To show how a prima facie argument does indeed exist here, he says: "It is appropriate to say that in the case of *udbhid* and so forth, these are names (*nāmadheya*) by resorting to etymological derivation (*yoga*) out of fear of dropping the possessive suffix *-matup*. However, there is no loss of their status as conventional terms."

Resorting to another elision out of fear of an elision is not appropriate in the case of the secondary sense (*gauṇapakṣa*); for instance, resorting to the elision of the suffix *-vat* out of fear of the elision of the possessive suffix *-mat* in the word *śyena*.

For the application of figurative terms occurs through the elision [of a suffix]. Therefore, it is better to resort to the elision of the *matup* suffix itself, because [the word] is understood as being connected with its literal meaning.

In the view that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), only that literal meaning of the word *śyena* which is directly expressed by the Vedic text is connected with the ritual action; however, [in the other case], it is not [so connected].

Therefore, since the direct (śrauta) syntactical connection remains even when the possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided, that [direct connection] alone is logical; whereas in the figurative (*gauṇa*) view, the direct meaning lacks connection with the ritual action, and thus it is weak. Thus the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) was restated.
He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), which applies to all examples: It is said in reply—
It was stated that [the conventional meaning] follows [the etymological].
The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) says: "Just as the conventional meaning does not follow the etymological, so too the etymological does not [necessarily] follow the conventional."
It does not follow conventional usage at all.
Therefore, what is the distinction of conventionality when there is mutual non-following? He reveals the intention of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):
"But here..."
An established usage (*rūḍhi*) that has been current since ancient times, by virtue of its independence, sets aside the etymological derivation (*yoga*).
The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) states his own position:
"It is true that established usage would set aside the etymological derivation, provided that the meaning of the sentence were preceded by the comprehension of the [etymological] cause."

it would have to be understood as such. In that case, because the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) at the stage of the primary cause (*nimitta*) is stronger, there would be a subversion of the etymological connection (*yogāpahāritva*);
that is, the etymological connection would be abandoned. However, if the status of being a primary cause is preceded by the comprehension of the effect, then— [p.

Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not override the etymological derivation (*yoga*). When the purpose of the sentence is understood, the comprehension of that purpose resides solely in the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). When one pauses and subsequently pursues the causal factors (*nimitta*), then, because the sentence has a single meaning, only the meaning of the verbal root is to be enjoined; for if one were to resort to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*). In that case...

Therefore, when considering how a single meaning can be established, one must rely on *yoga* (etymological derivation) itself; thus, *rūḍhi* (conventional usage) does not override *yoga*. Now, even if the sentence is intent upon enjoining a single thing, why should it be intent solely upon enjoining a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)? He says:
"It pertains to the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*) and is dependent upon the verbal action."

Since the comprehension of the task (kārya) is the object of an injunction only when there is the sense of an action (bhāvārtha), an injunction is not possible regarding a mere quality (guṇa) in isolation;

therefore, because it is conducive to the comprehension of the task inherent in an action, the etymological derivation (yoga) is perceived first, and thus the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) is not accepted.

For even in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) of words such as *ājya* and others has been demonstrated—as in "Because they went toward the race (*ājim īyuḥ*), that is the essence of the *ājya*s," and so forth. Otherwise, the statement regarding their etymological nature in the supplementary passage would be groundless. In this regard:

The opponent objects: "It is appropriate that *ājya* and the like are names [of sacrifices], but how can the *śyena* be a name? The questioner’s underlying intention is this: a word is a name by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Now, even in its figurative sense, the word *śyena*, which denotes the genus of the hawk, cannot possess coreferentiality with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). However, in the case of *ājya* and the others, which are etymological (*yaugika*), their status as names is indeed established through coreferentiality. The reply:

Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the word *śyena* is also a name. Now, one might object that there is no such coreferentiality at all; to this he replies: "For grammatical coreferentiality remains uncontradicted even in cases of figurative designation (*gauṇābhidhāna*), because the meaning of the suffix *-vat* is what is being enjoined."

For if the meaning of the suffix -vat were not that which is to be enjoined, then, because it would be subordinate to that [suffix], there would be no subordination to the verb; consequently, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not occur. But when the meaning of -vat is not non-enjoined, but rather merely the occasion for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) toward the object, then, because it is subordinate to the object, grammatical coreferentiality arises, and thus the status of being a name (*nāmadheyatva*) is established.

[The suffix] *matup* occurs [in this context]. However, if there were an elision of *matup*, a difference of substratum (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*) would be unavoidable; for while the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is what is to be enjoined, the ritual action (*karman*) is also to be enjoined.

Therefore, because enjoining multiple meanings contradicts the comprehension of a single meaning, it is better that there be an elision of the suffix *vat* rather than an elision of *matup*. Thus, its status as a name (*nāmadheya*) is established.
[The same applies] to the word *śyena* as well.
[This is so] because of the mention of a quality (*guṇa*) within a name (*nāmadheya*). For what purpose is this section?
[It is so that we may determine whether it is] a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), as long as that possibility might be entertained.

In that case, this section would be intended for the purpose of refuting that [position], yet such a possibility does not exist. For it has been established that names consist of both etymological (*yaugika*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings derived from their literal sense. Furthermore, it is possible to assert the status of "being designated by that" (*tatprakhyatā*) in the case of the *vājapeya*, because of the injunction regarding the cups of *surā* liquor. That *surā* would be of the nature of a drink, since it is so prescribed.

Because the form of the word (*peya*) has been prescribed as *vāja*. He states the rebuttal: "This section implies all [the preceding topics] during the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
He asks "Why? and answers: "Because of the presentation of a single mention (*tantra*) for the sacrifice.
By means of a single mention, the sacrifice offers itself for its own sake toward both the result and the quality.

Now, one might object that even because of the consequence of mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), the single mention should be abandoned; to this he replies: "And even when there is an injunction of a quality, under the view of a single mention, the word remains entirely independent."

Since both the status of being that which is enjoined (*vidheya*) and the status of being the subject of reference (*uddeśyatva*) are understood from a single utterance alone, and since it is possible for that very thing being enjoined to simultaneously possess the status of being the subject of reference, there is no requirement for another substratum (*āśrayāntara*) in the case of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); thus, the designation [of the word] as a name (*nāmābhidhāna*) is not tenable. Therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute the theory of simultaneous denotation (*tantrābhidhāna*). If that is so, then words such as *udbhid* would themselves be examples here; consequently, the point is that the citation of other examples would be redundant. He answers: "Certainly. (*bāḍham*)... [the text continues].
The *udbhid* and others are also examples here. The objector asks:

"Why, then, was only 'one desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*' cited as an example? He replies: "This is like the objection regarding the *śiṃśapā* tree; for even when the *udbhid* and others are cited as examples, one could likewise ask why the *udbhid* alone is cited."
Therefore, this objection which we raise is indeed not to be challenged. And he states another solution: "A certain distinction can also be stated here—that it is because the two actions are equal."

By this sūtra, the mention of the *dīkṣā*, *upasad*, and so forth refers specifically to what occurs within the Vājapeya; therefore, the Vājapeya is cited there in order to demonstrate the reason for its superiority.

Now, if this is the case, one might object that according to the evidence of the scriptural text (*darśana*), the Vājapeya alone was intended by the author of the sūtra as the illustrative example; to this, he says:

And that perception as well has all things as its object; since perception preceded by reasoning has all things as its object, and reasoning is uniform everywhere, perception too must have all things as its object.
