For this very reason, this section is meaningful because it refutes the designation [of the system] as a "tantra" (manual). Therefore, this is stated:
In this case, the position that [the term] is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) is indeed superior.

Why is it superior? To this he says: for in this way, the word-meaning such as "udbhid" becomes something connected with the action to be performed (kārya). On the other hand, under the position that it is a name (nāmadheya), the word-meaning would be merely the ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta).
Why? The answer [p.
because of that which has been prescribed.

On the view that it is the name of the ritual action, "udbhitva" means being denotable by the word "udbhit," but not the injunction (vidhāna) of the udbhid [sacrifice] itself. Therefore, it is not the cause for engagement [in the action].

Therefore, on the view that names are the cause, the mention of the cause would not be for the purpose of instigating action, whereas the sentence is for the purpose of instigating action; thus, there would be an inconsistency between the effect and the cause.

There would be a contradiction, for the action (*kārya*) consists of activity (*pravṛtti*), whereas the cause (*nimitta*) consists of a name (*nāman*). However, under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), that contradiction does not exist; therefore, the injunction of a quality is superior. But [it may be objected]:
in the case of an injunction of a quality, there is the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
It was stated in the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa* that [the word] must be accepted as having no literal meaning; he refutes this by saying: "That very [meaning] does not exist.
How does it not exist?
The answer is: for the meaning of the verb is understood as having a single form even within the relationship of cause and effect.
Whether it is understood as an effect or as a cause, the meaning of the verb is apprehended by one and the same form; it is indeed that which is being brought into existence.

For the meaning of the verbal root does not constitute the means (*sādhana*). When both [the root-meaning and the nominal stem-meaning] are understood, why should there be an indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)? Because the relationship is understood through a non-co-referential connection: "The sacrifice is to be performed by means of the *udbhid*, and by that sacrifice, cattle [are obtained]. Therefore, this meaning is established: "By means of the *vājapeya* [there is] a sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice, self-sovereignty."

There is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). But if this were the case, there would be a clear syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); to this he replies: "The expression is otherwise because of observation."

In ultimate reality, however, that which possesses the nature of both the probandum and the probans is expressed all at once by the verb. Thus it is said: "In the comprehension of the meaning of a word, there is no perception of distinction. But surely this is a property of the thing itself?

The meaning is that since it is only while being accomplished (*sādhyamāna*) that something becomes a means (*sādhana*), the word [itself] is not a property; thus, the word cannot denote both states simultaneously—that [the result] is "sovereignty through sacrifice" (*yāgena svārājyam*). For otherwise, the word would make it understood as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and otherwise as something to be referred to (*uddeśya*).
He refutes this: "True; however, because it possesses both natures, it is expressed in that way.
Even though both are denoted, the word 'yajeta' (one should sacrifice) is capable of conveying the two related entities because it possesses both natures."
Because the sacrifice possesses the nature of both the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), it is denoted by the word exactly as it is;
for although it is expressed as having both forms, it is nevertheless [denoted] as being related to both the result and the accessory (*guṇa*).

But the word "he should sacrifice" (yajeta) is capable of conveying [the connection] between the two related parties; if it is capable, then the injunction of a subordinate element (guṇavidhi) is established.

And validity is established. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "It is not so; for those two related elements—the result and the quality—are incapable of being connected with the sacrifice.

Indeed, the result is not capable of being connected with that which consists of both the goal and the means. Nor is the quality [capable], because the result is connected only with the means, and the quality is connected only with the goal. If they were capable of being connected,"
There being nothing,
what capacity for designation will it exercise?
Therefore, because each is capable of being related [to the result] individually, they are mentioned here separately.
Consequently, since two distinct meanings are enjoined, this sentence results in two separate functions: "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice" (*yajeta svārājyakāmaḥ*).
The injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vājapeya" would be mutually disconnected.

If this were so, what would happen? The answer is: the understanding of mutual connection would be abandoned; and a meaning that is not understood would have to be assumed. Thus, this very state of dependence arises. For otherwise, the assumption of a meaning not understood from the words would not be tenable. Now, regarding the claim that syntactic unity is achieved by resorting to the indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), he says: "And the indication of possessive sense is contradictory. Therefore, by the arguments stated in the *Udbhid* section and the *Tatprakhya* section...

Furthermore, the arguments were stated in the section concerning that designation; by those arguments, the position that it is a name is indeed the correct one. As for the inconsistency regarding the cause and the effect mentioned in the sentence, that does not exist, because there is no contradiction.

There is no inconsistency because the sign (nimitta) does not obstruct the effect. [Objection: But surely there is indeed inconsistency even if it is not conducive to action; to this he replies: "Inconsistency exists in the case of obstruction, not in the case of being non-conducive.
Although the name is not conducive to activity, nevertheless there is no inconsistency; such is the meaning.
Therefore, there is no fault;
there is no fault characterized by a contradiction between the effect and its cause.
As for its qualities: for what purpose is this section (adhikaraṇa) commenced?
A partisan (ekadeśin) offers the answer: "What is this question?
Is it not already known that the offerings to Agni and others are injunctions of qualities (guṇavidhi) and not names?"

The objector refutes this: It is correct that terms which are etymological (*yaugika*), those whose meaning is obtained through derivation, and those that are conventional (*rūḍhi*) function as names; however, the status of being a name is not possible in the case of "the *āgneya* [cake] on eight potsherds.
Why? He says: For the status of being a name was stated [only] because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of a verb.

In a sentence whose primary purport is the injunction of the meaning of a verb, since it is impossible for another thing to be the object of that injunction, even the other words must have the meaning of the verb as their primary purport; for this reason, they are called "nouns" (nāman). One might ask: "Let it be so; nevertheless, what follows? To this he replies: "And here, even the verb 'bhavati' (it exists) does not have the sense of an action (bhāvārtha), because its meaning is not something to be enjoined. This verb 'bhavati' does not have the sense of an action. Why is it not the sense of an action? To this it is said: "Because its meaning is not something to be enjoined."

If the meaning of the word *bhava* (being) were also of the nature of an existent entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), why would it not be of the nature of something to be enjoined (*vidheya*)? Yet it is not something to be enjoined; therefore, because it is not something to be enjoined, we understand that it does not have the sense of an existent action. Since it does not have the sense of an existent action, the sentence lacks the intent to enjoin that [action], and thus [the status of the term] remains as before. For if there were the sense of an existent action, the sentence would be intent on what is to be enjoined, and through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that, the designation of the word *āgneya* as a name (*nāmadheya*) would be established. Furthermore, there is no other reason for its being a name than the aforementioned form of coreferentiality with the meaning of the verbal root (*ākhyāta*) being enjoined.
With this intention, our question is:
"For what purpose is this section (*adhikaraṇa*) commenced? The meaning is that because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is weak, this section should not be commenced. The respondent says:
To this it is replied: here again, the very same dependence is suspected.

Having raised the objection regarding the dependence of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced in order to state its independence in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). The meaning is that it ought to be commenced.

This is the meaning. How is dependence [on another] suspected? The answer is: just as the status of being a name is not possible because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verbal action, so too the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) is not possible because no verbal action is heard.
For an injunction of a quality is dependent upon a verbal action; and here, no verbal action is heard.

When this would be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) based on something else, and when neither the status of an injunction of a quality nor the status of a name (*nāmatva*) is possible, then, due to the absence of any other alternative, the consequence of non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*) follows. And that [non-authoritativeness] does not belong to the word by its very nature, but rather is produced by its being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*). By virtue of being of human origin—

And therefore, because of the consequence of being of human origin, the entire collection of the Veda would necessarily depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: But surely, since the *Āgneya* [sacrifice] is heard as a connection between a substance and a deity, and since that [connection] is not possible without the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), the meaning of the verbal root must be the meaning of the action (*bhāvārtha*).

And therefore, in that case, either a name or an injunction of qualities is indeed possible. How [then] could there be a lack of authority? The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: "That is true, if a connection between a substance and a deity were heard in the text. The objector says: "But surely 'āgneya' (belonging to Agni) is what is heard."
The proponent says: "True, provided that it were not concerned with the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake baked on eight potsherds).

For the *aṣṭākapāla* is heard [in scripture] as belonging to Agni (*āgneya*). Since that [connection] is not possible here, the relationship between the substance and the deity would indeed be virtually unheard of. The objector asks: "If it were indeed concerned with the *aṣṭākapāla*..."

There would be a connection between the substance and the deity; what follows from that? The sense is that the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) would indeed possess the character of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatva*). The proponent states the reply: "From this it follows that the status of being an eight-potherd cake must be understood as unenjoined, because it is [merely] the object of reference (*uddeśya*)."

And there is no cake baked on eight potsherds that has not been prescribed. But surely that which is cooked on eight potsherds will be the referent— whether it be worldly or based on the scriptural injunction "he cooks it on potsherds"— and thus it will be designated as *aṣṭākapāla*.

The meaning of this is as follows: Alternatively, let it not be that the worldly [fire] is the intended referent because of the statement "he cooks in the potsherds"; rather, let it be based solely on the scriptural injunction. In any case, by this very statement, the status of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) can be established even for that which has not been previously enjoined.
The proponent refutes this: first of all, it cannot be based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), because the number eight is heard [in the text].

For indeed, without an injunction for the number eight, the state of being prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapālatā*) is not obtained. If it is argued that that number itself is what is enjoined, he refutes this:

—No, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). [It would result in the position that] the number is dependent on the *āgneya*, and the *āgneya* is dependent on the number.

[Specifically,] by way of restating the *āgneya*, the number eight would have to be enjoined: "That which is *āgneya* must be made into an eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*)," and likewise, "that which is an eight-potherd cake is *āgneya*."
B. Regarding the "conjunction with a deity" (*devatāsamyoga*):

since the quality of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) is expressed by way of reference to the eight-potsherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*), a prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is therefore not possible. Nor indeed...
It has been stated that [the cognition] arises;

therefore, it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*). If the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) was intended to show a lack of authority, then why did the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) say, "How indeed [could it be]?"? The respondent says: "Where was it said?"

The objector says: It was stated in the introduction whether this is a name or an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). This was presented at the time of the doubt. In that regard, "it is a name" is the formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while "it is an injunction of a quality" is the formulation of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Thus, at the time of adopting the prima facie view, there is a negation of the injunction of a quality.
And by performing [the action], it is stated that, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is a name (*nāmadheya*).
He provides the resolution: "It is true that it has been stated to be a name, but not..."

The meaning is that it has not been stated that "this is the name of the verbal root-meaning which is to be performed. What, then, has been stated? He says: "By the mention of the name, its status as a well-known referent is demonstrated."

The term *āgneya* does not function as a predicate (*vidheya-artha*), but rather as a well-known referent (*prasiddha-artha*), as it has been stated that even a name functions as a well-known referent. One might ask: "Granted that this is so, how is its dependence (*sāpekṣatā*) demonstrated? To this he replies:
"And since such well-known status is not possible without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), the dependence of the usage has been shown."

He states the established conclusion: this would indeed be so if there were a mutual dependence between the connection with number and the connection with the deity. But that is not the case. [Objection:
But surely this [mutual dependence] does exist.
[Question: How is it not so? [Answer: Because the injunction regarding the deity applies to the eight-potherd [cake].

He recalls the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "But was it not stated that this [self] is not well-known? The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) says: "Is it not well-known even as something denotable?"

The meaning is that it is well-known as something denotable. And it is by relying on its renown as a denotation that its injunction is possible. The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says: it is not well-known as something denotable, but rather as something to be accomplished (kārya).

Since it is stated that "the cake on eight potsherds must be prepared," its lack of established status is asserted. The final conclusion (rāddhānta) says: this very lack of established status as something to be produced is indeed desired; for it is precisely because it lacks established status as something to be produced that [it is so].

It is thus established. He concludes: Therefore, the non-establishment of the designation [of the term] subverts its injunction; however, it is not the non-establishment of its being something to be produced (kāryatā) that does so. Consequently, just as in the case of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), there is an injunction regarding the meaning of "eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*) as well. Furthermore, the fact that [the meaning] is understood through a well-known designation has been demonstrated by the Commentator when he says, "one does not take what has been cooked by another.
For if the meaning were unknown, the taking of what was cooked by another would not even be a possibility that required refutation by such a statement. [This applies] to the potsherds (*kapāleṣu*).

Because of the statement "he cooks," one does not take what has been cooked by another; therefore, this meaning of the *taddhita* suffix is also well-established, just like the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Just as the meaning of the root *yaj* is established through direct expression when there is the explicit hearing of the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), so too is the meaning of the *taddhita* suffix established. Consequently, there is no risk of it being dependent [on something else].
Because independence is established through the injunction of an action qualified by specific qualities;
nor is there, in this case, the possibility of the matter being already established— as is the case with the eight-pot-sherd offering in relation to the *agnihotra*.

Thus, it is also prescribed that just as in the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra," the deity Agni is not being enjoined because the deity Agni is already established, so too it is not possible here [to enjoin the deity]. Furthermore,
this [text] expresses a well-known meaning.
[Page 234] Regarding the *barhis* and the clarified butter (*ājya*):
what, then, is the intermediate connection? To this he says: "This section is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*)."
What, then, is the logical consequence here? The answer is: even with a meaning that is to be enjoined, the connection of the noun-meaning is observed, as in the case of "the eight-potherd [cake]";
furthermore, this word *ājya* is also seen in common usage to be based solely on the action [of preparation].
In common usage, this word *ājya* is based on the process of refinement (*saṃskāra*).

It is observed that the word *ājya* is employed only in the state of being consecrated (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, this [word] also is connected with the action (*kāryānvayī*). The connection of the word *ājya* with the purpose of the action means it is connected as something to be produced (*kāryatayā’nvayī*). The meaning of the word *ājya* is thus connected with the action. He demonstrates this very point: "One should make *ājya* by means of consecration. The meaning is:
"One should consecrate the *ājya* by means of melting."

But surely, even the word *ājya* is seen in certain regions to be used without reference to a ritual action, as in the expressions "ghee for sale" (*ājyaṃ krayyam*) and "having taken the sacrificial grass, the cows have gone.
Therefore, how can it be said with certainty that [the term] is based solely on a preparatory ritual (*saṃskāra*)?

It can be determined. He refutes [the objection]: indeed, the usage that is heard in the Veda ought to be universal (*sārvabhauma*). Usage that originates from only one region and is based on grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) cannot be universal. First, for those who employ words in the refined (*saṃskṛta*) form, their usage is based on refinement;
whereas for those who do not employ a word when refinement is absent, it is not so.

For them, it is quite clear that [the word] has the conditioned (*saṃskāra*) as its cause. Even those who employ it solely for the genus (*jāti*) employ it with respect to the conditioned; thus, its having the conditioned as its object is universal. And that alone is the Vedic usage. As for its denoting the genus in a particular instance, that is figurative (*gauṇa*).
Why is this so? The answer is: because of what is well-known (*prasiddha*).
For a word can possess a figurative sense only when its primary meaning is well-established, not when it is unknown;
for just as the word "fire," being well-known in the sense of a blazing flame, becomes used figuratively for a young boy by virtue of similarity to him, so it is for all [words].

Since the status of being the cause of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is well-established, the usage [of the term *saṃskṛta*] in the sense of "mere birth" is secondary, occurring in only one part of its meaning. However, for those who maintain that the term is used only in the sense of "that which is conditioned," the usage is primary because there is no other usage. Furthermore, this term is not universally established as denoting clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
And for that which is not so established, it is not logical for it to have a secondary meaning when applied to clarified butter elsewhere.

Those who consider sound to have its cause in *saṃskāra* (mental impression) do not employ a word even for another class (*jātyantara*) [of the object]; in that case, it is not appropriate for it to be figurative (*gauṇa*), because a primary usage (*mukhyaprayoga*) is not observed elsewhere. On the other hand, if its cause were action (*karman*), then when it is employed for a single part, such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*)...

Even in the case of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), since there is usage there based on the cause of action (*karmanimittaka*), the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) is established; for elsewhere, the primary usage (*mukhyaprayoga*) is established, as in the case of the word "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*). Therefore, because words such as *ājya* have their basis in preparation (*saṃskāra*), it is logical that they refer solely to the ritual purpose (*kāryārthatā*). To this it is replied: connection [of the word] with the ritual purpose is not tenable, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). [This is seen in the case of] the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
"The sprinkling of the existent, and with the sprinkling, the sacrificial grass (barhis).

Indeed, that which is consecrated by means of sprinkling and so forth is called "barhis. Since sprinkling and other rites are enjoined with reference to the barhis, it is not known to what [specific substance] they apply.

[The opponent says: "Sprinkling and so forth are enjoined. [The author asks: "If that is so, there is mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva). How then is there no mutual dependence in the case of the 'eight-potherd' (aṣṭākapāla) cake?

The answer is: "There is no mutual dependence because the designation is established through conventional usage (prasiddhi)," as it has been stated. But here, the designation arises solely from the function (kārya).
Thus, there is a discrepancy regarding the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), however, asks: "How is it with respect to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)? For it is heard in scripture: 'He fashions the sacrificial post'."

Furthermore, the word *yūpa* denotes a ritual action (*kārya*) and a consecration (*saṃskāra*); in that case, the mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident. Since there is no established knowledge from any other source, this is a recourse when no other way is possible (*agatikā gatiḥ*).
Just as in the case of *barhis* and so forth, there is establishment from another source because usage is observed for the mere genus (*jāti*), so it is here.

Since it does not exist in the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and since there is no other alternative course, this resort to a desperate measure is adopted: namely, that one makes the post by means of carving whatever is fit for carving and whatever constitutes the act of carving. What kind of desperate measure is this? He says in a single sentence: "Is it not understood from the scripture itself?"

The intention is this: if it were understood from the scripture, then the same would apply to the *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and other items as well. The answer is: when there is common worldly usage (*prasiddhi*), it is not understood from scripture; where something is already established through another source, it is not proper to employ a general term, because only the specific meaning is understood. In that case, this understanding derived from scripture is not perceived; that which is fit for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and serves as the object of the act of sprinkling is the *barhis*.

"That [substance] is consecrated by sprinkling. However, when the meaning of a word is not already established, because the purpose of the injunction remains unobstructed, it is postulated; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the injunction's purpose being frustrated. As for what was said—that a metaphorical application for a universal monarch (sārvabhauma) is impossible—[that is not so].

Regarding the argument that "because the Vedic sense is not well-known," and that a figurative sense is possible only when [the primary sense] resides in a specific part [of the word], it is replied here: worldly people do not necessarily employ a figurative sense only for a Vedic meaning that is already well-established, as is the case with the word *rājan*. For instance, even non-Aryans use the word *rājan* despite its Vedic meaning being unfamiliar to them.
Likewise, they employ figurative expressions such as the word *barhis* (sacrificial grass). He raises an objection: "In that case, the same fault applies even to the word *rājan* (king).

He says in a single passage: "For they employ a figurative expression for the purpose of conveying a resemblance to the primary object; even when it is not perceived as that [primary object], it is figurative."
To say that [a word] is "employed" [in this way] is a forced interpretation (*haṭha*);

for a secondary (*gauṇa*) term is employed precisely to convey a similarity to the primary meaning. Since that similarity cannot be known if the primary meaning itself is not understood, the employment of a secondary term would be without cause in the absence of a cognition of such similarity.

"It is without cause. To this it is replied: "The relationship between a word and its meaning does not depend upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); rather, it is the relationship that depends upon the intention.
The meaning of this is as follows: although the speaker employs [the word] with a figurative understanding and the person being addressed likewise understands it, nevertheless, a bystander...

A child, not having observed the usage [of a word] in its primary sense, understands only that [usage] as being primary. Having understood it thus, he would also engage in linguistic practice accordingly. Therefore, for a bystander, the relationship between a word and its meaning does not depend on the speaker’s intention; rather, at the time of linguistic practice, the bystander intends exactly that same primary relationship between word and meaning which he has apprehended. This very point is demonstrated by means of an example:

He demonstrates this: for it is said in the *Gopotalikā* and other texts that, due to the lack of understanding that [the word] is not produced by a [real] capacity, people employ it as if it were an eternal word (*anādi-śabda*), just like the word "beginningless" (*anādi*). Thus...
Furthermore, because the intention (*vivakṣā*) of some speaker is not fully understood, a mother may employ a word in a different sense that is devoid of her intended meaning.

This occurs when someone who knows the primary meaning of a word as referring to a genus (*jāti*) employs it figuratively (*gauṇa*) based on a partial similarity; thus, even with respect to something not belonging to that genus, the word is applied due to its connection with a figurative mental impression (*gauṇasaṃskāra*).

The word *barhis* and others have been employed here; for one who does not know their primary meaning, there is an intention to convey a secondary (gauṇa) meaning. Thus, for one who is unaware [of the primary sense], the cognition of the primary meaning proceeds. Just as in the case of "cow-calf" (*gopotalikā*) and similar terms, those who do not know [the etymology] have a cognition of beginninglessness (*anāditva*), which arises from incapacity [to understand the derivation], and upon that basis, the linguistic usage of word and meaning proceeds. But how is this understood?

[Objection: This primary linguistic usage regarding the term *saṃskṛta* (refined/processed) is based on error. [Reply: No, because such usage is observed both in common worldly practice (*loka*) and in the Veda (*veda*). Regarding the Veda first: having prescribed *ājya* (clarified butter), it sometimes praises it using the word *ghṛta*.

In that context, if the word *ājya* were to denote the specific refinement (*saṃskāra*), then in that praise the word *ghṛta* would have to be used as a mere figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). However, if it denotes the genus (*jāti*), then it retains its own primary meaning. Therefore, by examining the Veda, it is determined that [the word] indeed denotes the genus.
In common usage as well, there is the expression "the clarified butter (*ājya*) is for sale," "it is for sale," which is independent of any specific action.

This usage is observed even in the world to be independent of that for which the action is the means—that is, independent of that whose means is the action itself in the form of a consecration (*saṃskāra*). But surely, in those cases too, there is an unstated intention (*avivakṣitatva*)?
It can be said:
A. Even though the word primarily denotes the *saṃskṛta* (the refined), it is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) due to its connection with that;
or, even if it denotes the mere act of refinement (*saṃskāra*), it is used figuratively for the genus (*jāti*) simply by virtue of its fitness for that.

In that case, B., having been engaged [in debate], might not fully comprehend the intended meaning (vivakṣā); and because of this lack of comprehension of the intended meaning, it can also be said that for someone, a cognition of the primary sense has indeed arisen. Therefore, [p.

How is the certainty established? He provides the answer: "The resolution regarding reeds and so forth has already been stated. Furthermore, when there is a conflict regarding the nature of the genus (*jāti*) and its refinement (*saṃskāra*), or a conflict regarding the worldly usage of objects, the determination is made through the commonality with Vedic usage.

Therefore, here too, because of the similarity with Vedic usage, the primary sense (*mukhyatā*) applies to the genus (*jāti*). However, regarding the word *saṃskṛta*, its secondary usage (*gauṇaḥ prayogaḥ*) arises from its connection with the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belonging to that [genus]. If this is so, then the matter is already settled by that very same section (*adhikaraṇa*). It is replied: this section is commenced to dispel the doubt that a secondary usage can only occur for one who already knows the primary usage. As for the examples, both *barhis* and *vetasa* apply in both cases. But what is the relevance of this incidental discussion?

What is the purpose of defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The answer is: it is precisely to avoid non-determination; that is, to avoid non-determination regarding the meaning of words.

In the linguistic usage of words, there might otherwise be a lack of determination as to which [meaning] is primary and which is secondary. Consequently, because of this non-determination even in the case of the Veda, its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) would follow. Therefore, non-determination is indeed the motivating factor for the formal discussion (*adhikaraṇa*). But surely, by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)...

The distinction has been shown only with respect to the object (*karman*), not with respect to the cognition (*avagati*). He refutes this: precisely because there is a distinction regarding the object, for that very reason non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) is the purpose;
non-determination is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the formal inquiry (*adhikaraṇa*) for the sake of its cessation. If there were no distinction regarding the object...

In that case, there would be no distinction in practice; and due to the absence of a distinction in practice, there would be a lack of determination (*anadhyavasāya*) which cannot be removed—this is not a fault. To eliminate this, the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been commenced. However, if there is certainty (*niścaya*), then because of the presence of determination, the purpose is indeed established.

[Page 240] Regarding the *prokṣaṇī* waters: for what purpose is this a separate section? The answer is: an exception to the rules of application, based on traditional scripture (*smṛti*), is stated concerning those rites that occur universally and those that occur in only one part.

The application [of words] based on *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement) is universal, whereas that based on *jāti* (genus) originates from only one part [of the usage]. Having considered the recollection (*smṛti*) of these two, the exception is stated: that the word *prokṣaṇī* is etymological (*yaugika*). He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"But how can an exception to the application be stated on the basis of recollection, since the grammatical recollection has its root in actual usage? How [can it override it]?"

The sense is that [the opponent] is refuting the application [of the rule]. He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): For the application is indeed compatible with the traditional scripture (*smṛti*).
Indeed, an application that conforms to the scripture is certainly possible. Why? He says: because the connection of both parts is possible.
Even he who...

The application [of a term] based on a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is possible there, as is the application based on a genus (*jāti*). Consequently, since the application is not incompatible with *yoga* (etymological derivation), it does not sublate it; thus, in the case of "place the *prokṣaṇī* waters," the application is based on a refinement.
"We are distressed by the sprinkling waters"— this is based on the [caste] species. Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the determination is made according to the Smṛti.
The remainder has been stated.
Likewise regarding the *nirmanthya* fire. What is added here?

The answer is: this is excessive here. The traditional rule (*smṛti*) is also over-extensive, because we observe its application even when [the fire] has been churned not long ago, and likewise, we observe its application even when it is unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*).

"Let us cook it while it is being churned"—in this case, there is no basis for the term being a *saṃskāra-nimitta* (based on a preparatory refinement). Likewise, its status as a *yaugika* (etymological) term is also not possible, because we observe its usage even when the fire has been churned only recently; if it were etymological, its usage would apply only to that which has been churned for a long time.

It might be so; however, it cannot have "fire" as its cause, because it is used for fire in general. Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that there is no definitive conclusion even on the basis of traditional usage (smṛti).
He states the final conclusion: because the Smṛti text expresses the term without distinction, it is not capable of obstructing its specific application.
For if, in the Smṛti, the word *nirmanthya* were established as correct for both wood that has been rubbed for a long time and wood that has been rubbed recently...
If it were remembered [at that time], then the specific application would obstruct that memory; but this is not the case.

If it is argued that "it obstructs non-specific knowledge," meaning that the application obstructs the non-specific knowledge derived from memory, [the author] refutes this: it does not obstruct it, because the non-specific [knowledge] is already concluded by the specific [application].

If that which is non-distinctive in the Smṛti were to be applied as a distinctive feature by the force of usage, then there would be no fault. Therefore, this case is like the previous one; thus it was said, "Therefore, so it is," regarding the Vaiśvadeva. But how, again, does a doubt arise here concerning whether it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) or a name (nāmadheya)?

To the extent that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), it is more appropriate here for [the term] to be a name (*nāmadheya*). The reply: In this case, grammatical coreferentiality is more appropriately established under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Since the meaning of the verbal root is the primary sense of the suffix, it is not appropriate for it to be a name; rather, the view that it is an injunction of a quality is indeed more reasonable. Furthermore, even in the case of an injunction of a quality, there is no need for the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), because in the expression "the sacrifice of which Viśvedevas are the deity" (*viśvedevā devatā asya yāgasya*), the suffix has the sacrifice itself as its primary meaning, and thus coreferentiality is established through its primary sense. He objects again: If the injunction of a quality is indeed more reasonable, why...

The presentation by way of a name provides the resolution: because of the absence of a subject, a prescription of a quality is not tenable, since there is no subject for the quality to be prescribed. Why is there an absence of a subject? The answer is: by [the mention of] Agni and so forth.

Because the deities of the rites under discussion are already secured by the Vedic texts, those very rites that are under discussion are occupied by Agni and others who are enjoined by their original injunctions (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*); therefore, another deity cannot be prescribed therein. If it is impossible to prescribe another deity in the context of the established rites...

In that case, why does this not constitute a distinct ritual qualified by a deity? That too is not determined, because the *āmikṣā* dedicated to Viśvedevas is the subject under discussion. For in the injunction of a distinct ritual, there would be an injunction of a qualification—that is, an injunction of a qualified entity—and such occurs only when no other alternative is possible.

[This would be] logical if it existed; however, there is another possibility here: because of its association with the *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā* sacrifice, it can be construed as a name for the sacrifices under discussion by means of the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) logic. Therefore, even the status of being a name is not possible here, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established even through an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Nor is it an injunction of a quality, because the sacrifices under discussion are already restricted by qualities prescribed at their origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*). Thus he says: "Therefore, it is not a name."
Nor can independence with respect to qualities be understood;
such is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). A proponent of a partial conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*) says:
"If you think that it is impossible to determine independence, then let the determination be made through the injunction of qualities."

Because the relationship between the meanings of nouns and verbs is understood in that way. [Objection: But was it not stated that there is no object [for such a relationship]? [The author] refutes this: "That was poorly stated. [Objection: Again he asks: "In what way was it poorly stated?"
The answer: For the postulation of an effect arises from scripture, not scripture from the effect.

What is this that is being said? The answer: This and this; for the obstruction by a quality prescribed at the time of origin is the cause of non-comprehension, but not the sublation of what has already been comprehended.

The contradiction lies solely in the comprehension of a connection with another quality due to the obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origin; it does not, however, effect the sublation of what has already been comprehended. Even if this were so, he asks "What then?"—this word *vaiśvadeva* applies only to the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) in the context, and not to Agni and the others. [This is] in order to prevent the related meaning of the verb from being excluded from being denoted by the word *vaiśvadeva*.
[They are] capable.
He says [this] with a single passage: B. another related entity.

They preclude the status of being the object of another related entity, but they do not preclude the status of being denotable. What follows from this? The answer is: consequently, for the sake of establishing the denotability, Agni and the others—who are connected by way of origin—do not obstruct the attainment of another deity as a different related entity; just as [they do not obstruct] in the case of being something to be consecrated.

Since the consumption [of the *phalacamasa*] is connected as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of what remains from the sacrifice—an impossibility otherwise—the fact that the *phalacamasa* is a means of accomplishing the sacrifice is implied; thus, Soma does not obstruct it. Therefore, for the sake of establishing its designation by the heard term *vaiśvadeva*, one must postulate a function for the Viśvedevas.

It is logical; the meaning is that their inclusion as deities within the sacrifices under discussion is appropriate. However, the accomplishment of the sacrifice itself is not their function, for that is already accomplished by Agni and the others. Considering this, it is not reasonable to assume that the status of being denoted by the term *vaiśvadeva*—which is directly heard in the scripture—is otherwise than what it is, nor to assume that its referent is anything other than its true meaning. Since the connection as a deity is for the sake of making the designation possible, therefore, when the performance is carried out together with Agni and the others...
Because it is independent of conceptual construction, determination is logical;
[the author] states the final established conclusion: "If this is so..."

The assumption of a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is merely for the sake of establishing the application of the word; if that is so, let it be simply a name (*nāmadheya*). For it is for the purpose of making the designation possible that there is a connection with another quality.
It is conceptualized because it lacks logical justification. However, for those things enjoined by unequal means of knowledge, there is no such conceptualization;

for while Agni and others are enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), the Viśvedevas are enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*). In that case, the injunction is logically consistent as being a name (*nāmadheya*). But [one might object]: "Is it not so..."

If [the name] were a mere designation (*nāmadheya*), the meaning of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), being understood, would not be connected to the ritual action (*kārya*). For the meaning of the constituent parts—namely, that the Viśvedevas constitute the deity (*devatātva*) as perceived through that meaning—would then be unconnected to the ritual action; this is the sense. He refutes this: "It is not logical for that which is already connected to be further connected. And this meaning is already connected to the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture); therefore, the lack of connection with the ritual action is not capable of precluding the status of a name."

Even when it is connected in one instance and unconnected in another, its status as a name is established by the logic of the "man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*); thus, its function as a causal indicator (*nimitta*)—like the staff itself—is not contradictory.
Therefore, an option (*vikalpa*) cannot be postulated, nor can there be a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the ritual act. Consequently, it is logical to determine that this is a name (*nāmadheya*).
But how, then, is there the designation "vaiśvadeva" for the sacrifice to Agni and the others within the *vaiśvadeva* [section]?

[The objection is: "It is established [that the word denotes the substance] because, while it is devoid of a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the case of a quality-injunction, such a basis for application exists due to the re-enactment [of the injunction]. He refutes this: "That is true, provided that it is established solely through the act of enjoining; however, in the case of *āmikṣā*, there would be the undesirable consequence of its not being denoted [by the word]."

For since the Viśvedevas are already established in relation to the *āmikṣā*, they cannot be the object of an injunction; thus, the application of the term [the name of the sacrifice] as something to be enjoined does not succeed in an absolute sense. Now, one might argue that by abandoning the *āmikṣā* [as the primary referent], the designation as the object of an injunction will succeed; to this he says: "And the state of being the subject matter is equal [for both];
therefore, the sacrifice of *āmikṣā* is not [the intended meaning]."
It cannot be avoided. Here, an objection is raised: "Which of these two is stronger?

That is to say, between this naming of what is not a Vaiśvadeva as "Vaiśvadeva" and the naming of what is enjoined as that which is not enjoined—which of these two is stronger? He replies: "The naming of what is enjoined as that which is not enjoined [is not the stronger]."

This is possible. For that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is made known when it is unknown, whereas that which is denoted (*abhidheya*) is already known. And it is not possible for a single object to be both known and unknown at the same time. Furthermore, the denotation by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is possible for things possessing a common connection, as in the expression "the staff-bearers are going. This is the case in the view that [the word] is a name (*nāmadheya*).

Just as the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) applies by way of indication (lakṣaṇā) even to those who do not possess a staff through association, so too here the word "vaiśvadeva" will apply both to that which is not for the Viśvedevas and to that which is for the Viśvedevas. Therefore, this position—that the term "vaiśvadeva" denotes what is not for the Viśvedevas—is superior; this position is better.
Furthermore, this must be addressed here: why is it that the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" does not refer exclusively to the Āmikṣā sacrifice?

For in that case, no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) would have to be resorted to regarding the word "Vaiśvadeva. And even if the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) were to apply to that [Āmikṣā sacrifice] as well, nevertheless—

There is no inconsistency in this. To this it is replied: By the rule that the word *vaiśvadeva* applies to a hymn (*sūkta*) or an oblation (*havis*), it functions in its primary sense toward either a hymn or an oblation. Because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), which itself functions in the sense of a sacrifice, this word *vaiśvadeva* cannot restrict the application of the word *yajati*. Nor can there be a connection between the word *vaiśvadeva* and the root *yaj* through grammatical non-coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Because, by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *āmikṣā*, it would follow that it must be feminine; for when a coreferential connection is possible, a non-coreferential connection is untenable. [The mantras] preceded [by a known ritual] are not intended as injunctions. It has been stated that the authority [of the Veda] is established through injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, names (*nāman*), and injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

In this case, however, in the offerings on eight potsherds or twelve potsherds, there is neither the status of a mantra nor the status of a reminder; therefore, it functions as an injunction (codaka).

Since it does not serve to remind one of what has already been enjoined, it cannot even be a name. Furthermore, because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the "eight-potsherd" and other terms—as in the case of the injunction "when it becomes eight-potsherd"—there is no coreferentiality with the meaning of the action being enjoined. Moreover, its status as an injunction of qualities (such as the number eight) mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) remains indeed doubtful.
In that regard, first of all, there is no doubt concerning the prescription of qualities; it is possible.
Because of the absence of an object;

because it is absolutely impossible to enjoin a quality [where there is no substrate]. How is there an absence of an object? The answer is: because of the cessation of one quality and the arising of another.

In the injunction "one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," the sacrifice to Vaiśvānara is already restricted by the number twelve, which is prescribed as part of its very origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). As for the potsherds upon which the sacrificial cake is placed, since they are not [independently] enjoined, they do not constitute the subject matter because they lack independent purpose. Likewise, there is no doubt regarding the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) either.

The connection [is as follows]. Why? He says: because by means of the number twelve, other numbers such as eight and so forth are excluded. It is not a praise by virtue of being connected to that [other number], as in the case of "Water is indeed peaceful.

If it is argued that just as the praise of water as "peaceful" is appropriate when it refers to the water connected to the enjoined Vetasa reed, so too is it appropriate here; [we reply: praise by way of a connection is indeed appropriate.
However, this is not a praise of another number, because there is no connection between the number twelve and that other number. Therefore, [the objection] is merely a false appearance (*pratibhā*).
Furthermore, there is a further objection regarding independence.
This being the case, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) stands as follows:
A certain proponent of a partial conclusion considers its validity to arise through the prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*). What is his intention?
Thinking thus, does he not perceive that the origination [of the cognition] is obstructed by another quality?
Because he thinks thus: [the reply is] "No, it is not that he does not see;
rather, he certainly sees. This is because one who considers this to be a single sentence falls into the error of thinking it constitutes a single syntactical unit.
Due to the confusion of the sentence, one considers the act of offering (*nirvapati*) to be connected with all the numbers,
because of its syntactic unity: [one offers] on eight potsherds, nine potsherds, ten potsherds, and eleven potsherds.

"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds"— thinking that this prescribes an offering endowed with the total number [of potsherds], and considering this to be a single sentence because it constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the intention is that there is either a repetition of the ritual act or an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the subordinate elements (*guṇa*). [Regarding] Vaiśvānara...
The phrase "on twelve potsherds" is considered to be the introductory statement for the deity.
Therefore, by that single sentence, there is the injunction of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice endowed with the total number [of potsherds]. Because it is so enjoined, its origination is established;
hence, there is no obstruction by a quality already prescribed at the time of origination (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa*).

[Page 251] But as for the purpose of enjoining a quality (*guṇa*), it is said here that validity cannot be asserted on the basis of an injunction of a quality because of the absence of a subject matter (*viṣaya*). Now, it was argued that the ritual action having Vaiśvānara as its deity is indeed the subject matter.

Objection: That is not the subject [of the injunction], because it contradicts the twelve-pitcher [offering]. For [the text] beginning with "that which is on eight potsherds" (yad aṣṭākapāla) [prescribes] various [offerings].
B. nānā.

The injunction regarding the number of potsherds as being "eighteen" is contained in a single sentence. Therefore, the statement that there is no obstruction by a quality prescribed for the original production (utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa) is ill-stated.
How so?

The answer is: because the word *vaiśvānara* expresses a case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting a meaning distinct from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the term *vaiśvānaram* ends in the accusative case and expresses a meaning distinct from the nominal stem. Therefore, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dvādaśakapāla* is based on direct scriptural statement (*śrauta*). Consequently, it is first understood that "one should offer the *vaiśvānara* [cake] on twelve potsherds. As for the [cake] on eight potsherds...

Furthermore, because terms such as these are connected with the words *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster) and *punāti* (purifies), it is understood that they do not have the word *vaiśvānara* as their locus of meaning.

However, a connection must be postulated on the grounds that the praise expressed by the word *punāti* would otherwise be inexplicable. And it has already been stated that such a postulation is not tenable when a [direct] connection already exists.
The meaning of this is as follows: here, the status of being a single unified sentence (*sahavākyārthatva*) is not possible, because words such as "a cake on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*),
which end in the nominative case, are connected with the word *vaiśvānara*, which ends in the accusative case.

Because there is no syntactical connection with the word [dvādaśakapāla]. However, while one might wish to assume a connection with Vaiśvānara on the grounds that the praise would otherwise be inexplicable, such an assumption cannot even gain a foothold because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dvādaśakapāla* itself, which ends in the accusative case. Therefore, it remains established that [the sacrifice] is already occupied by a quality prescribed at its origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*). If, by the word *vaiśvānara*...
There is no connection between the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) and the others; if that is so, then it is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*).

He refutes this: "It is not intuition, because it is logically established as being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). But how is its status as praise established, given that the previous number has been set aside by another number? As it was said: [because it serves as a glorification].
The reply is: For the exclusion is by way of designation (abhidhāna), not by way of existence (sadbhāva) nor by way of non-existence (asadbhāva);
[for example], the number eight and so forth [is excluded] by the word "twelve."

It is not so designated. However, while the numbers eight and so forth can exist within the number twelve, their relationship is based on the presence [of those constituent parts] and is not caused by the act of designation itself. Since they do exist, it is logical to designate them through partial extraction (*avayutya*).
Thus, it is appropriate to designate the substances by extracting the numbers eight and so forth individually.
[Objection: But surely, if [the word] is separated [from its context], the understanding of the relationship would not occur;
and consequently, the praise would be untenable. [The author] replies:
Separation may be possible for the sake of denotation, but the state of being related cannot itself be separated.
The meaning of this is:
it is possible to apply the word "eight" to denote those eight potsherds which constitute a single portion of the twelve potsherds.

However, it is not possible to establish that they actually possess the status of being included within the number twelve in an ultimate sense. Therefore, because their actual connection [to that number] is not established, the praise of the number twelve is indeed justified by way of praising them. Now, one might ask: "How can there be a non-establishment for the sake of verbal expression, but not in an ultimate sense? To this he says: "For verbal expression follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not the objective reality (*vastu*).

Therefore, even though the number twelve is real for them, nevertheless, when there is an intention to express only a portion [of it], it is entirely appropriate to use words such as 'eight' and so forth."

Therefore, because the relationship [between the parts] is not being established, the praise is appropriate, just as in the expression "the waters are peaceful. And thus it has been shown: "The rim and hub of this wheel are beautiful."

Through the praise of the parts, there is praise of the whole; therefore, by the praise of the number eight, which constitutes the parts, there is praise of the number twelve. [Objection: But let it be that the number twelve is prescribed as part of the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), since there is no application of the number nine for the sake of a result.

To the objection that the injunction of the number eight and so forth might apply to that very same action, he replies: "Even the injunction of a connection between a quality and a fruit is not possible on this basis alone. Why not? The answer is: "Because it is understood to form a single syntactical unit with the purpose of praise."

Furthermore, because a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result if there were a connection between the qualities and the fruit, and because the unity of the sentence has been demonstrated through both the opening and the conclusion, its independence is established by virtue of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). That is established. It has been stated that praise is possible through a connection even when [the qualities] are mentioned separately.

Even though there is thus a separate mention [of the quality], nevertheless, because the state of being related has not been separately joined [to the substrate], it has been stated that by the praise of that [quality], there is also praise of the related entity. However, where the state of being related is not understood in any way whatsoever due to mutual lack of connection,
and the enjoining of a quality is not possible;

Because of impossibility, as in such cases as "the sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd" (ekakapāla) or "the sacrificer is the grass-bundle" (prastara), how can there be authority in those instances?
The meaning is that there is simply no authority.
B. Nor are qualities enjoined.
But is it not established in the section concerning the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya-adhikaraṇa*) that there exists a secondary relationship even for words denoting different meanings?
"It exists.
Because of that, since a mutual connection is possible, the praise of the *prastara* and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is justified. He refutes this:
"That very point is not accepted."

Only a figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) is implied. Why is it not accepted? The answer is: a figurative sense is simply not possible because [the word] is connected with a different meaning. How is it not possible?
The answer is: for in a figurative expression...
It is logical that qualities alone possess the status of being denotable.

Regarding this so-called figurative denotation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*), if it is the case that qualities themselves are what is denoted, then the comprehension of specific qualities is established; not otherwise. Thus he says: "For otherwise..."

In the expression "Devadatta is a lion," the word "lion" conveys only valor with respect to Devadatta. Likewise, in the expression "The boy is fire," the word "fire" does not apply to the boy in the sense of his being actually flaming, but rather conveys his tawny color. Thus, [the literal application] is not tenable.
To the question "Why?", he says here: "The activity of the lion species" (C).

The word "lion" uttered by the mouth, while expressing qualities, would express all those qualities whatsoever that are connected with the genus, because there is no distinction in the means of expression. Now, if you think that it expresses only as many as one intends to speak of— then that very [point remains].

If it is argued that "it is understood" means that only the quality intended to be expressed is understood and no other, [the author] refutes this: in that case, the word follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not the denoted object (*abhidheya*).

In that case, the word follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) rather than the actual object (*vastu*). Even though the object does not exist, the word nevertheless functions by the power of the speaker's intention. What follows from this?
The answer is: that which has a superimposed state of being is figurative (*gauṇa*).

[The opponent] arrives at this conclusion: having superimposed the state of being fire upon the boy—which does not actually exist there—and desiring to speak of it, a figurative word is employed; thus it follows. Nevertheless, he asks: "What of it? [The response is: "And in the case of superimposition, there is no connection with another object—that is, no connection of the word 'fire' with the boy. Why? The answer is: for superimposition has as its object only an already apprehended thing.
It grasps only an object that has already been apprehended and does not touch an unapprehended object;
just as in the cognition of silver regarding mother-of-pearl, it is grasped as "that very thing" and not as "something similar to that. This is the cognition: "This is indeed silver."

It is not, however, "similar to silver. Therefore, it perceives only non-existent silver, and not something like mother-of-pearl which is similar to silver. Furthermore, whatever is perceived as the object of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is precisely the object of figurative (*gauṇa*) language as well; therefore, in the praise of the grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), [the term "fire" is used figuratively].
The word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is not [the subject]. In that case, let it be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
The reply is: even that is not possible because of impossibility.
For a quality being enjoined is not seen to serve a functional purpose (kāryārtha).
In this context, it is prescribed for the sake of the function; yet that is not tenable in either case.

It has been shown that the injunction of the *prastara* and the single potsherd does not apply to the function of the sacrificer, nor does the injunction of the sacrificer apply to the function of those two.

The author of the Commentary has stated that this is an injunction regarding the sacrificer. Therefore, this very same suspicion regarding a [separate] injunction arises; to this, it is replied: it is true that an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, but an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) cannot be precluded. [Objection: But surely, because of its connection with another meaning...
It was stated that because there is no connection with the primary meaning, it is not an explanatory statement (arthavāda). He refutes this: "What you have said is incorrect. How is it incorrect?
The answer is: for figurative usage (gauṇatva) is indeed possible precisely through a connection with its own primary meaning.

The meaning is that a word, having denoted its own primary referent (*svārtha*), becomes secondary (*gauṇa*) by relying on an intention directed toward something similar to that referent which has been brought to mind by it. But was it not argued that this is not the case because there is no cognition of any quality (*guṇa*) connected with the primary referent?

He refutes [the objection]: "The distinction [between words] arises from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); this too has already been stated. He objects: "It is true that you have said this; it has also been stated that in the case of the speaker's intention, there is no connection with the denotable object (*abhidheya*).
Regarding the speaker's intention...

In the case of a restrictive [injunction], that which is the expressed own-meaning (*svārtha*) of the word "sacrificer" does not become a related entity; for in that case, there would be a superimposition (*adhyāropa*). A word expresses an unreal object constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpanā*), not an ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-artha*); consequently, praise (*stuti*) would be untenable.

Likewise, the occurrence of [words like] "sky-flower" and so forth is explained: since a word has as its object mere conceptualization independent of an external referent, the employment of the expression "sky-flower" is justified.
But if the word were connected with the denoted object, it would be logically untenable; for what would be connected with what?

Herein, the word "what" (kiṃ) is connected with which meaning? To this it is replied: you are indeed ignorant of the non-restriction of words; for when the denoted object is not intended to be expressed, [the word functions otherwise]. You are truly ignorant of the scope [of linguistic usage].
The utterance of a word would be without basis;

for it is the object that, for the sake of its own cognition, necessitates the word, and thus the utterance of a specific word is appropriate. In the absence of that [object], however, the utterance of a specific word would be groundless. Furthermore, the designation through superimposition by means of another word is likewise not at all tenable.
Here he objects: "O dull-witted one, do not speak thus! For it is by way of having a superimposed object that the referent of the word 'lion' is intended;
since words have superimposed objects, the meaning of a superimposed lion is what is intended."

Nor, however, does it [the word "lion"] apply to the boy by way of a connection with those qualities. Furthermore, this object "lion" cannot possibly exist as something superimposed apart from the word "lion.
Therefore, the utterance of the word "lion" is not without a basis.

"Since it is precisely that object which is superimposed that the word is uttered for, the utterance of a specific term is not without cause. The proponent says: "But surely this has been stated by us;
we have stated the specific cause."
B. The prohibition of binding is not [due] to the absence of the boy, but rather because of his connection with Aruṇa; C.
the utterance of the word indicating gender.

[Page 261] Why is it that the meaning of "lion" alone is superimposed upon Devadatta? If it is argued that this is because one perceives the qualities of a lion in Devadatta—that is, because one perceives the qualities of a lion in Devadatta—the author refutes this: in that case, it follows that the representation must be based on a connection with the primary referent.

The word "lion" denotes Devadatta by virtue of his connection with, and similarity to, that which is the primary meaning of the word "lion. Since the essential nature of the substance (Devadatta) is already apprehended through the word "Devadatta," the purpose here is the communication of mere similarity. Furthermore, since the lion's similarity is based on a connection with qualities, the purpose is the communication of the lion’s qualities. If it is asked, "How is the specific quality understood? the answer is: from the observation of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because figurative usage (*gauṇa*) is preceded by such [observation].

That this usage is secondary (gauṇa) is understood through the force of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara). For, having learned through another means of valid cognition that this word for one thing has been applied to another, the determination of its secondary nature occurs. And in that case, it is understood that the word is applied to that [other object] by virtue of its connection with whatever quality is perceived through that other means of valid cognition; thus, the establishment of the comprehension of that specific quality is achieved. He states this in a single passage: "Even in the case of words such as 'cook' (pācaka), their primary meaning is restricted to a particular [individual] by the force of another means of valid cognition."
It is established [as secondary].
What is the reasoning for saying it is not secondary?
If every word functions solely through a connection with an object, then how [can there be words like] "sky-flower"? Regarding the object...
The use of the word [“existent”] refers to being. The reply is: “Just as ‘a sky-flower.
The word “iti” here is intended to indicate that cognition; by this, the following is stated.

Just as there is the cognition "it is like a sky-flower," so too is the employment of the word "sky-flower. For instance, one cognition has only the sky as its object, while another has only the flower as its object. Although there is no apprehension of a mutual relationship between these two, one who does not perceive their lack of connection nevertheless engages in the linguistic practice of perceiving a relationship. This should be described according to the principles established in the *Nyāyavīthī* as being based on the commonality of the relata when they are mentioned in proximity. Therefore, the status of [the statement] as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is established. What happens?

Regarding the question "What is the purpose? and so forth, it is explained in the Bhāṣya: [The answer is] "The genus" (jāti). In the case of the genus and other such categories as well, validity is to be applied in exactly the same way.

There too, validity is established by resorting to the status of being an explanatory praise (arthavāda). If this is so, why then are there separate topical sections (adhikaraṇas)? To this he says: "But the separate topical sections are due to the difference in the refutations; the application is also [different]."
These are for the purpose of illustration.
In that regard, the statement "the Brāhmaṇa is Agni" is a secondary application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) based on similarity due to originating from the same source; this is the resolution.
The statement "the sacrificial post is the sun" [is figurative] because of the similarity to a sacrificial post. The statement "others than cows and horses are indeed non-animals;

cows and horses are animals" indicates that the word "animal" (paśu) is used figuratively (gauṇa) with respect to cows and horses alone, by way of praise. Similarly, in the cases of "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks" and "he lays down the *prāṇabhṛt*-bricks," [the usage is figurative] on account of abundance (*bhūman*).

The separate treatment of these topics is intended to demonstrate the resolution that "definition" (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs through the inherence of the defining characteristic (*liṅga-samavāya*). Therefore, it is established that even words with secondary meanings (*gauṇa-artha*) possess authority as *arthavādas*, as do those with metaphorical meanings (*lākṣaṇika-artha*). But how can even the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in passages such as the *sṛṣṭi* (creation) hymns be the objects of definition (*lakṣya*)? For in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the Gaṅgā, which serves as the defining characteristic, does not itself become the object of definition. The answer is: because of their connection to the same action as the objects of definition. That is, the defining characteristic is connected to the same action as those things which are the actual objects of definition; and since that action [itself] is the object of definition...

For being a cause (*nimitta*) is indeed the reason for being characterized by an adjunct (*upadhāna-yogitā*) when something is to be defined (*lakṣyatva*). And this state of being joined with an adjunct exists even for the *sṛṣṭi* and other [mantras] which serve as the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that they function as both the defined and the defining characteristic. How, then, can the word *paśu* (animal) be used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) for horses and the like in the context of [the prohibition of] non-animals and so forth?
How is the word "animal" (*paśu*) applied by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to horses and the like?

In the case of horses and the like, [the term] is applied only in its primary sense (*mukhya*). And here, the non-acceptance of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not the deciding factor, because the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) is intended in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). The meaning is that in every respect there is only the primary sense, neither the secondary nor the figurative. Regarding the subsequent [point], since usage is preceded by prohibition—because a generic term (*jātiśabda*) is prohibited from being used for other members of that same class, when it is employed for others of that class, it receives its application only through the secondary sense.
For in this case, among other animals, they are not "animals" [in the primary sense].
Having performed the prohibition [of the term "animal"] specifically with respect to the species of cattle and horses, the word "animal" (paśu) is applied to them only in a figurative sense.

Why? Because when a genus-term (*jātiśabda*) is prohibited with respect to members of that genus, it becomes the object of the prohibition precisely as a quality inherent [in those members] that is to be prohibited.
Since the genus (jāti) does not depart [from the object], the genus cannot be negated; nevertheless, he asks "why? and replies:
"Furthermore, because of the negation of the quality (guṇa), when [the word] is applied to another member of that same genus, it is understood as having only a figurative meaning (gauṇārtha)."

The meaning is that, since the qualities have been negated in the preceding statements, it is appropriate that there be a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding those very qualities. Therefore, even the word denoting the genus (*jātiśabda*) is secondary (*gauṇa*), because it functions through its connection with the qualities of the object; thus, there is no contradiction. Consequently, its independence (*anapekṣatvam*) is established.

"Regarding doubtful cases. [The opponent objects: "But surely, in the case of *yava*, *varāha*, *vetasa*, and so forth, the removal of doubt was already accomplished by means of the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*); therefore, this is redundant"—this is the sense of the objection. He answers: "True; however, that [removal of doubt] concerned the meaning of the words themselves. In those various instances, the word-meaning, which was being doubted as to whether it was innate (*autpattika*) or not, was determined by the supplementary passage."

Here, an objection is raised: "Does the word have a referent, such that the doubt concerning its object is removed? Or is it that there is no such thing at all? This is the sense [of the objection]. He replies:
—Certainly it exists;

for through the distinction of insertion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*uddhāra*), one understands the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word-meanings. If it is certain that a word denotes only its own meaning and that there is no sentence distinct from the words, then how can the innate (*autpattika*) relationship between sentence and sentence-meaning be established through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*)?

Objection: It is true that there is an innate relationship between a sentence and its meaning; however, it has been stated in the section on *tadbhūtāni* that the meaning of a sentence is conveyed by the sentence part by part.

"Because it is connected with the purpose of action," as we have stated in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*. Therefore, in that case, there is doubt regarding what has become that [purpose]; but here, the purpose of the sentence is the purpose of action.

This, then, is the distinction between the sentence and its meaning from the word and its referent; this has been demonstrated at length. Therefore, even due to doubt regarding the purpose of the action, there is a lack of authoritative validity.
Due to the contradiction between the opening and the conclusion, there is doubt regarding the very meaning of the passage.

This being the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), some who belong to a single school of the final conclusion (rāddhāntaikadeśin) consider it appropriate to determine the meaning of the concluding portion on the basis of the opening statement (upakrama).
Because there is no contradiction.
To explain how there is no contradiction, he says: for a universal resides both in itself and in its particulars.
If by that...

It has been said by someone that even if it is smeared with something else, the expression "smeared" is still applicable; likewise, although it is smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the word "clarified butter" must be explained in the concluding portion by virtue of the opening statement, just as in the case of the phrase "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks," which applies to both those bricks that are *sṛṣṭi* and those that are not.
Just as in the injunction "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks," [the term refers to all of them].

Furthermore, the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi) and likewise the word "clarified butter" (ghṛta) must be explained as applying both to what is clarified butter and to what is not clarified butter. To this it is replied: this would indeed be so, if by that [reasoning]...

In other cases, the general sense [of a word] might be established by another sentence; however, here, because of the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*), the comprehension of the syntactic connection extends only as far as the specific detail.
