In a single sentence, the meaning of the sentence is understood by considering the mutual relationship of the words. In that context, because the word *akta* (anointed) is connected with the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter), it is understood that its referent is specifically clarified butter. Otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *ghṛta*, but not in the word *akta*.

There is a certain contradiction between the word and its meaning. Therefore, it is established that the status of being for the sake of action (kriyārthatva) depends upon the supplementary part of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa).
Thus, it is proven in the context of the vākyaśeṣa.
It is established that the capacity of a sentence to convey the meaning of a sentence depends upon the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter).
Or rather, it follows from the sense (*arthāt*). Even where there is doubt regarding the performance [of an action], the scripture itself is considered to be doubtful;
therefore, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a lack of authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*).
[Page 270] But is this not improper? For since there is doubt regarding the performance [of the ritual], the scripture itself must be doubtful.

This is because performance is preceded by the scripture. (It is established that [the scripture] brings about the understanding of the meaning of the sentence. Even though the performance is doubtful, nevertheless, it is not...
The meaning is that the treatise (*śāstra*) is doubtful. He refutes this: "True, as you have said;

however, even when there is doubt regarding the performance of what has been taught about established entities (*siddha*), the teaching concerning established entities is not itself doubtful. But in the case of the teaching concerning things to be accomplished (*kārya*), doubt regarding the performance indeed arises."
The scripture. The objector says: Is there any performance that is not preceded by scripture, such that the scripture would be doubtful when that [performance] is doubtful?

For if that [the scripture] were the prerequisite, even the performance would be subject to doubt, whereas the scripture itself is not doubted. It is true that when there is a connection [to a result], it is preceded by scripture;

the meaning is that at the stage of its origination, it is preceded by scripture. Performance consists in the existence of the object of the injunction (*niyoga*); the injunction does not establish the performance as its own means of valid cognition.

Therefore, when even that [the injunction] is doubtful, the scripture itself is doubtful, because the scripture culminates in that. Consequently, a doubt regarding the meaning of the injunction is justified;
for a doubt regarding its performance is also justified, since that [injunction] culminates in it. He states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "But that..."
That which is the intended meaning must be determined through the force of the context;
and it has been determined by the author of the Commentary. He concludes the subject matter of the chapter: "Because it is a synonym for that."

Therefore, having established the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) by refuting any dependence on injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, traditional law (*smṛti*), names, or ritual performance; [the author proceeds].
It has been stated that "validity" is the subject, and it was promised that there shall be an investigation into the cause of that which possesses validity.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first book in the *Ṛjuvimalā* composed by the great teacher Śālikanātha.
In the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*,
[this is] the second chapter.
First Pāda:
Those whose meaning consists in bringing about [an action] (bhāvārtha).
In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been established; the means of valid cognition has been treated.
It has been stated that "the conduct" (vṛtta) is what is meant; this refers to the commentary.
For the first chapter indeed ought to be cited as the reason [for the following]. And it is not by the entire chapter that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is [established].
The definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.

What then? It was stated by way of a portion of it, namely through the definitions of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. Anticipating the objection that this does not serve as the reason for the division of the treatise (*śāstra*), he says:
"In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition has been set forth," which means that it has been explained how verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition.

The meaning of this is as follows: the meaning of the commentary on the phrase "in the first chapter" is this—the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that independence (*anapekṣatva*), by which mode of being independent verbal testimony is characterized as a valid means of knowledge; that independence is the definition.

[The word] "liberated" (mukta) [is used]. By this, the entire meaning of the chapter is proclaimed. Furthermore, we shall explain that independence (*anapekṣatva*) serves as the reason for the distinction between scriptures (*śāstra-bheda*). Now, one might object: "The investigation of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth was already performed in the first chapter; however, the manner in which the word possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) has not been stated.
Thinking thus, he asks: "Why? (*kutaḥ*)?
Thus he introduces the commentary as a response: "Since injunctions, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and traditional codes (smṛtis) have been determined according to their true nature,

and since the distinction between a subordinate injunction (guṇavidhi) and a name (nāmadheya) has been examined, and the determination of doubtful meanings through the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) and through the context (artha) has been stated."

Therefore, the definition of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been stated. But how, when this much has been said, is the meaning of "the definition of a means of valid cognition has been stated" expressed? To that he says:
"And these..."

Explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, when understood otherwise than they truly are, do not obstruct validity; however, when correctly comprehended, they do not undermine it. Therefore, because they have been determined according to their true nature, it is said that "the definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated."

The determination of the truth regarding injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, was stated solely for the purpose of establishing authority (*prāmāṇya*); thus, in the first chapter, only the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) was set forth. Therefore, it is rightly said that "in the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid knowledge was stated. By the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating, "That must not be forgotten," the author indicates—by saying that this independence (*anapekṣatva*) must not be forgotten—that the discussion of difference and non-difference is dependent upon that very independence, since he demonstrates that the recollection of that [independence] alone is useful. Why [is this so]?...

Is the statement regarding difference and non-difference dependent upon dependence on something else? The answer is: for it is the difference and non-difference of the effect that is being stated, and that is based on independence.
Why? He says: for when a word depends on something else, the distinction of the effect cannot be expressed from the word alone.
He summarizes: "Therefore, that must not be forgotten," by which [he means] "because of its independence. In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows.

The distinction between treatises (*śāstra*), the subject matter of the chapters (*adhyāya-artha*), the distinction of the objects to be established (*sādhya-bheda*), and the distinction of the ancillary factors (*anubandha-bheda*) are stated here as the causes for that [distinction]. Furthermore, that object to be established is cognizable solely through verbal testimony; therefore, the independence of verbal testimony is required. Moreover, that distinction of ancillary factors which is the cause for the distinction between treatises also depends upon the distinction of effects (*kārya-bheda*). For if the *apūrva* were to differ by virtue of its connection with sacrifices and the like, then the status of the sacrifices and so forth as ancillary factors would likewise differ.

The scripture (*śāstra*) would also be divided by virtue of its presenting distinct subordinate elements (*anubandha*). However, if the unseen potency (*apūrva*) is not divided by the subordinate element of the sacrifice, then, due to the absence of a difference in subordinate elements, the scripture is not divided. Therefore, even for the sake of establishing a difference in subordinate elements, a difference in the *kārya* (the task or result) must be asserted. And since that [difference in the task] cannot be stated without dependence and independence, it depends upon that independence. Subsequently, the primary and secondary elements are examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct.
Thus [ends] the commentary. After the classification of the treatises (*śāstrabheda*), he states that the classification of the treatises should be explained next.
He asks for the reason there: "Why 'next'?"

By the inclusion of the word "alone" (eka), he says: for even other distinct characteristics, such as "remainder" (śeṣa) and so forth, depend precisely upon the absence of dependence on anything else; it is only through this [absence of dependence] that the meaning can be determined from the word.

Therefore, by what distinction is the definition of the differentiation of the scriptures (*śāstrabheda*) commenced immediately after the definition of independence (*anapekṣatva*)? The answer is: it is true that even the remaining [definitions], such as being a supplement (*śeṣa*), can be determined from the words themselves only in dependence upon independence, but not independently of it.
G. Furthermore, with the intention that "this [very thing] immediately follows," the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Immediately after [the primary], the primary and secondary [factors]."
Thus [it is asked]: why then is this very [topic] presented immediately after [the definition of means of knowledge], and not the definition of the "remainder" (śeṣa) and so forth?
The answer is: because everything that follows is preceded by a distinction of purpose (kāryabheda).

The state of being preceded by a difference in effects, however, is due to being preceded by a difference in treatises, because a difference in effects serves as the cause for a difference in treatises. And how there is precedence by a difference in treatises—[p.

The definition of the "remainder" has been shown in that manner in the first [chapter] of the third [book]. He raises an objection against the statement of the Bhāṣya—"the primary and secondary [factors], whether distinct or non-distinct, will be examined"—by asking: "What is this 'primary and secondary'?"

He says in a single passage: "If it is connected thus, 'first the primary and secondary [elements] will be examined,' then one thing would be proposed as a thesis while something else would be what is actually examined."

Consequently, there is a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the examination (*parīkṣā*). He explains this very point: for immediately following [the section on] "Difference and Non-difference" (*bhedābheda*), the examination of "Principal and Non-principal" (*pradhānāpradhāna*) is seen, not the examination of "Substance and Quality. [Objection: But surely the other [examination] is for the sake of that [former], according to the rule: "But those by which a substance is intended to be produced, in that case [it is a quality]."
And the examination of the primary and the secondary is indeed seen immediately following [the statement] "it is understood.
He refutes [this objection]: for that which is established by the third...

That [distinction] has been brought forward here for the sake of conventional usage, for the purpose of establishing the distinction between functions, which serves as the cause for the distinction between the scriptures.
And so it was stated by the author of the Commentary:

In the third chapter, it was stated by [the author] himself: "Now, in that case, regarding those things for which a substance is intended to be prepared (*cikīrṣyate*), there a quality (*guṇa*) should be understood"—thereby excluding the status of being for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) for verbal roots whose purposes are visible. However, here the definition of all subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) is being stated. [The opponent says: "They are primary (*pradhāna*). [The author replies: That is incorrect.
Therefore, the claim that they are both primary and non-primary is incoherent.

It is said: the terms "principal" (*pradhāna*) and "non-principal" (*apradhāna*) denote the objectives (*sādhya*) and the adjuncts (*anubandha*). By the word "objective," the fourfold set beginning with origination (*utpatti*), the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*), the intermediate operation of the instrument (*karaṇāvāntaravyāpāra*), and the entitlement characterized by sovereignty (*aiśvaryalakṣaṇādhikāra*) are expressed. These objectives are designated by the term "principal," while the adjuncts of the injunction (*niyoga*) are designated by the term "non-principal."
They have become the objects [of inquiry]. Therefore, those primary and secondary [actions] will be examined as to whether they are different or non-different;
the meaning is that the difference and non-difference of both the goals (*sādhya*) and the subordinate factors (*anubandha*) will be investigated.
First, the difference among the subordinate factors is as follows: "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations."
The differentiation of the scriptures arises from the differentiation of those [subsidiary acts].
There is also no difference in the *anubandhas* (the constituent elements), as in the case of: "One who, knowing thus, performs the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice.
And because of that non-difference, there is non-difference of the scripture. Likewise...

There is also a difference in the effects [of actions], which constitutes the distinction between these two scriptural injunctions: "He threshes the rice grains" and "He sprinkles the rice grains. The effect of threshing is the removal of the husks and chaff, permeated by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*). The effect of sprinkling, however, is an unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, one threshes the rice grains and [sprinkles] the rice grains.

There is a distinction between these two scriptural injunctions, such as "he sprinkles" (*prokṣati*). Although these two scriptures are mutually distinct, they do not differ from the injunction of a mere *bhāvārtha* (action-verb), because there is no difference in their *anubandhas* (subsidiary elements). For the *anubandha* is the object of the *niyoga* (the mandate), and we shall explain that threshing (*avaghāta*) and the like are not objects of the *niyoga*. Furthermore, a difference in the *sādhya* (the end to be accomplished) that is independent of one another is a cause for the distinction between scriptures. Now, the task of threshing and so forth does not have as its *sādhya* an *apūrva* (unseen potency) that is independent of the *āgneya* sacrifice and others. However, in the case of subordinate actions (*guṇakarmāṇi*), a distinction between scriptures is indeed appropriate due to a difference in their *sādhya*s that are independent of one another.

This has been stated in the *Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*: "But is it not the case that even in the injunction of a quality for the cup (*camasa*), this would be a separate scripture (*śāstrāntara*)? No; this is merely another sentence (*vākyāntara*), not a separate scripture. A separate scripture occurs in dependence upon the injunction of another quality that performs an identical function, but not in dependence upon the injunction of a mere accidental quality (*bhāvaguṇa*). (Bṛhatī 2.3.24)

And here, what is intended is the equality of effects that are mutually independent. By this, it should be understood that there is a distinction between scriptural injunctions (*śāstra*) such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), due to the difference in the goals to be accomplished (*sādhya*), namely the restricted unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*). Likewise, in the *Paurṇamāsī* section (*adhikaraṇa*), the relationship between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is explained.

Even in the case of two different manuals (*śāstra*), although the procedures (*itikartavyatā*) are to be performed, a distinction will be stated based on the difference between the manuals and the difference between the goals (*sādhya*). For the goal of the procedure is the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇa*); however, for the instruments, there is a further intermediate operation.

Actions (*kāryāṇi*) are of the nature of activity. Likewise, regarding the statement "practice for as long as one lives," a distinction between scriptures will be described based on the difference in the goals (*sādhya*) of the qualification for living (*jīvana-adhikāra*) and the qualification for desire (*kāma-adhikāra*). [This] will be maintained. And there is non-difference of the goal.

In the injunctions "He offers the *samidh*s" and "He offers to *Tanūnapāt*," because they share a single goal through what is called "contextual connection" (*adhikāra*)—namely, the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*)—the scriptural rules concerning the *samidh* offerings and those concerning the offering to Agni, though distinct due to the difference in their subordinate elements (*anubandha*), are nevertheless non-distinct because the goal (*sādhya*) is the same. Therefore, it is well said that the primary and secondary rites will be examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct.

This alone is the meaning to be described and no other; this is the explanation of the word "immediately following" (*ānantarya*). And this is the connection between the chapters (*adhyāya-sambandha*), which states the reason for the immediate succession.

In the commentary, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because"—because this connection to the chapter exists, therefore the definition of the differentiation of the scriptures (*śāstrabheda*) must be presented immediately after. We have already shown how this serves as a logical reason (*hetu*).

Thus, six types of differentiation of ritual action (*karmabheda*) will be explained here: difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*).

The restatement of the commentary: He objects—how is it that "difference" (*bheda*) is "a different word" (*śabdāntara*)? This objection is raised by taking the word *bheda* as denoting the action (*bhāvasādhana*). He replies: "It is differentiated (*bhidyate*) by this," thus *bheda* is a word denoting the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*).

The word "distinction" (*bheda*) refers to that which is distinguished from other words and so forth; the meaning is that both that [action] and its object constitute the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).

Through the six means of distinction—beginning with "other words"—there is only a distinction among the various *bhāvārthas*, but no distinction among their subordinate elements (*anubandha*), nor a distinction among the scriptures (*śāstra*), nor a distinction among the injunctions (*niyoga*). This is by way of number.

In the case of the phrase "seventeen [animals] for Prajāpati," there is no difference in the status of the adjuncts (*anubandha*), because the injunction (*niyoga*) is established by their proximity to the substances and deities conveyed by the nominal stem *prājāpatya*. This is because they constitute the object of a single injunction; and in the case of a simultaneous connection (*tantrasambandha*), the status as the object of the injunction does not differ, just as in the expression "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Furthermore, the author of the *Nibandhana*, who maintains that the power of the word is primary, considers the connection between substance and deity to be the object of the injunction. On this point, there are these verses: [The verses follow here.]
In the second chapter, the Guru described the differentiation of the treatise according to its goal and its contextual adjuncts within his commentary.
However, when that which is to be proven is independent of one another, it constitutes a distinction between the treatises;
because of the specific differences among the means of proof, those distinctions have been declared in many ways.

The distinctions between the auxiliary elements (anubandhas) are established through differences in terminology, repetition, the mention of specific qualities, and different procedural methods; these are the causes for the differentiation of the scriptures.
Even though there is identity with the self as a continuous series, [the Lord] differentiates the mere entities;
because they are differentiated by Him and because He is the differentiator without distinction, number is also enunciated in this very context.

Since the word *bheda* (difference) has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), it is therefore said that there is a "difference of action" (*karma-bheda*). The out-of-order presentation of the [criteria] such as "different words" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth, without regard for the order to be explained later, is for the purpose of demonstrating that order is not relevant here.

The meaning is that when "different words" and the others function as differentiators of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), they have no mutual requirement for a specific sequence. Here, an objection is raised: "That which is to be explained later is mentioned here in the form of a proposition (*pratijñā*"; i.e., it is stated with the intention of being a formal proposition).
For what purpose? The Naiyāyikas maintain that it is logical to state the proposition (*pratijñā*) at the very time of stating the reason (*hetu*).
Those who engage in the practice of logic (*nyāyavyavahārin*) believe this for the sake of introducing the reason—that is, for the sake of stating the reason.

For it is the proposition (*pratijñā*) that is being stated, yet it is appropriate to state it precisely at the time of expressing the reason (*hetu*). He replies: "True; where an object is to be stated as something to be proven (*sādhya*), there it is indeed so. However, this mention of the 'sur' [prefix] is for the purpose of establishing the distinction between the connection (*anubandha*) experienced as a reason (*hetu*). He will do so.
When this has been said, the intellect of the listener— whose mind is drawn by the desire to know that [subject]— being concentrated,

proceeds with ease toward the classification of the treatise as it is being explained. By stating, "This is called the chapter characterized by various rituals," he demonstrates the established usage of the term among former teachers, in order to declare the beginninglessness of the system (nyāya).
This principle is beginningless;

it is merely being recorded in its own treatise by Jaimini and others through some specific occasion. Therefore, this is distinct from the introduction (*upoddhāta*), as well as from what is relevant or incidentally relevant (*prasaktānuprasakta*); thus, it is for the purpose of avoiding the fault of investigating matters not previously promised.

Furthermore, even that which is considered other than what was promised due to the division of the treatise (*śāstra*) is treated as an introductory supplement (*upoddhāta*), just as this very first [topic] is. And there is that which follows from what is relevant (*prasaktānuprasakta*)—such as the definition of *mantras* and their divisions. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. First, this is considered: in the first chapter it was stated that "Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction (*codanā*). An injunction is a sentence (*vākya*) that expresses an action; and the meaning of a sentence resides in its words (*pada*).
In that regard, is Dharma expressed by each individual word, or is it expressed by all [the words] together as one?
The restatement of the commentary (*bhāṣyānubhāṣaṇam*). He objects:

"It is indeed appropriate that this first point should be considered—whether dharma is expressed by each individual word or by all [the words] together as a single syntactical connection (*saṃbandha*). The particle *iti* should be understood here [at the end]. What is the purpose of this passage, which states that "this was said in the first chapter"?
To what context does this treatise belong? Therefore, we do not know how it is to be explained.
To this, it is replied: Is the *dharma* [to be understood] word by word?

It is said: when only this much has been stated, someone might think there is a contradiction with the method of one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhāntaprakriyā*), because of the assertion of an innate connection (*autpattikasambandha*) between the sentence and its meaning.
For when [the meaning] is [conveyed] by the sentence itself—

When the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is being expressed, the word-meaning (*padārtha*) has no separate meaning of its own. Therefore, how can it be suspected that the meaning denoted by each individual word is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*)? For one who considers this to be a contradiction with the established method (*prakriyā*), the answer is given in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "In the first chapter... He explains the meaning of this: "It is true that in the first chapter this was stated—that Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction (*codanā*); and an injunction is a sentence."

Therefore, it was stated in the *Codanā-lakṣaṇa* sūtra that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is precisely the definition of a sentence itself. Nevertheless, it was also stated that even within a sentence, there is a meaning belonging to the individual words. [The author] who composes this treatise maintains that the words themselves—denoted by the term "sentence"—express the meanings of the words as already interconnected, and thereby express the meaning of the sentence, according to the principle: "Those [words] which have come into being [as such] are enumerated for the sake of action."

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the established procedure. Consequently, this is logical: is the property (dharma) expressed by each individual word, or is it expressed by all of them together as one?

Now, this might be objected as improper: for it is not the case that every single word denotes dharma; rather, one might suspect that it is only the word ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth that expresses dharma, which consists of the *apūrva*. Anticipating this, he explains: "This is what is meant: does the connection with the task (kārya) belong to the meaning denoted by each individual word, or to that [meaning] which is dependent upon its mutual relationship [with other words]?"

When the meaning expressed by a word is connected with the task—that is, when it constitutes the object of the mandate (*niyoga*)—then the mandate is said to be expressed by that very word, because the knowledge of the mandate does not arise from the word "mandate" alone. But how can it be suspected that an object understood as being mutually connected [with other words] has a connection with the task only when it is unrelated to the meanings of the other words? For, due to the understanding of mutual connection, the connection of all [words] with the mandate is not perceived.

He refutes [the objection]: For it is observed that in the case of the *aruṇa* (red) and other such instances, there is an understanding of the connection with the action (*kārya*), even though the substance and the quality are mutually related to one another.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in understanding a mutual relationship when there is a connection with the purposeful action (*kārya*).

But was it not stated that in those cases there is no understanding of a mutual relationship between the substance and the quality, because the relationship with the purchase (*kraya*) is understood through the force of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*)? He refutes this: "True, indeed; by virtue of being for the sake of this [action] (*aidamarthyena*), there is none."

It has been stated that there is a mutual relationship; however, this does not mean that it does not exist even as the relation between quality and the possessor of quality (guṇa-guṇin), but rather that it certainly does exist. For otherwise...
If a mutual relationship were not perceived, then there would be no restriction at all;
for one might purchase [the cow] with a non-red *ekahāyanī*, or even with a multi-colored *ekahāyanī*. Yet, such a restriction does exist;
therefore, there is indeed the perception of a mutual relationship. The same applies here to the noun and the verb.

Is the connection with the *niyoga* independent of the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*), or is it established only while not abandoning that relationship between the action and its factors? Thus, the doubt is justified.

That which does not abandon the relationship between action and its factors is "not abandoning the relationship between action and its factors"; for that indeed is the relationship with the *niyoga* (injunction). What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? This means: regarding this doubt, what is logical? The word "attained" (*prāpta*) here functions in the sense of the word "logical" (*yukta*). The answer is: it is logical that the connection with the *dharma* applies to each individual word. Why?

The answer is: because the utterance of all words has the injunction (*niyoga*) as its purpose. All words indeed have as their primary aim the communication of word-meanings that are subordinated to the injunction. This is because the utterance of all words is for the sake of a task to be accomplished (*kārya*). [Objection: But surely, the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) is also understood here;
therefore—

Since the purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) of both the action (*kriyā*) and the factors of action (*kāraka*) is understood [from their mutual connection], it is logical that all of them possess purposefulness toward the mandate (*niyoga*) directly, without abandoning that [connection]. He refutes this: True, a relationship characterized by action and its factors is understood; however, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the factors of action having the action as their sole purpose, because the object of the mandate is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) independently.

If there is no "thisness" (the relation of belonging) between the action and its factors, then one might think that even the relationship between the action and its factors does not exist; with this in mind, a certain person of dull intellect objects: "But how can a factor, being devoid of activity itself, bring about the fulfillment of the meaning of the injunction?"

For that which has become a *kāraka* (a factor of action) produces the object of the *niyoga* by virtue of being subordinated to it through its purposefulness (*idamarthyāpannatayā*). [Objection: How can there be the status of a *kāraka* without a relationship between an action and its factors? Or how can an object (*karman*), not being brought into being and thus lacking its own existence, bring about the fulfillment of the *niyoga*? [The author] answers: Let this relationship between action and its factors exist as a matter of fact.

The relationship between the quality and the possessor of the quality is like that between substance and quality; however, "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya) exists solely for the purpose of the injunction,
for "being for the sake of that" is indeed something else.
G. Karma.
G. It is precisely the sense of "command" (niyoga).

And the intention is that there would be another relationship between the action and its factors (kriyākāraka). Therefore, there would be a distinct dharma for each word. To this, it is said: this is not tenable. Why? He says: for if the status of being the object of the injunction (niyogārthatā) did not belong to those words that do not abandon their perceived meaning, then there would be a distinct dharma for each word. This is the meaning.

Because the purport (*tātparya*) is everywhere more powerful, even a mutually established relationship is permissible provided that, by accepting it, the purport toward the injunction (*niyoga*) is not lost. However, where the comprehension of the relationship is itself required for consistency, the abandonment of that [relationship] would result in the very abandonment of what is heard in the text (*śrutahāna*). And this is not the case here.

G. adds: Nor is it logical that this cognition [of the relationship] should result from the Vedic text alone; for if there were a connection with the *dharma* at every word, the understanding of a mutual relationship would be abandoned due to the absence of a cause. Indeed, the entry of substance and quality into a single action called "purchase" (*kraya*) is the cause for the understanding of their mutual relationship. But here, because there is a difference in the injunctions (*niyoga*) due to the difference in the adjuncts (*anubandha*) at each word, [the two] enter into distinct injunctions.

Even though it is understood that the relationship between the noun and the verb is inherently seedless (independent), it must nevertheless be abandoned [as a mere possibility]; rather, that [relationship] is required by the injunction (*vidhi*).

For without an action (*kriyā*), the status of being a factor of action (*kāraka*) is impossible, and without a factor of action, the accomplishment of an action is not possible. Therefore, it is logical that one or the other is assisted by the other for the sake of the injunction. And since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is fulfilled even through a mediated sequence, there is no fault.
In this way, the postulation of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and inference will be minimized.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: In this very commentary, it is understood as follows: if dharma were [inherent] in each individual word (*pratipada*), then a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) would have to be postulated for every single word. And these [results] are to be known through inference from the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). For logicians designate inference from the unperceived by the term "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Thus it has been said: "And touch does not belong to those things that are perceived; therefore, air has an unperceived mark (*liṅga*)."

Thus, the connection between the sections of this treatise is as follows: in this way, from an inference based on what is not perceived (*adṛṣṭānumāna*) concerning an unprecedented object (*apūrva-viṣaya*), there arises a conceptualization based on an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭānumāna*). Here, an objection is raised: "What, then, is this conceptualization based on an inference from what is not perceived? For even from verbal testimony (*śabda*), that which is perceived is indeed perceived."

For if there were the postulation of an unobserved entity (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*), then it would be appropriate to say, "In this way, there will be a postulation involving the consequence of inferring an unobserved entity"—and indeed, G. adds, "in this way, such a postulation of an unobserved inference will be minimal. But in this case, there is no postulation of an unobserved entity.
Because the *apūrva* (the unseen force) is denotable by words. He refutes this: "True, as you have said, there is no postulation of an unseen entity [merely] because of a name.

If one were to postulate a *dharma* for every single word, then in the case of the relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayi*), the inference of a restrictive rule would result in an *adṛṣṭa* (unseen entity) that lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). [Thus, it would follow that] an *adṛṣṭa* would be established as a means of valid cognition.

The meaning is that [the agent] attains [the action]. Since it is impossible for that which is devoid of action to function as a *kāraka* (participant in an action), an action must be understood as being supported by the *kāraka* through its status as a *kāraka*. Furthermore, by means of the action, [the *kāraka*] itself...

The agent (*kāraka*), being the substratum (*āśraya*), must be apprehended as already established in its own right; and upon that [substratum], the understanding of the restriction [of the action] occurs. Based on this very action, one might conceive that "this agent accomplishes this specific application," and based on this very agent, one might conceive that "this is the action"—such a conceptualization involving an unseen relationship between substratum and superstratum would be devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*). This is because it differs from the logic of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow) rule. Furthermore, how could there be the conceptualization of an inference of many unseen factors? The answer is: first of all, in this way, the status of being a substratum belongs to the agents, and the status of being a superstratum [belongs to the action].

Furthermore, regarding actions, there is the relationship of the means and the end for their accomplishment, as well as the specific restriction [of cause and effect]. Moreover, in the case where one side is favored, there will be the postulation of a consequence involving the inference of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). What is this so-called "postulation of a consequence involving the inference of the unperceived"?
The answer is: the unperceived is that which lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

That which is indeed unperceived lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). Since inference is an inference based on a necessary rule (*niyamānumāna*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*) that would involve the relationship of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayitva*) is an "inference from the unperceived" (*adṛṣṭānumāna*); thus, it is a "consequence consisting of an inference from the unperceived. The conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of such a thing is extremely slight (*alpīyasī*).
[Page 285] But surely, no such conceptualization occurs; why then do you say it is "extremely slight"?

He refutes [the objection]: even in the case where one side is favored, there exists the conceptual construction that the object of the injunction (*vidheya*) is indeed the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), and that the favor (*anugraha*) belongs to that alone. Furthermore, as for this "favor":

That which is being performed is not to be accepted as consisting of its own form alone, because that would contradict the meaning of the *niyoga* (the injunction). But is this not already established by the words themselves; why then is it being postulated? He replies: we shall explain in the ninth [book] that its understanding arises from the effect (*kārya*).

By accepting that [the injunction] is prompted by something not previously known (*apūrva*), the employment of the term "postulation" (*kalpanā*) becomes consistent. Anticipating the objection that if the understanding [of the injunction] arises from the effect (*kārya*), it would then not be verbal (*śābda*), he says: "But it is verbal because its root is the effect understood through words. Therefore, it has been rightly stated: "In this way, there will be a postulation of an inference of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) involving the least possible [assumptions]."
Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya concludes that there is "one apūrva," and [the opponent] objects: "What is this 'one apūrva'? He replies: "Indeed, it is this very thing;
this meaning is perfectly clear. Again he objects: "It is not so, it is not so."

"From one [action], the *apūrva* [arises]"—this is the context from which it follows. Therefore, it must be concluded that "from one [action] the *apūrva* arises," and not that "one *apūrva* [arises]. To this, it is replied: when...
If the ritual duty pertains to each individual word in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then there must be a distinction of injunctions for each word.
Why?
The answer is: because of the difference in the subordinate elements (*anubandha*) for each word.

Furthermore, when there is a prescribed application (*vidhi-niyoga*) of mutually connected elements according to the rule, then there is only one subordinate factor (*anubandha*). And for this reason, it is concluded that there is only one *apūrva*. [Objection: Even so, would there not still be an *apūrva* from each individual [element]?
"Why was it not withdrawn? By what means of a result is it withdrawn?
To this he says, in order to demonstrate this very difference in the effect regarding the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) on page 286:
The Blessed Commentator has summarized [the conclusion] by means of the result: "Therefore, there is a single apūrva";
and the observation of a difference in the effects [is presented] as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because of their mutual lack of connection.

[The opponent argues: "The understanding of mutual relationship [between words] would result in being without a basis. This is said for the sake of establishing the reasoning of the Siddhānta. Here, because the utterance has the *niyoga* (the mandate) as its purpose, all words have a direct connection with the *niyoga*. And since it is improper to resort to an indirect (*paramparā*) relation when a direct connection is possible, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that all words have the *niyoga* as their object. The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: if all words had the *niyoga* as their object, there would be a contradiction with the understanding of their mutual relationship; therefore, since there is a distinct *niyoga* for each word, those [words] which enter into different *niyogas*...

Because a connection [between the two] is untenable, it is logical that there be a distinction of objects according to their respective applications (*viniyoga*). Thus, the objecthood of one belongs to that which is supported by the other. Furthermore, if one were to rely on a mutual relationship, the comprehension of the application (*viniyoga*) would result; however, it is precisely the comprehension of the application (*niyoga*) that is established.
Thus it is the authority.
When [an action] is something new from a single [word], then there is doubt: does it arise from words denoting existence (*bhāva*), or from words denoting substance and quality (*dravya-guṇa*)?
Regarding this, he asks: by the mention of "words denoting existence," what is being included?
The proponent of a partial view (ekadeśin) offers an answer: "Of verbal roots alone.
He then raises an objection: "If that is so, then by pointing out this doubt, [it must be specified] whether [the suffixes apply] to nominal words or to verbal roots?"
It must be stated: what is this being said—is it from words denoting states (bhāva-śabda) or from words denoting substances and qualities (dravya-guṇa-śabda)? [To the objector, p.
He asks: G. What is there, or what is superior here, such that even in the author of the Bhāṣya’s presentation of the doubt, there is nothing additional?
It is questioned whether it is more appropriate to derive [the meaning] from noun-words (*nāmaśabda*) or from verb-words (*ākhyātaśabda*). The objector says: "The noun-word is repeated unnecessarily;
for when the inclusion of substance-words (*dravyaśabda*) and quality-words (*guṇaśabda*) is being made, verb-words are not included."

The inclusion of both types of words [nouns and verbs] is achieved by means of two terms. When the term "bhāvaśabda" (action-word) is employed—that is, when recourse is made to the category of action-words—the inclusion of substance-words and quality-words must be effected as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). For at that time, the word is indicated by way of its denotation; thus, the distinct terms "substance" and "quality" must be uttered as the denotata in order to bring the general category of "word" to mind. However, in the case of the inclusion of "ākhyāta" (verb), since the word is indicated by its own form (*svarūpa*), the term "nāma" (noun) serves to indicate the very form of the word itself.

Thus it must be employed. And consequently, there is no utterance of two words for the sake of brevity. The supreme resolver says: "For you are ignorant of the intended meaning; for if it were stated whether [the suffix] comes from verbal roots (ākhyāta-śabda) or from nominal stems (nāma-śabda), then it would be determined."

If it were held that the *apūrva* arises only from verbal roots (*ākhyāta*), then the statement "the cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*) would lack a ritual action as its purpose.

The connection between the substance and the deity would not be the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), because the word *āgneya* is a noun (*nāman*). Furthermore, the meaning of the verb "it exists" (*bhavati*)—which denotes an action—would have to be the object of the injunction, because it is a verbal root.

Regarding the word *bhavati*: both of these [interpretations] are undesirable. This is because the meaning of "becoming" (*bhavati*) cannot be that which is enjoined; for an already existing thing (*bhūta*) cannot be enjoined to become, and that which is not yet existent (*abhūta*) cannot be enjoined because it does not itself exist. Therefore, the meaning of "becoming" is not something to be enjoined. Furthermore, it is the relationship between the substance and the deity that must be enjoined.
Therefore,
so that an undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti) does not arise, the mention of nouns and verbs was not made.
By the Blessed Commentator [it is said]: "What then?
By whichever nature the verbal root's status as having an injunctive meaning is possible, and by whichever nature the noun's status as having an injunctive meaning is possible..."

Therefore, it is not possible for the Bhagavat, as the author of the commentary, to have presented [the matter] by means of that very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is possible [only] to ask: by what intrinsic nature does the meaning of the verbal root possess the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), or by what [nature] is the name not excluded?
Thus it is possible.
To the two questions, there are two answers respectively:
since the meaning of the verb consists in the sense of "being," it possesses injunctive force; whereas since the name denotes a substance or a quality, it does not possess injunctive force.
We shall explain how this is so further below.
Here, the commentary asks: "What, then, is existence (bhāva), or what are the words for existence?
It explains this as follows: "What indeed is this thing called 'existence' that is distinct from the meaning of a verb? And what is a word for 'existence' that is distinct from a verbal word?"

He explains the *Uttarabhāṣya*: "But the reply, however—the meaning of these [verbs] 'one should sacrifice,' 'one should give,' and 'one should offer' is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*); and these are words denoting action (*bhāvaśabda*). Now, one might object: "Are not these the words 'sacrifice' (*yāga*), 'giving' (*dāna*), and 'offering' (*homa*)?"

This is the explanatory passage (*parihārabhāṣya*) [of the *Bhāṣya*]. He explains it: "But is this not that very same meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*), and are these not those very same verbal words (*ākhyātaśabda*)?"—this is the objection. "It is not so; for these are words such as 'sacrifice' (*yāga*) and so forth"—this is the explanatory passage of the rebuttal (*parihārabhāṣya*). He explains the resolution:
"The solution, however, is that the meaning of the verb alone is not [the cause] in cases such as 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*), 'one gives' (*dadāti*), and 'one offers oblations' (*juhoti*)."
What, then, is understood? It is also the production of another object;

that is, it is understood as the production of an object other than the agent. Not only is the temporal sequence [of prior and posterior] understood—as in the case of "it becomes"—but the mere temporal sequence is the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*). The meaning of the verb is the mere temporal sequence.

"One should not meditate in that way"—here, in the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is the production of another [entity]. That quality of being the meaning of the verbal root does not exist in the case of "it exists" (*bhavati*), because there it is understood as the arising of the agent itself. What we have stated here has also been stated by the Author of the Bhāṣya: "And from this, the meaning of *yajati* and so forth is understood, namely, 'one should bring about' (*bhāvayet*)."
By this commentary [the author says]. Now, thinking that the meaning of this commentary is something entirely different, he asks: "What has been stated by this commentary? The answer follows.
— From this, both the relation of priority and posteriority and the state of being a producer of another are understood;
in that regard, where the effect and the meaning of the sacrifice and so forth are understood from it, [that is the case].

By this, the understanding of sacrifice and other acts as consisting of prior and subsequent stages has been stated. "He should bring about" (bhāvayet) conveys the understanding of producing something else. Furthermore, this meaning has been clarified by the author of the Bhāṣya: "One should strive in such a way that something comes into being."
The meaning is that human effort conducive to the production of something else is understood. Therefore, even these verbal forms (*ākhyāta-śabda*) are called "words denoting action" (*bhāva-śabda*).

For that object whose nature is to bring about the production of something else consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages is the "meaning of action" (*bhāvārtha*), and words having that as their referent are "words denoting action. Consequently, there is also the inclusion of words denoting substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*).
Indeed, if the term "noun" (*nāman*) were used [in the definition], the counter-correlative would not be specified; for among nouns, some...

Because its meaning consists in the nature of consciousness (*cidbhāva*). Now, if someone should think: "Even so, that intrinsic nature by which there is purposiveness toward action (*kriyārthatva*) would not be specified as being non-purposive toward action (*akriyārthatva*).
He replies to that: "Because they produce the cognition of substances and qualities, they do not have action as their purpose, nor do they have names as their purpose;

for we observe that names such as 'āgneya' (dedicated to Agni) and so forth do have action as their purpose. What, then, is the prima facie position? That they are alike. What is the intention [of this objection]?
This is the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya.

The reply is: whether it be the substance that exists for the sake of the action, or the action that exists for the sake of the substance, in any case, the connection with the effect is precisely one that does not abandon the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka). If the injunction (niyoga) has the action as its object, then everything else is for the sake of that [action].

According to logic, a substance exists for the sake of action; however, when the substance is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), then the action exists for the sake of the substance. In both of these positions—this being the position that action exists for the sake of the substance—the relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*) is not contradicted. Therefore, since no specific distinction is perceived, either one may be the object of the injunction. Nor does this result in a lack of authority due to indecision, because the performance of the rite is indeed determined. It is of a single form.

For in both cases, there would be performance [of the rite], and because of the lack of determination regarding that performance, there would be a lack of authority [for the Veda]. To this it is replied: in this way, the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka) is not established. For when the action has the substance as its purpose, then the injunction (niyoga) has the substance as its object; in that case, the relationship between action and its factors is simply abandoned. Why?

The answer is: at that time, the substance (*dravya*) is the object (*karman*), being the primary element in the action (*kriyā*) because it is what is intended to be reached by the action. And that which is intended to be reached becomes the object. Furthermore, the object is not the *kāraka* itself;
for we shall explain that "the arising [of the result] residing in the *kāraka* is the object."
The *kāraka* [is defined as follows]: that state which arises from the position of a *kāraka* is the *karman*, not the state of the *kāraka* itself.

If the *karman* is not a *kāraka*, how then is there the traditional rule (*āgama*) stating "the second case ending occurs when the *karman* is the *kāraka*"? Likewise, [the rule] "that which is desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsita*)...
And [the statement] "darkness is the object" (*tamaḥ karma*) occurs in the section concerning grammatical factors (*kāraka*).
By reflecting upon this traditional authority (*āgama*), it is understood that the status of being a factor (*kārakatva*) belongs to the object (*karman*). Regarding the object...

Because of the indication of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the rule *kārake dvitīyā*, and because it is stated that "the factor (*kāraka*) which is most desired to be reached (*īpsitatama*) is the object (*karman*"), [the author] provides the resolution: the meaning of the sūtra is that the factor in which the fruit of the action is produced is the object.

The status of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to a factor of action (*kāraka*) by virtue of its participation in the fruit of the action; it does not consist, however, in the mere production of the action. And the status of being a factor of action exists precisely through the production of the action, and not otherwise. Why is the meaning of the Sūtra such? To this he says: otherwise, the mention of the term "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) would be purposeless.

For that which brings about the accomplishment of an action is not the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) by means of that action; rather, the state of being the recipient of the fruit produced by the action is what constitutes the most desired object by means of that action.
Therefore, it is also established that the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used for the *kāraka* known as the object (*karman*).
Because it is connected with two states,
therefore the verb (ākhyāta) serves the purpose of action, the purpose of injunction (niyoga), and presents the object of that injunction.

At that very time, the status of substance and quality as *kārakas* (factors of action) is established, and they are heard [in the text] precisely as *kārakas*; it is not for the sake of favoring this [fact] that the meaning of the verbal suffix alone is determined to be the meaning of the *niyoga*. Therefore, he says: "From those words which denote an action (*bhāvārtha*) and are terms for ritual acts (*karmaśabda*), such as 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*) and so forth, the action (*kriyā*) is to be understood."

Here, the author of the Sūtras, by stating that "action should be understood from those words whose meaning is being" (bhāvārtha), has stated that the very fact of having "being" as their meaning (*bhāvārthatva*) is the reason, since no other reason is provided.
With this in mind, he asks: "Why?
He explains that: "Why? is the question; what is it here?
Otherwise, how could its status as a *bhāvārtha* (an action denoting a process) be lost?

Even that status of being a *bhāvārtha* would be lost if it were not the object of an injunction (*niyoga*). In that case, this would indeed be a valid reason; however, the point is that this is not the case.

The answer is: Certainly, it is lost; for the status of being a verbal action (bhāvārthatva) belongs to a word denoting an action only when there is a sequence of prior and posterior (pūrvāparībhāva), since the term "action" denotes that sequence. Nevertheless, he asks: "And what of it? He replies: And that sequence of prior and posterior occurs here only when [the substance or quality] is for the sake of that [action], namely the sacrifice. Otherwise, as in the case of "one desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a milking vessel," there would be only the comprehension of a substratum (āśraya). It is not so here.
And it is understood that the *praṇayana* (carrying forward) is to be accomplished by means of the milking of the cows (*godohana*).

The meaning of this is as follows: for when there is "being-to-be-accomplished" (*sādhyatva*), there is the state of being a verbal action (*bhāvārthatva*); and when a verbal action is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), and substances and qualities serve the purpose of that [action], then the state of being "to-be-accomplished" is realized in the verbal action. But in the case of substances and qualities...

If [the word] has the sense of an injunction (*niyoga*), then the understanding of the meanings of the verbal suffixes would occur only as the substratum (*āśraya*) [of that injunction], and not as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), as in the case of "one desiring cattle should fetch [water] in a *godohana* vessel. But is it not the case that even in "one desiring cattle should fetch [water] in a *godohana* vessel," the fetching (*praṇayana*) is indeed a process consisting of prior and subsequent stages?
It is understood that the *godohana* is indeed an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*). He offers a rebuttal: "True, it is so understood;
however, it is not understood as having the sentence-meaning 'one should pour water with the *godohana*.'"

In this sentence, because the *godohana* (the milking vessel) constitutes the meaning of the sentence and because the *praṇayana* (the act of carrying forward) serves to assist it, a reversed relationship of goal and means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is understood. However, this worldly relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*) is what is actually conveyed by the word. Therefore, even in the view that there is no restrictive rule (*aniyamapakṣa*), the sentence is understood to have the nature of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*) so long as it does not abandon the relationship between action and its factors through such a restriction.

When, first of all, the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) is action (*kriyā*), then there is no abandonment of the perceived relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*). However, in the case of substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*), since they are stated to exist for the sake of action, by the aforementioned reasoning, there is indeed an abandonment of the relationship between action and its factors; thus, there is no lack of restriction. Rather, it is only that which has "being" as its meaning (*bhāvārtha*) that constitutes the meaning of the injunction. Therefore, this was said: "precisely because it has 'being' as its meaning. [p. 293]
This is what is meant: it is precisely because the relationship [between the word and its meaning] is understood in this very way.
Since the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) has the nature of an injunction (*niyoga*), it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
whereas substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) have only the nature of being means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). It is exactly thus.

The meaning is that the relationship is understood [only] in this way, and not otherwise. Now, he elaborates upon that object denoted by the word *bhāva* (action), which is distinct from a sequence of prior and posterior states—[an object] for the sake of explaining which the term *bhāvārtha* was employed instead of employing a verbal form (*ākhyāta*). He elaborates on that object, which is distinct from a sequence of prior and posterior states, namely the sense of "bringing about the production of something else."

—As for those who say that one should bring something into being (*bhāvayet*), they would say that one should bring heaven into being (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*) because of its connection with the word "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). Here, this is the intended meaning: having observed the activity occurring immediately after hearing a sentence containing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, it is determined that the optative suffixes and the like denote an object that impels to action. And since it is understood that the "task to be accomplished" (*kārya*) is what impels to action, it is concluded that the optative suffixes and the like also make that very thing known. Furthermore, the task to be accomplished is said to be that which is achievable through effort (*kṛti*) and is primary with respect to that effort. As it has been said: "That which is achievable through effort is the primary [object]."

As for that which is called the "effect" (kārya), its designation is not possible without designating an effort (kṛti); therefore, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others also designate effort. And since effort itself is the operation of the instigator toward that which is to come into being, it is termed "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*). Consequently, from expressions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the production of something else is understood. And that production of something else, through its connection with the word "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), is the "production of heaven" (*svargabhāvanā*).

It is understood [thus]. Here, an objection is raised: "Why is it said that 'one should bring about heaven' (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*) by virtue of its connection with the word *svargakāma*? It would be more appropriate to say 'one should bring about the one who desires heaven' (*svargakāmaṃ bhāvayet*). For the relation of one word-meaning (*padārtha*) is with another word-meaning; and here, the word-meaning is the one who desires heaven, not heaven itself. Therefore, this appears to be incorrect. To this, it is replied: True, [the word] *svargakāmaḥ*...

The meaning of the word is the person (puruṣa), because this word has the person as its primary referent; and that very person is [connected] with other word-meanings expressed by the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth.
It is connected with the effect by way of being that which is to be enjoined; however, this connection, which culminates in the production of heaven, has heaven as its ultimate goal.
Thus,
the author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated here that the "ultimate purpose" (aidaṃparya) consists in reaching as far as the connection with heaven; this is what is meant by "finality" (paratva).

Now, one might ask: for what purpose has the production of something else been elaborated by resorting to heaven (*svarga*), rather than being elaborated again by resorting directly to the *apūrva* itself? To this he says: "For the purpose of demonstrating that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*).

This is the intended meaning: if the word "one who desires heaven" culminates in the *bhāvanā* (productive operation) directed toward heaven, then only at that point, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the locus of the *apūrva*, would the *apūrva* be a causal effect distinct from the action.

[The instrumental nature] is established. Otherwise, the action itself would be the result (*kārya*). Consequently, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) would be only an object (*karman*), not an instrument (*karaṇa*).

It is only when there is a result distinct from the action that the instrumental nature of the meaning of the verbal root with respect to that [result] is established. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of demonstrating this instrumental nature? To this he says: "For it will be stated that once this section is settled, there will be an inquiry as to whether [the word in question] is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*). This is what is meant: the mention of "the meaning of the verbal root" (*bhāvārtha*) is made here for the purpose of refuting [the view that the word is] a name.

The establishment of the names of the *śyena* and other such words occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This establishment of coreferentiality, in turn, exists when the sacrifice functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the words *śyena* and so forth are joined with the instrumental case-ending. Therefore, without the establishment of the instrument, it is impossible to explain the very apprehension of the verbal root's meaning (*bhāvārtha*); thus, in order to demonstrate its status as an instrument, its productivity with respect to heaven (*svarga*) has been shown. But how can there be such a focus as "one should bring heaven into being"?

Regarding such sentences as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the answer is: we shall explain how they have such a purport in the section on qualification (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*), specifically under the sūtra *vṛtty-arthaṃ cābhi-saṃyogāt*. Therefore, the Commentator concluded: "From them, action should be understood. But what, then, is this "action" (*kriyā*) here?

The answer is: "the meaning of an injunction" (*vidhyartha*), which is the meaning that has the form of an injunction (*vidhirūpa*). Now, it has been stated that the performance of an action is the instrument for the result.

Furthermore, the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the fruit, not the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), because if it were the meaning of the injunction, it would follow that it is not the meaning of the sentence (*avākyārthatva*). It is replied: just as the meaning of the injunction [is understood].

We shall explain the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the section on the definition of qualification (*adhikāra*); nor does it have the status of a sentence-meaning or the status of being the object of an explanation,
because it is based solely upon its nature as an instrument for the sake of the Self (*ātman*).

As it has been said: "In order to establish the enjoined person who is favorable to the realization of the self, even heaven and the like are for us merely subordinate; the primary thing is the task (kārya) itself."

And here too, by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), in stating that "those [words] connected with sacrifice, gift, and oblation declare the production of heaven," it is stated that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) itself is the instrument (*karaṇatā*).

This is the meaning of this commentary: those words denoting action (*bhāvaśabda*), being connected by way of denotation with the things expressed—namely, sacrifice, gift, and oblation—declare the meaning of the injunction, which consists in making those [actions] the object [of performance].

They express a novel meaning (apūrvārtha) by means of denoting that object. And in that context, by employing the word "origination" (*utpatti*) for the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), it is stated that the meaning of the injunction serves as the instrument (*karaṇatā*) for the production of heaven.

The word "origination" (*utpatti*) is derived in the sense of an instrument, according to the rule: "That by which something is produced is 'origination'. Now, one might object: since sacrifice and the like are accepted as the instruments, how can the meaning of the injunction be the instrument?
To the objection that this is not tenable, he replies: "Because of its connection with that [apūrva], the sacrifice and so forth possess the status of an instrument;

for the verbal root-meaning possesses the status of an instrument precisely by way of producing the apūrva which has become the instrument, and not otherwise. Thus there is no fault. To the question "Why?", he asks: "How, then, can there be the status of an instrument for the object of the niyoga?"
The intention is that its status as an instrument (karaṇa) is understood.

The meaning of the question is: how can the object of the injunction (vidhyartha), which is of the nature of an effect (kāryātmā), serve as an instrument for the accomplishment of the result? But the respondent [on p. 296] says:

For this is what is enjoined: it shows the meaning established by the definition of the *adhikāra* (qualification for performance), namely, "one who desires heaven should achieve heaven by means of sacrifice and so forth.

For in the first section of the sixth book (*Ṣaṣṭhādya*), regarding the one desiring [a result] who is enjoined to an action, the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the accomplishment of that desire; of whom [is this stated]?
Having raised the objection that this is merely the function of the word, this point was stated with effort: "By what [means] would one accomplish heaven? By sacrifice and so forth.
What is demonstrated by this passage?
The answer is: it is that very same reasoning pertaining to qualification (*adhikārikī yukti*).

The very same reasoning that was stated in the section on "qualification" (*adhikāra*) regarding the fact that the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), is expressed by this passage. Why? He says: "For it will be established that qualification belongs to one who seeks to accomplish heaven."
He will state that "the qualification of one who desires belongs to the limit of the accomplishment of the desired object. Therefore, this is the meaning of the commentary:

for one who desires heaven indeed wishes to accomplish heaven. When there arises the expectancy, "By what means shall he accomplish heaven?", the injunction *yajeta* (he should sacrifice) is prescribed. And since the fruit is accomplished by the meaning of that word through the mediation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), and not otherwise, the *apūrva* is thereby understood.
Therefore, since the word that denotes it [the sacrifice] is what causes the *apūrva* to be understood, this is the resolution of the contradiction between the earlier and later statements.

Why is a contradiction between the earlier and later suspected? To this he says: "For previously it was stated that the fruit arises from the *niyoga*, whereas now you say the fruit arises from the sacrifice"—this is the contradiction. He resolves it: "By saying 'having produced the *apūrva* by means of that [sacrifice],' there is no contradiction."

Since the instrumentality of the sacrifice also exists by way of the accomplishment of the apūrva which has become the instrument, there is no contradiction due to this correspondence; therefore, the apūrva is understood.

He explains the commentary along with its supplementary gloss (*sopaskāram*): "From that, it is understood that the *apūrva* alone is the means to the fruit; 'the means to the fruit' is the supplementary gloss.

Since the status of sacrifice and the like as instruments [of action] is established through the mediation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), therefore the *apūrva* alone is the ultimate cause. Consequently, that which denotes it causes the *apūrva* to be understood; thus, we maintain that verbal roots (*bhāva-śabda*) are denoters of the *apūrva*.
Having thus restated the *Bhāṣya* by means of its opening phrase (*pratīkena*), [the author proceeds].
He states the intended meaning (*tātparya*): "Therefore, that which denotes it"—this is the conclusion (*nigamana*).

The meaning is that this is the summary. He states the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*): "Because the meaning consisting of the action (*bhāvārtha*), while accomplishing the *apūrva*, produces the fruit, and not otherwise due to its momentariness;
therefore, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) having that as its object is conveyed by the optative suffixes (*liṅgādi*) and so forth, and of that..."

Since that which is being conveyed depends for its comprehension upon the object [of the action], and since verbal roots (bhāva-arthāḥ) denote the object, it is said that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is understood from them; however, these verbal roots are not the direct denoters (*vācaka*) of the *apūrva*.

Demonstrating this, the author of the Bhāṣya explains the sūtra *tebhyaḥ kriyā pratīyeta* as follows: "When it is said that 'action is understood from those [words] whose meaning is existence' (*bhāvārtha*), that is not intended to mean that they are direct denoters; rather, it is by way of denoting their objects.
To the question, "Why is the sūtra explained in this manner? the author of the Bhāṣya replies: "But there is no word whatsoever that is a direct denoter of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency)."

Thus, some consider this commentary to be incorrect. For by this very commentary, it is stated that there is no word whatsoever that denotes the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality); and that is incorrect, because words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) do denote it. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But there is no word that directly denotes the *apūrva*"—this is intended with reference to the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). [R. *bhāvārtha*]

In the passage beginning with *bhāvārthāñ śabdān* (p. 298), the negation of denotative capacity is intended with reference to words whose meaning consists in an action (*bhāva*), and not with reference to words in general. Thus he says: "Furthermore, it is not that even words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) do not express an injunction (*niyoga*)."

Now, one might object: "Even if it is understood from the Sūtra that action (*kriyā*) is perceived from those [verbal roots], and thus it is determined that only those words whose meaning is 'being' (*bhāvārtha*) denote the mandate (*niyoga*), nevertheless, this doubt is not appropriate because there is no evidence for it; therefore, this statement is made not to refute such a doubt, but rather to show that no word directly denotes the *apūrva*. To this he says: "But how can there even be a suspicion that the verbal roots denoting 'being' are expressive [of the mandate]?"

The answer is: because the word *niyoga* (the injunction), such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, is never employed in isolation. If the meaning of an injunction were determined—or indeed enjoined—by the optative suffix and so forth when used alone, apart from the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), [then it would be possible].

In that case, there would be no suspicion that it expresses the meaning of a verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). Nor is there ever the usage of a word in isolation, because its application is invariably restricted to being followed by a verbal base (*prakṛti*); for it is only that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) that is employed.

Even when the meaning of the action (*bhāvārtha*) is expressed, it is employed only as a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), not in its pure form. Therefore, for those who hold the erroneous view that denotative power (*vācakatā*) follows only as far as the actual usage, denotative capacity conforms precisely to that which is employed—the word consisting of both stem and suffix; and it is exactly in that manner [that it functions].

For those who are deluded into thinking that [the phonemes] themselves possess denotative power, the limited scope of usage cannot be established through any means other than by way of the comprehension of meaning.

If even a single [phoneme] were expressive, why then is it not used alone? For there is no means for determining the extent of usage other than the mutual understanding of meaning; indeed, only as much as is required to convey the meaning is employed. To refute this view, it was stated that [the phoneme] is "not expressive. Now, if expressiveness is suspected on the grounds that its usage otherwise remains unaccountable, then that is not correct.
He states [the following] in a single passage to refute [this]: "Or rather, how else could the limited number of formal arguments (*prayoga*) be established,
by which [or for which] that argument..."
To the extent that the capacity to denote [meaning] following upon the application [of a word] is being refuted, he offers this rebuttal: "Is even the comprehension of meaning—
which is understood either from the existence [of the word] or from its distinction— to be denied?"
It is possible;
even without the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, by means of the very first [word].

In expressions such as "he offers" (*juhoti*) and "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), verbal roots denoting action (*bhāvārtha*) are perceived; yet, when suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) are employed with a different root, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is understood. Thus, through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the optative suffix and others alone denote the *apūrva*. However, the fact that the verbal root expresses the meaning of action, which is clearly apprehended, cannot be denied. Therefore, verbal roots denoting action do not possess the capacity to denote the *apūrva*.
If denotative capacity exists through distinction [of individual words], then what is the cause for the restriction of usage?
Why is the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix) etc., not used alone? The answer is: it is simply usage (*prayoga*).

The reason for the restriction on usage [is as follows]. Now, one might object that when usage itself is asked about as the cause, it is not a proper answer to say that usage itself is the cause; to this he says: "Just as with denotative power, the beginninglessness of usage has also been stated."

The denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of words is due to their beginninglessness (*anāditā*); their usage, moreover, proceeds through a lineage of the linguistic practice of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra-paramparā*), since beginninglessness has been established in the *Vimalāñjana*. Therefore, for subsequent persons, the very usage of preceding individuals is the cause of the restriction.
