"It has been stated that validity arises from independence. He challenges this: "How will independence effect validity in the face of a contradiction?"
The meaning is that [the reason] is ineffective with respect to validity. Why? He says: for contradiction brings about a mutual reversal, and reversal...

The consecrated king (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*) is cited as an example regarding invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). He refutes [the objection]: "It is true that the reverse is the case regarding the consecrated king's invalidity."

Thus, however, here, in the case of independence (*anapekṣatva*), error itself cannot obtain its own existence, because both [the cognition and the object] would be independent. For error is based upon non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*); and non-apprehension is not possible for that which is described as independent. If there were an obtaining of self-existence for error...
"In that case, there is no contradiction. He replies: "How is there no contradiction, given that there is indeed a contradiction because the performance [of the ritual] is a single act?"
Because of the unity of the word.

For a single injunction for performance (prayogavidhi) implies only a single performance. And when the performance is one, there is indeed a contradiction. He objects again: "What is this? It is like a Mahendra-illusion!"

"There is contradiction, there is no reversal. He refutes this: "This is this," because the treatise is a single unity. And thus, from the perception of contradiction, it is exactly so from that [source]. The meaning of this is as follows:

By one scripture, a contradictory practice is taught because it cannot be combined simultaneously. Nor is there a matter of relative strength or weakness despite the contradiction; rather, both are unerring, and there is simply a recourse to option (*vikalpa*), since they are mutually exclusive when performed simultaneously. But if this is so...

"Why does the same not apply to the Smṛti as well, such that there would be an absolute sublation of the Smṛti? To this, he says: "But the memory of that [Smṛti] is not like that. Why? Because the oneness [of the source] is unestablished.
That is to say, the fact that they belong to a single scripture is unproven in that case. He asks why, and then says: "It is inferential..."

For that is the reason there: it has been stated that once the opponent has been understood, inference finds no footing. Indeed, if the Veda were inferred, there would be the status of a single scripture; however, the possibility of inferring the Veda does not exist here because of its contradiction with the directly perceived Veda.
Therefore, the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*) is refuted here, as there is a disparity between the two cases—[the Veda] being established [by itself] and [inference] not being so.
As for that mutual dependence between the two contradictory authorities,
scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*), which was stated— namely, that "if scripture is authoritative, tradition is delusion; if tradition is authoritative, scripture is delusion"—
that has been refuted here by another means.

Since the delusion of memory is established by the contradiction of the inference of the Veda with the directly perceived Veda as its opponent, and since the delusion of the Smṛti is established by its being rooted in error; he summarizes the meaning of the two sections: "Therefore, the Smṛti...
The invalidity of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) has been refuted by its having as its cause something perceivable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, inference is also rejected.
As it has been said:
"Because a [contradictory] reason is observed."

Even a Smṛti rule whose meaning is contradictory may be established on the basis of observed custom (*ācāra*); for greed can be the root of such custom. Indeed, a certain priest, greedy for clothing, deceived a sacrificer of little learning by having him wrap the entire *audumbarī* post. Having understood that this custom was rooted in the Veda, the deluded author of the Smṛti [recorded]: "The entire *audumbarī* post must be wrapped."
Thus it is recorded in tradition. Therefore, since its basis is clearly perceived, it is not possible for it to have an inferred basis in the Veda that is entirely unperceived.
Or, [the phrase] "or another section" (adhikaraṇāntaraṃ vā) may be used; what is the meaning of "or another section"?

The meaning of this is as follows: this is not a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*) from the preceding section; for it was stated there that no inference of a further reason exists because the reason has already been seen. Here too, that very same point is being stated, and thus it does not constitute a separate section. He provides the rebuttal: the meaning is this—that it is the statement of a reason independent of the previous reasoning.
He explains this very point: the reasoning mentioned previously was dependent upon other reasonings; here, however, being stated as independent, it is called a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntara*).
First, contradiction (*virodha*) was the fundamental reasoning in the previous topic regarding the sublation of inference.

The perception of a reason (*hetudarśana*) constitutes an additional factor. However, in this case, the perception of a reason alone is the cause for contradiction with inference; thus, it constitutes a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntaratva*).
For this very reason, an example was cited regarding a non-contradictory subject: "They practice the gift of an elephant as a sacrificial post (*yūpahastin*)."

Thus [it is asked]: "But how is it that the observation of a cause—which is independent of any other reasoning—is not in contradiction with the inference from an effect? The answer is: "Precisely because of the observation of the cause. Since...

Thus, the cause is observed; for this very reason, there is a cessation of inferring a further effect. Indeed, when a cause is already seen, the inference of another cause does not proceed. And here, greed alone is seen to be the cause residing in the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), by which the sacrificer was so caused to act. When that conduct—
The author of the Smṛti, being deluded by the observation of [worldly] practice, composed the Smṛti. Therefore, when the cause is directly perceived, Vedic inference is not contradicted;
rather, it is non-contradictory, as in the preceding section.

This indeed becomes like the preceding section. Here he asks: in the absence of inference regarding the Veda, is there any necessity for adopting the usage of the Vedas among those things whose causes are perceived?
This applies even to other things whose causes are perceived.

Does their [inference] constitute an inference from the Veda, or not? If it does, then it must be graspable by a Vedic injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*); if it does not, then it is not so. The reply is: let it be graspable by a Vedic injunctive statement; let it be an inference from the Veda.
Up to this point... he objects: "In that case, where is the utility of stating the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), if there too the Veda is subject to inference?

The answer is: those [means of knowledge] that do not provide a visible benefit are not accepted as authoritative, whereas those whose objects are perceptible are accepted; thus, there is a distinction between the domains of validity and invalidity.

For when a specific result is seen to follow from a ritual—just as in the case of the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—the function of the scriptural statement is merely to enjoin a restriction, since that result is already implied by the ritual itself. Furthermore, greed cannot be the root cause of such a restriction, because a restriction is not something that can be practiced by a person out of personal desire.
For this very reason, even the Smṛti injunctions regarding the gift of a cow with golden horns and the like are not rooted in greed. Rather, one should act for the benefit of others.

Thus, since helping others is enjoined by the Veda itself through direct perception, and since the giving of wealth is implied by the force of that very injunction, the function of the scriptural statement is merely to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*). In that case, greed is not possible; therefore, this [giving] is not rooted in greed. For one, however, for whom no visible benefit exists within the sacrifice, the act of giving is understood solely from the scriptural statement. Since greed is possible in that instance, it is indeed rooted in greed. Therefore, in the context of the sacrifice, [the gift] serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), while the visible cause is [merely incidental].
It is logical to designate it as "non-authoritative" (*apramāṇa*) because its root—greed and the like—is merely presumed.

For this very reason, that which has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) is non-authoritative in the context of a ritual; as it was said regarding the gift of the cloth used in the *vaisarjana* oblation: since its purpose is seen, it lacks authority.

If it is argued that "there is no contradiction as long as there is no conflict with what is established by the learned" (*śiṣṭākope’viruddham*), then the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) remains established by the previously stated avoidance of invalidity when there is either a contradiction or a non-contradiction between the Smṛti and the Śruti. Now, the question arises: where does this contradiction exist, and where does it not?
It is considered for the purpose of rejection or acceptance:
if there is a contradiction, then the abandonment of the memory must be performed; if, however, there is none, [it need not be].

That is the "appropriation" (upādāna). Here, an objection is raised: for what purpose is the demonstration of the pervasion of the object? For this treatise is intent upon stating the nature of the *nyāya* (logical method), not upon being restricted to the objects of definition (*lakṣya*).
By means of this treatise, the statement of the nature of the *nyāya* is accomplished. Therefore...

When it has been stated that "in the case of contradiction there is rejection, and in the absence of contradiction there is acceptance" based on memory, why is it considered whether contradiction actually exists or not?

He replies: True, as you have said, this is merely the statement of the nature of the logical principle (*nyāya*), which is being demonstrated by its application to the subject matter. Even when the nature of the principle has been stated, it appears as if non-existent to those whose minds are focused on the practical task regarding a particular subject. Therefore, [this discussion] is for the purpose of removing that misconception.

This effort has been made by those of perfected intellect; for instance, in this very example, it appears contradictory to one who considers there to be a conflict between sequence and time that acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) would be prohibited.

The performance of the Smṛti-based ritual rinsing (ācamana) in the interval—when hunger and such conditions exist—contradicts that sequence which is determined by Śruti, namely: "Having made the Veda[-mat], one makes the altar. Likewise, it contradicts the principle of performing [the subsidiary acts] at the time of the principal act.

Regarding the limbs determined by the Śāstras: if the performance were carried out with only the right hand according to the Smṛtis, it would be subject to option (*vikalpyate*), or rather, it would be contradicted (*viruddhyate*) due to the occurrence of delay (*vilambāpatteḥ*).

Now, one might object that there is no contradiction at all, on the grounds that once the items prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti have been grasped, one relies upon their sequence and time; with this intention, he asks:
"How so? (*katham iti*).

The answer is: it is established in the section on *krama* (order) that performance [occurs] by virtue of the expansion of the injunction (*vidhivitāna*) regarding the meaning as it was heard. The meaning of this is: having grasped only those constituent elements (*padārtha*) delimited by direct revelation (*śruti*), the performance occurs by virtue of that expansion of the injunction which is perceived; this is established in the fifth [book], because those [elements] are directly revealed by scripture, whereas those based on inference—namely, the Smṛti-based ones—follow afterwards in order.

In case of conflict, they do not enter [into application]. Therefore, there is a conflict with the directly perceived injunction because of the contradiction with the expansion of the injunction; likewise, there is also a conflict regarding time, because the subsidiaries are implied by the time of the principal, and since the principal is directly perceived, there is a displacement of the time of the subsidiaries due to the displacement of the time of the principal.
If that [latter] were diminished, there would be a contradiction.

He states the established conclusion (rāddhānta): it is replied here that there is a contradiction only in the case of a contradiction with the meaning of the scripture (*śāstra*). And the scripture is for the sake of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), not for the sake of an injunction (*vidhi*).

It was stated in the second aphorism that [the Veda] is for the purpose of ritual performance (*vitāna*). This is because the authority of the Veda is asserted with respect to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). Why is it that the scripture does not exist even for the purpose of ritual performance, or why is it not for the purpose of injunction (*vidhāna*)? To this he says: "For it is only the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished) that is perceived as extended (*vitata*), because the ritual performance (*vitāna*) is eternally dependent upon the *kārya*."

The status of being an object of cognition does not belong to the effect independently; nor is there a contradiction between one effect and another effect, because [the sequence] is subordinate to the entities themselves rather than being a distinct category of entity.
There is no contradiction between the sequence—which is subordinate and dependent upon the entities—and those very entities. This is what is meant:

Once the nature of what is to be performed—consisting of the elements prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti—is understood, the determination of sequence occurs afterwards; thus, as B. and C. state, "the sequence comes later. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the ritual elements and the sequence.
How is there no contradiction regarding time? The answer is: for time is the accumulation of actions.

Therefore, because it depends on that—namely, because it depends on the effect—it will not conflict with the ritual elements (padārtha) belonging to the Smṛti which constitute the effect. On this point, the Bhāṣya states: “Furthermore, sequence occurs at a later time for those ritual elements that have already been obtained; and when the ritual elements are being obtained, there is as yet no sequence.”

Thus [it is said]. He objects: "What has been stated here that was not already stated? That very subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of sequence which was previously mentioned as the reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) need not be demonstrated again, since it has already been stated.
For when things are obtained even by means of establishing their status as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāva*), it is effectively stated that there is no *karma* at all. Therefore, how...

This is stated as another argument, as it were. He provides a resolution: there is indeed an intention here; he considers that sequence and time are nothing other than the collection of moments (*kṣaṇapracaya*).
For if those two were of such a nature [as independent entities], there would be no contradiction at all. Independent—

If, however, they were of the nature of distinct entities (*padārtha*), then contradiction would indeed be logical; so how could sequential time (*krama-kāla*) not consist of a collection (*vitāna-pracaya*) of such things?
The answer: In the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* [offering] on the full moon day," what collection of ritual acts (*karman*) is there?
[There is none, for] it refers to the constituent elements (*padārtha*) such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

Since the accumulation [of elements] is equal in the second and subsequent [days] as well, it is not logical for that accumulation alone to constitute the Pūrṇamāsī [day]. Furthermore, the understanding of sequence is observed through the nature of the action, as in the case of the statement: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati... and so forth.

Because the suffix *ktvā* is uttered here, the sequence is stated as something to be performed; therefore, an avoidance [of the conflict] by treating it as a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*) is not possible, since it is a task (*kārya*), and there is a contradiction in its being a task.

This objection is resolved by the following commentary. To demonstrate how it is resolved, he first sets forth the doubt: "When the ritual act in the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*) has been reached, is the spreading out of the initiation (*dīkṣāvitāna*) understood [to be performed], or is the Adhvaryu [the one who performs it] for the Gṛhapati?"
In this sentence, however, this sequence is understood as being independent and having its own task to perform, like the *samit* offerings and so forth;
it is not understood there as having an independent task. For there is no performance of one task within another task [B. & C. read: "not as another task"].
It is not understood. If there is an extension of the effect, it cannot be understood as an independent effect;
therefore, since the effect is not understood, the extension of the effect is also not understood—so with what is there a contradiction?
If the sequence is not stated as being another effect, then what is it?
The scope of this injunction, "the Adhvaryu [appoints] the Gṛhapati," is as follows:
we shall explain the latter at its proper occasion in the fifth [chapter]. It is also [to be understood] in regard to time.
And this very point is the solution stated in the Bhāṣya. How is this a solution? The answer is: what is intended by your reverence when you say "the word *paurṇamāsī*"?
For if that which is denoted is a single, all-pervading, and eternal time, then for that [time]...

Because there is no distinction even in the second [lunar day] and subsequent ones, it would follow that they are not denotable—or rather, it would follow that they are non-prescriptible. He himself says: "Therefore, in this case as well, it is precisely the accumulation of actions arising from the conjunctions and disjunctions of the planets that is expressed by words such as *paurṇamāsī*; [that is,] the accumulation of actions beginning with the conjunction of the moon and the sun."

That [lunar day] which begins with the first day (pratipad) and ends with the full moon is one thing; and that which begins with the first day and ends with the new moon (amāvāsyā), arising from the division [of the lunar month], is another. Since the terms "first day" and so forth are applied to the time [of the moon's phases] as distinguished by those limiting conditions (upādhi), it is logical that it is precisely that [conditioned time] which is denoted by those words, just like the word *sāman*. For example, the word *sāman*, when used for a mantra qualified by a melody (*gīti*), denotes the melody alone.

The same applies to words such as *pratipad* and so forth; however, this is the distinction: although they consist of a collection of actions (*kriyāpracaya*), there is a collection of enjoined effects (*coditakāryapraciti*).
The auxiliary (*aṅga*) is in one place [the time of the primary].
That time which is implied for the auxiliaries by virtue of being the time of the primary consists of the accumulation of the enjoined actions;
elsewhere, it consists of the accumulation of other actions.

The new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth constitute the auxiliary (*aṅga*). But how is it an auxiliary? It means that when [the new-moon day] occurs, the ritual is performed; that is to say, the ritual is performed at a time qualified by that [day]. Nor is it intended here that time, being a substance (*dravya*), possesses the status of an auxiliary.

Rather, that which is denoted by words such as "full-moon day" (*paurṇamāsī*) does not possess that status; for the status of an auxiliary belongs only to what is denoted by a word, and that must be expressed by a word.

It is understood: by that [means], through the medium of temporal limitation, even the accumulation of the movements of the sun and so forth constitutes a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the ritual action (*karman*).

In that regard, there is no contradiction in the case of those ritual items performed with the right-hand practice (*dakṣiṇācāra*), that is, with the right hand, due to the accumulation of other actions;
this applies to the time of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).
Because it is connected with that. As for the accumulation (*praciti*) of enjoined actions, it occurs at a time subsequent to the action itself;

thus, the accumulation of enjoined acts is based on the ritual elements (*padārtha*) of the Śrauta and Smārta rites as they have been enjoined. Therefore, there is no contradiction in its sequence, just as in the case of [other] sequential elements. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "And [acts such as] sipping water (*ācamana*)..."

He states his intention [when saying] "they create an intervention": it is the intention regarding the constituent parts of each ritual act; the sipping of water (ācamana) is a purification of the agent.

The agent is not a subsidiary (*aṅga*) by virtue of being a part of the performance (*prayoga*), but rather as a subsidiary belonging to each individual ritual act (*padārtha*). By that means, even acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*) possess the status of a subsidiary for each individual ritual act. Furthermore, one's own subsidiary does not constitute an intervention. Why? He says: for it is only when a ritual act together with its subsidiaries is connected with another ritual act that the understanding of their sequence is logical.

Since there is no contradiction [between the Smṛti rules and the Vedic injunctions], one must understand that Vedic ritual performances are to be carried out as being accompanied by the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and other such acts.
Because they are not observed in those [Vedic passages]. Even if there were a contradiction regarding the meaning of the words, what lack of authority would the Veda possess? It is not [the case].

This is the intended meaning. Since the doubt regarding the assertion that all [words] are denotative has already been dispelled by the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*) itself through the dual restriction (*ubhayaniyama*), [the opponent asks: "Because of the doubt, there is no comprehension.
If the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is uncertain, then the word and its meaning—

The claim that "there is no [other] meaning" constitutes a lack of authoritative evidence (*aprāmāṇya*). Nor is there any proof for assuming a dual denotative power (*śakti*) in both senses—as in the case of words such as *akṣa*—since it is stated that for both the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and the unlearned (*aśiṣṭa*), the primary power resides only in this [one sense], while in the other it is merely indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, even if grammar were authoritative, one could not determine where the primary sense lies and where the secondary; for if the science of grammar were not accepted, how could words such as *yava* and *varāha* serve as examples?

"It would not be so, because doubt is dispelled by the remainder of the sentence itself," he says. [Objection: "But has it not been raised that there is a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in cases where things are doubtful, on the grounds of 'from the remainder of the sentence'? [Reply: He refutes this: "True, it was raised. But where the word functions as a cause for meaning everywhere precisely through its possession of multiple meanings..."
When there arises a doubt as to what specific meaning a well-known word is employed here with, a determination is stated based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*),

as in the case of words such as *akṣa* which have multiple meanings. Furthermore, when there is a conflict among worldly people regarding the specific meaning of a certain word in some context, [the determination is likewise made].
The nature of the indicative mark (nimittatā) has not been understood; yet there is no doubt regarding its application,
for no doubt arises concerning its application.

"In what sense is this usage [to be understood]?"—the ablative case here is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (i.e., it means "from the usage"). Nevertheless, he asks: "What [is the purpose]?"—[the answer is:
"And the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) removes the doubt regarding the usage.
In whichever sense it is accepted, the consistency of the remainder of the sentence is established therein."

It is determined that [the word] is employed [in its primary sense]. The remainder of the sentence does not remove doubt regarding denotation; for this doubt exists precisely with respect to denotation.

Regarding doubt concerning denotation, there is a disagreement in linguistic usage: for some, the word "yava" is used for long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*), while for others, it is used for millet (*priyaṅgu*). Furthermore, there is no way to determine which usage is primary and which is secondary, because the linguistic application of the word is equal in both cases.
And it has been stated that the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda is rooted in the linguistic usage of words and their meanings.

In the *Saṃbandhaparihāra*, it is stated that because of this, a contradiction regarding the meaning of the Veda has arisen for those bound by worldly convention. Furthermore, this contradiction cannot be dismissed here on the grounds of inconsistency with the meaning of the Veda,
as follows:

The Smṛti rule regarding the complete wrapping of the Audumbarī post is set aside by the direct Vedic injunction for touching it, because the latter contradicts the meaning of the Veda; however, no such reason for setting aside [the Smṛti] exists in this case.

This is because the meaning of the sentence is compatible with both alternatives. Therefore, due to a conflict regarding the causal basis (nimitta), there is uncertainty concerning the meaning of the sentence.
Ignorance is non-determination; and from ignorance follows invalidity.
Or rather, it is according to the treatise.
He states the final conclusion: It is true that the contradiction cannot be refuted if there were no opposition;
however, here too, opposition is perceived. [The word] "ta eva" means "those very ones. For it is heard in scripture: "The cows run after the boar."

In such supplementary passages as these, there is a similarity between the boar and a cow; however, a black bird has no similarity to a cow. Thus, the understanding of the barbarians (mlecchas) contradicts the Veda. What follows from this?
The answer: A connection based on a specific cause is understood.

When the interpretation of the Mlecchas is rejected because it contradicts the Veda, it is determined that the word *varāha* functions as the causal basis for the meaning of the sentence precisely by conveying the sense of "boar" as established through the interpretation of the Āryas; therefore, the Veda is indeed determinative in this matter. Here, an objection is raised: But surely that very same...
"The conclusion follows from the remainder of the sentence.

To this he replies: "Even though this is a doubt regarding the designation, since the conclusion is reached through the remainder of the sentence, there is indeed a redundancy. He refutes this: "This does not follow at all."

He asks "Why? and says: For when the cause is doubtful, there is a need for a definitive determination; here, however, it is simply the misconception that is being refuted. [The terms] *varāha* and so forth mean nothing other than *sūkara* and so forth.

The misconception—that what is innate (*autpattika*) does not refer to the black bird and so forth, but rather that the black bird and such are the primary denotations—is here refuted; this is not a matter of doubt. Now, if the understanding of the *nimitta* (the cause or basis) comes from the Veda alone, then the absence of a worldly *nimitta* would be admitted, and not a worldly one.

[The opponent argues: "Because of conventional usage, as in the case of the sacrificial post (yūpa) and so forth. The proponent’s partial adherent (rāddhāntyekadeśin) says: "If there is indeed equality with words such as 'sacrificial post,' what is the fault in that?"
The objector refutes this: "Indeed, there is no other fault such as the killing of a Brahmin; for that very [act] is Vedic—"

The status of being a *nimitta* (ground/cause) is not established [in B and C]. How is it not established? Why? The answer is: when the worldly status of being a *nimitta* has not been apprehended, it cannot be apprehended from the Veda.
Even though this is understood from the Veda—that the word "varāha" denotes something similar to a cow—nevertheless...

The identification [of the *trivṛt*] with a pig is impossible, because similarity can exist for other things as well. Others, however, read the text as *anye tu pratipannāḥ*; their meaning is as follows: in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth, the status of being a Vedic basis is appropriate because it is entirely unknown in common worldly usage; here, however, since there is a well-known usage elsewhere in the world, the understanding of the basis does not derive from the Veda. This is incorrect, because regarding the word *trivṛt*, there is a counter-argument.

Even regarding worldly usage, since the understanding of its status as a cause arises from the Veda itself, the proponent of the final conclusion (*paramasiddhāntin*) justifies this: "Precisely because this understanding of its status as a cause arises from the Veda, for that very reason we do not call it 'Vedic. What then? It is said that the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) alone is authoritative, in accordance with the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*). And once this is established..."

Since the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭaprayoga*) is innate by virtue of its conformity with other parts of the Vedic texts (*vākyaśeṣa*), the understanding of the Mlecchas, which contradicts it, does not obtain such a status. [p. 103] Innate...
Because linguistic usage is established even by means of a secondary (gauṇa) sense.

Now, as to the question, "Why is it that the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) itself does not become secondary?"—to this he says: if the assumption of the innate connection (*autpattikatva*) of both were to arise from usage alone, then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*).
This results in a contradiction of conceptual construction (*kalpanāvyāghāta*).

For, by the authority of the linguistic usage of the Āryas, the usage of the Mlecchas would be considered delusive; and by the authority of the usage of the Mlecchas, the usage of the Āryas would likewise be considered delusive. Thus, due to this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), the assumption of an innate (*autpattika*) nature for words like "sūkara" and so forth would be untenable.
There is a contradiction here. However, it has been stated that in this case, the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of the Vedic usage established by other means is proven.

The superior strength of the usage of the Āryas is established through its conformity with the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*). And once that is established, the subversion of the opposing view is understood.
Because it would contradict the inference regarding the expressive and expressed powers of a word,
the usage of noble persons is therefore not figurative.
[The opponent] objects: Relying upon the preceding section, he states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "If, by the reasoning thus stated, the conduct of non-Aryans..."

[Objection: If it is argued that [the meaning] is established only figuratively (*gauṇa*), then those words which are not well-known as having a basis (*nimitta*) in the linguistic usage of the Āryas would have no basis at all in Vedic usage, such as *pika*, *nema*, *sata*, *tāmara-sa*, and so forth;
for the linguistic usage of non-Āryas does not [provide a basis for] the word-meaning.

Because they lack causality in that state, and because they are not observed in the linguistic usage of the noble ones (*ārya*), and because meaning is not understood from a word when its status as a cause is not determined, the status of being a cause would not belong to words such as *pika* in Vedic usage. If it is argued that let them not be causes, the author states the refutation: "In that very case, this same lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) would result."
If it is argued that— regarding what was previously stated as the definition of non-determination (anadhyavasāya)—
understanding of the meaning may arise from the study of etymology (nirukta), grammar (vyākaraṇa), and so forth,
just as in the case of words such as *jarpharī* and the like; [the author] refutes this:

There is no comprehension of meaning from those two— namely, etymology (nirukta) and grammar (vyākaraṇa)— because they are rooted in usage; for in the absence of observed usage, those very two would be baseless and thus unworthy of regard.
If the observation of usage alone is the root of those two, then how is the meaning of the base and the suffix inferred? As for those words...

In the world, those words whose meanings are perceived have their basis in usage; therefore, how is the determination of their meaning achieved through etymology (*nirukta*) and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) by relying on the division of roots and suffixes—especially in the case of words such as *jarpharī* and so forth? The answer is: precisely by virtue of their application (*viniyoga*).
This alone [is the reason].
It conceals— namely, the purposeful explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that constitutes a supplement to the mantra whose meaning has been determined and which has been employed [in the ritual].

For one who has ascertained the intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is the derivation of roots and suffixes following the usage of elders; however, a sentence stating an injunction (*vidhyuddeśavākya*) cannot be the cause for the derivation of words that are to be inferred, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for ascertaining its intended meaning. But where, on the other hand—

The statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśavākya*) would require a word whose meaning is to be inferred, and in that case as well, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, an injunction mixed with words such as *pika* and *nemi* lacks authoritative validity.

He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): It is true that there would be a lack of authority [in the scripture] if *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) were to contradict the inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*).

For in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* was adduced regarding the linguistic usage of non-Aryans concerning the *pika*, the *nemi*, and so forth, as being the meaning of words.

In the case of linguistic convention (*vyavasthā*), it is without a fixed sign (*animitta*), because it is a non-Aryan usage, like the referents of words such as "barley" (*yava*) and so forth. Now, if this is an inference from an effect—namely, an inference that the words *pika* and so on denote the cuckoo (*kokila*) and so forth, based on the effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning by those who do not follow Aryan conventions [p.

Would it then be invalid because that [contradiction] would refute it? Or rather, where there is a Vedic supplementary statement (*vedavākyaśeṣa*) regarding a specific object such as barley (*yava*) and so forth?

If there were a contradiction with the inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*) in that very case, then by what could the inference from effect— whose counter-argument has been refuted— not be prevented?
For him...

The counter-argument against inference from effect has been refuted; by what means could its prevention be effected? [Objection: Surely its prevention will be achieved through *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] itself. [Response (A): To this he says: "But what is the reason that it is not *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*? The answer is:
"For that would not even be a *sāmānya* (universal/commonality) if no counter-position were established."

A. In the case of the antidote (satipratipakṣe), being an ignoble convention (anāryavyavahāratva) that lacks an antidote is pervaded by the state of being signless (animittatvenaiva), and not merely by the state of being an ignoble convention alone. Therefore, there is no commonality whatsoever between an ignoble convention regarding objects such as *pika* [the cuckoo] which lacks an antidote, and an ignoble convention regarding objects such as *yava* [barley]. Consequently, [this applies to] the Mlecchas who lack an antidote...
Even that which is established by worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) is merely an instrumental cause for understanding the meaning of a Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

Therefore, in the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), the opposing view characterized by dependence—which arose when there was a conflict between the usages of Mlecchas and Āryas—has been refuted; and here, that same opposing view is refuted in the case of non-conflict. This [refutation] results in the independence (*anapekṣatva*) [of the Veda].
The authority of the *codanā* is established.
If it is argued that it is a treatise on ritual application (*prayoga-śāstra*), then what is the reason for its being established as such by virtue of its human authorship?
It is suspected that the *prayoga-śāstra* lacks independence [from human authority],
for the *Māśaka* and other such works are remembered solely as being of human origin; and whatever is the word of a person...

That [Vedic text] is dependent; therefore, how can its independence be questioned? The answer is: it is questioned on the grounds of both its being an effect (*kārya*) and its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He explains this very point: "The effect is the recitation of what has been studied, like other Vedic branches (*śākhā*); the means of valid cognition, moreover, is the word of the Teacher (*ācārya*), according to the principle that 'the word of the Teacher is authoritative' (*ācāryavacaḥ pramāṇam*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: when a certain work is recited again by Maśaka and others exactly as it was already recited in another *śākhā*, its independence (*anapekṣatva*) is understood through that consideration—this is indeed a Vedic sentence, and its independence is entirely logical. For a Vedic sentence does not become dependent merely because it is recited by a human being.

By the statement "the word of the Teacher is authoritative," it is understood precisely that it is independent (*anapekṣatva*). For there is no dependence for that which is authoritative; indeed, there is no authoritativeness in what is dependent.
But is this not a contradiction—to say that it is both of human origin and independent?
He refutes [the objection]: "What is contradictory here?

Things exist exactly as they are understood. And two things are understood here: its being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) and its independence (*anapekṣatva*). Its being of human origin follows from the fact that it is a recollection."
Therefore, that is established by those very two statements regarding the effect; thus, let there be both:
dependence [p.
108] and independence.

The intended meaning here is this: each individual sentence is indeed Vedic, and therefore possesses independence (*anapekṣatva*). However, because they are scattered across various recensions (*śākhā*), contexts (*prakaraṇa*), and independent discourses (*anārabhyavāda*), they are compiled and recited in a specific sequence by a person through his skill; thus, they possess human authorship (*pauruṣeyatva*).
This is not so, because there is no restriction [to a single person].
He states the final conclusion: "This is not tenable—that it is both of human origin and independent.
Nor should it be argued that it must simply be of non-human origin, for its [human origin] is established.

The *prayoga-śāstra* (treatise on ritual application) is of human origin because it is remembered as being composed by a person; nor can this be avoided by claiming it is merely a recitation, as in the case of the *Kāṭhaka* and other such texts.

Just as designations such as *Kāṭhaka* are established by virtue of the specific mode of recitation (*pravacana*), so it is not with the tradition that [the Vedas] were composed by a person. Even granting for the sake of argument that they were indeed composed by a person, he asks: "So what?"—and replies:

"In this context, 'composition' (*kṛti*) consists solely in the expression of an object perceived through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not in being an effect produced from phonemes and the like."

The "activity" (kṛti) is precisely that which consists in the expression by means of a word of an object already perceived through another means of valid cognition, and the employment of the word with that as its primary purpose; it is not, however, the status of being an effect and so forth belonging to the phonemes and other such elements.

Because phonemes are eternal, and because both the sequence of phonemes and the sequence of words in the Veda are dependent upon sound (*dhvani*), they are indeed of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). Therefore, once their human origin is established, their dependence on other means of knowledge (*sāpekṣatva*) is certainly difficult to avoid. As for the "effect" (*kārya*) that was proposed regarding what has been recited...
Regarding the claim that "the recitation is like [the texts of] other branches," it is said in response: this is not equal to other branches,
as is the case with those other branches.
All Vedic sentences are likewise not [identical] here, because the sentences of the *prayoga-śāstra* (manuals of performance) are distinct sentences.
How are they distinct sentences? To this he says: "The practice of performance is its purpose," because of the exclusion of the rules for accents and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Having excluded the rules for accents and explanatory passages, distinct sentences are composed by the authors of the *kalpa-sūtras* for the sake of practicing the performance as understood from the Vedas.

[These are] for the performers. Therefore, these other sentences [are distinct] from the injunction along with its explanatory passage (arthavāda) and its accents, because of their abandonment of those elements. Those other sentences devoid of them—which were composed by Maśaka and others—refer to that very same meaning which was understood through the sentence consisting of the injunction together with its explanatory passage and its accents. And he states another purpose: B. adds "the manual of performance" (*prayogaśāstra*); the perception of immediate sequence [indicated by the term] *prayogaśāstra* brings about the non-interruption of the ritual items.
The treatise states: for indeed, when the accents and other properties of the individual words are set aside, the word-meanings are understood immediately after the sentence has been heard.

The purpose of the teachers' recited text is that those [rules] which are perceived without interruption are easily performed. And for this very reason—that this treatise is for the sake of practicing the performance and for swift comprehension—it is designated as a "prayoga-śāstra" (a manual of performance). Thus, there is immediate succession.
For this very reason, it is designated by the word "kalpa. For here, "kalpanā" (construction) refers to the arrangement of the constituent elements, not their injunction;
for the arrangement of these elements consists precisely of those things already enjoined in the Veda, rather than being an original injunction itself.

He shows that, according to the view of creation (*vidhānapakṣa*), there is no operation of conceptual construction (*kalpanāvyavahāra*): for a conceptualization occurs only of something already perceived, like a gem.

Just as the fashioning of a gem is for the purpose of stringing it into a necklace, so too here the composition is for the purpose of stringing together the practical applications. As it has been said: "The word of the Teacher is authoritative," and this is understood from that very authority.

That is not so, because this statement lacks authority regarding this particular meaning. For it has been stated that a word possesses independence only with respect to the nature of a thing (*vastu-svarūpa*), but not with respect to an effect (*kārya*). Therefore, since this sentence is subordinate to something else, it follows the observed [usage].
Explanation:
In this context, either the Veda is intended as the teacher, or else the word of the teachers is the authoritative source.

That which is to be understood through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is intended here as the true meaning; therefore, it has been stated that the word of the Teacher (*ācārya*) and the word of the Veda are authoritative (*pramāṇa*).
Alternatively, the word of the Teacher refers to the word of Maśaka and others, which is authoritative.
The meaning is "it is true. But what, then, is the purpose of this inquiry?
He states it in a single continuous passage: because this scripture is devoted to the postulation of what is enjoined, we perceive no contradiction.
For since this treatise is devoted solely to the arrangement of those very ritual items that have been prescribed, no contradiction with the Vedas is possible.
Response: There exists here a conception that contradicts what has been prescribed—the conception that the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices may be performed on all lunar days (tithis).
And that...

Because of the scriptural mention of specific times such as the full moon (paurṇamāsī), [the Vedic injunction] is contradicted. And that which is contradictory must not be relied upon; it is to be disregarded.
Otherwise, if it were respected, there would be a contradiction, and consequently, the Vedic injunction (codanā) would lose its authority.

Therefore, so that they may be disregarded when they contradict the Vedas, the dependence of the Kalpasūtras is asserted; for if they were respected, the authority of the Vedic injunction (codanā) would be undermined by their conflict with it.
Because of the establishment of inference. Here, however, the example consists of both that which has a fixed object and that which does not have a fixed object.

That which is accessible through the *śākhāgraha* (the specific Vedic schools), the *smṛtis*, and established custom (*ācāra*)— namely, that performance which is restricted in its scope and is practiced by some but not by all, and which in ultimate reality is non-restricted due to the absence of a cause for restriction— is the example here.
What is this [example] that is both "restricted in scope" and "non-restricted"?
The answer: "This and this.

Here, one instance of the word *idam* refers to what has been said, and the other refers to what is yet to be said. That which has been stated is "this," and that which we shall state is also "this"—namely, the eastern, northern, and southern [directions].

Those who possess that [regional] pride perform the Holākā and other such rites. This is the established rule (*vyavasthā*): "This rite belongs to those from the East and so forth, and we are indeed those from the East and so forth"—it is by means of this pride that they perform the Holākā and other rites. And since there is nothing whatsoever to restrict that pride, there would be no fixed rule (*avyavasthā*).
But how is it that there is no determiner? The answer is: prescription (*vidhi*) is not a determiner, for it terminates solely in the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*).

The meaning of this is as follows: A Vedic injunction that is inferred on the basis of observing the practice of others does not, for its part, restrict that injunction to a specific person, because it has as its sole purpose the prescription of the act itself. Furthermore, even the term "rite" (*karman*), as in the case of the *Holākā* and so forth, is not restrictive, because it merely denotes a particular type of ritual action. Nor is anything else—be it a quality (*guṇa*), a caste (*jāti*), a physical configuration (*saṃsthāna*), or a location (*deśa*)—restrictive, because such factors are absent.
If there were a quality, a genus, or a bodily configuration residing solely in the performer here and distinct from other persons, then that might serve as a restrictive factor;
however, such a thing does not exist. Likewise, even a designation such as "Dākṣiṇātya" (Southerner) and so forth is not a restrictive factor.

[Objection: Surely, one who is born in a particular place is designated by that specific region—as a person from the East, the North, or the South—and therefore let this designation be the restrictive factor. [The author] refutes this: No, for a designation does not arise from birth alone, as it would apply even to those who have merely arrived [from elsewhere].
Because they are equal, the designation (*samākhyā*) is not restrictive.

[Objection: But surely the designation "born in the South" (*dākṣiṇāpatha*) applies as soon as one is born; therefore, let it be the restrictive factor. [Reply: It is said: even this is not restrictive, for there is the case of the son of a Southerner (*dākṣiṇātyasuta*).
Someone born in a particular place may follow only the ancestral customs and not those of the local region; likewise, another person born elsewhere may do the same.
However, physical traits such as red eyes and so forth are unreliable as determinants.
Therefore, it is established that there is no fixed rule.
But does this inquiry possess utility with respect to the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇalakṣaṇaupayikatva*)?

Regarding this inquiry— whether ritual objects such as the *holākā* and others are to be performed only by those from the East and so forth, or by everyone— is there any application toward the definition of the means of valid cognition, by virtue of which [the latter] would be relevant here?
[The opponent] begins: "Insofar as that [determining factor] simply does not exist. The respondent says: "How so? It does not fail to exist;
rather, it certainly exists. The challenger asks: "Whether a determining factor exists or does not exist, what does this have to do with [the doctrine of] independence?"
The respondent says:
"This very point to be stated hereafter has arisen. The proponent considers there to be invalidity because, although pride exists, its root is not perceived."
Since this observed practice is seen to be accompanied by conceit (*abhimāna*), an injunction (*codanā*) as its source is impossible;
thus, an injunction that merely prescribes the *Holākā* festival and similar rites is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because its subject matter is unreal.
Such an injunction is not authoritative. Here, the following consideration arises: should one perform only that which is seen being performed by others?

"And also by another" means that it should be understood as being for the purpose of clarifying the scope [of the rule]. Having clarified the scope—that all of them must be performed because there is no fixed restriction—the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) remains in mind: "If there is no fixed restriction, then there is a lack of authoritative validity."

"In that case, [the objection] regarding the Veda [remains]. However, in the final position (*rāddhānta*), the lack of authority has been refuted by the fact that the Vedic statement does not originate from pride (*abhimāna*). For if the Vedic statement were to originate from pride, then the statement would correspond exactly to the kind of pride that is observed.

If it were the case that [the Veda] must be established [by other means], then there would be a lack of authority for the *codanā*. But this is not so, because the *codanā* is independent. Furthermore, there is no basis for such a misconception.
Let this misconception be incorrect as it may.
Nevertheless, let the authority of the injunction (codanā) regarding the essential nature of action be established; thus he says:
"Furthermore, it is not possible to assert that the injunction is non-conformable with reality.

Because grammar is not a scripture for the production of correct usage. But how, given that the traditional treatise of grammar (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is without a foundation, can the lack of authority of the Veda be established?

This section is commenced in order to remove the doubt that one might entertain; he says in a single passage: "If words such as *gāvī* were also to possess beginningless existence, what would happen to the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)? For even words such as *go* [would be included] in this view."

Only words such as *sāsnādimat* (possessing a dewlap) and the like are denoters [of the cow], and not merely words such as *gāvī*. Consequently, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is indeed established. It is replied: Grammarians who know the Veda maintain that words such as *aśva* and *goṇī* have fixed meanings. The word *aśva* is the denoter of a horse alone, not of a pauper; and the word *goṇī* is the denoter of a sack alone, not of a cow.
This is the tradition of the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇas*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: they also provide an explanation of the Veda on the basis of its having a fixed meaning.

That very fixed meaning, such as *ghoṭakāvapana* (the place for unloading horses), is precisely what they explain when they interpret the words for horses and so forth found in the Veda as referring to a horse (*aśva*)—[p.

In passages such as "one should obtain," and so forth: if grammar were an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then this [usage] would be untenable; however, since it is rootless, its status as having a fixed basis for meaning would result in being without any authority. An objection is raised: "Let it be so; what harm is there to us?"
The reply is: the meaning of the Veda would result in having an indefinite cause, and consequently, due to the lack of a definitive determination, it would lack authority.
[This applies to] horses and so forth—

For a word is indeed heard in the Veda; in the absence of contextual indicators such as syntactic adjuncts (*upapada*) or context (*prakaraṇa*), there would be doubt regarding its application. Is this word employed with reference to a horse (*ghoṭaka*) and so forth, or is it employed with reference to a person devoid of wealth (*niḥsva*) and so forth? Consequently, if the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) were rootless, there would be a lack of authority due to indecision. However, if it has a foundation, then because certainty is reached through the determination that it refers specifically to a horse and so forth, the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is indeed appropriate once such a determination has been made. But [one might object]: [The objection continues: "But..."

Even though [the word] is correct in both senses, according to the principle established in the treatises (*śāstrasthanyāya*), its usage in the sense of "one who has no wealth" and so forth will be secondary (*gauṇa*), while its usage in the sense of "horse" and so forth will be primary (*mukhya*); therefore, the determination [of meaning] will occur by grasping the primary sense. To this, he says: "And the principle established in the treatises does not apply here. [B. adds: "Because a secondary sense is possible here due to similarity; [therefore,] between the secondary and the primary..."

Because there is no reason for such a distinction in this case. For in that instance, the primary status of the usage among the Āryas and the secondary status of the other was established due to its conformity with the remainder of the scriptural passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). Here, however, there is no such remainder of the passage. Furthermore, in that case, there was a figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) based on similarity;

here, however, no similarity is perceived between the means of sowing (*āvapana*) and so forth and cows and the like. [A. adds: "The distinction between the primary and the secondary is not perceived. Therefore, by the principle established in the scriptures, such a distinction is difficult to find here.

Therefore, determination is based solely upon grammatical derivation (*vyākaraṇa*); hence, the validity of that derivation must be investigated. This is what is being examined: whether words such as *go* (cow) have no beginning in reference to the animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, while words such as *gāvī* have a beginning.

And here the counter-argument (*pratiyoginī*) is this verbal formulation: "Both [the Veda and grammar] are beginningless. The Bhāṣya itself explains this: "Is it being deliberated whether this Smṛti has a possible basis or not?
If the grammatical Smṛti has a possible basis, then [it would apply to] the dewlap and so forth—"

The priority belongs to cows and the like alone; if it does not, then the priority would belong to all things as well. What, then, is the conclusion? He adopts the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Let us set aside for now the consideration of the root and the rooted; first of all, the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*) itself has an indefinite scope. What is this 'indefinite scope'?"
What is the purpose of this instruction? The answer is: this lack of fixed meaning [in common usage] exists because this treatise is undertaken for the sake of regulating linguistic usage;

that is, this treatise is for the purpose of restriction, so that the usage of "go" and other such words is correct only when applied to things possessing a dewlap and so forth, and not for "gāvī" and other such variants. It is not [for the purpose of teaching the actual denotations].

And by this [criterion], usage cannot be restricted. If it is argued that the restriction of usage arises from usage itself—that is, "only that which has usage in the world is correct"—he refutes this: "In that case, it is established that words such as *gāvī* and the like also possess beginninglessness with respect to their application to things possessing dewlaps and so forth."
Because those [forms] are also employed in the world. But how, then,
can usage be restricted by grammar?
Is it possible? The answer is: it is not possible in this way. First of all, this is the instruction: suffixes occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*).
And some of those [suffixes] occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
For example, the suffixes *tṛc* and so forth; some,
such as *tavyat* and so forth, are used in the sense of the object (*karman*), while others are used in all kārakas except for the agent (*kartṛ*).

Just as in the case of *ghañ* and other suffixes; having considered that in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) the direct instruction of words is not carried out by the first two chapters, it was stated: "First of all, this is the instruction."

But all of this is untenable. How is it untenable? It is untenable in this way: it is stated that "suffixes occur after a verbal root" (*dhātu*). What indeed is this "verbal root" (*dhātu*) from which suffixes arise? The proponent (*rāddhāntin*) says:
[Page 121] —
But surely, by this rule "bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ," having recited certain words in a specific sequence,
the technical designation *dhātu* (verbal root) is established. Therefore, the suffixes that follow those which are designated as *dhātus* by that designation [should apply].

Why would it not be logical that they exist? The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) objects: [If so,] even forms such as *gaṇḍayati* and *gaṇḍati* would result in being grammatically correct (*sādhutva*), yet this is not accepted.

But how, then, does the possibility of its correctness arise? It is said: from the root *bhū* (to become), [the suffix] *kvip* is applied according to the rule "kvip is used after all roots. When *kvip* has been applied, by the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating that "words ending in *kvip* do not possess the status of verbal roots," it follows that "the pure, isolated meaning of the root is designated as *bhāva* (being)."

Sweetmeats (*modaka*) have 'liking' as their meaning because they are the cause of liking. Here, 'liking' (*ruci*) is intended in the sense of pleasure (*prīti*); and since sweetmeats and so forth serve that purpose, they are said to have 'liking' as their meaning.

Therefore, upon the utterance of these [words], this fourth case occurs only in connection with them. Consequently, the connection with the word "let them be given" (*dīyantām*) does not obtain. And thus—

[Objection: Because it is not connected [to the sense of "liking"], the usage "let sweetmeats be given to Devadatta" would not be obtained. [Response: But surely the meaning of the verbal root *ruc* is understood as the meaning of the verbal root;
that is, the meaning of the root *ruc* is "the object of liking. In connection with that, the term *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is applied to the person who is pleased. Therefore—

"The fault previously stated will not occur. He refutes this: "Is this meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), having the sense of 'liking' (*ruci*), indeed without an object? The reply: "It is not without an object; if something is pleasing to someone, that thing is the object of the meaning of 'liking' for that person."
The reply is: then it is understood; because of the mention of the sweetmeats (*modaka*).
When the sweetmeats are mentioned as the objects, there is an understanding of the desire, which is the subject. And when it is understood—

In that case, since the fourth case would apply only when there is a connection with that [root], the expression "let sweetmeats be given to Devadatta" (devadattāya modakā dīyantām) would not be possible. If it is argued that the utterance of the verbal root is the basis for the designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), he refutes this: [in that case] the question and answer, "Do the sweetmeats please Devadatta? (*devadattāya modakāḥ kiṃ rocante*) would be untenable.

At that time, the expression “modakāḥ for Devadatta” is nothing but a corruption (apabhraṃśa). Consequently, the question “What [is the meaning]? is not tenable; likewise, the answer “They are being cooked” is untenable. If it is argued that the usage is based on that very [corruption], [we reply:]...

If it is argued that the employment [of the word] depends solely upon the utterance of a verbal root meaning "to desire" (*ruc*) with a northern direction as its object, and therefore it does not incur the status of being an *apabhraṃśa* (corrupt form) because [the required condition] is absent—[the author] refutes this:
the employment does not depend on that. Why? Because the question and answer would be untenable.

If the very dependence upon that [object] constitutes the instigation (*prayukti*), then what is the purpose of the question or its answer? Alternatively, if the question arises from a suspicion that the fourth case-usage is ungrammatical, and the answer is intended to dispel that [suspicion].
To this he replies: "Indeed, that utterance is for the purpose of refuting the objection, not for the sake of the grammatical correctness of the use of the fourth case (caturthī).

Therefore, the question and answer are untenable. Likewise, even in the case of the *apādāna* [ablative], the state of being a cause of fear establishes the status of the *apādāna* for any factor of action (*kāraka*) that is the cause of fear."

Because fear is dependent upon the operation of all the *kārakas*, all *kārakas* would themselves be the cause of fear; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all *kārakas* would function as the *apādāna*. However, in the case of [words such as] *upapada* and so forth, they do not possess the status of *kārakas* at all.

Therefore, within the section on grammatical factors (*kāraka*), it is not logical to restrict technical designations based on the influence of subordinate words (*upapada*) and the like; by this same line of reasoning, the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*) is also refuted, since the prescription of case-endings must be preceded by the determination of their respective domains.

For case-endings occur with respect to [grammatical relations] such as the object (*karman*); it is impossible to determine those endings when the object and other relations have not themselves been determined. Thus, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that presupposes the comprehension of the sentence-meaning cannot itself be instrumental for the comprehension of that sentence-meaning.

Grammar is indeed an auxiliary limb (*vedāṅga*) of the Veda, and its status as an auxiliary consists in its being a means for comprehending the meaning of Vedic sentences. That [status] would not exist [if grammar were useless], because the instruction regarding the substitution of case-endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*) is established through the prior comprehension of the meaning of grammatical sentences; that is, it is established from the comprehension of that [meaning].
Since the prescription for the substitution of case-endings occurs only when the sentence-meaning is established, and not otherwise, the [rules concerning] *kṛt* suffixes are likewise explained.

Because those [kṛt suffixes] are also prescribed for [grammatical relations] such as the agent (*kartṛ*), there is no power to determine a restriction when they are not restricted, since even kṛt suffixes lack the capacity for definitive determination. Furthermore, tiṅ suffixes, which have temporal conditions (*kāla*) and so forth as their limiting adjuncts, do not denote those [relations]. He asks, "What follows from that? and says: "And because [the relations] are not perceived through restriction..."

It is impossible to define [them]. Furthermore, when time and so forth are not perceived, it cannot be stated as a rule that "this suffix occurs after a verbal root when the meaning of the root is present," or that "this occurs when [the action] was past, or will be in the future. By whom, indeed, were time and so forth [ever defined]?
[Regarding the statement] "they are not expressed by means of a *tiṅ* suffix," the reply is:
it was stated by the Blessed One, the author of the *Bhāṣya*.
By Patañjali, who states that [the suffixes] occur after a verbal root (dhātu) when the meaning of the root (dhātvartha) is in the past tense;

now, one might object: "Granted that time and so forth are expressed by the suffix, nevertheless, the root itself will convey the past meaning of the root-meaning. To this he says: "And it is not possible for the determination of the root-meaning to be accomplished by the root-meaning alone."

Because there is no contradiction even in the three times—that is, across all periods of time—of the very meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Therefore, it is established that since [the relationship] is not perceived, it is impossible to define a restriction (*niyamana*). Likewise, this applies to the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as well.
They cannot be restricted, because their meanings—such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth—cannot be determined.

The suffixes *liṅ* and others are taught to denote injunctions and the like; yet these cannot be definitively established. And it is impossible to determine a restriction based on what is not cognized. But how [is this so]?
Why is there no determination of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth? The answer: because differentiation depends upon the force of the meaning of the accompanying word (*upapada*).
The differentiation of injunctions and so forth [arises from] the...

It is to be understood by virtue of the meaning of the words: that "this is an injunction" and "this is a command" is to be understood by virtue of the meanings of the accompanying words—that is, by virtue of the accompanying words denoting the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and the person who enjoins (*niyojaka*). A distinction cannot be apprehended from the words themselves. Furthermore, it is difficult to state a restrictive rule for those [words] whose own meanings are non-different.

Only where there is a distinction in meaning (*svārthabheda*) can it be said that this [function] belongs to *praiṣa* and so forth alone and not elsewhere, as in the case of *aśvagoṇī* and similar compounds. The meaning is that whereas it is possible in the case of *aśvagoṇī* and so forth, it is not possible here. And this has been shown from the perspective of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). Likewise, since the suffixes (*taddhita*) and compounds (*samāsa*) are defined by the requirement of semantic capacity (*samartha*), they are difficult to determine. What is this "statement of semantic capacity"?
[Objection: No. [Response: The grammatical rule is:
"The first member [of a compound] is optionally [retained] when the members are semantically capable," and "a word-formation rule applies only when the words are semantically capable.
To the question of how it is impossible to define those two—taddhita suffixes and compounds—he says: "The capacity [of words] consists in their being connected with a single meaning.

Those meanings which are connected with a single meaning are "capable" (samartha); from them arise taddhita suffixes and compounds. Furthermore, the specific types of compounds are for the purpose of defining that [capacity].

There is the denotation [of the base] and the denotation of specific secondary derivatives (*taddhita*). Both compounds (*samāsa*) and secondary derivatives are employed precisely to demonstrate the connection with a single meaning; and since those two are characterized by that capacity, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Likewise:

The addition of the rule regarding "compounds of non-coordinated meanings" (*asamarthasamāsa*) and the fact that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) do not arise from what is non-coordinated cannot be stated except by actual usage.

For, according to the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*), a compound of non-coordinated meanings is not logical; likewise, the non-arising of secondary suffixes from what is non-coordinated [is not logical].

It is logical; and this pair is indeed accepted. Therefore, the restriction follows from the very application [of the rule], and since that restriction is already established, the treatise has accomplished its own purpose. By this, he shows that the treatise is not useless, but rather meaningful; for it is by means of this that its own purpose is fulfilled.

That [compound] is purposeless because its function has already been accomplished. But what is the compound of those that are semantically incapable (*asamartha*)? He says: "First, the compound of those that are semantically incapable is, for example, *aśrāddhabhojī* (one who does not eat at a funeral feast).

This cannot be understood in a case where there is no distinction of meaning, such as in *dadhighaṭa* (a pot of curd), because [in that case] the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verb *bhuj* (to eat). Likewise [it applies] to *dadhighaṭa*.
[The compound] *dadhnā pūrṇaḥ* [is formed] because of the connection with the sense of "full";

*gorathaḥ* [is formed] because of the connection with the sense of "yoked" to a cow. Furthermore, secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) do not arise from [words that are not] semantically capable (*samartha*); for instance, in the case of *aṅgulyā khanati* ("he digs with a finger"), the suffix *thak* (forming *-ika*) does not arise in the sense of "one who plays with that" or "one who digs with that. Also, [the suffix does not arise] in the case of *vṛkṣamūlād āgataḥ* ("come from the root of a tree").

Because [the word] "tata" ends in *ā*, the suffix *aṇ*—prescribed by the rule *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ*—is not produced. Therefore, the grammatical treatise is a refuge for correct usage; it is not capable of restricting usage.
"It is worthy" (arhatīti).

Likewise, in the rule "a meaningful item that is neither a verbal root nor an affix is a nominal stem" (arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam), what is this property of being meaningful (arthavattva) for which the operation is intended?
"What is meant by 'inborn' (autpattika)? The proponent asks. "What is the distinction? The opponent refutes:

"If meaningfulness consists in being something to be produced (kārya), then, since the relationship between word and meaning is already established, and since words are employed for meaning in common worldly usage, the scripture would merely serve to restrict [the use of] words to matters of Dharma based on that productivity."

Thus, the Vārttika is not tenable. Furthermore, if the meaningfulness [of words] were innate (*autpattika*), then because the scripture would be devoted solely to explaining that, it would not be established as a means for the purpose of the scripture, nor as something conducive to the purpose of the scripture.

How is it that grammar serves as the means for explaining why this word—such as *go* and so on—is meaningful, while [corrupt forms] such as *gāvī* and so on are not? For that which is the goal (*upeya*) cannot itself be the means (*upāya*). Moreover, if this [grammar] is the means according to the Sūtra, yet its root is the goal, there is a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*). If this is the case:

The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself has not been definitively established; and consequently, neither the application of accentual operations nor the prescription of suffixes (*pratyaya*) based upon it is accomplished. Furthermore, in the rule "that which is not a verbal root and not a suffix" (*adhātur apratyayaḥ*), there is a logical inconsistency regarding the exclusion of its constituent parts.

The meaning of this is as follows: the meaning of the rule *arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam* is that a meaningful verbal form, distinct from both roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), receives the technical designation *prātipadika*. And here, by the phrase *apratyayaḥ*, there is the exclusion of suffixes alone, not of that which ends in a suffix, because there is no mention of the word "end" (*anta*). Nor [is it an exclusion] of anything by way of being a qualifier.

The word *pratyaya* has been employed [in the rule] because there would otherwise be an inclusion of that which ends in it (*tadantagrahaṇa*) according to the principle "that by which a grammatical operation is prescribed"; for the word *pratyaya* could also apply by virtue of referring to its own form (*svarūpaparatva*). Furthermore, it has been established in the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* that when a term is used in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*), there is no inclusion of that which ends in it. This is indeed a rule prescribing a technical name, not a prohibition of the name, since it forms a single syntactical unit with the exclusion (*paryudāsa*). And thus the author of the *Vṛtti* also [explains it] as an exclusion alone.

He demonstrates this by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not a suffix" in the preceding sūtra; for he states in the *kṛt-taddhita* sūtra: "By this [sūtra], the designation of nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is prescribed for that which ends in a *kṛt* affix and that which ends in a *taddhita* affix."
[Page 138] Now,

if this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the suffix (*pratyaya*) in general, how then is there a rule for the designation (*saṃjñā-vidhi*) of that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix or a *taddhita* suffix in the subsequent sūtra by means of the exclusion "non-suffix" (*apratyaya*)? For if there were a prohibition of the designation for that which ends in a suffix, this would be a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) specifically for that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix.

It might be argued that this [designation] would apply to that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix. It is said in response: this was stated precisely to refute such a doubt. The meaning is: "By the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of 'that which is not a suffix' (*apratyaya*) in the preceding rule, the designation is prescribed here for that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix. If this were the case...

If the designation of *prātipadika* were prescribed for every *kṛt*-suffix alone and every *taddhita*-suffix alone, then the mention of "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) in the preceding rule would not be necessary, because the restriction itself would have excluded them—namely, that if a suffix were to receive the designation *prātipadika*, it would only be the case for those ending in *kṛt* or *taddhita*. Yet, the mention of "not a suffix" has indeed been made. From this we understand that the designation is prescribed for what ends in a *kṛt* suffix and what ends in a *taddhita* suffix. As for those who...

They explain that there is a prohibition of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for that which ends in an affix (*pratyaya*); however, for them, what would prevent the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) from applying to the affix alone?

Such being the case regarding the meaning of the rule, the following objection is stated: [if the term *apratyaya* were taken as a single word], there would be an over-extension (*atireka*) to its constituent parts, namely, the words *na dhātuḥ* and *apratyayaḥ*.
Thus [it is said].

With a single continuous passage, he asks: "What is excluded by this? The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) replies: "Even though the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses meaning, the suffix (*pratyaya*)..."

It was stated that "a word consisting of a non-suffix and not being a verbal root" (*apratyayo 'dhātuḥ*) is for the purpose of ensuring that there be no designation as a *pada* [for a mere fragment]. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects:

if, on the basis of assuming a specific semantic capacity (*arthavattva*) for each individual [morpheme], it was stated that "a word consisting of a non-suffix and not being a verbal root" applies to a sentence...
In that case, the designation *prātipadika* would apply [to the compound],
because it too is connected with its own specific meaning. If it is argued that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of excluding that [designation]:
