If it is argued that although the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established by virtue of having meaning, the explicit mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), such that the designation does not apply to a sentence (*vākya*), [the author] refutes this: the exclusion of "non-root" (*adhātu*) and "non-suffix" (*apratyaya*) would be purposeless,
since even those two would be excluded by that same restriction.
Because it is so;

as he says: "Since for that [compound] as well, the application of the term 'compound' (samāsa) has ceased, when there is a single meaning, it is a negator, but not in the case of a different meaning.
If this is argued, [we reply]:

for when there is a restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*) regarding compounds, there is an exclusion of that which is of the same class (*samānajātīya*); and since a sentence and a compound possess the same meaning, they are of the same class.

Thus, by that [restriction], it is the sentence alone that is excluded, not the root (*dhātu*) or the suffix (*pratyaya*) of one who asserts a different meaning. Therefore, [the term] *arthavat* [applies to] that which is not a root...

If it is argued that the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix) [is necessary], he refutes this: "That is incorrect, because even in the case of a compound (*samāsa*), another meaning is admitted. Thinking that the rule for the suffix *vā* would be redundant, Kātyāyana, in order to reject the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* for the purpose of allowing an option between a compound and a sentence, stated: "Between a sentence and a compound..."

The state of being a *kārtha* (having a single meaning) has been stated. Therefore, the exclusion of the sentence (*vākya*) is not logically established. If, on the other hand, the exclusion refers to a sentence of a different class (*vijātīya*), then it would also apply to verbal roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). Alternatively, if the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of excluding meaningful aggregates (*arthavat-samudāya*), then [the rule applies to] the compound.

For a meaningful aggregate [is what constitutes a word], and by that, a sentence of the same class excludes another meaningful aggregate, not merely a verbal root or merely an affix. He objects: "In that case, the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* affixes should not be made;
for its purpose is as follows..."

It is stated [in the Vārttika]: "By the mention of *samāsa* (compound), when the exclusion of meaningful aggregates (*arthavatsamudāya*) is effected, the exclusion of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes and words ending in *taddhita* suffixes would follow;

let that not be the case. If the exclusion applied only to those of the same class, then since a compound consists of a collection of meaningful elements, it would have to result in the exclusion of only a sentence—which is a collection of meaningful words—and not of words ending in *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffixes.

Consequently, the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* [suffixes] is redundant; the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* is indeed superfluous. Now, one might argue that the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* will serve as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for *kṛdanta* (words ending in *kṛt*) and *taddhitānta* (words ending in *taddhita*) respectively; to this he replies: even in that case, [the rule would apply to] *prātipadikas* ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita*.
Because it is stated that "they become designations" (saṃjñā), it is intended that the aggregate alone is the designated object (saṃjñin).
And just as the aggregate possesses the status of being the designated object—
Success has already been stated in that regard. Precisely because grammar itself is so complex, it is difficult for usage to serve as its means.
Not only is grammar difficult to master, but even its status as a means toward usage is difficult to establish. Why?
He says that it is difficult to accomplish with respect to the application: "And by a difficult means, the knowledge of the goal is far removed.
Here, the word *ca* (and) implies *hi* (for).

The meaning of the word should be examined; furthermore, the examination of what has been poorly stated or left unsaid by commentators is itself the application [of the definition], which results in the removal of errors regarding that application.

He explains: For if one relies solely on the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), then whatever has been stated as the definition would be limited to exactly that; consequently, the examination of what is ill-stated or unstated would not be possible. However, when there is actual usage (*prayoga*), once that usage is understood, the examination of what is ill-stated or unstated becomes feasible. Furthermore, as for what the commentators say—that the definition is all-encompassing (*vyāpin*) due to the addition of "only" (*mātra*) or "syllable" (*varṇa*)—that too [is established] from usage itself, because of the addition of non-expressive elements.

It must be understood thus: for neither an additional *mātrā* nor an additional syllable (*varṇa*) is observed to be expressive of meaning or capable of accomplishing the intended object. Therefore, by definition (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), there is no comprehension of that meaning. At most, having learned the usage from elsewhere, one might resort to the principle that the addition of *mātrās* or syllables serves to complete it; consequently, the restriction would arise from usage alone, not from definition. Likewise, a specific statement regarding Vedic usage (*chandasi*) is untenable because the meaning of that [addition] is unknown.

For if its meaning were known, then it could be remembered that "in this sense, this word is correct. However, a Vedic peculiarity that is not established in common worldly usage cannot bring about the comprehension of a meaning. The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) states the objection: "If it is argued that [the knowledge of the meaning] is preceded by cognition—meaning that one first understands the meaning of the Vedic sentence through the force of logic (nyāya), and then the specific designation in the Veda (chandas) is made with reference to that meaning."

He refutes that [position]: "In that case, the instruction on its specific details would be useless. He states this in a single sentence: "For the auxiliary sciences such as grammar are employed for the sake of knowing the meaning of the Veda, not the meaning of the Veda for the sake of knowing the auxiliaries."

This is not the purpose of the meaning of the Veda: namely, "once that [meaning] is known, how might the ancillary sciences (*aṅga*) be applied? Therefore, by using the prefix *ut-* in the term *utprāsa*, he shows that the specific instruction regarding the *chandas* is merely an instruction; and thus, by the authors of the *Prātiśākhyas* and other such works, there is a mutual contradiction of meanings—
By this demonstration, the restriction [regarding the rules] from the *śāstra* and so forth has indeed been made clear.

For if the restriction were derived from the *śāstra*, then there would be no composition of mutually contradictory meanings by the authors of the various *Prātiśākhyas*. Therefore, the restriction does not derive from the *śāstra*. As for that which is intended as the primary meaning here...
The statement of the commentator— that [the objection] does not arise because there is no formal application— shows that the authors of the Sūtras were unaware of its underlying basis.
If they...

How could they know the fundamental application and yet compose a sutra that is over-extensive? Therefore, from the composition of such an over-extensive sutra, it is known for certain that the author of the sutra did not understand the correct application. And regarding the root [meaning], one must rely on the words of the sutra-author who has failed to fully comprehend the root.

This statement— that the restriction of application (prayoga-niyama) is indeed non-restrictive— is merely a hyperbolic remark; however, the designation of it as an "open-ended class" (ākṛtigaṇa) is the very foundation for the restriction established by the grammatical treatise.
For it is that [the treatise] which brings about the restriction through its rules; and by being brought to life by that, the restriction itself truly comes to life.

For the designation of "classes" (*ākṛtigaṇa*) is preceded by the observation of usage. If the understanding of usage were obtained from elsewhere, there would be no need for the treatise. The mention of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) is a drum-roll signaling the non-restriction of the treatise.

Just as a king, having struck a drum (*ḍiṇḍima*), acts according to his own will, so too does the author of the Sūtras by means of the inclusion of the term "bahula" (variously); thus it is called a "drum. And students are not able to comprehend this without knowledge of the actual usage (*prayoga*). If usage is already known, what is the use of grammar? Such is the [objection] against this traditional teaching (*smṛti*).

The Mīmāṃsakas, who accept that the knowledge of the beginninglessness of words such as "cow" arises from memory, have themselves admitted their own ignorance. Therefore, by asserting that the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda has arisen from a Veda whose cause remains undetermined, they have deluded the world that follows the path of truth.

By the Mīmāṃsakas. Or rather, this is simply the natural manifestation of faith arising from the straightforwardness of people in the world. Thus it has been said: "Because there is no scripture for the origin of usage, there would be no fixed rule regarding words. But surely, this inconsistency applies to the system of Pāṇini.
We know the rule of grammar as taught by others, such as Āpiśali and so forth.
He refutes this: it is not known whether there is a rule from another source as well.
B. The restriction regarding treatises and so forth [p. 142]:
it is not for another.
This very method regarding the designation of verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth for *piśala* and other such words is the means adopted in the grammatical treatise (*śabdānuśāsana*).
And here, this as well:

It must be asked: by what means did Pāṇini and others come to know that only words such as *go* (cow) are expressive, while forms such as *gāvī* are corruptions? For both types of words are identical in terms of usage and comprehension. If it is argued that this was understood from another grammar, no; for that would result in the fault of a "succession of the blind. Thus, grammar itself is poorly constructed and incapable of establishing rules for linguistic usage.

"Even if it were capable [of producing the effect], it would still be disregarded due to its lack of a root. This was indicated by the statement made with pride: "Let this consideration of the root be set aside for now. Regarding sound (*śabda*), there is a share in the fault of being produced through effort (*prayatna*). Let the means of instruction be set aside for now; rather, this alone is to be investigated: whether the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of sound is established even by way of having a beginning (*ādimattā*), or not.

The intention here is as follows: although it has been established that even for the Unborn (aja), instruction is a well-trodden means, nevertheless, because the Smṛti lacks a foundation, it is simply not to be respected; thus, its defense is fruitless. Therefore, one must first consider whether a source exists at all.
To establish that, it is investigated: does the usage of the word [for the Unborn] succeed—even if not born of attachment—by virtue of having a beginning, or not? In this regard:

If the establishment of linguistic usage occurs even by the force of incapacity, then the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is baseless; if it does not, then it is without foundation. The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) adopts the position: why is it not established?
For it is indeed established through the fact that words possess a beginning.

[The opponent says: "Regarding linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*): the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) says—thus, linguistic usage as having a beginning is not established. For the establishment of the linguistic usage of word-meanings occurs through an uninterrupted succession of the linguistic usage of elders, and that [succession] is indeed unbroken."

It has been stated in the *Saṃbandhaparihāra* and by us in the *Vimalāñjana* that there is a continuous tradition of usage (*vyavahāraparaṃparā*). And when there is no interruption, what occasion indeed could there be for corruption?
All—

Because words are established through a beginningless succession of conventional usage; at most, some name or technical convention may be employed for the sake of establishing one's own specific discourse.

A *saṃjñā* (technical name) is a rule that, by means of a specific qualifier, establishes the restriction that "this particular meaning is to be expressed by this particular word," such as "vṛddhi is āt, ai, and au. Alternatively, a *paribhāṣā* (interpretive rule) is a restriction regarding the relationship between the signifier and the signified established through a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), such as "a *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common substratum is called a *karmadhāraya*. For indeed, the state of having words with a common substratum is the defining characteristic for a *tatpuruṣa* compound being expressible by the term *karmadhāraya*.

And in that regard, there is a recollection of an author, as in this very grammar. However, no author of the relationship [of word and meaning] for words such as *gāvī* is remembered, unlike [the authors of objects] such as jars. Therefore, there is no occasion for [the Veda] having a beginning. But the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says: "True."

For all words whose relationship [to their meanings] is being sought, there would have to be establishment through an beginningless succession of usage by elders; however, there is no occasion for such beginninglessness, for that [beginning] does indeed exist. For it is observed that even when children have the desire to utter one word, they instead utter a different word.

Just as when one intends to utter the word *kartṛ* (agent) for Viṣṇu, one might instead utter *viṇṇu*, so too is it here intended: someone desiring to utter the word *go* (cow), due to an impairment of the vocal organs, a defect in the cause, or through negligence and the like, utters *gāvī*. Thereupon, another elder person, having understood the speaker's intention through context and other means, perceives the meaning from the word *go* and engages in linguistic usage by means of that [word].

In that case, two others who are unlearned determine this through mere error: "By means of the word *gāvī* alone, this person has understood this object without any mediation. Consequently, those two, having concluded through error that the word *gāvī* denotes that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, employ that word accordingly. Other children, following their usage, employ it likewise due to a lack of learning; thus, [the word] is characterized by having a beginning (*ādimattā*).

The establishment of conventional usage. Again, the proponent says: It is true that the utterance of other words by children is observed, and that [usage] is indeed limited to their own conventional practice. Since it has proceeded starting from that child's own conventional usage, it is remembered as such. As for that which...
Since that [word] whose origin is not being remembered is also produced by incapacity, it is indeed an expression born of incapacity.
Therefore, words such as *gāvī* and so forth— [are produced by incapacity].
It cannot be said that they are derived from a root (*dhātu*). This is stated by means of an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*):

"Words such as *gāvī* were uttered by someone who was unable to pronounce another word [intended], because they serve as a factor in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), like the word ‘tarkaka’. However, this inference based on general observation is not tenable; for the status of being a factor in linguistic usage—which arises from what is remembered—is pervaded by the state of being produced by incapacity (*aśaktijatva*) when [the original word] is remembered, and not when it is not remembered.

[The opponent says: "For [the word] *prabhava*, there is no generality at all. Furthermore, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) with respect to words such as 'cow' (*go*) and so forth. Likewise, there is the subversion of what is intended (*iṣṭavighātakāritā*), and contradiction with the definition (*lakṣaṇaviruddhatā*); for it would follow that even words such as 'cow' are produced without capacity. The proponent replies: "To this it is said: True, if it were observed that they are produced without capacity..."

We maintain that words such as *gāvī* are born of incapacity because we observe them being used by those who lack proficiency; however, having perceived their status as being born of incapacity through traditional usage (*smṛti*), we have stated the possibility of a source for that tradition based on the observation of their use by the incompetent.

The meaning of this is as follows: First, according to traditional usage (*smṛti*), only words such as *go* (cow) and the like are denoters of that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, not words such as *gāvī*. However, it is understood that these [corrupt forms] arise from incapacity (*aśakti*) and are introduced into the path of linguistic practice by those who are deluded. Nor is this tradition baseless, for we observe linguistic practice even through words born of incapacity; thus, the following is stated to dispel the suspicion that the tradition might be without foundation:

The observation of usage arising from incapacity (*aśaktija*) is useful. For if there were no observation of usage arising from incapacity, then even if another basis for the memory were postulated on account of the firmness of that memory, it would nonetheless remain entirely baseless. But when there is the observation of usage arising from incapacity, then the beginninglessness of that which exists within the beginningless tradition of grammar is postulated. Consequently, because words such as *gāvī* arise from incapacity, they possess a beginning. For who indeed...

[The author] postulates the beginninglessness of similar words—whose capacities for denoting a single meaning are possible through the generation of conventional usage (saṃbhāvyamāna-śaktija)—despite their having multiple names. Nor is there the fault of a "blind tradition" (andhaparamparā), because in this very manner, a foundational source is possible even for the authors of previous grammars. To explain this further, he states the objection:
"But surely, this very same inference has already been stated."
Because they are observed to arise from incapacity, corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and others are said to be "born of incapacity.

He refutes this: No, for that very point has already been stated, since what is being asserted there constitutes an inference (*anumāna*). And in that case, [the fallacies] such as the contradictory (*viruddha*)—[p.

[The word] *vasaraḥ*. Here, however, it cannot be said that there is an absence of a basis for the Smṛti; it is for this much purpose alone that the observation of [the usage] arising from incapacity (*aśaktija*) has been introduced. (B. adds: "Now, having further introduced the observation of [the usage] arising from incapacity...")
But how, then, does the refutation of the absence of a cause through the observation that [the effect] is not produced by incapacity eliminate the absence of a root cause? To this he says:
"And an absence that merely negates possibility does not depend on the establishment of non-production due to incapacity. The meaning of this is: the possibility of non-production due to incapacity—

The absence of a basis for the Smṛti is refuted by this alone, and not by establishing that the Gāyatrī and other such texts were produced from incapacity. For if no word could be produced from incapacity, then—since all words would be beginningless and their status as denoters would be established—the Smṛti would be without a basis.
But when it is possible for a word to be produced even from incapacity, then it cannot be said that the Smṛti lacks a basis. Therefore, the learned...
It cannot be said that the recollection is otherwise.
By virtue of being authoritative, he shows that the Smṛti is based on another grammatical system;
thus it has been stated: "In that case, this is merely a recollection and cannot serve as a restrictive rule."
He refutes [this], saying: "It is sufficient for it to be determined. He states this with a single passage: "But how, then, is it not [the case]?"

"Do you understand that it is sufficient for the sake of a restrictive rule (niyama)? The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says: "Precisely from that aforementioned explanation of the pervader (vyāpaka), and from the aforementioned explanation of the non-pervasion of the pervader."

By the term "pervasive" (vyāpaka), what is intended is that which pervades objects other than the intended object. But the proponent of the established conclusion (rāddhāntin) says: that explanation has been somehow resolved by the commentators on grammar.
Whatever has been established in some way, let that be accepted exactly as it is. Why? He says: for even that is indeed memory;
for even the memory of the learned authors of the Vṛtti, the Vārttika, and the Bhāṣya—that too is indeed memory, not only [the memory of others].
[This is] the view of the author of the Sūtra. By following the words of all those who are well-versed [in this matter], it is possible to determine the restriction.
And by doing so, one would not have to postulate a difference in capacity among similar words with respect to a single meaning.

The burden of postulating multiple powers is thereby avoided; for even today it is observed that this word serves as a cause for the comprehension of meaning only when mediated by the recollection of another word,
as in the case of *vinunnam* [understood as] *adritunnāṅgam*.

Therefore, for that elder person, even though the word *gāvī* intervened, it was the word *go* itself that produced the comprehension of the meaning; from the very observation of which that erroneous recollection arose, namely, that the word *gāvī* alone—or indeed the word *go*—is the expressive signifier (*vācaka*).

And precisely because another’s intention to utter one word is understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even when a different word is actually uttered, for that very reason [the cognition of] the case-ending—
Those learned in grammar accept transposition; when it is said "he has come from the Aśmakas," they understand it as "from the Aśmakas.

Otherwise, how could the transposition be known if the speaker's intention were not understood through another means of valid cognition? Therefore, even by this method, it is impossible to challenge the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
Because there is no injunction for practical application.
Regarding this, the Commentator asks: "Now, as for words such as 'cow' and so forth, do they [denote] the configuration (*ākṛti*)?

Having introduced the inquiry as to whether the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) [is the same] or whether it is the manifestation (*vyakti*), he asks: what is the purpose of introducing this [second] inquiry in the middle—namely, whether those very words that are worldly are the same as those that are Vedic, and whether their meanings are the same, or whether the Vedic words are different and their meanings are different? He asks: "Are those very words that are worldly the same as those that are Vedic? etc.
What is the purpose of this consideration— "and thus these are their meanings"— which has been introduced in the middle [of the discussion]? The answer:

—But is this not an introductory discussion (upodghāta) for the inquiry into the category of generic form (ākṛtyadhikaraṇa)? To the question "How is it an introduction?", he says: If those very same words [are used] and those very same meanings belong to them, then an objection to their authoritative status can be raised by way of the denotation of individuals.

If, however, words and meanings were indeed distinct entities, then on account of that very distinctness, there would be a lack of authority; for it is precisely because the relationship between signifier and signified has not been ascertained through the linguistic usage of elders, and because they thus fail to convey meaning, that their lack of authority is established. What is the point of asserting their lack of authority by way of [the claim that they denote] individuals?

By way of explanation: for at that time, it is not even possible for there to be a denotation of the individual; therefore, what is the use of this [argument], which does not touch upon the actual meaning?

By means of the presentation of the theory that [the word] denotes the individual (*vyakti*). Since this is the introductory context (*upodghāta*), it was said: "First, this must be examined. He raises the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*): "But how can there be a suspicion of non-identity? The answer is: "Because of the difference in designation (*vyapadeśabheda*).
He explains this very point:
Now, regarding the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), experts designate it as pertaining to "which words?"—distinguishing between worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*) ones.
From this, a distinction is understood. Likewise, they also designate a difference in form; for instance, the word *agni* with the cerebral *ṇ* (as in *kṛtaṇatva*).

They recite [the mantra]. Likewise, from the observation of such passages as "the gods by themselves" (*tathā devāsaḥ tmanā*), a difference in form is understood; for in common usage, there is the word "gods" (*devāḥ*) and also "by themselves" (*ātmanā*). Similarly, a difference in meaning also manifests from the Veda itself: [the word] *uttānā*...
"Indeed, the divine oxen carry [the burden]; the golden-leaved tree is the lord of the forest; and 'clarified butter' and 'honey' [are used].

For in the world, words such as "cow" and so forth do not have such meanings. But surely, if the words are one thing and the meanings another, then the comprehension of meaning from the Veda would be untenable.

Because the meaning of the Veda is the cause for the worldly linguistic usage of words and meanings, he offers this rebuttal: "Let that very thing not be," which was previously raised as an objection.
The meaning of this is as follows: "Let there be no comprehension of that very meaning"—this is what we intended to object to. By that, our desired conclusion is indeed established.

It is not appropriate to state this as a fault. Again, the proponent (rāddhāntin) says: "In that case, the Veda would be non-informative. By "informative," what is intended is "performance" (anuṣṭhāna); therefore, the meaning becomes: "If there is no comprehension of the meaning, then it follows that the Veda is non-informative, that is, non-performative."
The proponent, however, says: "It is said, 'Om.
Why? He says: Because a means of valid cognition cannot be something that follows after a purpose."

Therefore, if the performance that serves as the purpose does not occur, let it not occur; however, it is not right to postulate a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) on the basis of that [non-occurrence]. He states the established conclusion (rāddhānta): "In that case, we understand the purpose from the means of valid cognition itself.
What..."
That is the proof. The answer is: the realization that word and meaning are non-different.
Why? He says: for difference occurs either through effect or through essential nature.

He states [the answer] with a single argument: first, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of words such as "cow" is that very same thing consisting of the phonemes, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) [of them as identical]. Furthermore, their function (*kārya*) is also one and the same, namely, being the cause for the cognition of that which possesses a dewlap and so forth; therefore, there is neither a difference in essential nature nor a difference in function.

This is not tenable. For this very reason, by what means do we perceive their difference? The proponent of the prima facie view says: "But surely we perceive their difference through the presence of *ṇ* and other such sounds.

The word *agni* is different because it is expressed with a *ṇ*, whereas [the form] *abhi* is not so expressed; [the word] *devāsaḥ* is different because of the addition of another phoneme; [and the word] *tmanā* is different because of the elision of a phoneme."
[Objection: But [this] is a fault. [The author] states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "For that is a difference in phonemes (*varṇa*), not a difference in words (*pada*);

there is a difference only of the phoneme therein, not of the word, for that very same word is what is perceived. [Objection: But surely, by the refutation of *sphoṭa*, the word has been established as consisting solely of phonemes; therefore—

Regarding the claim that a difference in phonemes (varṇa) necessarily implies a difference in the word (pada), he says: "The status of being a word consists in being the cause for the comprehension of meaning, and that [status] is unitary.
The meaning of this is as follows: phonemes, when governed by the effect characterized by the comprehension of a single meaning, attain the status of a word in certain instances within common usage.
When those [phonemes] are heard in the Vedas, the cognition arises: "This is that very same word. In that case, if there were the loss of even a single phoneme from the word—
Even if another phoneme intervenes or [the word] enters into [another], nevertheless, the cognition arises that "this very same word has been modified" and not something else.

In common worldly usage as well, this understanding indeed occurs: "that very same word, having been modified, was uttered by him due to incapacity. And since incapacity is a defect of the person, those who are careful utter the word exactly unmodified in order to avoid it. But in the Veda, because of the absence of a speaker—

When the identity of the word is apprehended through its phonetic similarity (*styūvālabhbhaḥ*), the sentence-meaning is likewise apprehended as being that very same [meaning], because that word is understood to denote that specific meaning. In common worldly usage as well, the comprehension of meaning indeed occurs through the recognition of the intended word, except when there is a defect in the speaker’s incapacity resulting from the utterance of a corrupted word; or where there is the presence of many corrupted syllables, in such cases there is no recognition of the word.

However, where there is the utterance of a few phonemes, there is in common worldly usage a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the whole by means of a part; this is called "modification" (*vikṛti*). It should be understood in the same way in the Veda.
For example, in the word *urūka*, the word *ka* indicates *kasa* (fat), as in Jaimini Sūtra 9.4.22. This is a modification in the world, just as it is indicated by the word *vi*.
—But surely, because the meanings are different, the difference between the words is established by the difference between the effects? He refutes this: "The very difference in meaning..."

This is unestablished, because the meaning "flowing face upwards" is not perceived. For if some things were established as flowing face upwards, then they might be denotable by the word "cow"; however, no such establishment exists for them. Nor does this meaning [apply] when there is a difference in the referent.

Since it is possible to understand the word *satyuttāna* from the word *uttāna*, one who desires a different meaning for it must accept the meaning of *uttāna* as established in common worldly usage. If this is so, then by parity of reasoning, let it be the same for all words as well. Therefore:

Because of the non-existence of duality—that is, because of the non-existence of the duality consisting of difference in intrinsic nature and difference in function—it is established that there is oneness of the words, meaning oneness of the words and their referents. He raises an objection:
"If there is no difference in meaning, then how [is it that] 'the divine cows indeed carry with their backs upturned'?"
It should be described. The answer is: it has already been stated that this is for the purpose of praise.

B. [The meaning is as follows: Since the injunctions would otherwise lack authority, they must be explained by means of figurative description (*guṇavāda*) for the purpose of praise. Because they possess authority in this way, they must be described as having another purpose—that is, as having as their object some matter already established by other means of knowledge, in whatever manner possible. This applies if there is oneness...
How, then, is its designation made through differentiation? The answer is: for the purpose of establishing that the objects of the instruction are distinct.
Anu-

The designation [of these two] as distinct is intended to show that their respective domains (*viṣaya*) are different. To the question "Why is there a difference in the domain of the instruction (*anuśāsana*)?", he says: the difference in domain is established by way of being dependent or independent.
When those very same words [are used] in relation to other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—

When words are dependent [on other elements] and are employed for their own specific meaning, they are called "secular" (laukika); when they are independent, they are called "Vedic" (vaidika). Based on this distinction, the grammatical instruction is heard in the treatise on grammar: "in the spoken language" (bhāṣāyām) and "in the Veda" (chandasī).
And thus [it is stated]. This is an injunction regarding the application.
Here, the author of the Bhāṣya describes the inquiry as follows: "Is the meaning of a word the form (ākṛti)?"

"Or rather, it is manifestation (*vyakti*). That is incorrect—for the word is that which is uttered (*uccarita*), and that is the meaning of the word; moreover, all words have action as their primary purpose. To this he replies: "It has been stated that [words] denoting accomplished entities (*bhūta*) are connected with words denoting action (*kriyā*). This is now being examined: in what cases do [words] denote accomplished entities?
Is there no obstacle to the manifestation of the world?

Is it that elements are intent upon an effect (*kārya*), or that elements are intent upon manifestation (*vyakti*)? For words functioning in their own primary sense (*svārtha*) possess an intentionality (*tātparya*) directed toward an effect; in this regard, it is investigated: with respect to what do words currently existing possess this intentness toward an effect?

[Page 153] Does [the word] apply to the form (*ākṛti*) or to the individual (*vyakti*)? This is an investigation into the object that serves as the cause [of the word's application]: is the meaning of a word the form or the individual?
But surely, that from which something is understood must be its constituent [object].

The author of the Bhāṣya states that the generic form (ākṛti) is also understood here; therefore, it is precisely the state of being the generic form. How can there be doubt in this matter? He answers: both are cognized from this.
It consists of both form and individuality. If both are understood from this [word], how then did the author of the Bhāṣya state:
"Because the cognition of the universal [occurs] and because action is possible in the individual"?

The defender says: "What is it that is not tenable here, such that you ask? The objector says: "This is not tenable because action is impossible in the case of a manifested entity. For action is impossible...

The reason stated [applies] to manifestation (*vyakti*) being its inherent nature (*tadbhūtatva*), but not to the cognition (*pratyaya*). The respondent says: "Is comprehension (*avagama*) thereby refuted?
The sense is that it is not refuted. The objector says: "It is said, 'Yes'; comprehension regarding manifestation is indeed refuted."
Because comprehension and designation apply to the form (*ākṛti*).
For if there were comprehension of both, then comprehension would occur in the state of being the form itself.

It would not have been stated as a reason, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The respondent says: "The beloved of the gods, the objector, does not understand the text. The objector asks: "What is this lack of understanding of the text? The respondent’s answer is: "This is what constitutes a lack of understanding of the text."
In a single work, he states:

"It has been said that the collection of all words is for the purpose of action (*kriyārtha*); and by virtue of being for the purpose of action, their status as *bhūta* (established facts) is defined."

As for that [objection], even the fact that [words] function for their own meaning is also for the sake of action (*kriyārthatā*); for the purpose of action is mediated by the denotation of their own meanings.

The denotation of their own meanings is performed by words; and it is the individual (*vyakti*) that can have the capacity for action, not the class-character (*ākṛti*), nor can that which is not perceived serve the purpose of action.

The meaning is that since [the state of] "being" exists only in the individual (vyakti), the word "cow" and so forth denotes the individual itself. This is what is intended here: by the Bhāṣya statement, "And because action is possible in the individual," the demonstration of the possibility of action establishes that the individual alone is the denoted object.

This has been shown; it is not merely the possibility of action [in the individual]. If only the individual were capable of action and were what is understood, then how could there be an understanding of the universal?
The answer is: by the commentary stating "it exists" (*asti*), which demonstrates the possibility of its being the object of action, [the universal is established]. It exists—

This much can be said, but its status as being "already existent" (tadbhūtatva) does not follow from its being for the sake of action. [Objection: But surely, when there is comprehension of the universal (sāmānya), comprehension of the individual (vyakti) would not result?

"If, because of their difference, there is a comprehension of the universal from the word, then the comprehension of the individual does not follow, since the two are different. He refutes this: "Alas! What a failure of reflection even regarding experience!
He explains this very point:

—if the individual (vyakti) is not apprehended, it is not apprehended whose general property (sāmānya) it belongs to. Why? He says: "The apprehension [of a relation] depends upon another related term.
The meaning is that the general property is not apprehended as belonging to anything at all.

Now, [the opponent] might object: "Granted that it is not understood as being related, even so, what is the harm? To this he replies: "For a universal, if it is not understood as being related, is not understood as a 'universal' at all.
Why? He says: "Because a relation indeed depends upon another related term..."
If cognition arises [regarding] a universal as having the nature of a relation, then that which is not apprehended as a relation would remain unapprehended; specifically,
in this case, by way of the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier.

The relation [of the universal] is not apprehended, for the universal is the form (*rūpa*), whereas the individual (*vyakti*) is that which possesses the form (*rūpin*), because it is being manifested by that form. Indeed, there can be no cognition of a form devoid of that which possesses the form; if such were the case, it would not even be a form at all.
It might be so;

the meaning is that it would result in being of the nature of an independent category (*svatantra-padārtha*). If there is indeed comprehension even in the case of the individual (*vyakti*), why [is this not accepted]?

In that case, the presentation as distinct [from the universal] is for the purpose of showing the non-connection of the form [of the word], since the cognition occurs with respect to the universal and the action is possible only with respect to the individual. The answer is: it is for the purpose of demonstrating the lack of connection of the form [of the word] with the action, by virtue of its being for the sake of action.

Action is possible only in the individual (vyakti) and not in the generic form (ākṛti); the mention of them as distinct is because there is merely a cognition of the latter in that case. [The opponent objects: "Since the cognition arises with respect to the universal (sāmānya), action is possible in the individual. Even if there is thus no syntactic connection between that which has the purpose of action and that which does not have the purpose of action, he asks:
"What of it? He replies: "It is not logical for something that lacks syntactic connection to be the meaning of a word, just as in the case of the sentence 'Bring the lion of the cage.'"

[The two words] "in the cage" (*pañjarastha*) and "lion" (*siṃha*) are understood [together]. For one who understands that the lion is indeed in the cage, although there is an understanding of the cage when [hearing] the command "bring the lion," nevertheless the cage is not the meaning of the word, because it is not syntactically connected (*ananvita*) with the act of bringing. It is the same here as well.

Because it is not connected with a purposeful action (*kriyārtha*), the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not the meaning of a word. [Objection: If it is impossible for that which is unconnected to be the meaning of a word, why then is the argument "because there is a cognition of the universal" (*sāmānye pratyayāt*) put forward? [Response: It is to demonstrate this very point which is about to be stated, and not [to deny] the generic form itself. What point? [Response: The statement that [the generic form] lacks authority because it is the cause of what is unconnected.

This is to demonstrate that those among the proponents who maintain that a word’s meaning consists in the mere cognition of a universal—even without its syntactic connection (anvaya)—thereby imply that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) lacks authority because it would have no basis for syntactic connection; for, since they disregard syntactic connection, the universal would not be the word’s meaning, and thus the injunction would lack a connected object. Now, [one might object]: “But surely—”

Regarding the claim that only the individual (vyakti) is connected with the action, he says: even those who maintain the theory of the class-form (ākṛti-vādinaḥ) accept the connection of the individual in such cases as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). Now, one might object: "Just as there is a lack of authority for those who maintain the theory of the class-form, so too is there a lack of authority for those who maintain the theory of the individual. To this, he replies:
—Or, even if one accepts the position that [the universal] is either manifest (*vyakta*) or identical with the individual (*tadbhūta*), how can independence (*anapekṣatva*) be established?
The point is that it simply cannot be established. The reply: Whether it be established or not, the proponent of the universal (*jātivādin*) has at least resorted to an improper method (*apanyāya*).

Because it is accepted that the meaning of a word is a genus (*jāti*) that is not [inherently] connected [to individuals]; however, in the view that the individual (*vyakti*) is the referent, it is logical to postulate a cause that conforms to the effect. The individual—

It is logical to postulate a cause such that the practice, which is the effect, is accomplished from the word. But how is this position of denoting the individual (vyakti) logical, given that for one [who holds it], the tradition of usage among elders cannot be established as the cause of linguistic acquisition? Why can it not be so established?
The reply is: indeed, the linguistic usage of elders is understood as being based upon positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

For it is through positive and negative concomitance that the meaning of a word is determined; when a particular word is employed in connection with a particular object, [that object is understood as its meaning].

And that which is not employed when [the word] is absent is not the meaning of that word. Likewise, when a certain meaning is understood upon the presence of a word and is not understood upon its absence, that meaning is understood to belong to that word. And these two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—are based on the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha*). Elderly...

In linguistic usage, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are based on universals (*sāmānya*), not on individual instances (*vyakti*); for a word is applied even to another instance, and when a word is applied, another instance is cognized. Furthermore, a word is not applied when a universal is absent, nor [is it applied] when there is no word.

When [the word] is employed, the universal (sāmānya) is perceived; therefore, in the linguistic usage of elders (vṛddhavyavahāra), it is impossible to understand that the individual (vyakti) is the cause [of the denotation].

Nor do we find any other cause for the acquisition of linguistic meaning (vyutpatti) than the usage of elders, because the author of the relationship [between word and meaning] is not remembered. For if...
If there were an author of the relationship, then linguistic understanding would occur solely by virtue of convention; however, it has already been stated that no such author is remembered.
Now, one might object: even in the case of a generic form (*ākṛti*), its existence as such [is established].

It has been refuted [by the Mīmāṃsakas] that "the words of the Veda have action as their purpose" because the universal (ākṛti) lacks connection with action. With a single passage, he says: "But what, then, regarding these two [the universal and the individual], is the lack of purpose for action in the usage of elders?"
Between the two—following the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) and not following it—which is stronger?

Since the universal (*ākṛti*) lacks the capacity for action, it appears not to be the meaning of the word. Between the two—following the usage of elders and not following it—with respect to the individual (*vyakti*), which is stronger? The answer is: we say that the functional capacity (*kārya*) is stronger.
He asks "Why? and says:
For that is the seed of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), [the seed] of the entire cycle of causes; for everywhere, a cause is postulated by virtue of its effect, and there is no other cause.

In the process of conceptualization, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the comprehension of an effect associated with multiple meanings; this is the function of words. It is logical to postulate a cause that conforms to that [function]. Furthermore, the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) and so forth, together with their inherent nature (*tadbhūtatva*), constitute the cause; that is, both the usage of elders and their inherent nature [are required].
It is understood that the state of being that [cause] (tadbhūtatva) is more proximate to the effect than the millions of other causes;

and having observed the effect, one understands that very state of being that [cause] specifically as immediately preceding the effect, and a corresponding linguistic convention (vyutpatti) must be postulated.

He says in a single passage: "If that [convention] cannot be preceded by the linguistic usage of elders, then let it be postulated as either a *samaya* (conventional agreement) or something produced (*kṛtakatva*).
Here he raises an objection: "But surely, for children, [knowledge of meaning] arises from the very linguistic usage of elders..."

The cognition of the effect is observed. Therefore, since the cognition of the effect is established by that alone, the postulation of either a convention (*samaya*) or a creative act (*kṛti*) is not tenable. And it has been said: "For there is nothing that is impossible when something is actually perceived."
He refutes [this]: "In that case, the derivation is established. He objects again: "True, it is established from the perspective of direct perception."

Having reflected upon the perception, it appears as something established in accordance with how it is seen; yet, from the perspective of its causal basis (*nimitta*), it is not established. This is because, in the acquisition of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) through the usage of elders, there is an absence of a causal basis; thus, proficiency cannot be established by reflecting upon a causal basis. Nor is there a conventional agreement (*samaya*).

Or rather, the effect is not perceived. Therefore, in the case of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), the postulation of a cause is indeed refuted by this reasoning; it is refuted. [The author] provides the rebuttal: "It is seen as refuted by the method. (Note: Variants A, B, and C differ slightly in punctuation and phrasing regarding the negation.)
— If, however, it is the individual substance itself, as characterized by the universal,
that becomes the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning,
then what is the fault? None at all.

Because it is easy to grasp the relationship through a single indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). Again, he objects: "Indeed, there is no fault [in this], but you must state the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being an indicative mark."

"Why is it that the genus (*jāti*) alone, as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), does not become the denotable object (*abhidheya*)? He answers: "In this case, the fact that [the genus] serves as a means for the cognition of the effect (*kāryapratipatti*) is precisely the reason for its being a defining characteristic."
For indeed, as long as the individual instance (*vyakti*) is not apprehended, the apprehension of the action (*kārya*) is not possible.

If the individual instance is not cognized, then the apprehension of the action as connected with it cannot be established. Therefore, that [individual instance] is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). To the question, "But what is the use of those two being indicators? he replies:

—for indeed, a specific individual (*vyaktiviśeṣa*) that is not characterized by its universal (*sāmānya*) cannot be communicated, because there would be no grasping of the relationship [between word and object]; thus, everything is established regarding the theory that words denote [objects] as connected with an action (*kāryānvitābhidhāna*). [This explains] the cause of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) and the fact that the generic form (*ākṛti*) serves as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇatva*).

The meaning is that everything is thus established. Therefore, it has been demonstrated that Vyāḍi considers the individual instance (*vyakti*) to be the denoted object. And precisely because the individual instance is the referent, the applicability (*viniyojyatva*), the status of being something to be employed (*upādeyatva*), and [the relevance of] number and so forth are logically justified.

If the word-meaning were the generic form (*ākṛti*), then because that form cannot be the substratum for number and so forth, there would be no application of number in such injunctions as "one [cow] is to be given," and so on; for number indeed...

It is employed as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). And its status as a means of accomplishment arises through the determination of that means; for if the form (*ākṛti*) alone were the denotation of the word, then its status as a means would follow from its very employment as such, and because it possesses the nature of being a means, there could be no delimitation of it by number.

The application of number is not possible; thus, in cases such as *paśunā* (with an animal), by this very same method, the status of the number as something to be enjoined (*upādeya*) would not exist. He states this very point: "For a quality (*guṇa*) that is not supported [by a substance] does not participate in grammatical connection (*anvaya*), and the designation of 'otherness' (*anyatva*) is not tenable under the view that [the word refers to] the genus (*jāti*)."

Furthermore, the designation of "otherness"—as in "another [person] of that same color and that same age"—is not possible under the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the referent, because a universal is unitary. Therefore, it should be understood that the state of being "that" (the universal) is based solely on the individual (*vyakti*).
As for the "form" (*ākṛti*), it is said here: this position might indeed be established, if...

Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of the action to be performed (*kārya*). But the comprehension of the action to be performed itself is inconclusive (*anaikāntikī*). How is it inconclusive? The answer is: [as in the case of] the *śyenacit* (the hawk-shaped altar).
Regarding the statement "one should collect," it is not possible here to understand the identity of the individual instance with that [universal].
Why? He says: for here, what belongs to the individual...
The ritual action (*kārya*) is understood.
A. Why? He asks: "Why is it not understood? This is not the meaning of the sentence: that "that which is piled with *śyena*-birds is a *śyena-cit*.

For if that were the meaning of the sentence, the ritual action would pertain only to the individual [animal], since the individual alone would be the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of piling (*cayana*).

Because it is logically possible [to derive it otherwise]. Why is this alone not understood as the meaning of the sentence? The answer is: because of the traditional rule (smaraṇa) stating "when *karman* is the upapada.

When *karman* is the upapada, this *kvip* suffix is applied to the root *ci* (to pile). Therefore, [the compound] is *śyena-cita*, meaning "that which is piled in the shape of a hawk. Thus, *śyena-*...

The meaning is "consciousness. And it has been stated in the section on correct words (*sādhuśabdādhikaraṇa*) that the recollection of the designation is in accordance with the actual object; therefore, this word *śyena* [is applied] to the altar (*citau*).
It exists in the state of being built upon a level ground. Therefore, regarding the altar (citī) which is to be accomplished by a different substance—
distinct from the juice, blood, flesh, and so forth, and characterized by bricks— the word "śyena" (hawk) is used in the sense of a simile.
The meaning is that it exists as something similar to a hawk. Nevertheless, he asks "why? and says: for it is not possible to establish a similarity between individuals.
Thus the venerable authors of the Vārttika have said:
"Two or three people on this earth might create something resembling a single individual through painting or sculpture, but never by means of bricks."

Thus, it is observed that only the universal (*sāmānya*) possesses positive concomitance (*anvaya*), not the individual (*vyakti*), because it is possible to establish similarity based on the universal. Furthermore, it has been stated that only that which possesses positive concomitance is a [valid] category (*padārtha*). Therefore, the universal is not understood merely as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*); rather, the positive concomitance of the universal [is established].
It is understood;
however, it is so through its effect.
In some cases, this is because it itself is connected with the effect, and [because] that which is connected [with it].
The status of being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*) has been stated.
Here he asks: "And do even those meanings that are subordinate to a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) possess the property of being connected in a sentence (*anvayitva*)?"

Are those meanings which have become subordinate (*upasarjanībhūta*) in the simile also possessed of syntactic connection (*anvayitva*), such that you maintain that even the form of the hawk (*śyenākṛti*) lacks connection with the action? Since the form of the hawk does not enter into the performance [of the rite], it has no syntactic connection. To this, the reply is: "Certainly."
The property of being connected through cognition exists in the case of comprehension (*pratipatti*),
not in the case of the action (*kārya*);
since there is the cognition of a place similar in shape to the *śyena* [sacrifice] as something to be performed, it possesses connection through cognition, but not connection through performance.
He asks again: "Does that which is not connected to the action also possess connection, by virtue of which the form (ākṛti) possesses connection? The answer is:
"It has been stated regarding the words of explanatory passages (arthavāda) and the words of mantras."
Even those things that do not participate in the accomplishment of the action possess the quality of being concomitant. When this has been stated, someone might object:

"If the generic form (*ākṛti*) possesses the quality of being concomitant merely by being concomitant with the cognition [of it], then in cases such as 'one should sacrifice with a cow' (*gavā yajeta*), [the word] would have concomitance with its own primary meaning."
Why is it not accepted? The answer is: because the form (ākṛti) is not a constituent factor in the comprehension of the action.

This is because, in the comprehension of actions such as sacrifice, the form is not a constituent factor. At the time of comprehending the action, it is the individual (vyakti) alone that is perceived as being connected with the action; the form is relevant only at the time of learning the linguistic convention (vyutpatti).
B. Your non-connection with existence; C. Why is that?

A. The meaning is that even the form (*ākṛti*) appears [in the cognition]; the meaning is that the form serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). To explain this very point, he states the objection: "But surely, if it is a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), the form does not become a constituent part (*aṅga*) for the comprehension of the action. The reply: "It is neither a secondary indicator nor a constituent part, because, like a garment, it serves to bring about the specific understanding [of the individual]."

The meaning of this is as follows: an incidental attribute (*upalakṣaṇa*) does not become a constituent factor (*aṅga*) for the cognition of a particular object, just like clothing. For example, at the time of learning the linguistic convention, "This person who possesses clothing, who is dressed in white clothing, is Devadatta," the clothing serves as an incidental attribute; however, later, when it is said, "Bring Devadatta," at the time of performing the action, that [clothing] is not a constituent factor for the cognition of the specific person.

It does not exist; likewise, the configuration (*ākṛti*) also [does not exist as a permanent entity]. Having thus established that, for instance, in the case of "one should sacrifice with a cow" (*gavā yajeta*), it is the individual (*vyakti*) that is the recurring element, whereas in cases such as "one should pile the *śyena*-altar" (*śyenacitaṃ cinvīta*), it is the configuration, he now states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): therefore, in some cases the individual is the recurring element, and in others the universal (*sāmānya*).
Because we do not know where that state of having become real (bhūtatva) is logically situated,
the consequence of invalidity follows once again, as the basis [for validity] remains undetermined.
He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "To this it is replied. The connection of the individual (*vyakti*) is not determined as being through its actual existence (*tadbhūtatayā*);

that is, the connection of the individual as the denotation of the word is not understood. Why? He says: for if the individual were the connected [element], then there would be a connection with the individual alone.
Or, there is the concomitance (anvaya) of a single individual; the word "only" (mātra) has the sense of totality; thus, there is the concomitance of all individuals.

Or it might belong to a single individual instance. Yet neither of these two [possibilities] is perceived. Why? He says: for in every case, a concomitance (*anvaya*) is observed that does not abandon the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*).

The meaning of this is as follows: in the statement "one should sacrifice with a cow," the connection (*anvaya*) is perceived only in a general form, and this applies to the individual (*vyakti*) as well; it is not perceived through any other form. For every substrate (*dharmin*) is manifested by some attribute (*dharma*), and not otherwise. And upon the utterance of a word, the individual appears as distinct and possessing different attributes solely through the attribute that is the universal (*sāmānya*), and not through any other.
But has it not been stated that there is a cognition of the universal by way of secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*)?
The implication is that, because the individual (*vyakti*) is denotable by the word, the universal (*sāmānya*) cannot be non-denotable by the word. The reply is: "But that very [universal]..."
The nature of being an indicator (*upalakṣaṇatva*) is not understood.
Why?
He says: for that which is called an indicator does not indicate the object to be indicated by way of its own form (*ātmākāratayā*), as is the case where this...
"A crow is perched there; that is Devadatta’s house. One does not determine from this that the house has the form of a crow.
This is the intended meaning:

the cognition of the object intended to be indicated occurs by means of that which serves merely as its indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and not by means of whatever form [the object] actually possesses, just as in the case of the crow.
Regarding the comprehension of a specific house: when an individual is perceived as the meaning of the word "but" (tu), it is not perceived through any other form;
rather, it is made known.

[The word denotes] by way of the universal form alone. Because its cognition results in the apprehension of that [form], and because it culminates in that very nature, that [form] alone is the denotation of the word. As for what was also said—that for one who has seen a lion only while it is in a cage, the cage is understood precisely through the understanding of the lion;
in the same way, [the individual is understood] from the form (ākṛti).

The claim that there is comprehension from mere speech even regarding that which is not denotable by words is also incorrect. Why? Because people perceive the cage as being of a different form from the form of a lion; however, in the case of [the command] "bring the cow," no other form is perceived.

For indeed, just as the cage is understood through the understanding of the lion by means of their functional connection, so it would be here if it were the case that the individual (vyakti), being perceived in another form, becomes the cause for the comprehension of the configuration (ākṛti). But this is not so; for the word does not [denote] in any other manner apart from the configuration.

When [the word] is uttered, the individual (vyakti) appears. Since it is understood from that word in that very form, the universal (ākṛti) alone is the denotation of the word. Therefore, it is difficult to maintain that the individual follows along because no other form is perceived. Now, since the connection [of the word with its object] is for the sake of action (kārya), and since that [action] is not possible for a mere form alone, the cognition of the universal must be preceded by the individual; this is due to the [perceived] cause.

By Sāra. Its meaning is as follows: that which is connected with the action (*kārya*) alone is denoted by the word, and nothing else. And it is the individual (*vyakti*) that is so connected, not the mere form; therefore, it is the individual alone that is denoted by the word. When that [individual] has been understood, [the expression] "lion-cage"—
The form is understood through reasoning; thus, it is perceived precisely by following the underlying cause. He replies: "True, as one who has a father says."
He was properly trained in the sciences by his father; nevertheless, the comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) extends only as far as the apprehension of the form (*ākāra*).

It is only the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) that is perceived as the concomitant, not the individual (*vyakti*). The comprehension of the concomitance does not proceed as far as the individual, but rather terminates at the mere form alone. Now, this form may be conceived as standing in the place of a cage.
If, however,

the cognition of the form (*ākāra*) were conceived as being like the lion and the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) as being like the cage, then there would be either a concomitance with the mere individual or a concomitance with a single individual.
And yet that [universal] does not exist. The proponent says: "Let there be a connection with mere individuals, or a connection with a single individual; what contradiction is there for us?"
The author states the final conclusion: B. "The word would be non-determinative.

The word would be non-determinative because it is impossible to carry out the application [of the word] to all individual instances; thus, its application could not be accomplished through capability. When the application to multiple individuals is undertaken, there is no determination as to which individual's application is intended and which is not. Again, the proponent of the prima facie view asks: "By whom was it said that [the word] is non-determinative?"

The meaning is that it is indeed accepted that [the cognition] is verbal and not non-determinative (*anadhyavasāyin*). A. Regarding the final position, he states the conclusion: "But you must admit that the verbal [cognition] is indeed determinative (*adhyavasāyin*); for if it were non-determinative, how could it be possible to say that the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not subject to deviation?"
B. Inclusion of meaning (arthānvaya). C. Inclusion of another meaning (arthāntarānvaya):

for when there is inclusion of another meaning, it is possible to state the non-inclusion of that other meaning, as in the case of "Bring the cow," where the inclusion of the individual [cow] is certain, whereas the inclusion of a horse is not.
When there is a form, its recurrence cannot be understood; however, this is not the case when the recurrence has not been determined, as in the example: "The sugar-lumps are smeared."
"He places [the bricks]" refers to the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Just as in the case of "the pebbles are smeared," even when the connection [between the pebbles and the act of smearing] is not yet determined, the connection with clarified butter is accepted and is not untenable; so too, when the connection with the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not yet determined, [the connection with the individual is accepted]. Therefore, it is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
First of all, that position is incoherent.
Now, it might be argued as follows: the power of the word is inherent, while the connection [with the universal] arises from the effect; and the effect resides in the individual.
Yet, neither the mere individual nor its specific quality is apprehended; rather, it is the substance of the individual as already connected with "cowness" (gotva) that is cognized.

The meaning is as follows: that which is connected with an action (*kāryānvita*) is what is denoted by a word. And it is the individual (*vyakti*) that is connected with an action. In this regard, by the very nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*), the word "cow" does not denote merely an individual—whether of the same class or of a different class—nor does it denote any specific individual, such as a *śābaleya* (spotted) or an *aśābaleya* (non-spotted). Rather, it denotes merely an individual as connected with the universal "cowness" (*gotva*). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
[The opponent] refutes: "In that case, it follows that individuals connected with 'cowness' (gotva) are what are perceived. [The proponent replies:

"It is accepted that there is only the individual cow by way of the form of cowness. Therefore, cowness alone is the denotable object. Again, the proponent says: "Do not speak thus, for the purpose of the task..."

For a derivative suffix (*anvaya*) does not terminate in the cognition of the primary object itself; just as in the command "bring the man with the staff," it is not the bringing of the staff that is intended, yet the cognition [of the qualified person] occurs. The same applies to words such as "cow" and so forth.

Although the cognition of an individual is preceded by the cognition of the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), nevertheless, because cowness does not participate in the causal function (*kāryānanvayitvāt*), it is the individual alone that must be denoted by a word whose denotative capacity consists in its connection with a causal function. Just as in the command "Bring the man with the staff," the word "staff-bearer" denotes the person and not the staff. The proponent replies: "You are ignorant of the distinction."
He does not know the distinction between the staff and the cow-nature (*gotva*). Even though the distinction was stated, you did not grasp it. What was stated?

The answer is: this was stated—that where there is a distinction from another form, that other form serves as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), just as in the case of "the one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) alone.

When there is the cognition of a specific person possessing a staff, the form of the person is perceived as distinct from the form of the staff; thus, the staff serves as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, in the act of bringing [someone], there is no connection with the staff in the cognition of a specific person who may or may not possess a staff. However, where one is cognized specifically as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) and not merely as a particular individual, [the staff is an essential attribute].

In that case, it is possible to state the positive concomitance (anvaya) only of one who is thus constituted and specifically characterized by a staff; for when the specific [qualifier] is understood, the word "staff-bearer" does not apply to the staff itself.

Here he raises an objection: "If there is an understanding without distinction, does the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) apply to the staff itself—that is, in a case where it is understood solely as 'the staff' and not as a specific person possessing the staff? In that case too, the word *daṇḍin* would not apply to the staff, because of its connection with a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*). He replies: "It does not apply by way of being the cause [of the cognition]."

One does not proceed by merely observing the sign (nimitta), because the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) is understood [to imply more than that], due to its connection with a suffix; likewise, because in worldly usage it is established through convention that the person (*puruṣa*) is the cause only when accompanied by another object,
and not because of a comprehension of distinction [from the object] through the effect itself.

Having considered the functional requirement (*kārya*), the word *daṇḍin* also applies to the staff; where there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) solely by way of being a staff-bearer, it is indeed appropriate because it is not understood through any other form. However, in the case of cows and the like, since no difference in the cause (*nimitta*) is perceived, a distinction [of the word] as a cause even with respect to its correlates is not possible. How much less so, then, from the perspective of the functional requirement?

The universal "cowness" (*gotva*) alone is the cause (*nimitta*). The causality of words such as "cow" and so forth follows from their being impartite (*akhaṇḍatva*). And the effect is even more clearly of the nature of the comprehension of the connection with "cowness.
How then is there the apprehension of a particular in the injunction "he sprinkles the rice-grains," if there is no distinction based on the cause?

The meaning is: how is it that this very same word, in some cases, culminates in the comprehension of an individual (*vyakti*), while in others, it culminates in the comprehension of a universal (*sāmānya*)? The answer is: the comprehension of the particular arises from the effect (*kāryataḥ*).
The specific understanding of sprinkling and so forth arises from a consideration of their purpose. Why is this? He says:
for the purpose culminates either in the action itself or in that which possesses it.

In general, the function of ritual items (padārtha) culminates in that for which the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is enjoined. However, when that [direct object] is impossible, it culminates in that which possesses it—that is, in that which is connected to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) that motivates the act. Thus, since the function of sprinkling cannot directly reside in the *apūrva*, it resides in those things that possess it.
A. In the case of rice grains connected to the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of the motivator, the cognition of the task consists merely in the manifestation of its purpose.
But how, then, are those rice grains understood to possess that [unseen potency]?
The answer is: because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Since it falls within the section on the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and is grasped by the *apūrva*, the function of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is understood to reside solely in the rice and other materials that are directly connected to the *apūrva*. Therefore, it is not [connected to the sacrifice itself].

The opponent’s argument—that this [inference] is like that of a staff—is refuted; therefore, when the universal (sāmānya) is not [directly] connected, the result (kārya) itself remains unestablished. And it cannot be asserted that, while the result is established, the non-result (akārya) is also established.

Therefore, it is the universal alone that, being connected [with the word], is the denotatum. But surely, since words have as their object that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*), and since the individual (*vyakti*) is what is connected with that which is to be accomplished— [The opponent continues: ...the individual is indeed the denotatum. For it is observed that when the word "cow" is uttered, there is the cognition of a specific individual cow, and not of a universal. Furthermore, because the relationship between word and meaning is established through usage (*vyavahāra*), and since usage pertains to individuals, the word must denote the individual. Moreover, the universal is not perceived apart from the individual; therefore, the individual is the primary object of the word's denotation. As for the universal, it is merely a secondary attribute. Thus, the individual is the denotatum. And since the individual is connected with that which is to be accomplished, it is the individual that is the denotatum of the word. Therefore, the universal is not the denotatum. This is the position of the opponent.
Since it is established that this [universal] alone is the denotable object by virtue of its being the reality (*tattva*), let there be no finality regarding it. He refutes [this objection]:

It is true that there would be no finality if the operation were impossible even with respect to the universal (*jāti*). For the status of being the object of an operation exists only according to what is possible.
[The universal] exists precisely by virtue of possessing modification (*vikāra*), just like the instruments and so forth.

Just as the instruments and so forth possess the status of being objects of action even without undergoing modification, so too does the generic form (*ākṛti*). Now, [one might object]: "But what about those [instruments]?"
In the case of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, there exists a modification (*vikāra*) in their own operation.

172] An intermediate version (A) reads: "The very state of being connected with modification and operation is what constitutes the modification of instruments and so forth; it certainly exists. The reply: This is equally true for genus (*gotva*) and the like as well.

For even that [universal] is indeed already engaged in its own operation for the sake of establishing the operation [of the particular]. Now, one might object: we do not perceive any modification in a universal, as we do in the case of instruments and the like, either prior to its operation or after its completion. The reply is: there is no modification.

The *ṛta* is the cause for the accomplishment of the activity; however, when that [cause] exists, there is existence, and when it is absent, there is non-existence. Even if this were so, he asks "what then? and says: "And it has been stated that the cessation from the object of the injunction is not perceived as being devoid of the comprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*)."
Therefore, the very cognition [of the injunction] has the universal as its cause. Nevertheless, as to how it serves the purpose of performance, he says:
"Just as the accomplishment of the object being cognized does not arise from the cognition of that which is being cognized; for the meaning of the injunction, once cognized—"
Since it can be established that even the cause of cognition is useful for practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*), the connection of the universal with the effect is thus logically justified.
To the question, "If the universal is the denotable object (*abhidheya*), how then is there the designation of 'otherness' (*anyatva*)?", he says: "But as for the denotability of otherness...
"It is established through its being the material cause (*upādāna*).
That is to say, the designation of "otherness" is established in relation to the manifest individual (*vyakti*) which serves as the material cause.

Therefore, the comprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is necessarily preceded by the universal (*sāmānya*). However, in the case of the subject (*uddeśya*), it functions as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) by way of its effect (*kārya*), and not by virtue of being something other than that [subject].

The meaning is: "not by way of not being present in the individual form. Therefore, it is established that [the word refers] to those things which constitute the object as it is understood, i.e., "consisting of those" (*tadbhūtaiḥ*).
