This very point has already been stated in general terms: that cognition arises from the word in the form of a universal (*sāmānyākāreṇa*).
In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), there is the grasping of the form (*ākṛti*) of the two denotable objects (*abhidheya*).

The example provided is merely illustrative; it is not intended to be definitive. The meaning of the section is that even in the case of a non-concrete entity (*anākṛti*), there is no syntactic connection for one who has not grasped its qualifier. The same applies to the denotability of both action and quality; as in the word *sāman*—

Furthermore, both action and quality are denoted by the word *aruṇā* (red), yet from the word *sāman*, they are perceived as being of that very same nature as from the word *aruṇā*. Precisely because this principle applies everywhere, it has been stated: "In general, no cognition of a qualified object proceeds without first grasping its qualifier. Otherwise, it would have been stated: "No cognition of an individual proceeds without first grasping its form (*ākṛti*). [This is so] even when [the cognition] occurs in another individual.

"If it is applied [to another individual], then the individual is not the word-meaning; for it is said that the individual is devoid of all generalities and particularities"—this is the *Bhāṣya*. To explain this, he says: "If it is applied even to another individual, then the individual is not the word-meaning.

Thus [it is asked]. What is the intention? This is the questioner’s underlying thought: although [the word] is applied to another individual, why then does the individual not become the meaning of the word? He reveals the intention: for one who has cognized the relationship [of the word] with respect to one thing cannot [cognize it] with respect to another thing without relying on some single property (dharma).
For one who has already cognized that relationship, it is possible to understand the connection with another entity; however, there can be no application [of a word] to that which is unrelated.

If it is nevertheless applied, then something distinct from the individual (vyakti) must be admitted as its substrate. For it has been demonstrated by the statement "the individual is indeed characterized by its uniqueness" that the individual is devoid of all generalities and particularities.

The meaning of this is as follows: if a universal (*sāmānya*) is not accepted as the denotable object, then when a word such as "cow" has its relationship [with the object] known in one individual, it cannot be said that its relationship with another individual is known. A word whose relationship is unknown cannot be employed. And if it were employed, then [one would have to accept] one...

In that case, the relation must be understood by relying on a real entity (*vastu*) that exists in another individual (*vyaktyantara*). And that entity must be distinct from the individual itself, because it exists in other individuals; however, it cannot be that very individual, since an individual is not omnipresent (*asarvagata*). If it were present in another individual as well, its nature as an individual would be undermined, because an individual possesses a unique, non-common form (*asādhāraṇarūpa*). This has been demonstrated in the *Bhāṣya* by the phrase "devoid of all generalities and particularities" (*sarvasāmānyaviśeṣaviyuktā*).
“There is no such fault; for even in another individual, it will exist as being entirely devoid of all generalities and particularities,” so says the Bhāṣya.
He states the intention behind this: for the author of the Bhāṣya, who says "this is not a fault," the exclusion of all generalities and particulars will serve as a mere illustration.
The intention is that, for this reason, its application even to another individual characterized by that [universal] is not untenable. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya provides the reply:
"If it were a universal devoid of all particular universals (sāmānya-viśeṣa), then it would be merely a universal. To explain that, he says: "If [it were] devoid of all particular universals..."
If it is argued that [the word denotes] "separation," then in that case, separation itself would be presented as the denotable meaning, not the individual (vyakti),
because it is perceived precisely in the form of separation; thus, only separation would be the denotable meaning, not the individual.
Thus, it is stated that what follows as the denotable object is necessarily a universal (*sāmānya*);
whether it be "cowness" (*gotva*) or the exclusion of all universals and particulars (*sarvasāmānyaviśeṣaviyukti*). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya says: "It is not so."
Thus [it is said]. That is challenged by the statement "no," because the object which belongs to the universal— that is,
the common property— is [distinct from] the particulars.

Or rather, that which is the substratum of unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is the individual (*vyakti*). To whom is this answer given? He provides the resolution: the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely the state of being dissociated [from those properties].
[This is] for one who does not [properly] establish [the argument]. But how is this reply of his formulated?
It is as follows: it does not apprehend anything, whether a universal or a particular, by way of a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).
What, then, is the word? It is the denotation of the mere substratum of the word's general and particular properties.

This [word] denotes the substance itself as its object. But is it not the case that "mere substratum" (*āśrayamātra*) is also a universal (*sāmānya*), and therefore, if that were denoted, there would again be the undesirable consequence of denoting a universal? He replies: No, it is said; for a universal is the state of having a single form among things that possess different forms.
Furthermore, the substrate (āśraya) does not possess a different form from the substratum (āśrayin).
Nor is the so-called substrate something continuous that exists apart from universals such as "cowness" (gotva);

rather, it is only the universals themselves, such as "cowness," that appear as common [to individuals], and not some further property called "substrateness. Therefore, because they are non-different—
The application of the word is established through its usage.

Even with respect to another individual (*vyaktyantara*), since it is not perceived as being non-different from the [original] individual, the word is applied there as well. To this, the reply is: if such is the case regarding its application, then there is a contradiction.

Why is this so? He says: "For the word 'cow' is not applied to the individual horse, nor is such usage observed. And [this error] follows from your own hypothesis, because the absence of the cognition of difference and the cognition of non-difference are equivalent."
This has been stated in the Bhāṣya with the words, "If this [word] also occurs in another individual instance," and so forth. Here, an objection is raised:
"But surely non-perception was stated by you yourself;
therefore, since no usage is observed there, the word is not employed there."

Since the word "cow" is not observed to be used for a specific horse, one might think it will be used there [for that horse]. This is what was stated in the Bhāṣya with the words, "For whomsoever usage is observed," and so forth.
He refutes this: "In that case, then, the observation of usage..."
It is maintained that the reason lies in the employment of words. The opponent says: "Yes, it is so."
The opponent says:
If [the cognition] depends on the observation of usage, then how [can it occur] in the case of a cow born today?
The application of the word "cow" is established there, since its application is observed. It is observed.
And there is also the application of the word to that [individual]. Therefore, the individual is not the meaning of the word.
This is the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "yadi yatra prayoga" (if, where there is usage).

Furthermore, this claim that "usage occurs only with respect to the individual" is a mere assertion. If usage were restricted solely to the individual, then linguistic acquisition would arise from a conventional practice independent of other individuals;
[the word] would be restricted to only a single individual.
There would be a linguistic acquisition [of the word's meaning]; from that, another acquisition would be required for each subsequent individual.
And when there is a difference in those individuals and a difference in the acquisitions, one would have to say, "This is a cow" or "This is a cow."

There would be knowledge [of the object] such as "this is an axle" or "that is an axle. However, there would not arise the cognition "this is a cow" and "that is a cow" based on a single linguistic convention established upon a single individual instance. And thus, "the cognition of a universal would not occur."

Thus is the meaning stated by the Bhāṣya. Therefore, the position that [the word] denotes the individual (vyakti) is not possible, because no other derivation (vyutpatti) is understood, since the meaning is not cognized through a single derivation alone. B. reads *arthāntarāpratipatteḥ*. Here, he raises an objection:
— Then both must be stated.
It consists of both the individual (vyakti) and the genus (jāti); however, their status as subordinate or primary is to be determined by the purpose (kārya).

Having considered the purpose, or relying upon the purpose, it must be determined that in some cases the individual is primary and in others the form (ākṛti). Thus, according to the view that [the individual] is primary, whether it be worldly or Vedic—
It is doubted whether [the referent] is something to be modified (*saṃskārya*).

The meaning of this is as follows: where a word such as "cow" occurs in the primary category [of denotation], there the referent is the substance (*dravya*), that is, the individual (*vyakti*); for example, in the case of "he sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). For this very reason, doubt arises.

Is it the worldly substance, rice, that is to be sprinkled, or rather the Vedic [substance]? However, if the genus (jāti) is denoted, then because the genus is a single entity, no doubt would arise. On the other hand, according to the view that [the individual] is the thing to be taken up (upādāna), the word's meaning is indeed the universal (sāmānya) alone, wherever it is enjoined as something to be taken up.

In that case, only the universal (sāmānya) is expressed by the word, as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with a cow. This is what was stated [by Patañjali]: "Both [the universal and the particular] belong to the venerable Pāṇini. [The author] refutes this: he says—this position also is not possible.

He asks, "Why? and replies: "For the nature of being a material cause (*upādāna*) is established through its effect (*kārya*), and not through cognition (*pratipatti*). The meaning of this is: having observed the effect, it is understood that 'this is the material cause of that.'"

"You [assert] that this is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*); however, this is not known merely through cognition (*pratipatti*). For in cognition, no distinction is apprehended. Even where there is a defining characteristic, in that case too, it is only the universal (*sāmānya*) that is denoted by the word in usage. Through the power of that [universal], the individual (*vyakti*) is cognized. Even where there is a material cause (*upādānatva*), the cognition occurs in exactly the same way; thus, the universal alone is the meaning expressed by the word. Thus he says: "And the cognition..."
It is based on generality.
Why? The answer: because it occurs even without a word, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

"He who perceives the form (ākṛti) would necessarily perceive the individual (vyakti). However, for one who does not perceive the form even when the word is uttered, there is no comprehension of the individual. Why is this? He says: in the injunction "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), although the application refers to the individual, it expresses [the object] by way of its generic form.

Because it is cognized in that form, that alone is what is denoted by the word; however, the cognition of the individual occurs through its power. Here, an objection is raised: "If it is argued that [the universal] is determined from the individual..."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this is as follows: although it does not denote the denotation in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), nevertheless, that substance is determined precisely through the individual (*vyakti*); therefore, the individual alone is the denotable object (*vācya*). He refutes this: no, because it is not cognized as being contained within another individual.

Regarding the effect (*kārya*): if the substance were understood merely through its manifestation (*vyakti*), and only the manifestation were understood, then the effect would be understood as having reached even a manifestation connected with a different genus (*jātyantara*). But this is not the case; therefore, even when the usage is grounded in a manifestation, it is the substance itself that is understood by way of its universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), and not otherwise. However, in a usage grounded in the universal (*sāmānya*), [it is] one— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the relationship between substance (*dravya*), manifestation (*vyakti*), and the universal (*sāmānya*) in the context of linguistic usage and ritual action.)
It has been stated that a substance is determined precisely through its form; this very point is demonstrated by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) with the words, "This [occurs] due to a mental lapse.
Therefore, there is no lack of determination.
—Is it the individual (vyakti) that possesses the commonality, or is it the form (ākṛti)? Why? He says:

because of the cognition of a universal (sāmānya), that is, because of the cognition through a universal aspect; for there is a rule that the meaning of a word is necessarily the universal itself—it is precisely that which is determined (adhyavasāpya).
[This concludes] the section on verbal [cognition] in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, a commentary (*pañcikā*) composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra,
belonging to the first chapter.
The third quarter.
Now, the fourth quarter.
The purposefulness of the sacred tradition has been stated. But is this not a definition of the means of valid cognition?
In this chapter, it is said: "Words are explained according to their respective means of valid cognition."
Because of the declaration, "The investigation of its cause [is now undertaken]," he will state in the second chapter and thereafter: "The definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated."

Therefore, [the opponent asks]: "What is this that has been proposed? What is being said? Are words such as *udbhid* injunctions regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? The respondent asks: "Does this proposal not also fail to apply to the section on the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*)? The objector replies:
"Certainly, that is not possible at all. For it is only when validity is established that the consideration of determining a specific object becomes tenable."

The determination of the specific meaning. That reflection which is for the sake of retention is the reflection on the determination of the specific meaning. Furthermore, if there were invalidity, since the object would not exist, what kind of reflection on the specific meaning could there be?

He states another objection: "And it has been said that [the Vedic texts] have this purpose (aiding ritual performance). That which was explained as being possible through the injunction of a quality is also not tenable. For the impossibility of being a mantra or an arthavāda is not the reason for being an injunction of a quality. What then? Only the attainment of an action is the reason for being an injunction of a quality."

The Sūtra has been explained as meaning that because it is impossible for the word "udbhidā" to function as a reminder (*smāraka*) and because it is impossible for it to be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it must be intended as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). That interpretation is untenable;

for it is not the case that something which cannot function either as a reminder or as a matter of praise is necessarily an injunction of a quality. What then? [It is an injunction] regarding an action.

When [the action] has already been established, the hearing of its qualities is the reason for it being an injunction of qualities; as the Commentator himself has stated: "The injunction of a quality is purposeless with respect to an action that has not [already] been enjoined."

Thus, by saying this, it is stated that the prescription of an accessory (*guṇavidhāna*) is possible only when an action has been enjoined. Therefore, the very attainment of the action is the reason for [the status of] an accessory prescription. And if [this applies to] the meaning of the *mantras* and *arthavādas*—
The impossibility [of the injunction] would be the reason for it being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*);
in that case, even the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) would be an injunction of a quality.

Even for one desiring heaven, it is impossible for [the passage] to be either a mantra or an arthavāda. He raises another objection: as for what was said—that in the model sacrifice, the Jyotiṣṭoma, the injunction of an accessory will be purposeful—that too is incorrect, because even there, the word denoting the accessory is indeed heard in the form "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma."
Therefore, since even that [sentence] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)— because an injunction of an action (*karmavidhāna*) is impossible there as well—

how can there be an injunction of qualities such as *udbhid* based upon it here? Or, if in that case [of the *jyotiṣṭoma*] there were an injunction of a qualified [action] (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), [then...]
The intention is that since the action will also be prescribed there, an injunction regarding its qualities (guṇavidhi) will follow based upon it.
He refutes this: "Then why does a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna) not occur here as well, in the case of 'udbhidā'?"
He introduces another objection:
"Now, when it is established that [the sacrifice] is one and the same in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, then the other..."
"By the word 'udbhidā', there is an injunction of a quality in that very same [act].

He refutes this: "In this case, since the ritual act is already established through a qualified injunction by the word 'udbhidā', the injunction of a quality therein by the phrase 'jyotiṣṭomena' [is what is intended]."
Why is it not possible? Nor do we see any reason for such a restriction.
He states another objection: "distinguished"—
And the injunction is understood as pertaining to the production of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭakarmotpatti*).

When the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice has already arisen as an action qualified by its own accessories, the term "udbhid" is also understood as an injunction of a qualified [action] alone, not as an injunction of an accessory. Why?

Thus he says: "And it is not proper to enjoin another quality when a qualified ritual action has already arisen, because of the obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇāvarodha*). [As stated: 'And a quality [is enjoined] when there is a connection with something not previously established, [provided there is no conflict] between two sentences.'"
Because of the statement of the principle that "it is due to equality," he concludes:
therefore, there is neither inclusion within the definition nor the statement of a logical principle.
"Since the prescription of qualities is possible," [says] B. "We do not know how this is so here, nor do we know how this commentary has come to be stated. The respondent says:
"To this it is replied: [the means of valid cognition]..."

This is indeed the definition [of valid cognition]. Now, it was argued that in the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the consideration of the determination of a specific object is not appropriate.
He refutes this: "This is not presented as the determination of a specific object. What, then, is presented? The answer is:

Is there an injunction of a ritual action (*karma-vidhāna*) here, or is there merely an injunction of a quality (*guṇa-vidhāna*)? Under the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), there is an injunction of a ritual action;

under the view that it is an injunction of a quality, there is only an injunction of a quality and not an injunction of a ritual action—this has been set forth. Therein, he adopts the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*):

And when it is possible for there to be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi), it is not logical to assume an injunction of an action (karmavidhāna); for the sentence is intent upon the quality, like the case of "red cloth" (raktapaṭa).

The meaning of this is as follows: the application (niyoga) is understood according to the distribution (viniyoga), because that understanding is dependent upon the distribution. And by virtue of the distribution, [the action is understood] through the *udbhid*— [Fragmentary text ends here.]

In such cases, it is understood that there is merely an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhāna*). Consequently, just as the sentence "the cloth becomes red" is intended solely for the purpose of connecting the cloth with the quality of redness,

so too here, in the case of "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the sentence is intent upon enjoining the *udbhid* and other such qualities, and does not culminate in an injunction of a ritual action (*karmavidhi*).

Therefore, because the injunction of an action is impossible, [the text] lacks authority. How [is this] in the case of the position that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)? The answer is:
because it must rely upon a worldly action. For in a sentence intended as an injunction of a subordinate quality, a worldly action must necessarily be relied upon.
Here he raises an objection: what fault is there in relying upon a Vedic ritual, such that some worldly [basis] must be resorted to? Indeed, not...

There is no fault [in this]. However, there is the impossibility of Vedic ritual action. How is there impossibility? Because of the hearing of a subordinate term (*upapada*) in every instance, a single word is never employed [independently]. Since the sentence, due to the hearing of a subordinate term in every case, is intent upon enjoining the meaning of that subordinate term, it is impossible for it to enjoin a ritual action; thus, there is the impossibility of Vedic ritual action. Here, an objection is raised: "Even so, why is there a lack of authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*)?"
The answer is: regarding the meaning of the term, its application must be sought from another source, namely another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is from another [source]...

In that case, the activity [of the injunction] must be sought elsewhere, which leads to the undesirable consequence of its being dependent on something else. Since the activity directed toward the meaning of the verbal root depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) follows as a matter of course.
The opponent says: "But if, for instance, eating, sexual intercourse..."
If, as in the case of injunctions regarding movement and the like, there were non-dependence due to the prescription of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*), then how could there be invalidity?
Just as when one has already engaged in eating from another cause, [the rule] "one should eat food facing the east" [is a restrictive rule].
Thus,

just as in the case of approaching a woman [during her fertile period] in the injunction "one should approach her during her season," there is independence in both instances, so it will be here as well; therefore, there will be no lack of authority.

This is the meaning. He refutes this: "This might be so if all injunctions everywhere were solely for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*). However, some injunctions are perceived as being for the sake of ritual action (*karmārtha*) as well; in those cases, such a restriction (*niyama*) is not possible."

The meaning of this is as follows: if human purpose were the sole objective in every case—just as in the rule "one should eat food facing the east"—then there would be independence [from other factors].
However, some injunctions are understood to have ritual action (*karman*) as their purpose.

Since the nature of the action is established by that [scriptural statement] alone, and because it is observed through other qualities as well, no restrictive rule (niyama) is possible. Consequently, for the sake of establishing such a restriction, there must be recourse to another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). He objects: Furthermore, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," what is being restricted? Is it not the agent?

It is restricted. [The opponent] objects: "Just as this qualification of the agent is not tenable, so it has been demonstrated in the eleventh [book]. However, because the fruit (*phala*) is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), its restriction is impossible;

and because it is the primary element (*pradhānabhūta*) and thus not something to be undertaken (*anupādeya*), the fruit is not enjoined, and therefore its restriction cannot occur. Regarding the fruit...

If it is argued that action (*karman*) is what is being regulated, [the author] refutes this: it has already been stated that actions are not subject to injunction, because sentences have as their primary referent other categories of meaning (*padārtha*). Therefore, it must be understood that either another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought, or else it is merely the intuition of the blind (*andhapratibhā*).

Since no other means of valid cognition is possible, this [view] should be understood as a blind intuition lacking logical connection. Here, an objection is raised: why is there not an injunction for an action possessing a quality?
Why is the action itself, qualified by a quality, not enjoined? For example, as in the command, "Bring the man with the staff."

Just as there is a cognition of a person qualified by a staff, so too here, because of the cognition of an action qualified by a quality, that which is thus qualified alone is what is to be enjoined. To this, the reply is:

"Because the action possessing the quality is not understood. He asks, "Why? and says: "For in this case, the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is not expressed by the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth."

It is explained as follows: for that meaning, namely "possession" (*tadvattā*), belongs only to those words ending in the possessive suffix *mat*, and not to those ending in case-suffixes (*sub*). Now, [regarding the word] *udbhid*...

If it is argued that [the term] is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he refutes this: "In that case, dependence [on something else] follows as a consequence. He asks why, and says: "For one cannot maintain that there is secondary indication when there is a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)."

It is not known from the occurrence of the direct denotation (*śruti*) that the word "udbhid" and others function by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the object "udbhid-like";
rather, this is understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because their usage is observed to apply to that which possesses those qualities.

Therefore, it is the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for what was stated [in the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "Since the purposefulness of the Veda has been declared, therefore everything [in it] must have that as its purpose"—this is the reason for the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

To this it is replied: This reason does indeed serve to refute the name. But how, then, is the name refuted by this? Because its reference to this [object] (*aidamarthya*) is impossible, and because its status as an injunction (*niyoga*) is impossible. How is it that its reference to this is not possible?
The answer is: For it has been stated that the words of the injunctions, the mantras, and the explanatory passages (arthavādas) possess meaning by virtue of having the *niyoga* as their purpose;
[this applies] to that which has the *niyoga* as its purpose.

It has been stated that meaningfulness belongs to the injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśa*), the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and the mantra words. And this quality of having the *niyoga* (the mandate) as its purpose is not possible for a noun, because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*).
Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that, due to its being non-enjoined, a noun does not have its purpose realized through the *niyoga* by way of being itself enjoined."

But as to the question of whether this will be established by Śruti or Smṛti, he says: "Now, it has been stated that meaningfulness [of mantras] occurs through Śruti or Smṛti only for those things that are not subject to injunction (avidheya). And both of these [Śruti and Smṛti] apply here."
Since it is not possible for it to be a name,
therefore, in the view that it is a name— [p. 187]— the injunction...

Because the meaning of *gaia* (the name) cannot be [independently] enjoined, the meaning of terms such as *udbhid* must be the object of injunction. If it is an object of injunction, then it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Regarding this, the Commentator has stated: “A certain portion of this [name] is an injunction, which enjoins—that is, makes known—a meaning not previously known, as in the case of ‘with Soma’ (*somena*)...”
"One should sacrifice with Soma. This [objection] challenges it: "But how can the injunctive statement 'one should sacrifice with Soma' be cited as an example?
The respondent says: "Or rather, why should it not be possible?"

The objector says: "In this case as well, there is no injunction of a sacrifice, because of the hearing of an accompanying word (*upapada*). The respondent says: "Let there be no injunction of a sacrifice; rather, a quality (*guṇa*) is being enjoined.
By that..."

With this intention, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated that the word [of the injunction] expresses the injunction (*vidhyuddeśapada*): "A certain part of this is the injunction. Now, it may be objected that even an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, because words such as *udbhid* are well-known as names of sacrifices (*yāganāmadheya*).
It is replied: for such renown exists in the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
This is called "established usage" (*prasiddhi*).

Furthermore, in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), the word *soma* and the word *udbhid* do not denote a sacrifice. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely the usage of ritualists (*yājñika*) is also nothing other than the usage of elders?"

For the ritualists have stated that words such as *udbhid* and others are denotative of rituals (*karma-vacana*). Therefore, their established usage (*prasiddhi*) is indeed an established fact. [Objection: If their status as denotative of rituals is well-known, why is there a cognition of a quality (*guṇa*)? [Response: He refutes this: that established usage is not [the true] established fact, because the usage of ritualists is preceded by worldly usage. For in the world...
The words *udbhid* and so forth are well-known as names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), whereas on the contrary, *udbhid* and the others are established as denoting distinct objects.
Because it is well known as a term for a spade, it is therefore an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).
188] "In the model sacrifice, the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the injunction of an accessory will be purposeful."
Thus, this commentary appears to be incorrect.
Why is it incorrect? The answer is: even in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the word "Jyotiṣṭoma" is itself injunctive; therein also—

For it has been stated that the meaning of the root *yaj* must be sought from elsewhere; thus, the portion of the text ending with the word "ābhāṣānta" [is established]. Who, moreover, has said that even there the meaning of *yaj* does not exist?

"If it is asked, 'Is it to be sought?'—if that were so, then an injunction there would not be possible. The respondent says: "In that case, the status of being the archetype for a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is indicated."

He explains this very point: what is meant is this—when the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" prescribes an accessory (guṇa), it presupposes that the accomplishment of the sacrifice has been established from another source; if that were not the case, then even this [injunction] would be untenable.
This is the meaning.

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," if that which is intended as the substratum for the prescription of the accessory (guṇa) called Soma— whether it be the Jyotiṣṭoma or a worldly sacrifice— is indeed the very basis for the prescriptions of accessories such as *udbhid* and others, then let those also be prescriptions of accessories. Furthermore, the word "prakṛti" [refers to] the original form in the context of a prescription of an accessory.
This is for the purpose of definition. Therefore, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the accepted archetype (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that wherever there is acceptance of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there too terms such as *udbhid* and others are also injunctions of qualities; that is, all injunctions of qualities should enjoin a quality. Now...

To the question, "Why does this not become an injunction of a qualified entity? he says: "The impossibility of an injunction of a qualified entity has already been stated. To the objection, "In that case, let it be a name," he says: "Furthermore, in the view that it is a name, the status of being the object of the *niyoga* (the mandate) is not possible through the root *yaj* (to sacrifice)."

Because the sacrifice (*yāga*), which is the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), has already been apprehended, what is the use of another name? To this he says: "By virtue of merely expressing that which has already been presented as the object to be enjoined, it does not assist the injunction. Now, one might object: "Even if it does not assist the injunction, what of it? To this he replies: "And its authority (*prāmāṇya*) [is established] by virtue of its being useful for the purpose of the injunction."
This has already been stated regarding the injunction (*codanā*).

Therefore, even in your position, validity must be sought through another means of knowledge; it is understood by means of another means of knowledge and is not obtained easily. In our position, however, even the meaning of the words is already well-established through the linguistic usage of elders.
In your view as well, validity is equal [to that of other means of knowledge], and invalidity is likewise equal;
the only difference is that you must resort to either a non-worldly power of words or else [accept] it as a mere name.
To this it is replied: as for what was stated—that this sentence is concerned with qualities—that is true;
however, regarding its application (*viniyoga*), it is perceived as such through an examination of that application, and no further expectation of an application need be entertained.
What then?
It depends upon an entity, because its object is an entity; and this is an entity.
"One should sacrifice. Therefore, this injunction has that [sacrifice] as its object.
And it is not the case that there exists an injunction regarding a specific [particular] object already established by another means of knowledge, such that—

By abandoning that [previous view], there would be an injunction of a purely new quality (*kevalaguṇavidhāna*). Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "It is a different ritual act from the Jyotiṣṭoma. That is incorrect; for there is no ritual act named "Jyotiṣṭoma" [as a distinct entity] such that one could say, "it is a different ritual act from the Jyotiṣṭoma. Anticipating this objection, he says: "It is a different ritual act from the Jyotiṣṭoma."
This is what is meant: it is established that Vedic ritual action is distinct from worldly action.

The term *jyotiṣṭoma* is intended as an illustration for the basis of injunctions regarding subsidiary elements (*guṇavidhi*). And the author of the Sūtras will demonstrate this in the statement: "From them, the action is understood."

Therefore, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) alone is the object of the injunction (*vidhi*). How then can there be a repetition of the scriptural statement for the sake of a subordinate element (*guṇa*), if the mandate (*niyoga*) has the meaning of the verbal root as its sole object? The answer is: it is intended to convey the attainment of the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*).
It is not intended as an injunction [of the act itself].

As for what was said regarding the repeated mention being for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*): the necessity of performing the act as delimited by the *homa* has already been established; however, its delimitation by the specific quality has not yet been established. Therefore, with the intention that only the quality is being enjoined, the repeated mention is directed toward the connection with the quality, by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not.

The meaning is "scriptural injunction" (*śruti*). Here he asks: Is it not the case that there is an injunction (*niyoga*) according to the application (*viniyoga*), such that the injunction is described with due regard for the application? The answer is: This is indeed the method of the author of the Sūtras; [the words] "those whose meaning is the action" (*bhāvārthāḥ karma-*)...

To those who recite [the rule], "from them the action should be understood," is this sūtra— which serves as a counter-argument to the application according to the specific assignment— [meant to be] a restatement of that very application?

The answer is: certainly; for otherwise, according to the principle of application (*yathāviniyoga*), the injunctions for the *śyena* sacrifice and others would result in being mere ritual acts, like the rule regarding the red garment (*raktapaṭanyāya*). And this has already been refuted on the grounds that [the Veda] does not have non-existence as its purpose.
In the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), what, then, is the foundation for this methodological approach? The answer is: comprehension itself (*avagati*).
We say that it is the root;
for it is understood that the injunction (*niyoga*) has as its object only the meaning of the verbal root.
"But surely, even in the case of application (*viniyoga*), there is indeed comprehension; therefore, its abandonment is also not proper. He replies:
"By whom was it said..."

There is no comprehension whatsoever of the *niyoga* [in that sense]. However, we have stated that what is understood is the "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) having the entity (*bhāva*) as its object; for the entity has the nature of a task (*kārya*), and the *niyoga* has the task as its object—this was stated regarding the object (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the "thing to be done" (*karaṇīya*): for what purpose is the understanding of its application (*viniyoga*) now required? The answer is: we say it is for the sake of the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*).

That entity which has become the object of the injunction is the meaning of that [injunction]. If the application (*viniyoga*) is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), then how is it said to be subordinate to a quality (*guṇa*)?
In this case as well, there would first of all be subordination to the action itself (*bhāva*). The answer is: because the action is already established (*prāptau satyām*).

The sentence has the quality (guṇa) as its primary referent. Now, it may be objected that when an accompanying word (*upapada*) is heard, the mere action (*bhāva*) cannot be understood as the object of the injunction, because it is understood as the object only as conjoined with a quality, as in the case of "the cloth becomes red."

It was stated in the second quarter (pāda) that it is not only the cloth that is perceived. He provides the resolution: "By whom was it said that the word for the entity alone attains the status of an object?
It was stated that this [entity] is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), not its subordinate element (*guṇa*). Nor is it...
An injunction whose object is an existing entity is obstructed by its connection with another word;
however, as in the case of "the red-robed one" (*raktapaṭa*), it is understood as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) alone. But how [is this so]?
Qualities such as *rudbhida* (wood-cutter), being existent, attain the status of qualifiers of an entity (*bhāva*),
by means of which that entity qualified by them is enjoined.

Thus it is said. He offers a rebuttal: Is the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) established solely by way of being a quality (*guṇatā*)? For if that were so, he would be stating that only a quality can function as a qualifier of a thing denoted by a negative term (*abhāvārtha*); however, even a name (*nāman*) [can serve as a qualifier].
The relationship between qualifier and qualified is indeed observed in such cases as "This Brāhmaṇa is Ḍittha" and "This Kṣatriya is Ḍabittha.
But how, then, is it understood that [the word] possesses the nature of a name (nāmatva) here?
The answer is: because of the understanding of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Since the words *udbhid* and so forth are understood to be in grammatical coreferentiality with the root *yaji* (to sacrifice), they are names (*nāmadheya*).
[This is] the understanding [of the meaning]. But how is there an understanding of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)?
The meaning is that its identity of referent with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is understood.

He provides the answer according to the view of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*): "Because of the mention of the third case [ending] for the root *yaj*. For the sense of the third case exists there; that [sense] is [conveyed] by this [word]."

"It is accomplished," thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, the instrumental case-ending is heard in the case of "Udbhid" and other such terms; therefore, it is understood that "one should bring about the *apūrva* by means of the sacrifice called Udbhid. The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) refutes this: "This is improper, for [the relationship] is not based on a common case-ending (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)."
It is not the case that co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in having the same grammatical ending; rather, co-referentiality is the basis for the comprehension of a single referent.

For in co-referentiality, it is said that there is a single referent, and this is not based on a single grammatical ending, but rather on the basis of having a single referent. For if it were based on a single grammatical ending...

In that case, there would be no connection between the action and both the substance and the quality— as in the expression "with a red, one-year-old cow"— but rather there would be only a mutual connection between them,
as in the case of "a blue lotus."

Just as there is a mutual relationship between "blue" and "lotus" in the expression *nīlotpalam*, so too [one might expect] such a relationship between "red" (*aruṇā*) and "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*); yet this is not accepted. Precisely because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not arise based on the use of a single case-ending, it is for this very reason that coreferentiality is not perceived in expressions such as *gauraśvaḥ puruṣo hastī* (cow, horse, man, elephant), even though they share a single case-ending.

To the question, "How then is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) understood in the case of 'This is Devadatta'? he says: "And this grammatical coreferentiality in 'This is Devadatta' is understood through the fact of having a single referent (*ekārthatā*); therefore, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not the cause of grammatical coreferentiality."
[This was] regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Now, he states [his] own view: "To this it is replied: because the object is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), the state of being something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) is understood as residing in the meaning of the root (*yajyartha*), not in the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāmārtha*); and this connection is indeed perceived."
Regarding the two cases of *udbhid* and *yāga*: if it is accepted that [the name] is based on a quality (*guṇanimittaka*),
then in the case of "the sacrifice is *udbhid*" (*udbhidā yāgaḥ*), the word *udbhid* is a reference [to the substance] with the suffix *-matup* elided.
It must be postulated.
The meaning is that the fault lies precisely in postulating an unmentioned possessive suffix (*matvartha*). However, if it is a name (*nāmadheya*), then [p.
The relationship is caused by another word that is not conceptually constructed;
and this relationship is established because of the connection with the same case-ending.

And it is for this very reason that the introduction of the third-case designation (*tṛtīyānideśa*) is presented in the Bhāṣya. The meaning is that if there were a designation with different case-endings, then there would be no syntactic connection by way of being a name (*nāmadheya*); yet such [a difference] does not exist, because of the designation with a single case-ending.
As for what was demonstrated regarding "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*), in that case both [the quality and the substance] possess a connection to the action (*bhāva*).

In this case, however, since no other distinct entity is heard, of what would the third case-ending express the relationship? [It expresses the relationship] with something else, because it denotes a state (bhāva).
Just as, for example, in the case of *aruṇā* and *ekahāyanī*, there is a distinct entity [the purchase].

The body [of the text] is heard; B. reads: "In this case, a new efficient force (*apūrvabhāvanā*) not already occupied by the meaning of the sacrifice is not perceived. Rather, a different meaning is heard; a new efficient force is perceived as already occupied by the meaning of the sacrifice. Therefore, the connection of 'udbhid' and the like is precisely with the meaning of the sacrifice. Consequently, this instrumental case-ending has as its sole result mere designation, since the object is already established by the word's denoting the sacrifice."

Because of that. [Objection: But surely, in the case of a mere indication, the nominative case alone should occur. [Response: That is an instruction regarding non-distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not an instruction regarding non-distinction from the meaning of the word (*pada*).
And the nominative occurs when there is non-distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem.

It is not non-distinct from the word-meaning (*padārtha*). And this non-distinction from the word-meaning is not a non-distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This is demonstrated by the example: "The Brahmin named Ḍittha has eaten. But [one might object]: since there is no comprehension of a single unified meaning, what will the case-ending (*vibhakti*) accomplish?

The word *udbhid* cannot denote the sacrifice itself; therefore, it is better to assume here merely the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*). Alternatively, both [the name and the accessory] may serve the purpose of an injunction, as in the case of the red one-year-old cow (*aruṇaikahāyanī*) which serves for the purpose of application. He refutes this: first of all, there is no status as an object of an injunction for both.
It has been stated that an injunction (*niyoga*) has action as its object; and since a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not denote an action,
it [cannot refer] to the meaning of a noun.

The direct status of being the object of an injunction is untenable. Here, an objection is raised: "Let it be that, through its connection with its constituent parts, the name denotes an action (*kārya*);
by means of that, its status as the object [of the injunction] is established. He refutes this: "It is true that, by virtue of the conventional meaning of its parts, the name denotes an action."

In the view that the name has a non-distinct meaning, since it is connected [to its referent] as a distinct word-meaning, who can deny its status as having an established meaning? And it has already been stated that having an established meaning is not the object of an injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, because it conforms to the connection with its constituent parts, it is established that the name has a non-distinct meaning.
And because it is non-distinct, the lack of contact with the injunction is avoided.
For in the sacrifice, the connection with the injunction is direct; likewise, for that which is its name, contact with the mandate is established by way of its meaning.

Now, it might be argued that since the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) conveys exactly the same meaning as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the latter lacks a distinct purpose and therefore cannot be a name. To this, he replies: This would indeed be so if the means of knowledge were to conform to the purpose.
But the purpose follows from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, even the fact that there is no purpose—which is derived from the *pramāṇa*—is not a fault. And this [assertion] is merely a concession (*abhyupagama*), because a purpose does indeed exist. Thus he says: "And the meaning of another sentence is seen..."
The names [of the sacrifices] possess a secondary meaning (*pāriśeṣya*).

Furthermore, the purpose of connecting qualities and results is observed even in other sentences; therefore, their lack of purpose is not at all established. Consequently, it is proven that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is independent [of other means of knowledge].

Regarding the statement that "in which there is an instruction on qualities," and the claim that "the name also will become meaningful through its connection with qualities and results"— considering that to be improper, the propriety [of our position] is established in a specific context. By this, the fault of lack of connection to the chapter (*adhyāya*) is addressed.
He offers a rebuttal: as to how it is unreasonable, that is now stated—first, for the purpose of connecting a quality (*guṇa*), it is said, "there are fifteen *ājyā* [stotras].
By means of the word *ājya*, having designated a specific stotra by its name, the quality of the number fifteen is enjoined therein. Therefore, by that connection with a quality—

The name [of the sacrifice] is meaningful because it serves to connect it with a result; for instance, in the statement, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," a connection with a result is established for the sacrifice under discussion by means of the word *citrā*, as in: "Curd, honey, ghee, water, parched grain, and rice—this mixture constitutes the offering to Prajāpati. Thus, the connection with the fruit is effected through the term *citrā* in reference to the sacrifice already in hand.

In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is as follows: It is indeed appropriate that [words] such as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" function as names, because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the root *yaj* ("to sacrifice"). Likewise, it is appropriate for *ājya* and so forth to function as names, because of their coreferentiality with the meaning of the verb "to praise" (*stu*), as in "they praise with the *ājyas*" and "they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*."

This is the state of being a name through praise. However, where grammatical coreferentiality with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is not perceived—as in the case of "the fifteen *ājya* [hymns]"—there is no comprehension that it is a name.
He asks: why? And says:

Even though the meaning is derivative (*anugata*), it is designated as a name because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for even those words such as *udbhid* and others possess a derivative meaning.
In those cases as well, the status of being a name was stated on account of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, such coreferentiality does not exist here;

for precisely because of the statement "the *ājyāni* [offerings] are fifteen," the word *ājya* does not possess the status of a ritual name. Therefore, [the term in question] is a name by way of its connection with a quality (*guṇopabandhena*).
It cannot be said that [the name] possesses meaning.
Here, an objection is raised: it is indeed appropriate that a name has meaning when it is connected with a quality (*guṇa*).
"It is not the case that there is no purposeful function"; for since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible when the fruit is connected [to the action],
why would there be no purposeful function when the word *yājin* is uttered?
It can be said [that this applies] to the statement, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā. He refutes this, saying:
"It is not purposeful."

It can be said that by the very word *yajeta* (one should sacrifice), which denotes the subject at hand, the connection of the fruit with the specific sacrifice is established; for why? He says: because in that case, the specific sacrifice is obtained simply through proximity (*sannidhāna*).
Not by name. Here, an objection is raised: let it be that there is no understanding of a specific sacrifice by way of its name; however, as for being a name—
It cannot be prevented because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He refutes this, saying: "And by whom was it stated that the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) is negated?"

"It is performed. The objection is simply that there is no purpose [for it]. But how can there be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhāna) in the case of "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā"?
The intention is this: even if there is no purpose, why should it not be a name (nāmadheya)?

It may be asked: "How is this an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi)? The answer is: "The injunction of a quality is as follows. For here, a specific sacrifice already known is enjoined for the sake of a fruit.
[Objection: "Let it be so; even then, what of it? He says: "For when the specific [sacrifice] is already known, [the role of] the other word—"
The understanding [of the term] does not result in a lack of distinction;
why? The answer is: precisely because it is already well-known—as in the expression "curd, honey, and ghee."

The sacrifice, which has been specifically determined from the sentence as "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*), has its specific form determined by the root *yaji* itself, which denotes the subject under discussion. For in a case where the meaning of an injunction is understood only through words connected to its own sentence— namely, through the understanding of the meanings of the words connected to its own injunctive sentence— it is from that very source that the specific [form] is determined.

[Page 201] The understanding [of the word's meaning] is as in "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. However, that which is already known from another sentence does not serve for its own comprehension within its own sentence; it is not a word to be understood through the words connected within its own sentence.
It requires syntactic connection (*anvaya*). And for that which does not require such connection, there can be no verbal co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*) are the causes of a relationship. In the case of "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*), the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) does not require a name for the sake of ascertaining its specific nature, because that specific nature is already ascertained from another sentence. Therefore, due to the absence of syntactic connection, it cannot be a name.

Therefore, in the case of the word "citrayā," variegatedness (citratva) is to be understood as that which is enjoined. To this, an objection is raised: "In those cases where the specific detail is understood from the accompanying word (upapada) itself, since that which is enjoined is not the subject under discussion, let there be the purpose of the name (nāmadheya) by virtue of its power."

Not at all, because of the understanding of a specific distinction. He refutes [the objection]: here, first of all, it has been stated that [the name] does not exist in an absolute sense. Furthermore, even when applied to something not under discussion (*aprakṛta*), the status of being a name (*nāmadheyatā*) is of no benefit.
Even if a sentence joined with a name not under discussion enjoins a sacrifice for the sake of a result, [it remains so].

Even in that case, there is no connection of the name by way of being a designation. Why? He says: because it is indeed another action (*karmāntara*), since the action is enjoined with respect to the fruit; and because the action is not previously mentioned (*aprakṛta*), it constitutes a different action. And in that regard, the meaning of the two words—
The injunction:

even by name, a similarity to the primary action is enjoined based on its auxiliary benefit. Even by means of a word denoting a verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), there is an injunction of a verbal root-meaning; thus the verbal root-meaning has been demonstrated, as shown in the case of "He performs the *agnihotra*" at the *Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*.
Therefore,

the name [of the mind] is not purposeful either by way of being connected to the fruit of the primary karma that has already arisen, or by way of being connected to the fruit of another karma that is currently arising. Consequently, it is appropriate that it be called "variegated" (*citrayā*).

This is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the animal sacrifice; in that case, this injunction of a quality must be inferred. Since clarified butter, vegetable offerings, milk-offerings (*sānnāyya*), and so forth lack variety, the requirement for further specification is not satisfied by the statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice."

Because of that [logical] reality, since it is impossible for it to form a single syntactical unit with that [other injunction], one must split the sentence; thus, the word *citrā* alone is for the purpose of enjoining a quality (*guṇavidhi*), while "one who desires cattle should sacrifice" (*yajeta paśukāmaḥ*) is the injunction of the fruit for the sacrifice already under discussion (*prakṛta*). Furthermore, the word *citrā* is extended (*utkṛṣṭa*) to apply to the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*).

It is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, in the case of "the Ājya-stotras are fifteen," it is an injunction of fifteen Ājya-hymns. Therefore, the statement that [the sentence] is purposeful by way of connecting an accessory with a result is incorrect.
To this, the reply is given: [In response, it is said: Here it is stated.
"This is not incorrect, for it is purposeful through its connection with the fruit of the qualities. Why is this so? He says: "Where another quality is enjoined," as for example:

In the case of the variegated [sacrifice], there is femininity, and likewise the number fifteen in the clarified butters; in that context, it is only as a name for an action already previously established that [the term] becomes meaningful. For a quality cannot be enjoined with respect to what is not an action, according to the stated principle that "the performance [of a ritual] is dependent [upon a prior injunction]."
For the prescription of a quality occurs through the prescription of an action that is already colored by qualities; therefore, there is no prescription of a quality in the case of a non-action.

Furthermore, an action is presented by its name, since the name possesses purposefulness through its connection with a quality. And because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), once the status of being a name is established for "ājyaiḥ stuvate" and so forth in another sentence, the statement "the ājyas are fifteen-fold" can indeed function in this way as well.

[A name] is intended to designate that which possesses the name. Therefore, it is logical that a name is meaningful through its connection with a quality. This is appropriate in the case of *ājya* and so forth, because two things cannot both be enjoined due to the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Since one must function as the subject (*uddeśaka*), and since the word *ājya* itself functions as the subject by virtue of denoting the substance of the ritual action.

The name possesses a meaningful referent; however, how can there be meaningfulness in the case of the word *citrayā*? For in that instance, the specific object is understood precisely because it is the subject under discussion.
It cannot be said that this [injunction] is devoid of purpose.

The answer is: certainly it can be so; for even in that case, if [the action] were not already produced, an injunction regarding its fruit would be untenable, because it would contradict the scriptural mention of a subordinate quality (guṇa).
He demonstrates this very point: because no distinction is perceived— that "this is for the sake of the fruit, not for the sake of a subordinate element"—
the hearing of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is solely for the purpose of connecting it with the fruit, not for the purpose of connecting it with a subordinate element.

No distinction is perceived; and when no distinction is perceived, there would be non-determination (anadhyavasāya), and from non-determination follows invalidity. That [objection] has been refuted by [establishing it as] a designation (nāmadheya).
Because the name is subject to being enjoined and because there is certainty regarding the connection with the fruit,

it is proper [to say] "by the *citrayā*. Here, the *pūrvapakṣa* commentary states, "And these are not etymological (*yaugika*)," which he [the author] challenges by [stating] their etymological nature— *yaugikatva*.
Where is the rejection [of the opponent's view] useful?

He provides the answer: this is the intended meaning—because if [the term] were etymological (yaugika), there would be the establishment of denoting the sacrifice under discussion, just as in the expression, "Give wages to the cook."
Even in the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word denoting a specific person, the establishment of the expression of the "cook" under discussion is achieved;

likewise here too, in the view that [the term] is etymological (*yaugika*), there would be the designation of the sacrifice under discussion, and consequently, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not tenable.
It is established. Therefore, it has been stated that these [words] are not derivative (*yaugika*).
Now, one might ask: even if they denote a genus (*jāti*), why do they not function as names (*nāman*)?
To this he says: "But when denoting a genus, there is only the state of being something to be enjoined (*vidheya-tā*)."

It is logical that it denotes the genus (*jāti*). For the denotation of an individual (*vyakti*) depends upon specific qualities (*viśeṣa*). Moreover, a word that denotes an individual cannot be etymologically derived (*ayaugika*). Thus, in the case of "citrayā," it refers merely to the quality (*guṇa*).
Because it is so designated, its status is equal to those words that denote a genus (jāti).

Therefore, this [word] also does not denote the primary subject matter (prakṛta). And in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Citrā," it is a reference (anuvāda) to a sacrifice because it is already known, and not an injunction (vidhi) of a sacrifice.
What is demonstrated by this commentary? The answer is:

the state of being devoid of expectancy (*anākāṅkṣitatva*). Because of the lack of expectancy on the part of the noun *citrapada*, since this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), its specific quality is already known.
A name does not require a specific cognition; and for that which is not so required, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Due to the absence of that [coreferentiality], it is not a name. Therefore, in the injunction of a result, its status as a name is not understood to be of assistance. Consequently, if one were to postulate a quality and a result, the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) would be rendered non-intentional.
What is it that this proponent (pūrvapakṣin), by speaking thus, intends to refute?

Is it not rather the very connection between the quality (guṇa) and the fruit (phala) that is being stated? That [connection] is certainly not what should be suspected; for what the proponent must establish is that the name has no meaningful purpose (arthavattā) through a connection with a quality and a fruit. That alone is what he should suspect, namely, that which would indeed provide the name with its meaningful purpose. And yet—

Even in the case of a connection between a quality and a fruit, there is meaningfulness for the name. Thus he says: "Because even in the connection between a quality and a fruit, the meaningfulness of the name does not arise through that very connection; on the contrary, this must be refuted by the proponent who asserts the meaningfulness of the name."
Therefore, this fragment of the commentary that has been revolving in the mind is indeed entirely irrelevant. The respondent says: "To this, it is replied" [p.
In the conceptualization of a quality and its fruit, it is indeed not possible to set it aside; therefore, the proponent refutes the connection between the quality and the fruit.

Why is it not possible to set it aside? He says: "It is possible. The answer is: because there is no intention to express (*avivakṣā*) the sacrifice (*yajati*). And when there is no intention to express, [the sacrifice] remains unsupported.
The meaning is "bhāva" (the action itself), and a quality (*guṇa*) that does not depend on the *bhāva*-action cannot be enjoined for the sake of a result.

Why, then, is the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) not intended [as the primary object]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the engagement [of the agent] in another way is the cause for the connection between the ritual act and the quality-result."

Since the action proceeds from something other than the injunction itself, the understanding arises that the fruit results from a subordinate element (guṇa) when it is not being enjoined. And there is no other motivator for the sacrifice (*yajña*) than the injunction for one desiring cattle; for nothing else has the power to motivate the performance of what constitutes the purpose of the sacrifice.
Therefore, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not intended to be emphasized [as the primary object of the injunction]. However, the word *citrā* is indeed connected with "one desiring cattle."
Therefore, as long as the connection with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*) is not abandoned, nothing remains of the word *citrā* except its status as a name (*nāmadheya*).

Consequently, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), even by resorting to the connection between the quality and the fruit (*guṇaphala-sambandha*) for the word *citrā*, absolutely rejects the connection with the desire for cattle. For he thinks:

If I were to absolutely exclude the connection of the word *citrā* with "one who desires cattle" even by means of a relationship between a quality (*guṇa*) and a result (*phala*), he [the opponent] would think as follows:

"If I admit the connection of the word *citrā* with 'one who desires cattle' even through a relationship between a quality and a result, then, since that [connection] is impossible, once it is rejected, the status of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) would be abandoned. Otherwise, because the words *citrā* and *paśukāma* [would remain], there could be no possibility of their forming a single sentence."

The word *citrayā* would thus result in being merely a name (*nāmadheya*). Therefore, by that very effort, I utterly reject the possibility of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) even through the connection of a quality with a fruit. Consequently, because there is no mutual expectancy between the two—the term "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*)—[the sentence cannot be a single syntactical unit].

In some cases, the word *citrā* should be understood as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) corresponding to a quality; since there is no connection between the meaning of the verbal root and the qualified agent, [the word] is not devoid of meaning.

The *pada* (the word "citrayā") is not required by the word expressing the desire for cattle (*paśukāmapada*). Nor is it required as a name (*nāmadheya*) by the sacrifice, whose specific nature is already known, for the sake of knowing its own particularity. This injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is to be understood only where this quality called "variegated" (*citrā*) is capable of being enjoined; it is not so elsewhere.

He also explains the Bhāṣya which supports the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "Even in the assumption of a quality-injunction (guṇavidhi), there is no recourse to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). For it has been stated that the defect in resorting to figurative indication is that the meaning would then become cognizable through another means of knowledge (pramāṇāntara).
Indeed, having understood the object through another means of knowledge and having ascertained the intended meaning (tātparya) therein, [one proceeds].

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs everywhere, and that is a great defect in the Veda; for it would entail that the mantras, the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), and the injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśas*) depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Furthermore, it has been stated that this [indication] is not present here either, due to the absence of a connection between words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For in the case of "udabhidet," indeed—

If it were a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by resorting to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice, then the fault of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) would have been stated. However, in this case, there is no prescription of a quality by resorting to coreferentiality; rather, it is precisely through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in: "That which one should sacrifice with a *paśu*—that [sacrifice] should be variegated. Therefore, since there is no fault of possessive indication, it is established that this is a prescription of a quality.

Therefore, it is established that [the name] is meaningful through its connection with the fruit of the qualities; this is stated [by the opponent]: "In this case, an injunction of qualities is not possible, for when there is an injunction of the meaning of a name, the object [already] established..."

Since an injunction [of a quality] is impossible by itself, its injunction occurs through its entry into the action; however, the meaning is that the quality itself is not enjoined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) for its own sake. What follows from this? This results: wherever this injunction of a quality is established, it must be enjoined there as something serving the purpose of the ritual action (*karmaupayikatā*).

The quality [of being variegated] is prescribed for the animal, because such variegation is possible in the case of an animal. Even if this be so, what follows? To this he says: "In that case, when variegation is being prescribed..."
Another quality of this animal must be prescribed, namely its being a ewe (*svītvam*).
Consequently, even if there were a displacement [of the quality], there would be another syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, if—[p.
In the case of the Sārasvatī [offering],

even if there were no injunction regarding its femininity— or whether it were enjoined or not— the connection with the term "desiring cattle" (paśukāma), which is understood [from the context], would have to be abandoned; furthermore,
the attainment of the qualities belonging to the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] would have to be set aside in the Sārasvatī.

For in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, a specific color is fixed; that [color], having been extended by analogy (atideśa), must be set aside. Therefore, because a syntactical split (vākyabheda) is inevitable, this [injunction] applies to the Agniṣomīya—which serves as the archetype (prakṛti) for all sacrifices performed with living beings as the material—since its connection to its own sentence has already been rejected.
In that case, both the quality of being variegated (*citratva*) and the quality of being female (*strītva*) would have to be enjoined again after having already been obtained;

consequently, there would again be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible. Hence, it is logical to assume that this [sentence] serves as the basis for the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) of what is perceived as connected with what is not perceived. And that [unity] here cannot exist without the two names.
Thus it has been stated. Therefore, its status as a name is established.
By this, it is also demonstrated that [the passage] possesses purpose through its connection with a fruit.

For if it were a subordinate quality (guṇa), there would be uncertainty as to whether this sentence is intended for the purpose of connecting a quality or for the purpose of connecting a fruit; such uncertainty is avoided by its being a name.

That this is refuted has already been shown. Likewise, in the view that "there are fifteen *ājya* offerings" constitutes an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), there would be the injunction of two qualities, because both the number and the *ājya* offerings would be enjoined; and that is not possible because of the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore, one word within the mantra must be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the indicator [of the action]. And that [word] refers to the ritual act...

[It is] related. Therefore, it is logical that the word *ājya* itself—which denotes the ritual action already established in another sentence—is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, the mutual—

The comprehension of the relationship is not abandoned here, as in the case of the statement, "There are fifteen *ājya* [chants] here. Furthermore, what was said—that even in the view that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is also incorrect. Why? Because wherever the *ājyas* are enjoined by the words "there are *ājyas*," that [sentence] must be expressed with the verb *bhavati*.

Therefore, the meaning is that the hymns (stotra) come to possess clarified butter (ājya). For this reason as well, they come to possess clarified butter here; that indeed is the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). As for what was stated—that the status of being a name for the ritual action is unestablished—that is established because it serves as a characteristic mark (lakṣaṇa) of the action.

Since the word *ājya* denotes the ritual action (*karman*), its status as a name for that action is established; furthermore, the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists everywhere, as seen in such passages as "when they went toward the race" (*yad ājim īyuḥ*). Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya has raised an objection: "Why then are the *ājyas*, qualified by the number fifteen, not enjoined in connection with the hymns (*stotra*)?"
B. adds "ājyānīti" [p.
209], and this he objects to: what has been set forth by this that remains unrefuted?
The answer: This has been proposed.
[The objection is that] while the meaning of two words is established elsewhere, here the meaning of another word is also being enjoined. What will happen as a result of this?
The answer is: the intention is that there is no repetition of the sentence.

Since the two word-meanings, existing in a state of mutual qualifier-qualified relationship, are enjoined by this single injunction, there is no further operation; thus, there is no repetition (*anāvṛtti*). Of this...
The commentary on the rebuttal of the objection states: "Because there is no word that denotes [things] as qualified.
He explains this:
"In this way, it is indeed established."
If the meaning of both words were to be enjoined by a single injunction, then their relationship would have to be established prior to that injunction—just as in the case of "Agni Pāvaka.
Just as the quality of being "pāvaka" (purifying) is already established for Agni prior to its formal injunction, so too [would it be here]. But this is not the case.

[210] Likewise, in this case, it is established that there are exactly fifteen *ājya* [stotras], as stated by B. Therefore, he says: "But that [number] does not exist [as a separate entity]. Consequently, the connection between these two is based solely on the injunction (*vidhi*) and its subject matter (*uddeśa*). Thus, it is impossible for the meaning of both words to be the object of an injunction (*vidheya*).
Now, why is it that an injunction for two things that are unrelated— such as Agni and Prajāpati— is not possible?
Just as in the Agnihotra sacrifice,
by the injunction "to Agni and to Prajāpati," there is an injunction for Agni and Prajāpati, who are mutually unrelated, by means of a single injunction, so too here.

The meaning is: why does it not occur? B. The answer: It does not avoid [the objection]; this application of two unrelated things is not possible because it is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it must be accepted as being caused solely by the statement of an injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*).
Consequently, it is established that even this is a name (*nāmadheya*).
"And another scripture is like that. But by what distinction is this section commenced here to remove the suspicion that it might be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)?
