The answer is: because there is no implication of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible even through an injunction of a subordinate quality.

[The opponent’s] position: This term *agnihotram* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, even without the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of possessive meaning (*matvartha*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established.

Because of this specific feature, there is a suspicion here that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). And this has been demonstrated: "In this [act], there is an offering (*hotra*) to Agni."
"‘This is the agnihotra’—this compound (B.

& C. is indeed expressive of the *homa* (oblation), because the *homa* itself is the meaning of the other member [of the compound]. Even by means of enjoining a subordinate sense, there is a quality..."

An injunction indeed occurs, as in the case of "the priests wear golden garlands. Therefore, in this instance, Agni, though functioning as a subordinate element (*upasarjanībhūta*), is enjoined as the deity.
It is reasonable that in "he offers the *agnihotra*," there is an injunction of a subsidiary quality (*guṇavidhāna*). But as for "he pours the *āghāra* libation" (*āghāramāghārayati*)...
How so?
The answer is: there is no purpose here for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), nor is it even perceived here that [the word] expresses an object of action (karman).
Thus, this is indeed an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).

The word *āghāra* does not denote an action, but rather refers to the substance to be poured; its preparation (*saṃskāra*), namely the act of pouring (*āghāraṇa*), is enjoined as an accessory. This very point is stated: "where the substance to be poured..."

In that very context of the *upāṃśuyāja*, this pouring (*āghāraṇa*) is prescribed. But surely, since a sacrifice whose substance is to be poured is accomplished in the *āhavanīya* fire, it already possesses the act of pouring (*āghāra*) by necessity;
for all sacrifices (*yajatis*) are performed while standing, are accomplished in the *āhavanīya*, and the term "offering" (*homa*) refers to the action of pouring a long stream [of clarified butter].

[Objection: Since [the act of pouring] is already established in a sacrifice where the substance for the *āghāra* is prescribed, what is the purpose of enjoining the *āghāra*? [Response: Because an injunction has the function of bringing about what has not yet been established. The answer is: this is a distinct *āghāra* from the *homa-āghāra*;
it is a further refinement of the substance intended for the purpose of refining that substance—this is the intended meaning.

Since an injunction brings about what has not yet been attained, it functions as the object (*karman*); and for one who considers the word *āghāra* to be formed with the suffix *-ghañ* according to the rule "the suffix *-ghañ* occurs after a root when the agent is not the subject and when it denotes a name," it follows that this very act of pouring (*āghārya*) is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), and for that very reason, it applies to the *upāṃśuyāja*.
It has been demonstrated that this is an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

Therefore, in this example, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based solely on the fact that it does not denote an action (*akarmavacanatva*). However, in the case of the *agnihotra*, even though it denotes an action (*karmavacanatva*), [the same conclusion holds].
It has been stated that the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) is not contradicted because there is no need for a secondary indication (matvarthalakṣaṇā).
To this it is replied: here an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, because the qualities are already established. He explains this very point:

those qualities which are presented here as things to be enjoined are obtained from another source. First, as for Agni, [he is obtained] from the passage beginning with "And to Agni and Prajāpati... and so forth.

Since this [meaning] is already obtained from the sentence "and," it is not something to be enjoined; therefore, the word *agnihotra* is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), but rather a name (*nāmadheya*).
One performs the pouring continuously, one pours straight— based on such statements as these.

But surely, since these sentences are intended to enjoin continuity and other qualities by referring back to the act of pouring (*āghāraṇa*) through the word "he pours" (*āghārayati*), how can the pouring itself be established from them?

Now, it might be argued that the sentences concerning "continuity" (*santata*) and so forth enjoin the *āghāra* (sprinkling) as qualified by continuity. That is not so; for, as in the case of "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), those [sentences] recited in proximity to the injunction for the *āghāra* are understood to have the purpose of enjoining a subsidiary quality (*guṇa*). To this it is replied: first of all, the futility of the injunction for the *āghāra* itself is unavoidable. For instance, let that [injunction] be absent; in its absence, the sentences concerning continuity and so forth would themselves be the enjoiners of the qualified *āghāra*.

[The sentence] "Let them be" is not an injunction (*vidhi*). Nor should it be argued that if sentences concerning the *santati* (continuity) and so forth were intended as general injunctions, a distinction [between acts] would result;

for no distinction is perceived among subsidiary acts (*guṇakarman*) when there is no difference in their purpose, as is the case with the purchase of *soma*. The statement "He offers the *agnihotra*" serves this purpose: if sentences such as "He offers with curd" were injunctions of distinct qualified acts, it would entail a distinction [between the primary act and these], which is not the case. Furthermore, since meaningfulness is possible...
Therefore, its meaninglessness is logical. However, the sentence "He pours the *āghāra* libation" possesses purposefulness by virtue of enjoining a sacrifice (*yāga*).

For if that were not the case, then the sentences concerning continuity (*santata*) and so forth would merely be injunctions regarding continuity and the like for the *upāṃśuyāja* itself. But since this status as an injunction of a sacrifice is established, [the sentences in question serve to qualify it].

In that very context which prescribes the sacrifice (*yāga*), since the *āghāra* (sprinkling) is already established as having clarified butter (*ājya*) as its substance, these sentences—such as "continuously" (*sāntatyādi*)—are intended to enjoin specific qualities (*guṇa*) based on that established *āghāra*. However, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) has here raised a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by assuming an injunction of the substance itself; he then establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) because the substance is already obtained through the phrase "fourfold-drawn" (*caturgṛhīta*). In that regard, how [is it so] in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*, given the statement: "This [butter] is indeed fourfold-drawn"?

There is no injunction for clarified butter (*ājya*), for the *upāṃśuyāja* cannot be designated by the word "āghāra. If it were called "āghāra" because it consists of a substance poured as an oblation (*āghārya-dravyaka*), a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*) would result. It is replied: by the statement "this is indeed fourfold-drawn (*caturgṛhīta*)," it is taught that one should perform the rite with fourfold-drawn clarified butter. And since that [rite] lacks a specific substance [of its own], it remains established as the *upāṃśuyāja* itself. And of that, the clarified butter—

Since it possesses the nature of a substance (*dravyakatva*), the word *āghāra* is merely a restatement of what is already established by the sense of the matter; thus, there is no fault. And this has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya as follows:

"Even if the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is argued on the basis of an injunction regarding the substance or an injunction regarding the refinement of the substance used for the pouring (*āghāraṇa*), nevertheless, because an injunction is possible through another scriptural authority, the injunction [of the word itself] would be untenable; therefore, it is a name (*nāmadheya*). He now raises an objection against this very conclusion: "What is this—"
"What is meant by 'connected'? The proponent asks. "What is it that is disconnected here?
The objector says: "This is what is disconnected here:
that it should be stated as an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the case of the ladle-oblation (*darvihoma*)."

The proponent [of the prima facie view] has stated that the injunction "to Agni and to Prajāpati" applies to the *darvihoma*, and likewise, the pouring of the *āghāra* oblation applies to the *upāṃśuyāja*. Furthermore, [the proponent has argued that] the continuous [pouring] and other such features do not apply to the *upāṃśu*...
In the *śūyāja*, there are injunctions of subsidiary qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
He concludes: "This appears like the word 'ether' (*viyat*)."

He composes [the following]: "To this we reply: under the view that this is an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), this injunction—'one offers the Agnihotra'—applies only to the *darvihoma*. Likewise, it applies to the *upāṃśuyāja* and the *āghāra*."

The meaning is that the statement "he pours the *āghāra* oblation" implies that, failing to find a proximate substrate, the injunction regarding the deity—"to Agni"—and the injunction regarding continuity—"he pours the *āghāra* continuously"—both apply to the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. Consequently, since these two [rites] are already enjoined by those [injunctions], it is not possible for the terms "Agnihotra" and "*āghāra*" to be injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*); thus, what was stated is indeed consistent. It is with this very intention that [the author] has spoken, without having realized this point.

He objects: "In that case, being named after it (*tatprakhyatā*) is not the reason for the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), because [in the case of] the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*, there is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhāna*).

And here, in the phrase 'what to Agni,' there is an absence of proximity (*sannidhāna*). If the injunction of an accessory had been suspected to occur in its own place, then it would have occurred right there."

The principle of "being designated by that" (*tatprakhya*) would be the reason for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) due to the proximity of passages such as "that which [is offered] to Agni. However, in the case of the *darvihoma* and the *upāṃśuyāja*, since there is a suspicion that they are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*), and because passages such as "that which [is offered] to Agni" are not proximate there, it is impossible to demonstrate that "there is another scriptural authority designating that. The respondent says: "Certainly, it is a reason for the final conclusion. How so? The answer is: "Even the principle of being designated by that (*tatprakhyatā*) [applies]."
For this is indeed a *darvihoma* sacrifice.
In that view, even the injunction "to Agni" is a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*), because it depends upon the context.
In that very case, it occurs just as in the statement "he performs the Agnihotra.

Just as, under the view that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), the sentence "he performs the Agnihotra" extends to the Darvihoma by virtue of its dependence on a common [element], so too does the phrase "that which is for Agni" [extend]. Likewise, the statement "he continuously pours the libation" [extends] to the Upāṃśuyāja.
Thus, because the injunctions for consecrations depend upon a substance that serves a purpose— just as in the case of "he pours the Āghāra libation"— [the opponent] objects:

"If, then, because of the existence of other scriptural texts that indicate that [name], there is no injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) in the case of the *darvihoma* or the *upāṃśuyāja*, then their status as names would also apply only to those very *darvihomas* and the *upāṃśuyāja*. He refutes this: "The gods do not know what has not been established [by scripture]."

"Priyaḥ" means one who is ignorant of logic (*nyāyānabhijña*). Since the prescription of qualities is established from another source, and because a name cannot be the object of a prescription— as stated in the rule "vidhāne siddhenāmnaśca" and so forth—
since the meaning of the verb is what is prescribed in the sentence "agnihotraṃ juhoti," what else could be understood from this statement?

When the status of being an injunction of qualities has been refuted, then it must be an injunction of ritual action (karma-vidhi). And once the meaning of the verb has been enjoined, this [phrase] "to Agni and to Prajāpati" remains applicable solely to that context, by virtue of the subject matter (prakaraṇa).

And thus, by that very connection with the quality, this name also belongs to that same other action which is enjoined by this rule. As it has been said: "Therefore, it is established that this is the name of this [action] alone. In this way, when the injunction of a quality in the form "one pours the libation" (āghārayati) is ruled out, what else could the injunction enjoin other than the meaning of the verbal root?
He alone is capable; that very thing to be enjoined is the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha),
because of the connection between the substance and the deity, just like the root *harati* [is related to its object], so too is *yajati*.

Just as in the case of the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastarapraharaṇa*), there is the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) due to the connection between the substance and the deity, so too the pouring of the libation (*āghāraṇa*) is indeed a sacrifice. Therefore, qualities such as "continuous" (*santata*) and so forth also belong to that very [act]. Consequently, this term *āghāra* [also] refers to the sacrifice.
It is established that this refers to the name of that very [substance].

This being the case, what is the meaning of the expression "he pours the āghāra continuously"? The meaning is that he brings about the āghāra continuously. But if the injunction of the deity is expressed by the words "to Agni," then how is there no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here?
Because, insofar as [the text says] "to Agni and to Prajāpati," multiple qualities in the form of Agni and Prajāpati are enjoined.
It must indeed be understood that there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
He refutes this: "There is no syntactical split known as the injunction of multiple qualities when there is the injunction of qualifiers for a single factor (*kāraka*).
This is the meaning.

For here, since Agni and Prajāpati are construed as qualifiers of a single factor called the deity, there is no injunction of multiple qualities regarding Prajāpati; how, then, could there be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)? Indeed, it is the injunction of another related entity that is termed "multiple qualities," not the injunction of another substance.

For where there is the injunction of multiple related factors for an action that is not itself previously connected to an action, there is the injunction of multiple qualities (*anekaguṇavidhāna*). On the other hand, where only a single factor related to the action is enjoined—provided that it is based on a single substance—it is the meaning of that very factor as being endowed with multiple substances; in such a case, there is no injunction of multiple qualities.

It is indeed so. Here, Agni and Prajāpati are taken as the substrata of the deity (*devatā*), not as the deity itself. And it is the deity as connected to the ritual action that is enjoined in connection with the action, not the substratum of the deity. Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Even so, the deity’s connection to the ritual action occurs through each of the substrata individually.
The recurrence of the ritual action is also justified by the statement "it will arise"; thus, this constitutes a single treatise. And because of the word "and" (*ca*), it is faultless.
Furthermore, there is its designation.
In this regard, the Commentator [Śabara] maintains that only the words *śyena*, *iṣu*, and *saṃdaṃśa* are names [of sacrifices].
He establishes [the point]. Fearing that someone here, being focused solely on the examples, might fail to grasp that *ājya* and the like are indeed non-examples, he says:

"In this context, the conventional (*rūḍhi*) words such as *śyena*, *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and so forth, are the examples. But what is the distinction between this section and the section concerning *udbhid*, by virtue of which this section [is distinct]?

The objection has been raised: "Just as in that case [the *agni* sacrifice] the status of being a name for the ritual action was asserted to avoid the fault of *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication of possessive meaning), so too here it is certainly possible to maintain the position that it is a name. The reply is:
"There is this distinction: in the case of a ritual action, [the application of the name] must conform to the grounds for its usage (*pravṛttinimitta*)."
"Etymological derivation (*yoga*) does not, however, follow established usage (*rūḍhi*).

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding these words such as *ājyapṛṣṭha* and others, if they are taken as names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), their etymological nature must be asserted; if they are taken as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), they possess established usage. And established usage [prevails] over that which is etymological.

The conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger because the etymological meaning (*yaugika*), by virtue of following its constituent parts, is dependent, whereas the conventional meaning is independent. Therefore, rather than relying on the conventional meaning, it is better to assume a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); thus, the status of this as a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is again raised here, and so this is treated together with the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa*.

This is the distinction: since words such as *udbhid* and others are etymological (*yaugika*) in both positions, how then is the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) reached? It is said: because the sentence is intent upon enjoining an action, it is improper to enjoin the meaning of the subordinate term (*upapada*). As for the fact that in some cases an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) is nevertheless resorted to, that is because the connection with another word has no other possible recourse. However, where there is an available, albeit delayed, etymological derivation, there [an injunction of a qualified entity] does not occur.

The injunction of an action qualified by a quality is established by resorting to the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Here, he raises an objection regarding this specific example:

"Even under the view that [the term] is a name (*nāmadheya*), it is not necessary to assume a conformity with etymological derivation (*yogānuvartitva*) for the word *śyena*. Rather, even on the view that it is the name of an action, one must accept a figurative designation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*), namely, 'it is called *śyena* because it is like a hawk (*śyena iva śyenaḥ*). And conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not preclude figurative usage. Rūḍhi—

Because the secondary designation (gauṇābhidhāna) is based on a primary cause, the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* is therefore without proof; thus, there is no possibility of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in that regard, and it is better to simply accept the secondary nature [of the term].
He [the author] refutes this: "In order to remove this very ignorance, the venerable Author of the Commentary [has said] this—"
It was cited with joy.

Precisely because a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is difficult to find in this example, for that very reason the Commentator has cited only those examples among all conventional (*rūḍhi*) words where, even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the status of being a convention is not lost. [Regarding] the prima facie arguments—
Someone might think, out of a sense of partiality, that this is not a valid example. To show how the prima facie argument stands here, he demonstrates it as follows:

"It is proper to say that in the case of words such as *udbhid*, they are names because they rely on etymological derivation (*yoga*) for fear of dropping the possessive suffix *-matup*; however, this does not entail the abandonment of conventional (*rūḍhi*) words."
Resorting to another elision out of fear of an elision—

such as resorting to the elision of the suffix *vati* in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice out of fear of the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*— is not appropriate under the view that the term is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).

For the application of figurative (guṇa) terms occurs through the elision [of a suffix]. Therefore, it is better to resort to the elision of the *matup* suffix itself, because [this] conforms to the syntactical connection with the literal meaning heard [in the text]. In the view that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), the literal meaning of the word *śyena* itself becomes connected with the ritual action.

A. reads "na tu" instead of "tenatena," [arguing that] even when the possessive suffix *matup* is elided, the connection of the literal meaning still occurs; therefore, that [literal sense] alone is appropriate. However, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is raised again, stating that in the case of a secondary (gauṇa) sense, there is no connection of the literal meaning with the object, and thus it is weak. He states the final established conclusion (rāddhānta), which applies to all examples: It is said in reply—
It was stated that [the primary sense] follows [the secondary].

The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) says: "Just as the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) does not follow the etymological derivation (yoga), so too the etymological derivation does not [necessarily] follow the conventional meaning."
It does not follow established convention at all.
Therefore, what is the distinction of convention if there is no mutual following? He reveals the intention of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
"But here..."
An established usage (*rūḍhi*) that has operated previously prevails over etymological derivation (*yoga*) due to its independence.
The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) states his own position:
"It is true that established usage would prevail over etymological derivation, provided that the meaning of the sentence were preceded by the comprehension of the etymological cause."

If it were to be understood [in that way], then, because the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is stronger at the stage of the primary cause (*nimitta*), there would be a subversion of the connection (*yoga*); that is, the etymological connection would be abandoned. However, if the status of being a primary cause is preceded by the comprehension of the effect, then— [p.

Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not override etymological derivation (*yoga*). When one understands the function of a sentence, the comprehension of that function resides solely in the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). When one ceases [from the primary action] and proceeds to follow the causal factors (*nimitta*), then, because the sentence has a single purpose, only the meaning of the verbal root is to be enjoined; for if one were to resort to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple meanings. In that case, when considering how a single purpose can be accomplished, one must rely on etymological derivation alone; therefore, it is not [the conventional sense].

By convention, the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is set aside. Now, even though the sentence is intent upon enjoining a single thing, why is it that it has as its sole purpose the injunction of a mere accessory (*guṇa*)? He says "no":

the comprehension of the task (*kārya*) is dependent on both that which possesses the sense of "being" (*bhāvārtha*) and that which does not possess the sense of "being" (*abhāvārtha*); since the object of an injunction exists only when there is the sense of "being," an injunction is not possible in respect of a pure accessory alone.

Therefore, because it is more consistent with the understanding of the effect residing in the meaning of the word *bhāva*, yoga is apprehended first; thus, even in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is not accepted for this reason.

For the etymological nature of words such as *ājya* has been demonstrated in passages such as, "Because they went toward the race (*ājim īyuḥ*), that is the reason for the *ājya*s being called *ājya*s.
Otherwise, the statement regarding their etymological nature in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) would be groundless. In this regard—
He objects: "It is appropriate that [the term] *ājya* and so forth function as names, but how can *śyena* be a name? The intention of the questioner is this:
[regarding] the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)...

For the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) arises through the instrumentality [of the word]. And the word *śyena*, which denotes the *śyena* species, cannot have grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) even in a figurative sense. However, for words such as *ājya* and others, which are etymological (*yaugika*), the status of being a name is indeed established because of their coreferentiality. The subsequent [point] follows from coreferentiality.

Even in the case of "śyena," it is a name. Now, one might object that there is no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) at all; to this he replies: for coreferentiality remains uncontradicted even in figurative designations, because the meaning of the suffix -vat is what is being enjoined.

For if the meaning of the suffix -vat were not that which is to be enjoined, then, because it would be directed toward that [suffix], there would be no dependence on the verb; consequently, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would not occur. But when the meaning of the suffix -vat is not—

However, when it is the object of an injunction, that [word] serves merely as the ground for engagement in the action; thus, because it is subordinate to the action, it becomes a name (*nāmadheya*) when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

On the other hand, if the possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided, the state of having different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*) is unavoidable, because the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is what is being enjoined, whereas the action itself is the object of the injunction.
Therefore—

Since it is better to assume the elision of the suffix *vat*— as there would be a contradiction in understanding a single meaning from a word that prescribes multiple meanings— it is established that the word *śyena* is also a name (*nāmadheya*), rather than being a case of eliding the possessive suffix *matup*.
[The conclusion follows] from the hearing of the qualities in the name. For what purpose is this section?

This section would exist for the purpose of refuting [the view] if it were even possible that this were an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). But that is not possible; because for those [words] which are established by convention (*rūḍhi*) upon meanings already obtained through their etymological derivation (*yaugika*), [an injunction of qualities is impossible].

The status of being a name (*nāmatva*) has been established. Furthermore, it is possible to assert that [the term *vājapeya*] is a name based on the mention of that [sacrifice] in the *vājapeya*, because of the injunction for the *surā* cup-offering. *Surā* would be of the nature of a drink, since it is enjoined; and *vāja* is of the nature of a drink, since it is enjoined. He states the refutation: "This section, during the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), implies all names."
To the question "Why?", he says: because of the presentation of the mention of the sacrifice by way of *tantra*.
By means of *tantra*, the sacrifice offers its own purpose toward both the result and the accessory.

[Objection: But surely, due to the consequence of requiring mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), one must abandon the designation as a *tantra* (a single word serving multiple functions). To this, he replies: Even in the case of the *tantra*-designation, there is indeed no dependence of the word, because both the status of being that which is enjoined (*vidheya*) and the status of being the subject of reference (*uddeśyatva*) are understood from a single utterance; for it is possible for that very thing being enjoined to simultaneously possess the status of being the subject of reference.

Since it is impossible for there to be an expectation of another substratum (*āśrayāntarāpekṣā*) when a quality (*guṇa*) is being enjoined, the designation [of the name] as such cannot be maintained. Therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to refute the theory of the simultaneous denotation of both [the substance and the quality] (*tantrābhidhāna*). If that is so, then *udbhid* and the others are indeed examples here; consequently, from among the examples—
The sense is that the internal assumption (*antaropādāna*) would be useless. He refutes this: "Certainly, *udbhid* and others are also examples here. The objector asks:
"Why, then, was only 'one desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya' cited as an example?"
He refutes this: this objection is like that regarding the word *śiṃśipā*. For even among the examples cited, such as *udbhid* and others, one could ask why specifically *udbhid* is cited.
Therefore, this objection which we raise is indeed not to be challenged. And he states another solution: "A certain distinction can also be stated here—that it is because the two actions are equal."
By this sūtra, the mention of the *dīkṣā*, *upasad*, and so forth is indeed contained within the Vājapeya;
therefore, the Vājapeya was cited there in order to demonstrate the reason for its superiority.

Now, if this is the case, one might object that according to the evidence of the scriptural passage (*darśana*), the Vājapeya alone must be intended by the author of the sūtra as the illustrative example; to this, he says:
Moreover, that perception is indeed for all purposes;

since perception preceded by reasoning is perception, and reasoning is the same everywhere, perception as well is again for all purposes. For this very reason, this section is meaningful because it refutes the designation of a "system" (tantra). Therefore, this is stated:
In this case, the position that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is indeed superior.

Why is it superior? To this he says: for in this way, the word-meaning such as *udbhid* becomes something connected with the action to be performed (*kāryānvayin*). On the other hand, under the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), the word-meaning would be merely the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Why? The answer [p.
because of that which has been prescribed.

In the view that [the term *udbhid*] is the name of the ritual action (*karman*), "being an *udbhid*" means being denotable by the word *udbhid*, but it does not mean the prescription (*vidhāna*) of the *udbhid* itself. Therefore, in the view that it is a name, there is the mention of a basis for application (*nimitta-upādāna*) which is not the cause of engagement; whereas the sentence serves the purpose of bringing about engagement.
There would be a lack of consistency between the effect and its cause;
for the effect would consist of activity, while the cause would consist of name, resulting in a contradiction.

However, under the view that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), that contradiction does not exist; therefore, the injunction of a subordinate quality is superior. But [an objection may be raised]:

It was stated in the *Udbhid-ādhikaraṇa* that, under the view that [the word] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), one must resort to a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) which is not the literal meaning of the word. He refutes this by saying: "That very [indication] does not exist."
How is it that it does not exist? The answer is: for even in the case of a causal relationship, the meaning of the verb is understood as having a single form. When...

When [the meaning] is understood as an effect, and when it is understood as a cause, then the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha) is understood in only one form; for it is only while being that which is to be accomplished (sādhyamāna) that the meaning of the verbal suffix becomes the means (sādhana). When both are understood, why resort to the figurative indication of possession (matvarthalakṣaṇā)?

Because the relationship is understood through a relation between different substrata: "By means of the *udbhid*, a sacrifice is to be performed; and by that sacrifice, cattle [are obtained]. Therefore, this meaning is established:
"By means of the *vājapeya*, a sacrifice [is performed]; by means of that sacrifice, self-sovereignty [is attained]."

There is no indication by implication (lakṣaṇā) of a possessive sense (*matvartha*). To the objection that this being the case, there would clearly be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), he replies: "The expression is otherwise because of what is observed."

In ultimate reality, however, that which possesses the nature of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is expressed all at once by the verb. Thus it is said: "In the comprehension of the word's meaning, there is no perception of distinction. But surely this is a property of the thing itself?

For it is only while being accomplished that something becomes a means; thus, the word "sovereignty through sacrifice" does not denote a property of the word itself. The meaning is that a word is incapable of denoting both forms [of object and means] simultaneously. Otherwise, the word would cause one to understand [the sacrifice] solely as that which is to be enjoined.
And otherwise, it would be [the object] by virtue of being the intended referent.
He refutes this: "True; however, because it possesses both forms, it is denotable in that way.
Even when both are denoted, the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is capable of presenting the two related entities.

Because it possesses both forms; that is, because the sacrifice possesses the form of both the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it is denoted by the word exactly as it is. Even though it is denoted as possessing both forms, nevertheless, regarding the two related factors—the result (*phala*) and the quality (*guṇa*)— [The sentence continues: ...the result is not enjoined with respect to the quality. Why? Because the result is not intended to be enjoined. For the result is not enjoined with respect to the quality; rather, the quality is enjoined with respect to the result. Why? Because the result is intended to be enjoined. It is the result that is intended to be enjoined, not the quality. For the purpose of the result is to be achieved, not for the sake of the quality. Therefore, the result is not enjoined with respect to the quality. But how is the quality enjoined? It is enjoined with respect to the result. How so? By means of the sacrifice. How so? Because the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Since the sacrifice is the instrument, it is the sacrifice that is enjoined with respect to the result. And since the sacrifice is enjoined with respect to the result, the quality is enjoined with respect to the sacrifice. Thus, the quality is enjoined with respect to the result by means of the sacrifice. Therefore, the result is not enjoined with respect to the quality. This is the meaning. It is the result that is intended to be enjoined, not the quality. For the purpose of the result is to be achieved, not for the sake of the quality. Therefore, the result is not enjoined with respect
In order to present [the agent] as being related [to the sacrifice],
that word "he should sacrifice" (yajeta) is capable of presenting the two related parties. If it is capable, then the injunction of a subordinate element (guṇavidhi) is established.
And validity is established. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "It is not so; for those two related factors—the result and the quality—are incapable of being connected with the sacrifice.
Indeed, the result is not capable of being connected with that which consists of both the goal and the means; nor is the quality [capable], because the result is merely the goal."
Because of being related; and because a quality is related only to that which is being established. If these two lack the capacity to be related, [p.
What power of denotation will [the word] exercise?
Therefore, because each is capable of being related separately, they are denoted here as distinct entities;
and consequently, since two meanings are enjoined, [there is no fault].
This sentence would result in two distinct actions: "One desiring sovereignty should sacrifice" and "One should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," which are mutually unrelated.
If this were so, what would happen? The answer is: due to their mutual connection—

The verbal expectancy (*vākya-ākāṅkṣā*) is abandoned; and a meaning that is not being understood becomes something merely imagined. Thus, this very state of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*) has arrived. For otherwise, the postulation of a meaning not understood from the word would not be tenable. Now, as for the claim that syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is achieved by resorting to the indication of possessive sense (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), he says: "And the indication of possessive sense is contradictory. Therefore, by the arguments stated in the *Udbhid-adhikaraṇa* and the *Tatprakhya-adhikaraṇa*...

Furthermore, the arguments regarding the section on designation have been stated; by those arguments, the position that it is a name alone is logical. As for the inconsistency regarding the cause and the effect mentioned in the sentence, that does not exist, because there is no contradiction.

There is no inconsistency because the purpose of the sign (nimitta) is not frustrated. Now, one might object that there is indeed inconsistency even if it is not instrumental; to this he says: "Inconsistency exists when there is frustration [of the purpose], not when there is a lack of instrumentality."
The meaning is that although the name lacks utility for initiating activity (*pravṛtti*), nevertheless there is no inconsistency;
therefore, there is no fault.
There is no defect characterized by a contradiction between the effect and its cause.
[Page 228] As for its qualities: For what purpose is this section (adhikaraṇa) commenced?
A partisan (ekadeśin) offers the reply: "What kind of question is this?"
But surely, it must be known whether the *āgneya* and other such terms are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names (*nāmadheya*).
The objector refutes this: it is appropriate that they are etymological...

The status of being a name belongs to those [words] whose meanings are established through conventional usage; however, the status of being a name is not possible in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*).
Why? He says: for the status of being a name is stated on the basis of grammatical coreferentiality with the meaning of a verb.

Since in a sentence whose primary purport is the injunction of the meaning of the verb, it is impossible for another meaning to be what is enjoined, the other words must also have the meaning of the verb as their primary purport; for this reason, they are called "nouns" (nāman). One might ask: "Let that be so, but even then, what follows? To this he replies: "And here, even the verb 'bhavati' does not have the sense of an action (bhāvārtha), because its meaning is not something to be enjoined."

That which is expressed as "it comes to be" (bhavati) does not have the sense of an action (bhāva). Why does it not have the sense of an action? To this it is replied: because its meaning is not something to be enjoined (avidheya).
If even the meaning of "it comes to be" were of the nature of an action, why would it not be of the nature of something to be enjoined? And yet, it is not something to be enjoined.

Therefore, because it is not something to be performed, we understand that it does not have the nature of a positive action (*bhāvārtha*). Since it lacks the nature of a positive action, the sentence would lack the purpose of enjoining it; however, if it were a positive action, the sentence would be intent upon what is to be enjoined, and through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that, the status of the word *āgneya* as a name (*nāmadheya*) is established. And for the reason stated above, there is no coreferentiality with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) which is being enjoined.
With the intention that there exists another cause for being a name distinct from form, we ask this question:
for what purpose is this topic?
"It is not commenced" means that because the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is weak, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) need not be undertaken. The respondent says:
"To this it is replied: here again, there is indeed dependence."

It is suspected [that there is a problem]. Having raised the suspicion that the injunction (*codanā*) is dependent [on other means of knowledge] in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced in order to state its independence in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). The meaning is that it must indeed be commenced. How is the dependence suspected? The answer is: just as the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*) is not possible because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), so too [is it impossible] with respect to a quality (*guṇa*)...
The injunction [of the word *dadhnā*] also does not [apply], because no verbal root meaning (*bhāvārtha*) is heard;

for an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is dependent upon a verbal root meaning. And here, no verbal root meaning is heard upon which this injunction of a subordinate quality could depend. When neither the status of an injunction of a subordinate quality nor the status of a name (*nāmatva*) is possible, then, due to the absence of any other alternative...
Invalidity would follow as a consequence; and that [invalidity] does not belong to the word by its very nature, but rather is caused by its being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*).

And thus, because of the resulting status of being of human origin, the entire collection of the Veda would necessarily depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). [Objection: But in the case of "the Āgneya [offering]," there is the substance and the deity—
Because of the hearing of a conjunction,
and because that [conjunction] is not possible without the meaning of sacrifice, the meaning of sacrifice is the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha);
and therefore, in that case—

The designation of names or the prescription of qualities is indeed possible. How [then] can there be invalidity? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "True, if a connection between substance and deity were heard [directly]. The objector says: "But surely it is heard as 'āgneya' (belonging to Agni).
The proponent replies: "True, if [the word] 'aṣṭākapāla'..."
The *kapāla* would not be the object;
for it is heard that the eight-potsherd offering belongs to Agni, and since that [offering] is not possible [in this case], it is as if it were not heard.

The connection between the substance and the deity is primarily [established] through inference. The objector asks: if the connection between the substance and the deity were restricted solely to the eight-potherd cake (aṣṭākapāla), then...
Is it indeed possible? The intention is that even the eight-pot-sherd (aṣṭākapāla) offering possesses the character of being dedicated to Agni (āgneyatva).

The proponent states the reply: from this it follows that the status of being an eight-pot-sherd offering must be understood as not having been specifically enjoined [in this context], because it is merely the object of reference (uddeśyatvāt).

And there is no such thing as an "eight-potherd" (aṣṭākapāla) that has not been prescribed. But surely, that which is cooked on eight potsherds will be the worldly referent for "eight-potherd," or it will be based on the scriptural statement, because of the injunction: "one cooks [the offering] on potsherds."
The meaning of this is as follows:
Alternatively, let it not be that the worldly [fire] is the intended object, on account of the statement "he cooks in the potsherds. Rather, let it be based solely on the scriptural injunction.
In any case, by this very statement, the status of being dedicated to Agni (āgneyatā) can be established even for that which has not been previously prescribed.
The proponent refutes this: First of all, it cannot be based on direct scriptural statement (*vācanika*), because the number eight is heard [in the text].

For indeed, the status of being "prepared on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapālatā*) is not obtained unless there is an injunction of the number eight in the scriptural statement itself. If it is argued that that number is also enjoined, he refutes this:

—No, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). [The objection is: "In the case of the *āgneya*, there is the number; in the case of the number, there is the *āgneya*.

[That is to say,] by way of restating the *āgneya*, the number eight would have to be enjoined: "That which is the *āgneya* must be made eight-potherded (*aṣṭākapāla*)," and likewise, "that which is eight-potherded is the *āgneya*."
B. Regarding the "connection with a deity" (devatāsamyoga):

it is the state of being dedicated to Agni (*āgneyatā*) by way of reference to the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*). Therefore, an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible; nor indeed can it be so named.
It has been stated that [the cognition] arises.
Therefore, there is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). If the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is intended with the meaning of invalidity, then how [is it explained] by the Bhāṣya with the words "nāma"?
By whom was it said? The respondent says: "Where was it said?
The objector says: "It was stated in the introduction. What [was said] there?

"Is it a name or an injunction of a quality?"—this was presented at the time of the doubt. In that regard, "it is a name" is the formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while "it is an injunction of a quality" is the formulation of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Likewise, at the time of adopting the prima facie view, there is a negation of the injunction of a quality.
And by performing [the action], it is stated that, by process of elimination, it is a name.
He provides the resolution: "It is true that it has been stated to be a name; it is not [otherwise]."

The meaning is that it has not been stated that this is the name of the verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha) which is to be enjoined. What, then, has been stated? He says: "By the mention of its name, its well-known meaning is indicated."

The term *āgneya* does not serve as an injunction (*vidheya*), but rather expresses a well-known meaning (*prasiddhārtha*), as it has been stated that even a name (*nāmadheya*) possesses a well-known meaning. One might ask: "Even if this be so, how is its dependence (*sāpekṣatā*) asserted? To this he replies:
"Since a well-known meaning is not possible without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), the dependence of the usage is thereby demonstrated."

He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): This would indeed be so if there were a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*) regarding the connection with number and the connection with the deity. But that is not the case.
Why is it not so? The answer is: for the injunction of the deity applies to the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake baked on eight potsherds).

He recalls the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa): "But was it not said that this [Brahman] is not well-known? The proponent of the final view (rāddhāntin) replies: "Is it not well-known even as something denotable?"

The meaning is that it is well-known as something denotable. And it is by relying on the well-known status of being denotable that its injunction is possible. The proponent of the prima facie view says: "Not [denotable]..."
It is well known [as such], but by way of being an effect (*kāryatayā*).
For it is on the grounds that the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) is an effect that its lack of prior establishment (*aprasiddhatva*) is asserted.
The final conclusion (*rāddhāntin*) says: this is indeed accepted.

[The word] is not established as having the status of an effect (*kāryatayā’prasiddhatvam*). Precisely because it is not established as an effect, it is [therefore] enjoined. He concludes: "Therefore, the non-establishment of the denotation (*abhidhānāprasiddhi*) subverts the injunction (*vidhāna*); but it does not [subvert] the effect (*kārya*)."

Because of that, there is no lack of established meaning. Therefore, just as the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is established, so too is the meaning of the term *aṣṭākapāla* (the eight-potherd cake) established as an injunction.

Furthermore, the fact that the meaning is understood through a well-known expression has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya when he says, "one does not take what has been cooked by another. This applies even to a term whose meaning is not [otherwise] established.

For indeed, it is not the case that the taking of what has been cooked by anyone else would even be a possibility such that it would be appropriate to speak of its exclusion; because of the statement, "He cooks in the potsherds," one does not take what has been cooked by another. Therefore, just as the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is well-known, so too is this meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) well-established.

The meaning is that just as there is well-established understanding of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) when one hears directly "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), so too is there such understanding of the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix. Therefore, there is no contingency of mutual dependence, because independence is established through the injunction of a ritual action qualified by a subordinate element (*guṇa*).
And in this case, since it is not possible for the state of having eight potsherds to be already established— as is the case with the *agnihotra*—
it too is enjoined, just as follows.
In the injunction "one performs the agnihotra," the fire is not enjoined as the deity because the deity Fire is already established; likewise, that is not possible here.
Furthermore, this [text] expresses a well-known meaning.
Regarding *barhis* and *ājya*:

what, then, is the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) here? To this he says: "This section is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). But what is the occasion (*prasaṅga*) for it? The answer is: "The connection of a noun-meaning with a meaning that is even something to be enjoined is observed, as in the case of 'the eight-pot-sherd offering' (*aṣṭākapālam*)."

Moreover, this word *ājya* is observed in common usage to be based solely on the action [of preparing it]. This word *ājya* is seen in the world to be based on refinement (*saṃskāra*), because the word *ājya* is employed only in the state of having been refined. Therefore, this too is connected to the effect; that is, the word *ājya* is connected to the purpose of the effect.

It is concomitant by way of being an effect; the meaning of the word *ājya* is that which is concomitant with the effect. He demonstrates this very point: "One should make the *ājya* [into something] by means of a refinement (*saṃskāra*).
The meaning is: "One should refine the *ājya* by means of liquefying it."
But surely, the word *ājya* is observed in certain regions to have a non-ritual basis, as in the expressions "ghee is for sale" and "having taken the sacrificial grass, the cows have gone.
Therefore, how can it be said with certainty that [the term] is based solely on ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*)?

It can be determined. He refutes [the objection]: "The usage must indeed be based on the Vedic revelation (śrauta) as it pertains to all regions; for a usage originating in only one part [of the country] and caused by linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*) cannot be considered universal (*sārvabhauma*)."

A. First, for those who employ words in the *saṃskṛta* [language], since their usage is based on grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), they do not employ words when such refinement is absent; thus, for them, the basis of usage being refinement is quite evident. Furthermore, even those who employ words solely for the sake of the genus (*jāti*) employ them within the *saṃskṛta* as well;

therefore, having the *saṃskṛta* as their domain is universal. And that alone is the primary (literal) sense. As for the denotation of the genus in only one part [of its application], that is secondary (metaphorical).
Why is this so? The answer is: for a word that is already well-established, a figurative sense is possible in relation to its primary (literal) meaning, but not for one that is not so established.

For just as the word "fire" (agni), well-known in its primary sense for a flame, becomes secondary when applied to a young boy due to similarity with it, so too, since the fact that all [words] have their basis in refinement (*saṃskāra*) is well-established, the usage occurring in reference to mere genus (*jāti*) is secondary. However, for those who maintain that the word is used only in reference to what has been refined, the usage is primary because there is no other usage; yet this word is not universally established as denoting clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Furthermore, for that which is not well-known, figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) in relation to clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is not tenable. Those who consider a word to be based on a refinement (*saṃskāra*) do not employ that word even when there is a different genus (*jātyantara*); in such a case, figurative usage is not appropriate because primary usage (*mukhyaprayoga*) is not observed elsewhere. [This applies to] action (*karman*)—
Furthermore, since it is employed in a single part where ghee is present—
even when it is not processed— it is used there even when [the term] is based on the action.

The secondary usage is established, because the primary application is established elsewhere; the secondary usage is established in the case of *ghṛta*. Therefore, it is based on the cause of consecration.

It is more appropriate that words such as *ājya* (clarified butter) and others have only a referential function toward an action (*kāryārthatā*). To this it is replied: their syntactic connection as having a referential function toward an action is not tenable, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For there is sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in order for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) to exist, and there is sprinkling in order for the sacrificial grass to exist.

That which is indeed consecrated by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites is called *barhis*. Since sprinkling and other rites are enjoined with reference to *barhis*, it is not known for what those sprinklings and so forth are enjoined. If this were the case, there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*); how then [is it established] in the case of the "eight-potherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*)?
Is there not, then, a mutual dependence?

The answer is: it was stated that there is no mutual dependence from the standpoint of verbal designation because of its well-established nature; however, in this case, the designation arises solely from the effect, and thus there is a difference [from the previous case] regarding the charge of mutual dependence.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) says: How [is it] with regard to the sacrificial post (yūpa)?
For it is heard in scripture: "He fashions the sacrificial post.

And the word "sacrificial post" denotes a functional refinement; in that case, a mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) is evident, because there is no means of establishing [the term's meaning] from any other source.
This is a recourse for those who have no other way out (*agatikā gati*).

Just as in the case of *barhis* and the like, there is established usage elsewhere because they are seen to be employed in the sense of the genus alone, such is not the case with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Therefore, since no other alternative exists, this recourse is adopted: that which is fit for carving—that which has become the object of the act of carving—is made a sacrificial post by the act of carving.
"It performs [the function]"—what is this desperate resort?
He says it all in a single sentence: "Why is it not understood from the scripture itself?
The intention is this: if it were understood from the scripture, then the same would apply to the *barhis* grass and other such items as well. The answer is: "When [the scripture] exists..."

When a thing is already well-known, it is not understood through scripture; where its existence is established by other means, it is not appropriate to employ it as a general term, because only a specific instance would be understood. In that case, this understanding derived from scripture is not perceived: namely, that "that which is fit for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and serves as the object of the action of sprinkling is the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), and it is purified by that sprinkling. However, when a word's referent is not well-known, since the meaning of the injunction remains unobstructed, [the specific referent] is postulated.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the meaning of the injunction. As for what was stated— that the universal application (*sārvabhauma-prayoga*) cannot be secondary because the literal sense is not established— the following applies to one who occupies only a single location:

Regarding the claim that a secondary (gauṇa) meaning is possible, it is said in response: worldly people do not necessarily employ a word with a secondary meaning only when its primary Vedic sense is well-known, as is the case with the word "king" (rājan). For instance, even non-Aryans use the word "king" despite its primary Vedic sense being unfamiliar to them.
They employ figurative [expressions], such as the word *barhis* and others. He raises an objection: "In that case, the same fault applies even to the word *rājan*.

He states this in a single passage: "For they employ the figurative [expression] for the purpose of conveying a resemblance to the primary meaning; yet it is figurative even when there is no cognition of that [primary object]."
To say that it is "employed" is a forced interpretation (*haṭha*);

for a word is employed figuratively (*gauṇa*) precisely to convey a similarity to its primary meaning. Since the primary meaning is not known, its similarity cannot be known; thus, in the absence of the cognition of similarity, the employment of the figurative term would be without cause (*animittaka*) and without reason (*nirhetuka*).

To this it is replied: the relationship between a word and its meaning does not depend upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). For it is the relationship that depends upon the intention. The meaning of this is as follows: although the speaker employs [the word] with a figurative understanding and the person being addressed likewise understands it as such, nevertheless, a child standing nearby—who has never seen the word used in its primary sense—understands it only as having a primary sense. Having understood it in that way, he would also proceed to act accordingly in his worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*).

Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning for a bystander does not depend upon the speaker’s intention; rather, whatever primary relationship between word and meaning the bystander perceives, that very same one he intends when engaging in linguistic usage at a later time. This very point is preceded by an illustration [p.

He demonstrates this: for it has been stated regarding Gopotalikā and others that, due to their lack of understanding and because they are not born with the capacity [for correct usage], they employ words as if they were beginningless, like those who use the word "anādi" (beginningless). In the same way here, due to the speaker's lack of understanding of the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), some speakers employ [a word] devoid of its intended meaning in a different sense. This is the case with *jāti*...

By someone who knows the primary meaning of a word in its proper domain, but who has acquired only a partial knowledge, the word *barhis* and others—though belonging to a different class—are employed through a secondary (gauṇa) linguistic impression (*saṃskāra*) associated with that [primary] impression. In this case, for one who does not know the other, the primary meaning, there exists an intention to convey the secondary meaning. Thus, for one who does not know [the distinction], the cognition of the primary meaning proceeds. Just as, in the case of young cows and the like, those who do not know the lack of beginning [of the usage] have a cognition based on incapacity (*aśaktija*). And that is the basis for it.
This is the linguistic usage of words and their referents. But how is it understood that this primary linguistic usage regarding conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) is based on delusion?
The answer is: because such usage is observed in both the world and the Veda. First, in the Veda, having prescribed *ājya* (clarified butter), in some instances [the word] *ghṛta*...

In that context, he praises by means of the word; if the word *ājya* were denotative of a refinement (*saṃskāra*), then in that praise the word *ghṛta* would serve as a mere figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). But if it denotes a genus (*jāti*), then it has its own primary meaning; therefore, by examining the Veda, it is determined that it indeed denotes a genus.
In common worldly usage as well, one observes the expression "the clarified butter (*ājya*) is to be purchased," "it is to be purchased"—a usage that is independent of the means of action.

That is to say, even in the world, one sees such usage which is independent of that whose means of action is the action itself in the form of a consecration (*saṃskāra*). Now, one might object: "But even in those cases, there is an intention [to speak] that is not understood."
It can be said as follows: A.

Even though the word primarily denotes the *saṃskṛta* (the refined), it is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) in reference to something else due to its connection with that [refinement]; and even when it denotes mere refinement, it is used figuratively for the genus (*jāti*) simply by virtue of the latter's fitness for that refinement.

In this regard, B. it can also be said that because someone’s intention was not fully understood—due to a failure to grasp the intended meaning—a cognition of the primary meaning has indeed arisen; therefore, [the figurative usage is justified].
How is this determined? He provides the answer: "The resolution regarding the *vetasa* tree and so forth has already been stated.

Furthermore, because of worldly convention (*laukika-vyavahāra*), when there is a disagreement regarding the nature of universals (*jāti*) and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is worldly usage concerning objects that are not [merely] conventional.
In the case of a conflict, the determination is made based on the commonality of Vedic usage;

therefore, here too, because of the similarity with Vedic usage, the primary sense belongs to the genus (*jāti*). However, regarding the refined form (*saṃskṛta*), its usage is secondary due to its connection with the refinement belonging to that [genus]. If this is so, then by that very [reasoning]...

In that case, the matter has already been settled by the previous section. It is replied: this section is commenced to dispel the doubt that the secondary usage belongs only to one who has already understood the primary usage. As for the examples, they are *barhis* and so forth, as well as *vetasa* and so forth, in both cases. What, then, is the connection to the present topic?
What is the purpose of defining the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The answer is: precisely non-determination; that is, non-determination of the meaning of words.

In the conventional usage of words, there would be a lack of determination as to which [meaning] is primary and which is secondary. Consequently, even regarding the Veda, there would be non-determination.

Otherwise, there would be invalidity [of the cognition]. Therefore, indeed, non-determination is the cause for the [inapplicability of the] topic. But surely the Commentator has shown the distinction only with respect to the action (*karman*), not with respect to the comprehension (*avagati*). He replies: "Precisely because there is a distinction with respect to the action, for that very reason..."

The purpose [of the deliberation] is the absence of non-determination; therefore, it is the absence of determination that motivates the deliberation. If there were no distinction regarding the object (*karman*), then there would be no distinction in the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Due to the absence of a distinction in performance, the absence of determination cannot be removed; thus, it is not a fault.
This section (adhikaraṇa) has been commenced to refute that [view]; however, in the case of certainty, the purpose remains established through the very determination [of the matter].

Regarding the *prokṣaṇī* waters: for what reason is this a separate section? The answer is: because of the difference between that which arises from the whole world and that which arises from a single part.
An exception based on traditional authority (smṛti) regarding the two types of usage is now stated:
usage based on grammatical refinement (saṃskāra) is universal, whereas usage based on genus (jāti) is restricted to a single region.

[The author] asserts the origin [of the term]: having considered the traditional usage (*smṛti*) of those two, the exception (*apavāda*) is stated, namely that the word *prokṣaṇī* is etymological (*yaugika*). He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"But how can an exception to usage be stated on the basis of tradition?
For the grammatical tradition has its root in actual usage; how then [can it override it]?"

The meaning is that he refutes the application [of the rule]. He states the established conclusion (rāddhānta): for the application is indeed consistent with the traditional teaching (smṛti). For the application is certainly in accordance with the traditional teaching. Why? He says: because the connection of both parts is possible.

Even in that application which is based on a *saṃskāra* (preparatory refinement), *yoga* is possible; and even in that which is based on *jāti* (universal class), *yoga* is possible. Therefore, since the application is not in contradiction with *yoga*, it does not sublate *yoga*; thus, [in that case], one should bring the *prokṣaṇī* waters.
Thus, "the performance is caused by ritual refinement" refers to the cause of action, while "we are distressed by the sprinkling waters" refers to the cause of birth. Therefore...
Because of the contradiction, the determination is made on the basis of Smṛti.
The remainder has been explained.
The same applies to the case of the *nirmanthya* fire. What is the excess here?
The answer is: this is the excess here; the traditional authority (*smṛti*) is also over-extensive.

Because application is observed even when [the fire] has not been churned for long; likewise, because application is observed even in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in such and such ways—as in the case of saying "we shall churn this wood"—therefore, it does not have conditioned factors as its cause. Likewise, its etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) is also established.

This is not possible; for we observe the usage of the term even when the fire has been produced by friction only recently. If it were based on etymology (*yaugikatva*), the usage would apply only to that which has been produced by friction for a long time. Nor is it based on a genus (*jāti*), because the term is used for any fire whatsoever. Therefore, even from the perspective of traditional usage (*smṛti*), there is no definitive conclusion.

Thus thinks the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī). He states the established conclusion (rāddhānta): Because the Smṛti text expresses it without qualification, it is not capable of setting aside the application of the specific rule.

For if it were recorded in the Smṛti that the word *nirmanthya* is correct whether applied to wood that has been churned for a long time or to wood that has not been churned for a long time, then a specific application would contradict that Smṛti. But this is not the case. If it is argued that [the specific application] contradicts the knowledge of non-distinction [contained in the Smṛti], [we reply: no.

If it is argued that the application (prayoga) subverts the Smṛti rule because it lacks specification, [the author] refutes this: it does not subvert it, because the lack of specification is terminated by the specific details.

If that lack of specification found in the Smṛti were to be superseded by a specific detail through the force of the ritual application, then [the Smṛti rule would indeed be set aside]. However, that is not the case here.
There is no fault. Therefore, this case is also like the previous one; thus it was stated, "it is so.

Regarding the Vaiśvadeva: how, moreover, does a doubt arise here as to whether it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), given that there is a commonality of the verbal root’s meaning (*bhāvārtha*)?

Because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is more appropriate here that this is indeed a name. The answer is: in this case, grammatical coreferentiality is even more plausible under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), because the meaning of the verbal root is the primary sense of the suffix.
It is not logical that this is merely a name; rather, the position that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is indeed more appropriate.

Even in the case of an injunction of a quality, there is no need for the figurative indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), because the suffix denotes the sacrifice itself—as in "the sacrifice of which Viśvedevas are the deity"—and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established through its primary sense. He raises an objection again: if the injunction of a quality is indeed more reasonable, why [is it not accepted]?
The introduction by way of a name provides the solution: because of the absence of a subject for the injunction of a quality— that is, for the quality which is to be enjoined, there is no subject.

Furthermore, an injunction regarding a quality based on existence is also not tenable. Why? Because of the absence of an object. The answer is: because the rites under discussion are already occupied by deities such as Agni through direct scriptural statement (śruti).
However, those actions under discussion are already occupied by Agni and other deities prescribed for their origination;

therefore, another deity cannot be enjoined therein. If it is impossible to enjoin another deity in the context of the original action, why then is it not considered a different action characterized by a different deity? That too is not determined, because [the original action] remains the subject at hand.

Regarding the curd (*dādhikṣā*) dedicated to the Viśvedevas: for when there is an injunction of a separate ritual action, it constitutes a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), which occurs only in the absence of any other possible interpretation.

This is logical. Furthermore, there is another alternative here: because of its association with the *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā* sacrifice, it can be construed as a name for the sacrifices under discussion by means of the "stick-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) maxim. Therefore, even the status of being a name is not possible here, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established even through the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Nor is it an injunction of a quality, because the sacrifices under discussion are already restricted by qualities prescribed at their origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*). Thus he says: "Therefore, it is not a name."
Nor can independence [of the Veda] be understood on the basis of its qualities;
such is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position. A proponent of a partial conclusion (rāddhāntaikadeśin) says:
"If you think that it is impossible to determine independence, then let the determination be made on the basis of the injunction of qualities."

For it is thus that the relationship between the meanings of nouns and verbs is understood. [Objection: But was it not already stated that there is no object? [Reply: He refutes this: "That was poorly stated. [Objection: Again he challenges: "In what way was it poorly stated?"
The answer: For the postulation of an effect arises from the scriptural text (*śruti*), not the scriptural text from the effect.
What is this being said? The answer:
This is it; for the obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origination (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇāvarodha*) is indeed the cause of non-comprehension, and not otherwise.

When something already understood is being sublated, it is precisely the cognition of a connection with another quality that is contradicted by the obstruction of a quality enjoined by the originative injunction; however, the sublation of what has been understood is not actually performed. Even if this were so, he asks "What then? and replies: "And this word *vaiśvadeva* applies only to the meaning of the verb."

In the present context, it applies [to the deities], not to fire and the others; for fire and the others, whether related or unrelated, are not capable of excluding the meaning of the verbal root from being denoted by the word *vaiśvadeva*.
He says in a single sentence: [The words] exclude one related term being the object of another related term, but they do not exclude its being denotable.
What follows from that? The answer is: consequently, for the sake of establishing the denotability of the other related term...

The deities Agni and others, who are connected by way of origination, do not obstruct the attainment of another deity; just as the status of the *phalacamas* as a means of sacrifice— which is implied by its connection with the act of eating (which is a consecration subordinate to the sacrifice) as something to be consecrated— is otherwise inexplicable.

"Because Soma does not perish"— by this, for the sake of establishing the propriety of being designated by the term *vaiśvadeva* as heard [in the scripture], it is logical to postulate a function for the Viśvedevas;
the meaning is that their entry as deities into the sacrifices under discussion is appropriate, but the performance of the sacrifice is not their function.

[This refers to] these [offerings]. Considering that they are accomplished by means of Agni and the others alone, it is more appropriate to assume that the status of being denoted by the term *vaiśvadeva*—which is heard in the scripture—is otherwise [than literal], rather than assuming that the object to be denoted is otherwise [than what it appears]. Since there is a connection with [Agni and the others] as deities for the sake of making the designation possible, therefore, when the performance is carried out together with Agni and the others...
Because it is independent of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), determination (*adhyavasāna*) is appropriate.
He states the ultimate established conclusion (*paramasiddhānta*): "If this is so, [it is for the sake of establishing] the mere occurrence of words."

Regarding the assumption of a prescription of qualities (*guṇavidhikalpana*): if that is the case, let it be simply a name (*nāmadheya*). For it is only due to the impossibility [of another interpretation] that a connection with other qualities is postulated for the sake of making the designation possible. However, there is no option (*avikalpa*) between those things enjoined by means of unequal authorities.

For Agni and the others are enjoined by direct Vedic statement (śruti), whereas the Viśvedevas are [enjoined] by syntactical connection (vākya). In that case, the injunction is appropriately understood as being for the purpose of providing a name. Now, if it were merely a name—
The meaning of the individual parts, as it is being understood, would not be connected to the ritual action (*kārya*).

For if the status of the Viśvedevas as deities were perceived according to the meaning of the individual parts, it would not be connected with the ritual action; this is the sense. He refutes this: "It is not logical for that which is already connected to be further connected. Anvi-...
And thus, regarding the *āmikṣā*, this meaning is established: therefore, the lack of connection with the [specific] effect is not capable of precluding the denotation [of the word].

For even in a single instance, that which is connected [to one thing] may be unconnected [to another]; and by the logic of the "man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), its status as a name is justified, so that its being the cause [of the application of the name], like the staff itself, is not contradictory.
Therefore, it is not possible to conceive of it as a mental construction (vikalpa), nor is there a repetition of the ritual action; hence, it is logical to determine it as a name (nāmadheya).

But how, then, can the designation "vaiśvadeva" apply to the sacrifice to Agni and others (the āgneya-yāga) within the Vaiśvadeva-parvan, given that it lacks any basis for its application (pravṛttinimitta)?

In the case of an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), however, [the name] is established because it is enjoined again and because a ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) exists. He refutes this: "That is true, provided it were established solely through being enjoined; but in the case of *āmikṣā*, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the name] not denoting it."

For since the Viśvedevas are already established in relation to the *āmikṣā*, they cannot be the object of an injunction; thus, the application of the term as denoting something strictly to be enjoined is not established.
