[Objection: But surely, by abandoning the reference to the *āmikṣā*, the designation as an object of injunction will be established. To this he says: "And the state of being the subject matter (*prakṛtatva*) is equal."
Therefore, it is not impossible to avoid the sacrifice of alms. Here, an objection is raised: "Which of these two is stronger?
[The answer is: that which pertains to the non-Vaiśvadeva [offering].

Between the naming of that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) as "vaiśvadeva" and the naming of that which is not to be enjoined (*avidheya*), which of these two is stronger? He resolves this: the naming of that which is to be enjoined as something not to be enjoined is impossible. For that which is to be enjoined is made known because it was previously unknown, whereas that which is named [as a referent] is already known. And one...

In this way, it is possible for a single object to be both known and unknown; and it is also possible for there to be a designation by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for those who possess the same attribute.

In the case of the view that [the word] is a name, just as in the expression "the staff-bearers are going," the word "staff-bearer" applies by secondary indication through association even to those who do not possess a staff.

In the same way, here too, the word "vaiśvadeva" will apply both to that which is not a vaiśvadeva and to that which is a vaiśvadeva. Therefore, this position—that there is an application of the term "vaiśvadeva" to what is not a vaiśvadeva—is superior; this position is better.

Furthermore, this must be addressed here: why is it that [the injunction] "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" does not designate the Āmikṣā sacrifice alone? For in that case, no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would have to be resorted to regarding the word *vaiśvadeva*. And even if the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) were to apply to that [sacrifice as well], there would still be no inconsistency. To this it is replied: by the rule that the word *vaiśvadeva* applies to both a hymn (*sūkta*) and an oblation (*havis*), it [primarily] refers to the hymn.

Or rather, the term *havis* (oblation) functions in its primary sense; because it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), and since that [term] applies to the sacrifice itself, this word *yajati* cannot restrict it. Nor can the word *vaiśvadeva* be connected with *yajati* through grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because that would result in the word [vaiśvadeva] taking a feminine gender due to its coreferentiality with the word *āmikṣā*. Since the connection is possible through coreferentiality...
Because a connection between items in different grammatical cases is untenable;

those [passages] which possess a prior [basis] are not for the purpose of injunction. It has been stated that authority [is established] through injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, names, and injunctions of qualities.
Here, however, in the case of the "eight-pot-sherd" and "twelve-pot-sherd" [offerings], there is no status as a mantra.

Since there is no quality of being a reminder (*smārakatva*), and because it is an injunction (*codaka*)— due to the absence of reminding what has already been prescribed— even the status of a name (*nāmadheya*) is not possible, owing to the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the "eight-potsherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) and other such terms.

In the phrase "when it consists of eight potsherds," there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning of the action being enjoined; rather, its status as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), such as the number eight mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), remains indeed doubtful.

In that regard, first of all, there is no doubt concerning the injunction of a quality (guṇavidhāna), because it is impossible due to the absence of an object; for the injunction of a quality [occurs] exclusively—
Because of its arising. How is there an absence of the object?
The answer is: because of the cessation due to the production of another quality.
Vaiśvānara...

In the injunction "one should offer on twelve potsherds," the sacrifice to Vaiśvānara is already restricted by the number twelve prescribed at its origin; therefore, although the potsherds for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) are not yet restricted, they are not the subject [of the injunction] because they do not constitute the primary action itself. Likewise, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) also remains free from doubt.

The connection [is as follows]. Why? He says: because by means of the number twelve, other numbers such as eight and so forth are excluded. This is not a praise based on a relationship with that [number], as in the case of "Water is indeed peaceful.
Just as in the injunction "Water is peaceful," [the mention of] vetasa...
If it is argued that just as the praise of waters related [to the sacrifice] is appropriate, so too here [the praise of the number] is appropriate; [we reply:

praise of that which is related is indeed appropriate, but praise of another number is not, because of the lack of connection with the number twelve. Therefore, since this is merely a mental impression (*pratibhā*), the objection regarding the lack of dependence (*anapekṣatva*) is raised once again.
[Page 250] This being the case regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*),
a certain proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntaikadeśin*) considers its authority to be established through the prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*). Who is this?
Thinking thus, does he perhaps not see that cessation occurs through another quality (*guṇa*) rather than through origination?
Because he thinks thus. The answer is: it is not that he does not see;

rather, he certainly does see. Thinking that this is a single sentence (sahavākya), due to the delusion that it is one sentence and due to the delusion regarding the "together" (saha) construction, [he concludes] it is endowed with all numbers.

He considers the act of offering (*nirvapati*) to be a single syntactical unit; thus, he considers the offering to be endowed with all the numbers mentioned in the injunction: "One should offer on eight potsherds, nine potsherds, ten potsherds, eleven potsherds, or twelve potsherds."

Considering this to be a single sentence because it forms one syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the intention is that there is either a repetition of the ritual action or an option (*vikalpa*) among the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*). He considers the phrase "the Vaiśvānara [cake] on twelve potsherds" to be the introductory statement for the sake of the deity.

By that single sentence, there is the injunction of the sacrifice to Vaiśvānara endowed with all the numerical specifications. Because of this injunction, there is the origination [of the rite]; therefore, there is no obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origination.

"But for the purpose of enjoining a quality. To this it is said: validity cannot be asserted on the basis of enjoining a quality, because there is no subject matter [for such an injunction]. Now, it was argued that the ritual action having Vaiśvānara as its deity is the subject matter.
He refutes this: "That is not so."

The subject matter [of this section] concerns the contradiction with twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*). By the passage beginning "that which is on eight potsherds" (*yad aṣṭākapāla*), there is the injunction of various numbers of potsherds by means of a single sentence; therefore, what was stated—that there is no obstruction by a quality enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇa*)—is ill-stated.
How so?
The answer is: because the word *vaiśvānara* has a case-ending that denotes a distinct referent.

Because it is a word [denoting an object], the term *vaiśvānaram* ends in the second case and expresses a meaning distinct from the basic nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dvādaśakapāla* is based on direct Vedic statement (*śrauta*).

First, it is understood that "one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. However, because phrases such as "that which is on eight potsherds" and so forth are connected with the words *brahmavarcasa* (spiritual luster) and *punāti* (purifies), they are not understood to have the Vaiśvānara offering as their substratum.

Rather, a connection must be postulated based on the fact that the praise of the act of purifying would otherwise be inexplicable. And such a postulation is not tenable when a [direct] established connection already exists.
Thus it has been stated. The meaning of this is: here, the status of being a single sentence (*sahavākyārthatva*) is not possible for the words "eight-pot-sherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth.

Because the words ending in the nominative case are connected with the word *vaiśvānara* ending in the accusative, they lack a connection with the [other] words. While one might wish to postulate a connection with *vaiśvānara* based on the impossibility of explaining their praise otherwise, such a postulation finds no footing because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dvādaśakapāla* itself, which also ends in the accusative. Therefore, it remains established that [the sacrifice] is already occupied by a quality prescribed at its origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). This is so whether by the word *vaiśvānara*...
There is no connection between the eight-pot-sherd offering and the others; if that is so, then it is merely a flash of intuition (*pratibhā*).
He refutes this: "It is not intuition, because it serves the purpose of praise (*stutyarthatayā*)."
[Objection: How can it be established that [the mention of numbers] is for the purpose of praise, given that number has been refuted by another number? [Reply: The answer is:
the refutation applies to the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*), not to its actual existence (*sadbhāva*), nor to its non-existence (*asadbhāva*).

The number eight and so forth is not denoted by the word "twelve. However, the numbers eight and so forth can exist within the number twelve; and their relationship [to it] is based on their actual presence, not on the basis of being denoted. When they are present, it is logical that they be denoted through partial extraction (*avayutya*).
Having distinguished substances according to numbers such as eight and so forth, the designation is justified.
[Objection: But surely, if [the word] were separated [from its context], the comprehension of the relationship would not occur;
and consequently, the praise would be untenable. [The author] replies:
Separation may be possible for the sake of denotation, but the state of being related cannot be separated.
The meaning of this is:
it is possible to apply the word "eight" to denote eight potsherds that constitute a single portion of the twelve potsherds.

However, their actual inclusion within the number twelve cannot be established as a matter of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). Therefore, because such a connection is not established, the praise of the number twelve is indeed valid by way of praising those [entities]. Now, one might ask: how can there be a non-establishment for the sake of verbal expression, but not in terms of ultimate reality? To this he says: "For intention follows verbal expression, not the objective entity."

Therefore, although their actual number is twelve, nevertheless, when there is an intention to express only a portion of them, it is entirely appropriate to designate them by the word "eight" and so forth.
Consequently, because the relationship [of the parts] is not being treated as a composite whole, the praise is justified, just as in the case of the statement, "The waters are peaceful. And thus:
It has been shown that "its felly, nave, and spokes are beautiful";

through the praise of the parts, there is praise of the whole. Thus, by praising the number eight belonging to the parts, there is praise of the number twelve. [Objection: But let the number twelve, being enjoined for the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), serve for the sake of the fruit.

B. [p. 255] As for the objection that, since there is no mention of nine *yojanas*, one might as well assume that the injunctions regarding eight and so forth apply to that very same ritual action—the author replies: "Even the injunction of a connection between a quality and a result does not arise from this alone."
It is possible. Why? The answer is: because it is understood as a single syntactical unit for the purpose of praise (stuti).

Furthermore, if there were a connection between a quality and a result, a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda) would result. And that it constitutes a single syntactical unit has been demonstrated by means of the opening and the conclusion.
Therefore, since it is established as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), its independence is proven;
that proof is established. It has been stated that even by means of partial extraction (*avayutya*), praise is rendered possible through connection with the denotation.

Even though there is such a separate designation (*avayutyābhidhāna*), nevertheless, because the state of being related has not been excluded, it is said that by praising that [related object], the relative itself is also praised. However, where the state of being related is not apprehended in any way whatsoever—
Because they are not mutually connected,

and because it is impossible to enjoin them as subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), as in the cases: "The sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd" (*yajamāna ekakapālaḥ*) and "The sacrificer is the grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*).
Regarding such passages as these, how can they possess authority?
The meaning is that they lack authority altogether.
Furthermore, no qualities (*guṇa*) are being enjoined.
But is it not established in the section concerning the secondary and primary [meanings] that a secondary relationship exists even for words denoting different objects?
Because of the possibility of mutual connection between them, the praise of the *prastara* (the grass-bundle) and the *ekakapāla* (the single potsherd) is appropriate. He refutes this:
"That very point is not tolerated.
It is precisely the figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) that is being challenged. Why is it not tolerated? The answer is: "Not at all."
The state of being secondary (gauṇatā) occurs through a connection with another meaning. How is it not so?
The answer is: for when there is secondary denotation, it is logical that only the qualities (guṇas) themselves are the objects of expression.

Regarding this so-called figurative designation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*): if it is the qualities themselves that constitute the denotable object (*vācyatva*), then the comprehension of specific qualities is established; not otherwise. Thus he says: "For otherwise, the word 'lion' would convey only courage in Devadatta."
In the case of "Devadatta is a lion," as well as in "The boy is fire," the word "fire" cannot logically apply to the boy in the sense of his being tawny.
Why? To this he says: "Because of the lion-species... [and so forth].
C. By way of its application (*pravṛtti*), the word "lion" expresses qualities; it expresses all those qualities whatsoever that are connected with the genus.
One should establish [the meaning],
because there is no distinction in the means of establishment. Now, if you think that when there is the intention to express only that much,
that very [meaning] is understood;

If it is argued that "only that quality which is intended to be expressed is perceived, and no other," he refutes this: "In that case, the word follows the speaker's intention, not the denoted object;
for the word follows the speaker's intention, and not [the object]."
Regarding the object (*vastu*): although the object does not exist, nevertheless, the word functions by the force of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). What follows from this?
The answer is: it results in being figurative (*gauṇa*), having that state superimposed (*adhyāropita-tadbhāva*).
Having superimposed the state of fire—which does not exist—in the boy...

It follows that a word is employed figuratively because one intends to speak [of something else]. Nevertheless, he asks: "Why so?"—[the answer is: "And in the case of superimposition (adhyāropa), there is no connection with another object;
that is, the word 'fire' has no connection with the boy. Why is this? The reply is: "For superimposition is indeed..."
It concerns only an object whose meaning has already been understood; it grasps only an object that is already present and attained, and does not touch an object that is unattained,
as for example:

In the cognition of silver with respect to mother-of-pearl, it is apprehended as "that very thing," and not as "something similar to that. The cognition is "this is indeed silver," and not "something similar to silver. Therefore, it apprehends only the non-existent silver itself, and not something like mother-of-pearl that resembles silver. And that which is perceived—

The very object that is the referent of superimposition is also the referent of figurative (gauṇa) speech; therefore, the word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is not capable of serving as praise for the grass-bundle (prastara) and the single potsherd (ekakapāla). In that case, let it be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
The answer is: this too is not possible because it is impossible.
For a quality (*guṇa*) being enjoined is seen to be for the sake of an action (*kāryārtha*), yet here it is enjoined for the sake of an action, and that is not tenable in either way.
It is not.

The Bhāṣyakāra has stated that the injunction regarding the sacrificer is intended to show that the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *ekapāla* (single-pot offering) are prescribed for the duties of the sacrificer, nor conversely that the sacrificer is prescribed for the duties of those two. Therefore, this very same suspicion regarding the appearance [of a contradiction] arises here; to this, it is replied: It is true that an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, but an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) cannot be ruled out. But was it not said that it is not an *arthavāda* because of its connection with a different meaning, or rather because of its lack of connection with the primary meaning?
He refutes [the objection]:
"What you have said is incorrect. How is it incorrect?
The answer is: for figurative usage (gauṇatva) is indeed possible precisely through connection with its own primary meaning.

The meaning is that a word becomes secondary (gauṇa) when, having denoted its own primary meaning (svārtha), it relies upon an intention directed toward something similar to that meaning which has been brought to mind by it. Now,
it was argued that this is not the case because there is no cognition of any quality (guṇa) connected with the primary meaning.
He addresses the objection: "The distinction [of words] arises from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); this too has already been stated.

He raises a further challenge: "True, it has been said; however, it has also been stated that when there is a speaker's intention, there is no inherent connection with the denotable object (*abhidheya*)."

When there is a desire to speak that acts as a restrictor, whatever is the primary meaning (*svārtha*) of the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) does not become a related [referent]. For in that case, there would be a superimposition (*adhyāropa*); the word expresses a meaning constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpanā*) which is non-existent, rather than a real, ultimate meaning, and consequently, praise (*stuti*) would be untenable.

Likewise, the occurrence of [terms such as] "sky-flower" and so forth is possible because a word has as its object mere conceptual construction independent of an external referent; thus, the employment of the word "sky-flower" is justified.

However, if the word were connected to a denotable object, its application would be impossible. For what could be connected with what? In this case, with what referent would the word *kiṃ* ("what") be connected?

It is connected [to the objection]. To this it is replied: You are indeed ignorant of the rules governing words; for when the denotation is not intended to be expressed, you are truly ignorant of the scope of the word "lion."
The utterance of a specific word would be without basis.

For it is the meaning that necessitates the employment of a word for the sake of its own comprehension; thus, the utterance of a specific word is justified. In the absence of that [meaning], however, the utterance of a specific word would be baseless. Even by means of another word, [the meaning could be conveyed].
The designation "superimposition" (adhyāropa) is not at all untenable. To this, the opponent objects: "O dull-witted one, do not speak thus! [For] the object of superimposition..."
For by that [word], the referent of the word "lion" is intended to be expressed;
since words have superimposed objects as their domain, the superimposed meaning of "lion" is intended to be expressed, and not the boy's actual connection with those qualities. Nor is it that...
The meaning "lion" is superimposed [upon another object] even without the word "lion";
therefore, the utterance of the word "lion" is not without a basis.
The word belongs precisely to that meaning which is superimposed.
"It is uttered" means that the utterance of a specific term is not without cause. The proponent says: "But indeed, this has been stated by us;
the specific cause has been stated [and] the binding of what is prohibited has been refuted."
Furthermore, the utterance of the word *liṅga* is not due to the absence of the boy, but rather because of its connection with the dawn (*aruṇa*).

Why is it that the meaning of "lion" alone is superimposed upon Devadatta? If it is argued that this is because of the perception of its qualities—that is, because the qualities of a lion are perceived in Devadatta—the author refutes this: in that case, it follows that the representation must be understood as being based on a connection with the primary object itself.

The primary referent of the word "lion" is [the animal]; by virtue of its connection with that [referent] and its similarity to it, Devadatta is designated by the word "lion. In this case, since the essential nature of the substance (Devadatta) has already been apprehended by the word "Devadatta," the word "lion" is intended solely to convey the quality of similarity; and this similarity to a lion is based upon the possession of common attributes.

The intent is the realization of the qualities of a lion. If it is asked, "How is the understanding of these specific qualities attained? the answer is: from the observation of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because figurative usage (*gauṇa*) is preceded by such [observation].
It is understood through the force of other means of knowledge that this is a figurative application. Other means of knowledge...

For, having understood that this word "other" is employed in reference to another [entity] elsewhere, there is the determination of its figurative nature (*gauṇatva*). And in that case, since a certain quality (*guṇa*) is perceived through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is understood that the word is applied there by virtue of its connection with that quality; thus, the establishment of the comprehension of that specific quality is achieved. In a single treatise— [p.
I say: even the primary meaning of words such as "cook" is restricted to a particular [individual] by virtue of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
It is established [as primary].
What is the reasoning for saying it is not secondary?
If every word functions solely through a connection with an object, then how [can there be words] such as "sky-flower"?
The use of the word [“existent”] refers to an entity. The reply is: “just as ‘a sky-flower’.
The word “iti” here is intended to indicate that cognition; by this, the following is stated:

Just as there is the cognition "it is like a sky-flower," so too is the employment of the expression "sky-flower. For instance, one cognition has only the sky as its object, while another has only the flower as its object. Although there is no mutual connection between these two, and despite not perceiving any actual relation, one engages in the conventional practice of perceiving a connection. This occurs because one perceives the simultaneous utterance of those two terms as something common to their respective correlates.

Thus, this composition on the path of policy (*nayavīthī*) should be described in accordance with logic (*nyāya*). Therefore, the status of [the passage] as an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) is established. As for what the purpose is and how it is achieved, this is explained in detail in the Bhāṣya.
[The section on] *jāti* (genus). The same application of authority (*prāmāṇya*) should be made regarding *jāti* and the rest as well.
In those cases too, authority is established by resorting to the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
If this is so, why then are there separate topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*)? To this he says: "But the separate topical sections [are established] because of the difference in the refutations..."
B. "The application as well" is for the purpose of demonstration.
In that regard, the response is that the term "Brāhmaṇa" [applied to fire] is a figurative usage (*gauṇīvṛtti*) based on similarity due to originating from the same source;

"the sacrificial post is the sun" is so because of its similarity to the sacrificial post; "all other animals are indeed non-animals, while cows and horses are the true animals"—here the word "animal" is figurative when applied to cows and horses by way of praise; and likewise, "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks" and "he lays down the *prāṇabhṛt*-bricks" are so by way of abundance (*bhūmnā*).

The phrase "separate topical sections" is used to show the resolution that the definition [of the Veda] consists in its inherence in the indicative marks (*liṅga-samavāya*). Therefore, it is established that even those passages with figurative meanings possess authority as *arthavādas*, as do those with metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) meanings. But how can even those things which serve as the indicators (*lakṣaṇa*) in the accounts of creation and so forth also be the objects indicated (*lakṣya*)? For in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the Gaṅgā, being the indicator, does not itself become the object indicated. The answer is: because they share a single action with the objects indicated.
Because of connection (*yoga*).

First, as for those things which are the objects of definition (*lakṣya*), the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) has a connection with them through a single action. And since that action serves as the cause for their being objects of definition, the state of being connected to the conditioning factor (*upadhāna*) is indeed the reason for being an object of definition. Furthermore, this state of being connected to the conditioning factor exists even for those things that function as definitions.

[This refers to] creation and so forth. Therefore, because they stand in the relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no contradiction. How is it that the word "animal" (*paśu*) is used figuratively for horses and the like? How is the word "animal" applied by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to horses and such?

In the case of horses and the like, [the word] is applied primarily (*mukhya*) alone. And here, the non-acceptance of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not the governing factor, because in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the figurative (*gauṇa*) sense is intended. The meaning is that in every respect there is only primary denotation (*mukhyatā*) here, neither figurative denotation nor indication. This is because the usage [of the word] is preceded by a prohibition; for a generic term (*jātiśabda*) is prohibited from applying to other members of that same class.

In those cases where a word is employed, it receives its application only in a figurative sense. For here, having established a prohibition by stating that "among other animals, they are not [true] animals," the word *paśu* (animal) is applied only to cows and horses— which belong to the class of animals— and thus its usage is indeed figurative.

Why? For when a genus-term is negated with respect to something belonging to that genus, it becomes the object of negation precisely by way of negating the inherent quality, because the genus itself cannot be removed; nevertheless, he asks: "What then?"
Furthermore, because its primary qualities have been negated, when it is employed again in reference to another member of that same class, it is understood only in a figurative sense,
as in the preceding sentences.

The meaning is that when the qualities have been excluded, it is appropriate to provide a counter-exception (pratiprasava) for those very qualities. Therefore, even a word denoting a genus (jātiśabda) is used figuratively (gauṇa), because it functions through its connection with the qualities of the object; thus there is no contradiction. Consequently, the independence [of the Veda] is established.
[pp.

266–267] Regarding doubtful cases: But surely, in the instances of *yava*, *varāha*, *vetasa*, and so forth, the removal of doubt has already been accomplished through the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*)?

The sense is that this [objection] is therefore redundant. He refutes it: "True, but that [discussion] concerns the meaning of words (*padārtha*). However, when a word-meaning is being doubted as to whether it is innate (*autpattika*) or non-innate, it is determined in various instances by means of the supplementary context (*vākyaśeṣa*)."
Here he raises an objection: "Does the word have an object [meaning] such that the doubt concerning it may be removed? The implication is that it does not exist at all. He replies:
—Certainly it exists;

for through the distinction between insertion and deletion (*āvāpa-uddhāra*), one understands the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) between two word-meanings. If a word [denotes] only the word-meaning...
It is certain that there is no sentence distinct from its constituent words; how then is the innate relationship between the sentence and its meaning established?
[The author] answers: "True, [it is established] through the linguistic usage of elders. Regarding the sentence:
The relationship between the sentence and its meaning is innate;

however, it has been stated that "the meaning of a sentence is conveyed by the sentence through its constituent parts" (*tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthena samāmnāyaḥ*). [This concerns] the knower of the meaning of the sentence...
And [this applies] to us regarding the body; therefore, there is doubt concerning that which has become such. But here, the meaning of the sentence lies in the sense of action.

This, then, is the distinction between the sentence and its meaning from the word and its meaning; this has been demonstrated in detail. Therefore, even because of doubt regarding the purpose of action, there is a lack of authoritative validity.
Due to the contradiction between the introduction and the conclusion, there is doubt regarding the very meaning of the sentence.

This being the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), some who hold a portion of the final conclusion (rāddhāntaikadeśin) consider it appropriate to determine the meaning of the concluding passage on the basis of the opening statement (upakrama).
Because there is no contradiction.
To the question "How is there no contradiction?", he says: For a universal resides both in itself and in its particulars. If by that...

If it is argued that [the term] "anointed" (akta) applies because it is anointed by something [other than ghee], even so, despite being anointed with ghee, the word "ghee" must be explained in the concluding passage on the basis of the opening statement, just as in the case of the phrase "he lays down the sṛṣṭis," which applies to both those bricks that are actually sṛṣṭis and those that are not. Just as in the expression "he lays down the sṛṣṭis," [the term refers to all bricks].

Furthermore, the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi) should be explained in the same way, as well as the word "ghee" (ghṛta) whether applied to ghee or to what is not ghee. To this it is replied: this would indeed be so if, by that means...

In another sentence, there would be a general application; however, here, because it constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the comprehension of the connection extends to the specific detail.

In a single sentence, the meaning of the sentence is understood by examining the mutual relationship of the words. In that context, because the word *akta* (anointed) is connected with the word *ghṛta* (ghee), it is understood that its scope is restricted solely to ghee. Otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *ghṛta*, but not in the word *akta*.

There is a certain contradiction between the word and its meaning. Therefore, it is established that the status of being for the sake of action depends upon the supplementary portion of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa). Thus, it is proven by means of the supplementary portion.
It is established that the capacity of a sentence to convey the meaning of a sentence depends upon its connection with the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter).
Or rather, it is by implication (*arthāt*). Even where there is doubt regarding the performance [of a rite], it is the scripture itself that is considered to be doubtful.
Therefore—
Validity [is established] in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). But is this not improper? For since there is doubt regarding its application, the scripture itself would be doubtful.

Since performance is preceded by the scripture, it is established that [the scripture] conveys the meaning of the sentence. Although the performance may be doubtful, nevertheless the scripture is not doubtful; this is the meaning. He refutes [this objection]: "True, as you have said."

In the case of an instruction regarding an accomplished entity (siddhānuśāsana), even if there is doubt regarding its performance, the instruction itself is not doubted. However, in the case of an instruction regarding a task to be accomplished (kāryānuśāsana), doubt regarding the performance indeed extends to the scripture as well.
The objector says: Is there any performance that is not preceded by scripture, such that the scripture would be doubtful when that performance is doubtful?

For if it were preceded by scripture, then the performance itself might be doubted, but the scripture would not be doubted. True, [the performance] is preceded by scripture when there is a connection [to a result].

The meaning is that at the time of its origination, it is preceded by the scripture (*śāstra*). The performance [of an action] consists in the existence of the object of the injunction (*niyoga*); the injunction does not establish the performance as its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, when even that [performance] is doubtful, the scripture itself is doubtful, because the scripture culminates in that [performance]. Consequently, [the doubt regarding the scripture] is logically established.
There is doubt regarding the meaning of the *niyoga*.
This is because that [doubt] extends even to the doubt concerning the performance [of the action]. He states the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Furthermore, that which is the *ni-*"

The meaning [of the word] must be determined through its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), and it has been so determined by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*). He concludes the subject matter of the chapter:
"Because it is a synonym for that."

Therefore, having established the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) by demonstrating its independence through the performance of injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, traditional law (*smṛti*), and technical names;
It has been stated that "validity" is the subject, and it was proposed that there shall be an investigation into the cause of that which possesses validity.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first book in the *Ṛjuvimalā* composed by the great teacher Śālikanātha.
In the *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*,
[this is] the second chapter.
The first quarter:
those whose meaning consists in being.
In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been completed; the means of valid cognition has been discussed.
Thus it has been said—this refers to the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

For the first chapter (*adhyāya*) is to be cited as the reason (*hetu*). Nor is the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) stated by means of the entire chapter; rather, what is it? It is stated by means of a portion of it, namely the definitions of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. Furthermore, that [definition] does not possess the status of being a reason for the division of the treatise (*śāstra*), and so on.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been established," meaning that it has been stated how verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition.

The meaning of this [commentary] is as follows: the meaning of the phrase "in the first chapter" in the *Bhāṣya* is this: by whatever manner—namely, by way of what is called "independence" (*anapekṣatva*)—the word [of scripture] is independent.

"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is defined; thus, independence (*anapekṣatva*) has been stated as the definition of valid cognition. By this, the entire subject matter of the chapter is proclaimed. Furthermore, we shall explain how independence serves as the reason for the distinction between scriptural texts (*śāstra-bheda*). Now, one might object: "The investigation of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth was performed in the first chapter, but the manner in which verbal testimony possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*) was not stated. Thinking thus, [the author] says:

He asks: "From what? He introduces the commentary as the answer: "Because injunctions, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and traditional codes (smṛtis) have been determined according to their true nature" [p.

The injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) and the designation of names (*nāmadheya*) have been examined. It has been stated that the determination of doubtful matters is achieved through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and through the sense (*artha*).

Therefore, the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been stated. But how, when this much has been said, is the definition of the means of valid knowledge considered to have been stated? To this he says:
"And these..."

Exegetical passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, when understood otherwise than they truly are, do not obstruct validity; however, when correctly comprehended, they do not invalidate it. Therefore, since they have been determined according to their true nature, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.
Thus it has been said:

since the determination of the true nature of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth was stated solely for the purpose of establishing authority (*prāmāṇya*), it is precisely the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) that was taught in the first chapter. Therefore, it is rightly stated that "the definition of the means of valid knowledge was taught in the first chapter. By the phrase "that must not be forgotten," [the author] indicates...

By stating that "that independence [of the Upanishads] should not be forgotten," the author of the Bhāṣya has shown that the discussion of difference and non-difference is dependent upon that very independence;
for he demonstrates that it is precisely the remembrance of that [independence] which is useful. Why, then, is the discussion of difference and non-difference dependent upon independence?
The answer is: For the difference or non-difference of an effect is stated; and that is based on independence.
Why? He says: because when a word is dependent upon something else, it is not possible to state the distinction of the effect from the word alone.

He summarizes: "Therefore, that must not be forgotten" means that because it is independent (*anapekṣatvāt*), what was stated regarding its independence must not be forgotten. Herein lies the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*).

The distinction between treatises (*śāstra*), the subject matter of the chapters (*adhyāya-artha*), the distinction of the goals to be established (*sādhya-bheda*), and the distinction of the auxiliary factors (*anubandha-bheda*) are stated here as the causes for that [distinction]. And since that goal to be established is to be understood solely through verbal testimony (*śabda*), the independence (*anapekṣatva*) of verbal testimony is required. Furthermore, that very distinction of the auxiliary factors which is the cause for the distinction between treatises is also an effect—

[The distinction] depends on the difference [in auxiliaries]. For if the *apūrva* were to differ due to its connection with the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, then the status of the sacrifice and other elements as auxiliaries would differ;

and because they would present different auxiliaries, the scripture (*śāstra*) itself would also differ. However, if the *apūrva* does not differ through the auxiliary character of the sacrifice, then, due to the absence of a difference in auxiliaries, the scripture does not differ. Therefore, even for the sake of establishing a difference in auxiliaries, one must indeed speak of a difference in the *kārya* (the task to be accomplished). Not otherwise.

And this [subject], G., cannot be spoken of without reference to dependence and non-dependence; thus, it has a dependence upon that non-dependence. Immediately thereafter, the primary and secondary [factors] are examined as being distinct or non-distinct—this is the commentary (bhāṣya).
Following the division of the treatise (śāstra-bheda), G., immediately after the division of the treatise...
He says, "it should be stated.
He asks for the reason therein: "Why [is it said] 'immediately after'? He answers by means of the mention of "one": "For even another..."

The other characteristic [of the means of knowledge], namely independence (*anapekṣatva*), can only be determined from the word when it is itself dependent upon the remaining factors and so forth. Therefore, by what distinction is the definition of the difference between the scriptures (*śāstrabheda*) commenced immediately after the definition of independence? The answer is: True.
Even the remaining [means of knowledge], such as presumption (*arthāpatti*) and so forth, can be determined from verbal testimony only when they are dependent upon it, and not independently;
for the word "immediately following" (*anantaram*) is used with the intention that this very [verbal testimony] is what follows immediately after.

The author of the Bhāṣya stated that "the principal and subordinate [elements] follow immediately after. But why is this alone mentioned as the immediate [topic], and not the definition of the subsidiary (śeṣa) and so forth?
The answer is: because everything that follows is preceded by a distinction of effects;

and this being preceded by a distinction of effects is due to its being preceded by a distinction of scriptures, since a distinction of effects serves as the cause for a distinction of scriptures. And how it is preceded by a distinction of scriptures...

The definition of the remaining [categories] has been shown in that same manner in the third chapter and the first; now, the primary and secondary [factors], whether distinct or non-distinct, will be examined.
Thus, he challenges what was stated in the commentary: "What is this [meaning of] 'primary' and 'secondary'?
He says in a single passage:
"If it is connected with the idea that 'the primary and secondary [factors] will be examined,' then one thing has been proposed as a thesis while something else is being examined."

It would follow that there is a contradiction between the thesis and the examination [of the subject]. He explains this very point: for the examination of difference and non-difference is seen immediately following, whereas the examination of the primary and the secondary is not.

But is it not the case that the examination of what is primary and what is secondary is indeed seen immediately following [the previous section], with the rules "the rest [are for its purpose]" (2.1.3) and "but where a substance is intended to be prepared, there a subordinate quality is understood" (2.1.4)?
He refutes this: for that [distinction] is established in the third [chapter],
and it is brought here for the sake of conventional usage, in order to establish the distinction between effects, which serves as the cause for the distinction between the scriptures.

And likewise, it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself in the third chapter: "Now, in that case, regarding those [actions] by which a substance is intended to be prepared, there a subordinate quality (guṇa) should be understood"— thereby, the status of being for the sake of the *apūrva* is excluded for those things which have a visible purpose.

[This refers to] those whose meanings have not been explained; however, here the definition of all the remaining ones is being stated. Thus, [the claim that they are] "principal" is inconsistent. Therefore, [the distinction between] "principal and non-principal" is incoherent.
It is said: the terms "primary" (*pradhāna*) and "secondary" (*apradhāna*) denote the goal (*sādhya*) and its concomitants (*anubandha*).

By the word "goal," the fourfold [process] beginning with origination (*utpatti*), the assistance of the instruments (*karaṇopakāra*), the intermediate operation of the instruments (*karaṇāvāntaravyāpāra*), and the entitlement (*adhikāra*) characterized by sovereignty are intended.

It is said: those [actions] to be accomplished are denoted by the term "principal" (*pradhāna*), while likewise, the subordinate elements (*anubandha*) which constitute the objects of the injunction (*niyoga*) are denoted by the term "non-principal" (*apradhāna*). Therefore, these principal and non-principal elements will be examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct from the things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
The meaning is that the difference and non-difference of the names and the subsidiaries will be examined.
First, regarding the difference of the subsidiaries: [they are] "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations.
Due to that difference, there is a difference among the scriptures.
There is also no difference in the consequence (*anubandha*), as in: "One who, knowing thus, performs the Full Moon sacrifice.

Due to that non-difference, there is no difference in the scripture (*śāstra*). Likewise, there is a difference in the task (*kārya*) between these two scriptures: "He threshes the rice" and "He sprinkles the rice," because of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) of threshing.

The purpose of threshing (*vighana*) is the removal of the husks and chaff, whereas the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is an unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, there is a distinction between these two scriptural injunctions: "one threshes the rice-grains" and "one sprinkles the rice-grains. Although these two scriptures are mutually distinct, they do not differ from the injunction of the mere verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), because there is no difference in their respective adjuncts (*anubandha*). For the adjunct is the objective domain of the mandate (*niyoga*), and threshing and the like are not the objective domains of the mandate.

We shall explain this with the word "you" (*tvam*). Furthermore, a difference in the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) that is independent of one another is a cause for the distinction between scriptures (*śāstra*). Now, the function of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth does not have as its object to be accomplished the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the *Āgneya* sacrifice and others independently. However, in the case of subordinate acts (*guṇakarman*), a distinction between scriptures is indeed logical because of the mutual independence of their respective objects to be accomplished. As it was stated in the section on "Another Context" (*Prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*): "But surely, even in the case of an injunction of a quality (*guṇa*) regarding the *camasa* cup, this would be a different scripture; [the answer is] no, because of the sentence..."

This [text] is indeed not a separate scripture; rather, a separate scripture depends upon the prescription of other qualities that perform an identical function, but it does not depend merely upon the prescription of a quality of existence. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.24)

And here, the intended equality refers to effects that are mutually independent. By this, it should be understood that there is a distinction between scriptural injunctions—such as "one offers with curd"—due to the difference in the goals to be accomplished, namely, the restricted unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*). Likewise, in the *Paurṇamāsī* section, the relationship between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is explained.

Even regarding the two types of *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirements), a distinction will be stated based on the difference between the scriptures and the difference between the goals (*sādhya*). For in the case of *itikartavyatā*, the goal is the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇa*).

However, for the instruments themselves, the goals are the intermediate operations (*vyāpāra*) consisting of further actions. Likewise, this applies in the case of lifelong repetition (*yāvajjīviko ’bhyāsaḥ*).

A distinction between scriptures will be described based on the difference in their respective goals (*sādhya*)—namely, the goal of the qualification for livelihood (*jīvana-adhikāra*) and the goal of the qualification for desire (*kāma-adhikāra*). Furthermore, there is non-distinction regarding the goal, because in such cases as "he sacrifices the *samidh*" (*samidho yajati*), "he sacrifices *tanūnapāt*" (*tanūnapātaṃ yajati*), and "the eight-potherd cake for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), they share the single goal known as qualification (*adhikāra*). Although the scriptures concerning the *samidh* sacrifice, the *āgneya* sacrifice, and so forth, are distinct due to the difference in their formal adjuncts (*anubandha*), nevertheless, they are not distinct with respect to the goal.
They are distinct. Therefore, it is well said that the primary and non-primary [factors] will be examined as to whether they are distinct or non-distinct.

This very meaning is to be described and no other; this is the explanation of the word "immediately following" (*ānantarya*). And this is the connection of the chapter (*adhyāya-sambandha*), which states the reason for the immediate succession.

In the commentary, the word *ca* (and) has the sense of "because"—that is, because this is the connection between chapters, therefore the definition of the differentiation of rituals (*śāstrabheda*) must be undertaken immediately after. We have already demonstrated how this serves as the reason.
Thus, sixfold differentiation of ritual action will be explained here: difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), and context (*prakriyā*).
"Name" (*nāmadheya*) is a restatement of the commentary. He raises an objection: "How is there a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) based on a different word (*śabdāntara*)?
[The answer begins with] "The state of being... (*bhāva-*).

This objection is formulated by taking the word *bheda* as having an instrumental derivation (*sādhana*). He provides the resolution: "It is differentiated by this, therefore it is a *bheda*; thus, it has an instrumental derivation."

The word "distinction" (*bheda*). The meaning is that which is distinguished from other words and so forth, and that is the action (*karman*), which is the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). Through the six [criteria] beginning with "other words" (*śabdāntara*), there is only a distinction among the meanings of the verbal roots (*bhāvārtha-mātra-bheda*); there is no distinction of the subordinate factors (*anubandha-bheda*), nor a distinction of the injunctions (*śāstra-bheda*), nor a distinction of the apūrva-impositions (*niyoga-bheda*). For instance, in the case of "seventeen [animals] dedicated to Prajāpati," the nature of the subordinate factor is not divided; for the substances and deities presented by the nominal stem *prājāpatya*—

The injunction that brings about their proximity is for the sake of the relationships [between the elements], because they constitute the object of a single injunction. Furthermore, in the case of a *tantra* (simultaneous) relationship, the status as an object of the injunction does not differ, just as in the expression "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

And the author of the *Nibandhana*, who maintains the primacy of the word (*śabdabalavādī*), considers the relationship between the substance and the deity to be the object of the injunction. There are verses on this point:
"In the second chapter, the Teacher [discusses] the composition of the Commentary..."
He described the differentiation of the treatises by way of the distinction between the goal to be accomplished and its attendant consequences.
However, when that which is to be proven is independent of one another and constitutes a distinction between the scriptures,
those distinctions are declared in many ways due to the specific differences among the means of proof.
The suffixes (anubandhas), however, differ through differences in designation, repetition, quality, and grammatical procedure; these are the causes for the distinction between grammatical treatises.
Even though there is identity with the self as its continuous connection, [the Self] differentiates the mere states of being;
because there is no distinction between being differentiated by that [Self] and being the differentiator of that [Self], number is also formulated in this very context.

Since the word *bheda* (difference) has an instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*), it is therefore stated as "difference of action" (*karmabheda*). The out-of-order presentation of "different words" (*śabdāntara*) and the other criteria, without regard for the sequence to be explained later, is for the purpose of demonstrating that sequence is not relevant [to the differentiation of actions].
Regarding the differentiation of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) by different words—
The meaning is that there is no mutual sequential dependence among the internal [factors] and so forth.

Here, an objection is raised: "What is about to be stated is being mentioned here in the form of a proposition (*pratijñā*"; it is proclaimed with the intention of a proposition. For what purpose? According to the Naiyāyikas, it is proper to state the proposition at the very time of stating the reason (*hetu*)."

Those who follow the principles of logic maintain that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is stated for the purpose of introducing and articulating the reason (*hetu*); however, it is only at the time of articulating the reason that it is appropriate [to state it]. He replies: "True."

In cases where the object to be proven is stated as that which is to be asserted (*pratijñeya*), it is thus; and this is for the sake of easy comprehension (*sukhagrahaṇārtha*). Because it facilitates the concentration of the listener's intellect, it serves as the cause for the distinction between treatises (*śāstrabheda*). As the reason (*hetu*)—*anu-*... [text truncated]

He will provide an exposition of the distinctions among the continuities of the elements (*bhūtānubandha*). When it is said, "he will do," the intellect of the listener—whose mind is drawn by the desire to know that—is concentrated and thus proceeds with ease toward the classification of the treatise (*śāstra*) as it is being stated.

By saying, "they call this chapter 'The Characteristics of Various Rituals' (*nānākarmalakṣaṇa*)," he demonstrates the established usage of the term by the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*), in order to declare the beginninglessness of the system (*nyāya*).
This principle is beginningless;

it is merely being recorded in its own treatise by Jaimini and others through some specific purpose. Therefore, this is distinct from the introduction (*upoddhāta*), as well as from what is incidentally related (*prasaṅgānuprasakta*), in order to avoid the fault of investigating matters not previously promised.

Even that which is considered other than what was promised due to the division of the treatise is treated as an introductory topic (*upoddhāta*), just as this very first [section] is; and there is also that which follows from what is relevant (*prasaktānuprasakta*), such as the definition of *mantras* and their divisions. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. First, then, this is considered: it was stated in the first chapter that the *codanā*...

Dharma is that which has the characteristic of being an object. And an injunction (*codanā*) is a sentence that expresses an action; furthermore, the meaning of a sentence resides in its constituent words.
In this regard, is Dharma expressed by each individual word, or is it expressed by all of them together as one?
The restatement of the commentary. He raises an objection:

"It is appropriate that this first point be considered—whether dharma is expressed by each individual word or by all of them together as a single syntactical connection"—and here the particle *iti* should be understood. What is the purpose of this passage stating that "this was said in the first chapter"?
To what context does this treatise belong? Therefore, we do not know how it is to be explained.
To this, it is replied: Is the *dharma* [to be understood] word by word?

It is said: when only this much has been stated, someone might think there is a contradiction with the method of one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhāntaprakriyā*), because of the assertion of an innate connection (*autpattikasambandha*) between the sentence and its meaning.
For when [the meaning] is [conveyed] by the sentence itself—

When the sentence-meaning is being expressed, the meaning of the individual words has no separate existence apart from it; how then can it be suspected that the meanings denoted by each individual word constitute the object of the injunction? For one who considers this to be a contradiction of the established method (*prakriyā*), the following answer is given:

The commentary begins with the words "In the first chapter," and so forth. He explains its meaning: "It is true that this was stated in the first chapter—that Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā); and an injunction is a sentence."

Therefore, it was stated in the *codanālakṣaṇa* sūtra that the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is indeed defined by the sentence itself. Nevertheless, it was also stated that the meaning of the individual words also exists within the sentence, according to the principle: "The mention of those [words] which have already come into being is for the sake of the action. Thus, the words themselves—being the denotations of the term 'sentence'—express the meanings of the words as connected [to one another], and thereby express the meaning of the sentence.

Since the author is a creator of conceptual constructs, there is no contradiction with the formal grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). Therefore, this is logical: is the property (*dharma*) expressed by each individual word, or...
"All [words] together" means this:

[an objection is raised]—"But this is incorrect; for it is not the case that every individual word denotes dharma. Rather, it is the word itself, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, that expresses dharma in its nature as the *apūrva*. Anticipating this doubt, he explains: "The following is what is meant: Is it by each individual word..."
Regarding whether the connection with the action belongs to the meaning expressed by the word alone, or to that which is dependent upon its mutual relationship [with other words]:

if the meaning expressed by a word possesses connection with the action—that is, the status of being the object of the mandate (*niyoga*)—then the mandate is expressed by that very word; for the knowledge of the mandate does not arise from the word "mandate" (*niyoga*) alone.

Not so, because [the meaning] has not yet arisen. But how can it be suspected that a meaning understood as being mutually related possesses a connection with the action (kārya) only when it is unrelated to the meanings of other words?
For, due to the understanding of mutual relationship, the connection of all [words] with the injunction (niyoga) is not perceived.
He refutes this: for it is observed that in the case of the dawn and so forth,
there is an understanding of the connection with an effect even between a substance and a quality which are mutually related.

Therefore, there is no contradiction in understanding a mutual relationship when there is a connection with the action (*kārya*). But was it not stated that in those cases there is no understanding of a mutual relationship between substance and quality?

Because the connection with the purchase is understood through the force of the third case ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*). He refutes this: "It is true that it has been stated that there is no mutual connection by virtue of being for the sake of one another (*aidamarthyena*); however, this does not mean there is no connection even in the form of quality and possessor of quality (*guṇaguṇitayā*)."
It does not mean that it is non-existent;
rather, the meaning is that it certainly exists. For otherwise, if a mutual relationship were not perceived, then there would be no restriction at all.

The purchase could be made with a one-year-old cow that is not red, or even with a multi-colored cow that is red; yet there is a restrictive rule (niyama), and therefore the mutual relationship between them is indeed understood. Likewise here, what is the relationship between the noun and the verb—whether it be that of action and agent, or...?

The doubt is thus established: is the connection with the injunction independent of the relationship between the two [the agent and the action], or does it occur precisely while not abandoning the relationship between the action and its factors?

That which does not abandon the relationship between action and its factors is "that which does not abandon the relationship between action and its factors"; for that indeed is the connection with the injunction (*niyoga*). What, then, is the prima facie view? This means: in this doubt, what is initially reasonable?
This word *prāpta* [is used here].

It occurs in the sense of the word "yukta" (joined). The answer is: it is logical that there is a connection with *dharma* for every individual word (*pratipadam*). Why? The answer is: because the utterance of all words has the purpose of enjoining (*niyoga*).
All words indeed are intent upon conveying the meanings of word-referents as established through their purposefulness in relation to an injunction;
for the utterance of all words has action as its ultimate purpose. But is it not the case that here the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka) is also understood?
By that...

Since the purposefulness (*aidamarthya*) of both the action (*kriyā*) and the factors of action (*kāraka*) is understood, it is logical that all of them possess purposefulness toward the injunction (*niyoga*) directly, without abandoning that [relationship]. He replies: "True, the relationship characterized by action and factor of action is understood; however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the factors of action having the action as their sole purpose."
[Reply: This is not so; for the meaning of the *niyoga* (the injunction) is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) independently.

If there were no *raidadarthya* (subservience to a purpose) between the action and its factors (*kāraka*), then one of dull intellect might raise an objection—thinking that even the relationship between the action and its factors would not exist—asking: "But how can [the *niyoga*] be devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*)?"
The *kāraka* brings about the purpose of the *niyoga*;

for it is by becoming a *kāraka*—that is, by being subordinated to the purpose of the *niyoga*—that it effects the realization of the *niyoga*'s objective. How can there be the status of a *kāraka* without the relationship between action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*)? Or how could an object (*karman*) be such if it were not being acted upon?

How can that which has not itself attained existence bring about the performance of an injunction? He answers: Let this relationship between action and its factors exist by virtue of the purpose (*artha*).

The relationship between the quality and the possessor of the quality is like that between a substance and its qualities; however, "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya) exists solely for the purpose of the injunction,
for "being for the sake of that" is indeed something distinct.
G. Action.
G. It is precisely the state of having the sense of an injunction [p.

And the intention is that there would be another relationship between the action and its factors (kriyākāraka). Therefore, there would be a distinct dharma for each word. To this, it is said: this is not tenable. Why? He says: for if the status of being the object of the injunction (niyogārthatā) did not belong to those words which do not abandon their perceived meaning, then there would be a distinct dharma for each word. This is the meaning.

In all cases, because the overall purport (*tātparya*) is more powerful, even a mutual relationship that is perceived is admissible provided that, by accepting it, the purport toward the injunction (*niyoga*) is not lost. However, where the comprehension of a relationship is indeed required for consistency, the abandonment of that [relationship] would result in the very abandonment of what is heard in the text (*śrutahāna*). And this is not the case here.

G. adds: Nor is it logical that this cognition [of the relationship] should be abandoned on account of the Vedic revelation (śruti). For if there were a connection with the dharma at every word, the understanding of a mutual relationship would have to be abandoned, simply because the cause for it would be absent. Indeed, the entry into a single action called "purchase" is the cause for understanding the mutual relationship between a substance and a quality. In this case, however, because there is a difference in the injunctions (niyoga) due to the difference in the subordinate elements (anubandha) at each word, [the two] enter into distinct injunctions.

Even though it is understood that the relationship between the noun and the verb is "seedless" (lacking an inherent basis), it must nevertheless be abandoned [as a mere appearance]. And that [relationship] is required by the injunction (*vidhi*).

For without an action (*kriyā*), the status of being a factor (*kāraka*) is impossible; nor can an action be accomplished without a factor. Therefore, it is logical that one or the other is supported by the other for the sake of the injunction. Furthermore, since the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is fulfilled even through a mediated sequence, there is no fault.

"And thus, the postulation of unseen factors through inference will be minimal," so says the Bhāṣya. Regarding this Bhāṣya, it is understood as follows: if Dharma were to reside in every single word, then one would have to postulate distinct *apūrvas* for each word; and those [unseen factors] are—
[These are] to be understood through reasoning (*mānagamyāni*). For the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] is what is expressed by the term "inference of the unperceived" (*adṛṣṭānumāna*) for logicians.
Thus it has been said: "And touch is not among those [qualities] that are perceived; therefore, air has an unperceived mark (*liṅga*).
Consequently, this is the connection of the text: in this way, even in a very small [amount], the unperceived...

"In the case of a mental inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) regarding an unprecedented object, there arises a conceptualization of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Here, an objection is raised: "What, then, is this conceptualization of a logical consequence of an inference from what is not observed? For even from verbal testimony, only what is observed is indeed observed."

For if there were a postulation of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), then it would be appropriate to say: "In this way, there will be a postulation involving the consequence of inferring the unseen" (G. adds: "in this way, there will be a very slight [postulation]"). But here there is no postulation of the unseen, because the *apūrva* is denoted by the word itself. He replies: "True, as you have said."

"By name, there is the postulation of the unseen" means that when one postulates a property (*dharma*) for every single term, and a relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayi*) ensues, the inference of a restrictive rule becomes "unseen"—that is, it lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

The sense is that since it is impossible for something devoid of action (*kriyā*) to function as a factor of action (*kāraka*), an action must be apprehended as the substratum by virtue of its being a factor of action. Furthermore, by the action itself... [the substratum is established].

By means of that which is already established (*niṣpanna*), the agent (*kāraka*)—which serves as the substratum—is to be grasped; and therein lies the comprehension of the restriction (*niyama*). Based on this very action, this agent accomplishes this specific application (*niyoga*); and based on this very agent, this is the action. Such a conceptualization of an unseen relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayi-prasaṅga*) would be devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*), because it differs from the principle of the *aruṇaikahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow). And in that case, there would be much...

How is there the conceptualization of an undesirable consequence involving the inference of the unseen (*adṛṣṭānumānaprasaṅgakalpanā*)? The answer is: first, there is the status of being a locus for the factors of action (*kāraka*) and the status of being the object (*karman*) that depends upon them; furthermore, for the sake of establishing those, there is the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanatva*) and the specific restriction [of their application]. However, in the position favored by either [of the two views], there will be a conceptualization of an undesirable consequence involving the inference of the unseen to a lesser degree. What is this "conceptualization of an undesirable consequence involving the inference of the unseen"?
The reply: "Adṛṣṭa" means that which lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
That which is indeed unperceived is without a means of valid cognition; it is an inference based on a rule (*niyamānumāna*).

The "consequence of the inference of the unperceived" (*adṛṣṭānumānaprasaṅga*) refers to that contingency of the relationship between locus and occupant (*āśrayāśrayitva*); the conceptualization of this "consequence of the inference of the unperceived"—being both an inference of the unperceived and a consequence—is the simpler one.
[285] But surely it is not at all the case that the conceptualization "What is this so small a thing? does not occur? He provides the answer: "Supported by one or the other..."

Even in the case of an alternative view, there exists the conceptual construction that the object to be enjoined is indeed the meaning of the injunction, and that the favor (anugraha) belongs to that very [meaning]. Furthermore, as for this "favor":

That which is being performed is not to be accepted as consisting of its own nature alone, because that would contradict the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*). [Objection: But is this not already established by the verbal testimony itself? Why is it being postulated here? [The author] answers: We shall explain in the ninth book that its comprehension arises from the fact of its being an action to be accomplished (*kārya*).

[This is] by virtue of accepting that [the injunction] is prompted by an unprecedented [result]. Thus, the expression "conceptual construction" (kalpanā) is justified. Anticipating the objection that if the understanding [of the result] arises from the effect (kārya), it would not then be verbal (śābda), he says: "But it is verbal because its root is the effect understood through words. Therefore, it has been rightly stated: "In this way, there is no assumption of a conceptual construction involving the inference of a small amount of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)."
The author of the Bhāṣya concludes that "therefore, there is one apūrva," and [the opponent] challenges this: "What is this 'one apūrva'? He replies: "Is it not this very thing?"
This meaning is indeed very clear. He raises an objection again: "Not so; not so," because of the context [of the statement] "from one [action], the apūrva [arises].
Therefore, it should be concluded that "from one [action], the apūrva [arises]," and not that "one apūrva [arises from one action]. To this, it is replied: when...
If the ritual act (dharma) pertains to each individual word in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), then there must be a distinction of injunctions for each word.
Why?
The answer is: because of the difference in the subordinate elements (anubandha) associated with each word.
Furthermore, when there is a connection between mutually related [actions] according to the rule (*vidhi*), that is the application of the rule (*vidhiniyoga*);

at that time, there is only one subsidiary element (*anubandha*). And for this reason, it is concluded that there is only one *apūrva*. Now, one might ask: "Even so, why is it not concluded that 'the *apūrva* arises from a single [action],' such that the conclusion is made by way of the fruit (*phala*)? To show this very distinction of effects (*kāryabheda*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: [the following].
The Blessed Commentator has summarized this by means of the result, stating: "Therefore, there is a single *apūrva*," and he also points out the observation of a difference in the effects.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it would follow that the comprehension of mutual connection among words—which are themselves mutually unconnected—is without a basis; therefore, for the sake of establishing the reasoning of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), [the following is argued]: since the utterance of words has the *niyoga* (injunction) as its purpose, all words have a direct connection with the *niyoga*. And since a recourse to an indirect (mediated) relationship is untenable when a direct relationship is possible, the prima facie view is that all words have the *niyoga* as their object. However, the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that... all [words...]

If [the injunction] were the object of the *niyoga* (the mandate), there would be a contradiction with the understanding of the mutual relationship [between the parts]. Since the *niyoga* differs for each word, it is impossible for relationships to obtain among those things that enter into distinct *niyogas*. Therefore, the status of being an object must correspond to the *viniyoga* (the application); the distinction of objects is what is logical. Thus, one or the other is the object as supported by the other. Furthermore, if one relies on their mutual relationship, the very understanding of the *viniyoga*—which is itself based on the understanding of the *niyoga*—is the authority.
When something new arises from a single word, then a doubt arises: does it arise from words denoting action (*bhāva*), or from words denoting substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*)?
On this point, he asks: "By the mention of 'words denoting action,' what is meant?
A partisan (the *ekadeśin*) gives the answer: "Only verbal roots (*ākhyāta*)."

He raises an objection again: "In that case, while demonstrating the doubt, it ought to have been stated whether [the difference arises] from nouns or from verbs. Why is this being said instead: 'whether from words for action (bhāva) or from words for substance (dravya) and quality (guṇa)'?"
He asks the objector:
"What is there, or what is added here?"

Even in the author of the Bhāṣya’s presentation of the doubt, there is nothing further by which one could be urged as to whether it is more appropriate to derive [the notion of agency] from nominal words or from verbal roots. The objector says: "The nominal word has been mentioned twice."

It is excluded. When the mention of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) words is made, there is no inclusion of verbal (*ākhyāta*) and nominal (*nāman*) words by means of those two terms. When the mention of state (*bhāva*) words is made—that is, when recourse is taken to state words—it must be understood that substance and quality words are mentioned as their counterparts.
For at that time, the word is indicated by way of its denotation; thus, the distinct denotata of substance and quality words are presented by the word.

These two [words] should not be uttered. However, since the mention of a verb (ākhyāta) involves a reference to the word by its own form (svarūpa), it is precisely the noun-word "nāma" that must be employed as the indicator of the word-form.
Consequently, the non-utterance of two words is for the sake of brevity (lāghava). Thus, the supreme resolver [concludes].

He said: "For you do not understand the intended meaning. If it were stated whether [the apūrva] arises from verbal roots (ākhyāta-śabda) or from nominal stems (nāma-śabda), and if it were thereby determined that the apūrva arises only from verbal roots, then [in the case of] 'The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni' (āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ), there would be no reference to action."

It might be argued: the connection between the substance and the deity would not be the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), because the word *āgneya* is a name (*nāman*); whereas the meaning of the verb "to be" (*bhavati*)—being an action and expressed by the verbal root—would be the object of the injunction, because the word *bhavati* is a finite verb (*ākhyāta*). And this is undesirable.
Neither of the two [is the object of injunction], because the meaning of the root *bhū* (to be) cannot be enjoined.
